Title: Gartner Report: The Attack Path is Closing Faster than Most Teams Can Patch
Context: Rapid7’s vulnerability management capabilities support this operational path by bringing attack-surface visibility, threat intelligence, business context, and attack-path...
Full Text:
Security teams have never lacked vulnerability data. The harder problem is deciding which issues create a credible path to business impact, then acting before that path can be used. As frontier AI makes it faster and less expensive to connect weaknesses, operational assumptions, and legitimate system behavior, that decision window is becoming even tighter.

The Gartner® report, Mythos Reprioritizes Cybersecurity Outcomes and Investments, examines what this shift means for cybersecurity priorities and investment. Rapid7 is offering complimentary access to the research, which we believe can help security leaders reassess how they prioritize exposure and infrastructure teams reassess how they plan response and recovery.

Why does AI change the vulnerability management equation?

Gartner states, “Mythos collapses the distance between theoretical weaknesses and executable attack scenarios, forcing cybersecurity to optimize for outcomes, not activity.” For leaders already managing more vulnerabilities than their teams can address, the pressure comes from the growing speed at which separate weaknesses can become a credible attack path.

The change also extends beyond one model. Gartner states, “By 2027, Mythos will be overtaken by new frontier-AI-enabled models, signaling that this moment is not about Mythos, but a new era of AI-assisted vulnerabilities and functional exploits.”

At Rapid7, we believe this requires a more attacker-aware view of exposure. A large backlog can contain thousands of issues with very different implications for the organization. Leaders need to understand which exposures are reachable, how they could be combined, which business services they affect, and what action would reduce risk most effectively.

What should security leaders measure instead?

Vulnerability counts, backlog size, and generic remediation targets show how much work a team has completed. They provide less clarity on whether an attacker’s options have narrowed or whether the organization can respond and recover more effectively.

Gartner advises, “Organizations must shift focus from volume and activity to speed of decision, effectiveness of response, and tangible reduction of enterprise risk in an environment where attacker reasoning scales rapidly.”

The report examines outcome-driven measures including “Attack path analysis coverage,” “Patching cadence,” “Compensating control deployment cadence,” “Mean time to remediate,” and “Technology debt.” We believe this gives leaders a stronger basis for connecting security investment with reduced exposure, faster action, and business resilience.

How can teams move from prioritization to action?

Better prioritization only creates value when teams can act on it. Gartner recommends, “Use attack path analysis to prioritize your patches, virtual patches, and compensating controls. This can scale down to a consideration of critical services mapped into critical business outcomes and exposure.”

Rapid7’s internal, practitioner-led exploration of Claude Mythos Preview through Project Glasswing reinforces our view that faster discovery is only the beginning. A model may help identify and validate a potential vulnerability, but reducing exposure still requires teams to understand affected systems, apply business context, choose the right remediation or compensating control, verify the result, and maintain detection coverage.

Rapid7’s vulnerability management capabilities support this operational path by bringing attack-surface visibility, threat intelligence, business context, and attack-path analysis together, helping teams identify which exposures matter most and coordinate remediation through existing workflows.

What does an outcome-led program look like?

An outcome-led program gives executives a clearer answer to a more useful question: which attacker opportunities did we reduce, and how quickly could we respond? It also supports ongoing decisions about technical debt, recovery planning, and where limited resources can deliver the greatest reduction in business risk.

Title: Debian, Ubuntu patch APT flaw that could hand attackers root
Context: Linux administrators’ trust in package managers is being tested by a newly disclosed vulnerability in APT, the package management system used by Debian, Ubuntu, and their...
Full Text:
Linux administrators’ trust in package managers is being tested by a newly disclosed vulnerability in APT, the package management system used by Debian, Ubuntu, and their derivatives, that could allow attackers to install unverified software with root privileges.

Tracked as CVE-2026-109518, the vulnerability could let an attacker positioned to manipulate HTTP traffic between an APT client and an archive server install an attacker-controlled package without verification.

Debian disclosed the flaw on November 4, crediting security researcher Max Justicz. Ubuntu subsequently rated it High, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.7.

“I used an AI for two hours and found a zero-day that would let a nation-state hack any server running stock Ubuntu,” Justicz said in an X post. Successful exploitation could allow arbitrary code execution with root privileges on a vulnerable machine.

Both distributions have issued fixes.

Redirects and retries turn hardlinks into an attack surface

The problem lies in APT’s handling of HTTP redirects and resumed downloads.

“APT can merge two different package downloads after an HTTP redirect gives them the same URI,” Debian’s advisory said. “Improper file handling when resuming an HTTP download allows a man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacker to replace a package after verification, resulting in the execution of arbitrary code as root.”

APT developers provide a more detailed explanation: an attacker can exploit redirects and transient HTTP server errors that trigger download retries, causing APT to override existing hard links with a chosen payload. Because Debian packages are installed with root privileges, successfully substituting a package can lead to arbitrary code execution as root.

Ubuntu described the required attack position as an on-path attacker able to manipulate traffic between the package client and the archive server. A malicious mirror or proxy could provide that position, but the attack requires specific download conditions.

Retry settings decide who is exposed

The vulnerability depends on APT’s Acquire::Retries setting being non-zero. APT developers say this has been the default since version 2.3.2, although scripts may have enabled retries on older installations. Ubuntu specifies that the default retry value of three applies from Debian 12 (Bookworm) and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish) onward. Older releases are not exposed by default, but may still be vulnerable if retries have been enabled.

Debian 13 (Trixie) is patched in APT 3.0.4, while Debian 12 (Bookworm) received the fix in version 2.6.2. Ubuntu has also released patched packages for supported releases, including 22.04 LTS, 24.04.LTS, and 26.04 LTS. Ubuntu 26.10 was also affected, with its fix being published when Ubuntu’s November 4 advisory appeared. The fix addresses the underlying file-handling issue. In a commit authored on October 12, APT developer Julian Andres Klode changed the download code to open destination files exclusively, unlinking existing files before copying over any partially downloaded content.

The change prevents downloads from writing through existing hard links, which could otherwise redirect writes to unintended files.

Ubuntu recommends updating APT and temporarily disabling retries during remediation. It also advises using HTTPS for package downloads, which protects against traffic manipulation in this attack scenario. For enterprise security teams, the priority is to identify vulnerable installations, check retry configurations, and ensure patched packages reach production systems and the Linux images used to provision them.

Title: Post-Quantum Questions to Ask Your Vendors
Context: To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-...
Full Text:
CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available.

Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to update, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts.

Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC.

Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

Title: US Government Partners Urge Hardening Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems
Context: Threat The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery...
Full Text:
Overview

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization.

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access.

Threat

The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.

Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors:

Authentication bypass;

Arbitrary code injection; and

Weak configurations.

Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects:

Change of temperature, which could:

Affect the service life of the system;

Create a fire hazard;

Cause loss of inventory; or

Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage.

Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition).

Mitigations

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement:

Eliminate public internet exposure: Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [CPG 3.S]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices.

Isolate operational technology (OT) devices: Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [CPG 3.I].

Enforce credential security: Change default passwords [CPG 3.A], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [CPG 3.B]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [CPG 3.F].

Apply patches: Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [CPG 2.A, 2.B]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance.

Restrict access: Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [CPG 3.H].

Have reliable backups: Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [CPG 3.O].

Monitor and report: Enable logging [CPG 3.Q] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity.

For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets.

Review setpoint ranges: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations.

Resources

The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations:

CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology

CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security

CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance

United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT

Contact Information

The authoring organizations recommend U.S. organizations report suspicious or criminal activity related to information provided in this fact sheet:

Contact CISA via CISA’s 24/7 Operations Center at contact@cisa.dhs.gov or 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For more information on reporting a cyber incident, refer to CISA’s Voluntary Cyber Incident Reporting web page. File a claim with FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or contact your local FBI field office. When available, please include the following information regarding the incident:

Date, time, and location of the incident;

Type of activity;

Number of people affected;

Type of equipment used for the activity; and

Name of the submitting company or organization, and a designated point of contact.

Contact HHS via HHSCyber@hhs.gov or the HHS 24/7 Operations Center at 202-619-7800 for assistance mitigating potential disruptions to the delivery of healthcare resulting from health and medical supply chain impacts.

Title: GhostMap Bug Leaves Android Phones Stuck in Reboot Loop
Context: Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset
Full Text:
Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset.

Bitdefender said it discovered the issue when an Android package (APK) it collected from the wild crashed the emulators in its labs. It found that the problem wasn’t malware, but a bug in the Android OS itself.

“The operating system mishandles two fields inside a ZIP entry, the compression method and the declared uncompressed length. Reading such an entry causes a SIGBUS (a signal sent by the CPU to stop a process that accesses an invalid memory space) in whichever process touches the file,” it explained in a blog post.

“We call it GhostMap: the malformed entry causes Android to map the file across memory that was never allocated, and the crash occurs when a process reads from that empty space.”

Read more on Android bugs: Google API Keys Quietly Gain Access to Gemini on Android Devices.

Bitdefender said that the crash loop persists after a reboot and continues in safe mode, meaning the only way out is a factory reset which erases all locally stored data.

The bug affects all Android versions from Android 10 and above, but Google has so far failed to address it, claiming the issue is outside the scope of a security fix, the report noted.

It was notified by the security vendor on August 20.

How Threat Actors Could Abuse GhostMap

Bitdefender warned that cybercriminals could theoretically hide the technique in a fake app to disable a victim’s phone, or use the threat of GhostMap as leverage for extortion.

It shared several possible scenarios:

Brick a victim’s phone by first creating a malicious app containing a deliberately malformed resource that Android’s system service needs to read. When it does, the resource triggers a crash in system_server which renders the phone unusable. This could be used for extortion

Make a malicious app impossible to remove. In this scenario an icon contains a malformed resource which triggers a crash when Android tries to display it. The launcher, the app list in Settings, and the app's own info screen all crash when the user tries to access them to uninstall

Disable security tools. Mobile security apps, malware-analysis sandboxes and automated scanning pipelines need to use Android's resource-parsing code to examine suspect apps. By embedding a malformed resource in an APK, hackers could trigger GhostMap to crash anything inspecting it

Delivery through an app update. An app looks trusted on download but, in theory, the malformed file could be introduced later. That would mean it could pass app-store checks and security scans to infect a much larger number of potential victims at once

“This is a flaw in Android itself and, as of publication, no fix is available, so users have limited options on the device to prevent it. The most practical defense is to recognize the file before the bug is triggered,” Bitdefender concluded.

“That's possible because the malformation is visible in the file's structure, without installing or running the app. A scanner can distinguish a crafted file from a normal one by inspecting it, not by executing it.”

The vendor detects this issue as Android.Riskware.Ghostmap.rA.

Title: Zyxel patches a zero-day hiding behind an old fix
Context: Zyxel has patched a zero-day vulnerability that attackers exploited to compromise 996 GS1900 network switches across 48 countries, exposing device configurations, network...
Full Text:
Zyxel has patched a zero-day vulnerability that attackers exploited to compromise 996 GS1900 network switches across 48 countries, exposing device configurations, network information and hashed root credentials. The attack began around August 17, according to cybersecurity firm GreyNoise, but researchers initially blamed a different vulnerability that Zyxel had already addressed.

The newly identified flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-107441, is a CVSS 8.8 out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the switches’ web management interface. It allows unauthenticated attackers with network access to execute operating system commands through specially crafted HTTP requests.

The flaw affects ten GS1900 models, including GS1900-8, GS1900-24, and GS1900-48. Zyxel listed firmware versions ending in .2C0 and earlier as vulnerable, with model-specific fixes in versions ending in .3C0.

Zyxel released a fix for CVE-2026-7273 in June, addressing a separate buffer overflow in the same switch series. GreyNoise initially attributed the attacks to that vulnerability, prompting CISA to add it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in September.

However, security researchers at Binary discovered an exploit targeting a previously unknown flaw that remained effective even on switches running the June updates. The researchers reported the vulnerability to Zyxel on September 29.

The attackers used a script to collect device configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information. Such data can give intruders a useful map of an organization’s network and potentially help them move deeper into its infrastructure. Zyxel released firmware updates on October 22 and published its advisory on November 3. Administrators should update affected GS1900 switches, including those already running June security fixes.

Title: Zyxel GS1900 Patch Fails to Block Zero-Day Exploit Allowing Root Command Execution
Context: Zyxel GS1900 network switches that received the vendor's earlier fix for an actively exploited flaw are still open to the exploit attackers used, researchers at Binarly found
Full Text:
Zyxel GS1900 network switches that received the vendor's earlier fix for an actively exploited flaw are still open to the exploit attackers used, researchers at Binarly found.

The exploit lets anyone who can reach a switch's web management interface run commands on it without logging in. Zyxel has released new firmware for 10 GS1900 models that closes the hole.

The earlier fix is the 2.90 Patch 2 firmware, named in a June 16 advisory for a flaw tracked as CVE-2026-7273. The new 2.90 Patch 3 firmware fixes a flaw now tracked separately as CVE-2026-107441, which the exploit relies on. It was posted on October 23, and the vendor announced it in an advisory earlier this week.

The researchers, who reported the flaw to the vendor on September 29, call it a zero-day. Attackers already had a working exploit for it by then.

GreyNoise, which monitors attack traffic through a network of sensors, reported on September 21 that attackers took data from 996 GS1900 switches around August 17. It tied the attacks to CVE-2026-7273, and the researchers say the exploit it described matches the one they found.

Neither GreyNoise nor Binarly says the attacked switches were running the earlier fix, and the vendor's advisory does not say whether the new flaw has been exploited.

Which Switches Need the New Firmware

Zyxel's security advisory lists the affected and fixed firmware for each model:

Switches on Patch 2 or any earlier firmware need the Patch 3 build for their model. The builds are posted with their firmware release notes.

The advisory lists no workaround for owners who cannot update yet. It also does not say whether updating removes access an attacker may already have, or what owners should check if a switch may have been compromised.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on September 21 and gave federal agencies until September 24 to apply the vendor's fix, the Patch 2 firmware. The listing came the day the earlier attacks were made public.

The researchers' vulnerability advisory says the new flaw is present in all 10 of those Patch 2 builds. It also says "an attacker only needs network reachability to the management service", while the vendor's advisory describes a "LAN-based, unauthenticated attacker".

The researchers rate the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS severity scale, against 8.8 in the vendor's CVE entry, and say the attacker's commands run with root privileges.

Why the Earlier Fix Did Not Stop the Exploit

Binarly's technical analysis traces the flaw to the program that handles web requests on the switch. It is an out-of-bounds write, meaning the program writes data beyond the memory allocated for it.

The program stores each request parameter in a fixed area that can accommodate 140 parameters. It never checked the size of a parameter, and before Patch 2 it never checked how many parameters it had stored.

The exploit sends a 140th parameter that is too large, causing it to overrun the end of that area and overwrite the program's parameter counter. The next parameter is then written outside the area, allowing the attacker to swap the function the program is about to call for one that runs the attacker's command.

Patch 2 added a check on the counter, but the check runs only after the oversized parameter has been copied. By then the counter holds the attacker's value, so the check does not stop the write. The researchers say the exploit works against Patch 2 without changes.

They tested it on emulated firmware and on real hardware, though they do not say which model. The exploit's own list of supported firmware includes the Patch 2 build for the GS1900-24.

According to the researchers, Zyxel told them that CVE-2026-7273 was about the missing counter check, and that it treats the missing size check as a separate flaw, now CVE-2026-107441.

In the Patch 3 code, the counter is checked before a parameter is copied, and the copy is limited in size. The researchers say this fixes the flaw.

What Is Known About the Attacks

GreyNoise's attack report says the attackers used the exploit to download a data-collection script onto the switches and left the collected data to be picked up. The data included switch configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information. Of the 996 switches, 564 still used factory-default credentials.

The report does not say which firmware the switches were running or how the attackers reached them. It says the attackers are the same as, or related to, a group that Acronis tracks as Red Heron and describes as Chinese-speaking. Acronis linked a backdoor called JITTERLY to Red Heron in an earlier campaign that targeted Gitea servers.

The researchers found the exploit on September 17 in an open folder on a server that also acted as a command server for JITTERLY.

Their advisory offers two explanations. Either the Patch 2 update was a faulty fix for CVE-2026-7273, or the attacks exploited a different flaw from the one CISA listed.

The researchers say they will soon publish a smaller version of the exploit as a proof of concept. CISA's KEV catalog data, last updated yesterday, does not list CVE-2026-107441.

Title: How Adversaries Are Turning the Vulnerability Ecosystem Against Defenders
Context: Among them was a modified version (SHA256 hash: fd6b46d148af22da6163f18ce43b35ebb827cc6e140f03f0f514bc2a6f548743) of a public POC exploit for a FortiOS and FortiProxy...
Full Text:
Fortinet FortiOS and FortiProxy Authentication Bypass Vulnerability (CVE-2024-55591)

In February 2026, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations identified an open directory controlled by the Iran-nexus adversary STATIC KITTEN on IP address 157.20.182[.]49 containing 1.9 GB of data and more than 20,000 files. Among them was a modified version (SHA256 hash: fd6b46d148af22da6163f18ce43b35ebb827cc6e140f03f0f514bc2a6f548743) of a public POC exploit for a FortiOS and FortiProxy authentication bypass vulnerability (CVE-2024-55591) first released by a well-known industry source on January 27, 2025.4

Where the public POC exploit executed a single user-provided command, the modified version contained 13 hardcoded payloads designed to enumerate targets, create users, and establish persistence. The modifications reflect a systematic approach to turning a demonstration tool into a more comprehensive exploit.

Table 1. Payloads for modified CVE-2024-55591 exploit

Payload Name

Description

test

Creates the backdoor admin user FortiWiFi with password FortiWiFi123 and assigns this user the super_admin profile, granting full system access

test2

Lists all user groups in the victim system, likely to facilitate reconnaissance in order to understand the victim system’s existing group structure

test3

Displays all local user accounts, allowing the attacker to enumerate existing users

test4

Modifies the FortiWiFi admin account by assigning it the ssl-vpn-groupamoss access profile

test5

Creates the FortiWiFi user with password FortiWiFi123, adds this user to the ssl-vpn-groupamoss group, and then displays all user groups to verify the user was successfully added to the group

test6

Creates or modifies a user group named ssl-vpa-amoss and adds multiple users to this group, including the backdoor FortiWiFi account (created by test1 or test5) and users with transliterated Hebrew-language names (i.e., shachar, sigal, amos, sima, lev, and gabi)

test7

Queries the ssl-vpn-groupamoss group configuration’s help information, likely to understand available options for follow-on activities

test8

Creates the backdoor user darlen with password 1234

test9

Similar to the test payload, creates the FortiWiFi user with password FortiWiFi123 or updates the existing FortiWiFi user to use that password

test10

Creates the FortiWiFi user with password 1234 and adds this user (along with numerous other users, many with transliterated Hebrew-language names) to the VPN-Users group, potentially to hide the backdoor account among legitimate users

test11

Creates a system admin account named FortiSetup with super_admin privileges and an encrypted password (decrypted password is gwm1607pmw); this account provides a more sophisticated backdoor than those created by other payloads, as FortiSetup has root VDOM access

test12

Displays the FortiAdmin account’s configuration, likely to facilitate reconnaissance

test13

Creates a user named offices with an email address and an encrypted password (decrypted password is @lolo@123456); POC_ZZ_1.py‘s developer may have added this email address to make the new user appear legitimate

Whether STATIC KITTEN modified the public CVE-2024-55591 exploit themselves or obtained this modified version from another source remains unknown. However, as of this writing, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations has not observed any other adversaries using this modified POC or infrastructure hosting it.

AI’s Impact on the Vulnerability Research Ecosystem

AI advancements are undoubtedly accelerating the speed and scope of how vulnerabilities are discovered and weaponized.5 One only has to look at the substantial increase in the number of vulnerabilities in recent Microsoft Patch Tuesdays compared to prior to the advent of frontier models earlier this year.6

Detecting and attributing adversaries’ direct use of AI for vulnerability research purposes remains hard to identify due to inherent visibility gaps and the fact there is no single identifier that distinguishes AI-generated exploit code. Complicating things further, is that the patterns suggesting AI assistance (such as well-commented code, improvements to existing POCs, or structured code organization) are also consistent with the output of someone with high technical capabilities.

Nonetheless, threat actors are leveraging AI to augment their vulnerability research. CrowdStrike Intelligence assesses they will almost certainly continue to do so through at least three vectors:

Direct interaction with frontier models by trying to “jailbreak” AI safeguards and bypass any export control restrictions

Modifying open-weight proprietary models for malicious use by extracting safeguards; these are not/less monitored for abuse by frontier AI companies

Adopting AI-led/assisted public vulnerability research published by industry sources

The third point, while not a direct use, is the easiest to detect. One only has to look at the CopyFail vulnerability detailed in this blog post, whose discovery was allegedly facilitated by AI.7 Or the mass exploitation of wp2shell in July 2026, which is the first critical unauthenticated WordPress Core remote code execution (RCE) purportedly discovered in nearly a decade and was allegedly discovered using GPT5.6 Sol Ultra and $25 USD worth of tokens.8

Outlook

Adversaries will almost certainly continue using public vulnerability research as part of their offensive toolkit through the foreseeable future. As more POC exploits become routinely available within hours of disclosure, at least partially driven by AI-assisted vulnerability research, the number of threat actors using them will almost certainly increase. Over the next year, this will likely manifest itself in the rise of widespread exploitation campaigns resulting in contested environments, like the cPanel CVE-2026-41940 exploitation example covered in this blog post.

This expanding pool of adversaries leveraging public vulnerability research, combined with the rapid speed at which adversaries are operationalizing public research, reinforces three key points.

The first is that patch prioritization is harder than ever. As vulnerability disclosures continue to increase in volume, predicting which ones will attract public research (and therefore adversary attention) becomes a genuine intelligence challenge. Because adversaries have access to the same advisories and public exploits that defenders do, organizations that rely solely on CVSS scores to drive patching decisions are relying on the wrong signal. Real-world exploitability, ease of exploitation (i.e., if there is a public exploit or exploitation guidance), and adversary intent are what separate the vulnerabilities that matter from the ones that do not.

The second is that the time to patch is effectively zero. The data from the first half of 2026 shows this: 91% of vulnerabilities with POCs that CrowdStrike has seen exploited were weaponized and used in the wild within 48 hours, with the fastest observation occurring just 35 minutes after a POC became available. Adversaries treat public vulnerability research as the starting gun, and legacy patch cycles measured in weeks or days cannot compete.

Lastly, more threat actors can participate in exploitation. As the case studies show, adversaries across skill and resource levels are operationalizing public research, some using POCs with minimal modification and others refining them (as UMBRAL BISON and STATIC KITTEN both demonstrated). When motivation and intent are the only remaining barriers to exploitation, the volume of participating adversaries significantly increases.

The vulnerability research ecosystem is one of the security community's greatest assets and most significant challenges. Defenders who treat public research as a threat actor's green light, and who build the intelligence, patching timelines, and detection capabilities to match, are the ones who will keep pace.

Full Text:
SonicWall has warned of two vulnerabilities impacting end-of-life Global Management System (GMS) systems that it said will not be patched.

Details of the security flaws, which affect SonicWall GMS 9.5.2 and earlier versions, are below -

CVE-2026-109593 (CVSS score: 9.1) - An unauthenticated file read vulnerability that could allow an attacker with network access to read internal GMS files, potentially exposing sensitive information.

CVE-2026-109594 (CVSS score: 6.8) - A post-authentication SQL injection vulnerability that could allow an authenticated attacker to access or modify information stored in the GMS database under specific conditions.

"The affected product has reached End-of-life (EoL)," SonicWall said in a Tuesday alert.

"As a result, no remediation or security update will be released for these vulnerabilities. Organizations using the product should be aware of the associated security risks and are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the SonicWall Network Security Manager (NSM)."

The development comes less than a month after SonicWall shipped fixes for CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS score: 10.0), a critical pre-authenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw that could have allowed an attacker to reach internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations.

The vulnerability has since come under active exploitation in the wild, with telemetry data from Previdian recording 2,541 attack attempts from eight unique IP addresses from Singapore and the U.S. since October 9, 2026. As many as 30 exploitation attempts were registered on November 3, 2026.

Title: The Classics Return: Vulnerable E-Mail Scripts, (Wed, Nov 4th)
Context: This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail
Full Text:
One of the early web application vulnerabilities I remember was CVE-2000-0411 [CVE]. This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail. The vulnerability was pretty straightforward: Adding additional parameters to the URL leaked environment variables. Other vulnerabilities allowed setting the "To" address and were heavily abused by spammers. And if parameters were passed directly to the sendmail binary, similar vulnerabilities could allow arbitrary code execution.

Today, I noticed a slight resurgence in scans targeting e-mail scripts on our honeypots. Today, there are numerous scripts like the old "formail" scripts, and it is hard to link a specific vulnerability to any of these scans. But my main suspect is spammers looking for webforms that allow setting arbitrary "To" headers. The URLs I am seeing:

"/sendmail.php" "/test-mail.php" "/testemail.php" "/config/mail_config.php" "/mail_config.php" "/email-test.php" "/mailtest.php"

In particular, the "Test" part of the filename suggests that the attacker is not looking for production scripts, but for test scripts left behind during development. This, along with the requests for credential/secret files that top our "Leaderboard," points to a more fundamental issue: Code hygiene. Do not leave behind development artifacts that should never have reached a live website.

For example, some excerpts from a random "mailtest.php" script that came back in a Google search [mailtest]:

<?php

/* DONT FORGET TO DELETE THIS SCRIPT WHEN FINISHED! */

$server = array( 'HTTP_HOST', 'SERVER_NAME', 'SERVER_ADDR', 'SERVER_PORT', 'SERVER_ADMIN', 'SERVER_SIGNATURE', 'SERVER_SOFTWARE', 'REMOTE_ADDR', 'DOCUMENT_ROOT', 'REQUEST_URI', 'SCRIPT_NAME', 'SCRIPT_FILENAME', ); $to = ( isset( $_GET['email'] ) ? $_GET['email'] : FALSE ); $subject = 'Mail Test Successful for ' . $_SERVER['HTTP_HOST']; $message = '';

??????? foreach ( $server as $s ) { $message .= sprintf( '%s: %s', $s, $_SERVER[$s] ) . PHP_EOL; };

$success = mail( $to, $subject, $message, $headers );

The comment at the top says it all: This is not meant for production use, and even on a development site, it should likely be deployed only briefly for debugging. The script takes any "To" address from the "email" GET parameter and exfiltrates/displays part of the server configuration. It can be useful to scan your own hosts for some of these URLs as an additional control, but you really want to catch these issues during application deployment.

Title: Chrome 157 fixes 213 security issues, including 7 critical flaws

Full Text:
On November 3, Google issued Chrome 157 to the stable channel for Windows, Mac and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.38/.39 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.38 for Linux. It includes 213 security fixes, including seven vulnerabilities rated Critical by Google.

Chrome for Android was also updated to 157.0.8103.38. It will become available on Google Play over the coming days.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates. If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome 157.0.8103.39 is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Technical details

Some of the security fixes deserve a closer look.

Google rates seven vulnerabilities in the update as Critical. One, a memory corruption flaw in ANGLE, affects Chrome for Android. It could potentially allow a remote attacker to run code outside the sandbox through a specially crafted HTML page.

Mobile protection, anywhere, anytime.

CVE-2026-121229: Memory corruption in ANGLE, which could allow a remote attacker to potentially execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page.

ANGLE is Chrome’s graphics translation layer. A buffer overflow occurs when a program puts more data into an area of memory than it can hold, overwriting data in adjoining memory. An attacker can exploit this to make the vulnerable process run malicious code.

Chrome vulnerabilities that enable remote code execution outside the browser sandbox are particularly valuable to attackers because they can turn a visit to a malicious or compromised website into direct code running on the underlying operating system, often without requiring additional exploitation steps.

CVE-2026-121035: Use-after-free in Prerender.

Chrome’s Prerender component helps pages open faster by loading and preparing a page in the background before you navigate to it. If you then visit that page, Chrome can display the prepared version almost instantly instead of loading it from scratch.

This goes beyond just downloading content: Chrome also starts rendering the page and running its JavaScript.

A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code.

CVE-2026-121156: Buffer overflow in Dawn.

Dawn powers WebGPU in Chrome, allowing websites to use a device’s graphics processor for rendering and computational tasks. It checks and translates WebGPU instructions into commands that the device’s underlying graphics system can understand.

A buffer overflow occurs when a program writes more data to a block of memory than it can hold. This can cause a crash or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run code.

Title: Hackers Exploit BTCPay Server Flaw to Steal Cryptocurrency
Context: 1 or earlier of the open-source payment platform, and that attackers had used a different method to exploit a vulnerability fixed in version 2
Full Text:
Hackers have stolen cryptocurrency from hot wallets on outdated BTCPay Server instances, with blockchain analysis tracing about $1.63m in Bitcoin and Litecoin to addresses linked to the thefts.

BTCPay Server said in an incident update on November 2 that the thefts hit servers running version 2.4.1 or earlier of the open-source payment platform, and that attackers had used a different method to exploit a vulnerability fixed in version 2.4.2, released on August 7.

It had seen no impact on servers already running 2.4.2 or later when it issued its warning.

An analysis by blockchain intelligence company Bitquery traced 18.38 Bitcoin and 3405 Litecoin to two addresses named by BTCPay Server, moved in 682 sweeps between October 30 and the morning of November 2. It said the thief signed in to the servers as an administrator and swept their hot wallets.

The flaw had already been exploited in August to steal funds through LND, a Lightning Network implementation, though BTCPay Server said at the time that on-chain wallets, including hot wallets, were not affected.

Read more on hot wallet breaches: Bitget Restarts Bitcoin Withdrawals Following $387.5m Wallet Breach

Sweeps Continued After BTCPay's Warning

Bitquery said 87% of the traced funds moved in a single wave on the afternoon and evening of November 1. It counted 267 further sweeps, worth about $150,000, after BTCPay Server told operators at 22:25 UTC that night to shut down their instances.

The firm could not tell how many servers were hit, since the blockchain records wallets rather than systems. It also left out other addresses and coins, including Lightning funds, making its figure a floor.

BTCPay Server added that some activity at the two addresses appears to predate the reported thefts, so their balances should not be treated as confirmed losses. The project has not published a loss total.

BTCPay Server Urges Hot Wallet Users to Rebuild

BTCPay Server urged operators of version 2.4.1 or earlier to move to a fresh server with a new wallet and seed, even if they had since updated, warning that "updating alone cannot remove access an attacker may already have gained."

It said wallets whose spending keys are held off the server, including hardware wallets, were unaffected, and advised keeping only operational funds on the server.

Operators should also preserve logs and transaction records, replace exposed credentials and avoid restoring the old server onto a new one, the project said.

The fix had been available since August 7. The wallets that were emptied sat on servers that had never installed it.

Title: Introducing Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities
Context: Note that requests matching these rules are not a count of compromised systems or successful exploits; the chart aims at providing practitioners a sense of what the focus level...
Full Text:
You run security at your organization. It’s 7:00 am, and you’re having breakfast. You receive a ping: a new critical vulnerability has been disclosed. Your team scrambles to compare vendor advisories, read technical research, check which systems run the affected software, and answer familiar questions from the business: are we affected, and what are we doing about it? Another disclosure arrives before that work is finished.

AI is changing both the volume and speed of critical vulnerability discovery. It can analyze large codebases at scale and surface deeply nested flaws that may have existed for years without being found through human review. That discovery momentum will put more pressure on security teams to understand the impact of each disclosure on their infrastructure.

To help security teams prepare, today we’re introducing Zero Wire: a public vulnerability intelligence feed on Cloudflare Radar, bringing the clarity of a news wire service to critical security developments. It helps security leaders and practitioners understand significant vulnerabilities and decide what to do next.

How it works

Zero Wire lives inside Cloudflare Radar under the security section.

Each briefing brings together a plain-language explanation of the vulnerability, who should investigate it, recommended actions, and links to the evidence and vendor guidance. The format is deliberately simple: an index card with what you need to know, without the drama. A CISO should be able to understand the issue quickly and ask the right questions. An engineer should be able to follow the same briefing to the technical guidance needed to investigate and remediate it.

We also offer a pre-compiled prompt you can use with your agent to assess the impact on your infrastructure. Cloudflare contributes security research, observations from our network, and practical knowledge of the controls that can help reduce exposure. The information is useful whether or not you are a Cloudflare customer.

Zero Wire brings that context together with authoritative external sources, giving readers a starting point for assessment and a place to return as an issue develops.

Our focus

Rather than a catalog of every CVE, Zero Wire complements vendor advisories and vulnerability databases, linking readers to the evidence and technical guidance needed to act. Zero Wire focuses on critical CVEs in Internet-facing software, such as vulnerabilities in web applications, the runtimes and libraries they depend on, and services exposed to the Internet, where a proxy can help mitigate exploitation.

We select significant issues that security teams need to understand and assess. Each briefing explains the potential impact, which deployments should be investigated, what is known about exploitation, and the available mitigation and patching guidance. A vulnerability’s severity and evidence of active exploitation are distinct: readers need both to make informed decisions.

A dedicated Cloudflare protection, such as Web Application Firewall (WAF) rules, is not a prerequisite for inclusion. Some issues require vendor updates or changes beyond the traffic Cloudflare can inspect. Where Cloudflare controls can help, we explain their scope and configuration requirements.

A walk through Zero Wire

Start on the Zero Wire homepage. Each card introduces an issue, identifies associated CVEs where applicable, and summarizes why it matters and what to do. You can search for a published briefing using a CVE or issue name, and follow technology tags to related entries. One briefing can cover several related CVEs when understanding them together makes the response clearer.

Find what needs attention

The homepage separates briefings into two categories. “Needs attention” brings together issues requiring active assessment or action, including those with known exploitation or developing guidance. “Reference” keeps briefings available when guidance has stabilized. Moving to “Reference” does not mean every affected system has been patched: an older vulnerability can still matter to an organization that has not completed remediation.

The status and last-checked date help you interpret each card. Known exploitation, an ongoing investigation, and an available vendor fix describe different things. Read them alongside the briefing’s evidence rather than treating them as a verdict on your own environment.

Understand what happened and who should investigate

When you open a briefing, the overview tells you what happened, why it deserves attention, and which teams should investigate. The explanation connects the technical issue to its practical consequences, such as service disruption or risk of data exposure.

For example, the recent php2shell vulnerability concerns flaws in the PHP runtime. That distinction matters for teams running applications such as WordPress or Magento: updating application code or a plugin alone does not repair the underlying runtime. The briefing helps readers identify the right system owners and directs them to the PHP security guidance for affected versions and remediation.

Turn the briefing into an action plan

What to do now gives your team a short set of next steps. Depending on the issue, that can mean identifying affected deployments, checking versions with a hosting provider, applying vendor updates, reviewing suspicious activity, or keeping compensating controls in place while patching.

The purpose is to make the next conversation concrete. For a PHP deployment, ask which runtime is actually running, whether the vendor’s fix has been applied, and who owns the update. Follow the linked vendor advisory for detailed applicability and remediation instructions, which can change as the investigation develops.

Assess your exposure with an AI agent

In this section, we share a prompt that can be used with your AI agent to quickly assess the impact on your infrastructure. The prompt asks for a read-only assessment of deployed software, relevant vendor fixes, exposure, and compensating controls, with per-asset evidence, unknowns, and next actions. It helps your team investigate its own environment; copying the prompt does not itself scan or change systems.

Check the evidence and follow what changed

To help you learn more about the vulnerability, each briefing links to external documents such as CVE records, research, and relevant exploitation evidence, including CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. These sources answer different questions. A vendor advisory establishes affected versions and remediation guidance. An exploitation report provides evidence of attacker activity.

If applicable to a briefing, Cloudflare can add context about traffic seen on our network, for example by showing traffic matching WAF rules that indicates exploitation attempts. Those distinctions matter. Observing an attack attempt does not establish that a particular organization was compromised. Equally, a lack of observed attempts on Cloudflare’s network does not establish that exploitation is absent elsewhere. Briefings distinguish what the sources establish from what remains unknown.

Where available, charts add context to that evidence. The php2shell briefing shows the volume of HTTP requests matching Cloudflare WAF managed rules over time. Note that requests matching these rules are not a count of compromised systems or successful exploits; the chart aims at providing practitioners a sense of what the focus level is by threat actors on a particular vulnerability.

Finally, update chronology records important developments, such as new advisories or changes to the evidence and response guidance. Together with the last-checked date, it helps returning readers understand what has changed since their previous visit.

Understand Cloudflare’s role

The Cloudflare section provides links to whether we offer compensating controls or provide a way to mitigate the vulnerability impact on your infrastructure.

If a particular CVE can be addressed with a WAF rule, the briefing reports its availability and essential configuration requirements. When applicable, paid Plans and free Plans links take customers to the relevant dashboard configuration. The next step is explicit: “Review your WAF configuration to determine whether you are protected”. A link allows you to review your security posture, it does not automatically enable a rule or verify a deployment.

Note that a WAF mitigation is a compensating control for the traffic it covers, it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Blocking the requests can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. The security teams should always follow the vendor remediation guidance.

Stay informed with Zero Wire

A useful vulnerability briefing should leave you with a clearer understanding of the issue and a concrete next step. Day Zero brings those essentials together: what happened, who should investigate, what to do now, and where to find the evidence.

Visit Zero Wire vulnerability intelligence, share the relevant briefings with the teams responsible for your systems, and return for new entries and updates. When the next disclosure arrives, we want you to spend less time assembling the basic facts and more time acting on them.

Title: Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware
Context: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow...
Full Text: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050. In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating. Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday. “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.” One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said. Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices, allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on water systems across at least 12 US states over the summer. The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote. While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted. Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher. One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote. The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote. “If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post. While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®

Title: What exploited vulnerabilities have in common: A data-driven analysis of real-world attacks
Context: Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead,...
Full Text:
In this article

Classifying the vulnerability landscape

Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild

Where defenders should focus

Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast

Impact, exposure and where to focus

Next in line

How Microsoft Security helps defenders act

References

Learn More

The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation.

Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond.

Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack.

Classifying the vulnerability landscape

To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform.

Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve.

Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction.

Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content.

Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold.

Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges.

Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls.

Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen.

Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets.

Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification of data or system state.

Denial of service: Disruption of system or service availability.

Cross-site scripting (XSS): Script execution within a victim’s browser context.

Arbitrary file access: Unauthorized access to or placement of files.

Spoofing or redirect: Spoofing, redirection, or other forms of UI deception.

We also classified vulnerabilities by the platforms they affect, including Windows, Linux/Unix, mobile, network appliances, IoT/OT, virtualization hosts, and developer packages. A CVE can span multiple platforms. Developer packages are treated as a separate category because they are often cross-platform and represent a significant share of the overall vulnerability population.

Most CVEs in the analysis affect application code, including servers, web applications, browsers, productivity software, libraries, and firmware tooling, while a smaller share affects OS and system code such as kernels, drivers, and firmware.

This analysis covers CVEs published through September 2026 using Microsoft’s catalog of tracked vulnerabilities. Each CVE is counted once in the impact analysis and across each relevant platform in the platform analysis.

Figure 1 – The full published-CVE population as of September 2026, broken down by impact class and affected platform, and an OS vs. application split. Breadth dominates – many impact classes spread across many platforms, with about 77% of CVEs in application code and 23% in OS/system code.

Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild

The subset of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild is much smaller than the overall CVE population, and looks very different from it. Fewer than 1 in 200 published CVEs are ever used in a real attack, and those that do get used are overwhelmingly concentrated in the takeover classes that maximize threat actor impact and exposure.

The difference becomes clear when we look at impact. Exploitation is heavily concentrated in vulnerabilities that give attackers greater control over a system. Server-side RCE rises from 20% of published CVEs to 37% of exploited CVEs, local privilege escalation from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%. By comparison, XSS falls from 15% to 4% and denial of service from 16% to 7%. OS vulnerabilities show a similar shift, increasing from 23% of the overall CVE population to 41% of exploited vulnerabilities.

These patterns are consistent with threat actors favoring vulnerabilities that can provide meaningful access and control. Remote code execution and privilege escalation can create footholds that support subsequent stages of an attack, while vulnerabilities that primarily cause a crash or limited script execution may offer less utility for broader compromise.

Importantly, a vulnerability’s stated classification does not always reflect what an attacker can reliably achieve in practice. For example, some vulnerabilities described as enabling RCE may ultimately result only in denial of service under real-world conditions. Understanding the demonstrated impact and exploitability of a vulnerability is therefore critical to effective prioritization.

Figure 2 – The 2,056 exploited-in-the-wild CVEs distribution, compared against the full published population: ghost lines mark each class and platform’s share of all ~380K published CVEs, and badges show the shift in percentage points. Takeover classes and OS code rise, while high-volume XSS and DoS fall.

Where defenders should focus

Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast

Patching is slow, and far slower on critical systems than others. Across platforms, servers are the critical assets and the slowest to patch. Microsoft Security Exposure Management data from 2026 shows that the median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers. It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on MacOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest.

Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure. According to VulnCheck, 29% of the exploits in 2025 were launched within 1 day of CVE publication. According to CISA, the mean time from CVE publication to CISA KEV catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. 2026 data up to September already have that number dropping to 20 days, with a median of only 3 days since publication. Industry research suggests that advances in AI are a significant factor in the time reduction required to develop exploits, further increasing pressure on defenders to respond quickly.

Impact, exposure and where to focus

Two things determine a vulnerability’s value to a threat actor: impact and exposure. Impact is what successful exploitation provides, such as remote code execution or privilege escalation. Exposure is an asset’s position in the environment and the opportunities it creates for further compromise. An asset’s exposure is shaped by the identities, privileges, and connections available from it.

Servers often use service accounts, application identities, or cloud-managed identities with permissions beyond their operational needs. Compromising such a system can provide access to additional resources, sensitive data, administrative privileges, or trusted network paths. Together, impact and exposure determine the blast radius: a vulnerability that enables full control of a highly exposed system can enable widespread on-premises or cloud compromise.

Threat actors do not exploit at random: they go after the vulnerabilities that give the highest impact and exposure: full control of a system and the privileged identities and critical assets it has access to. As defenders, focusing on these vulnerabilities first can deliver the highest return on remediation investment.

Takeover vulnerabilities like remote code execution, authentication bypass and local privilege escalation lead here. They drive the broadest exposure and the largest blast radius, account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities, and stopping their exploitation interrupts attacks at the earliest stage, before compromise can propagate across the environment.

Next in line

A second slice deserves attention where context makes it severe: denial of service against availability-critical assets is recoverable in general, but can be mission-ending in parts of your environment where uptime is everything; disclosure of credentials or secrets can be minor as an insulated incident, but it feeds the same privileged-identity path mentioned above.

Figure 3 – The three remote-takeover classes analyzed across 1,239 exploited CVEs), each drilled down by affected platform and split into OS vs Application code. Bar length is the CVE count per platform; the dark segment is OS/system, the light segment is application.

How Microsoft Security helps defenders act

Threat actors do not begin with a vulnerability list. They begin by looking for a reachable way in. Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management approaches the environment from that same outside-in perspective, continuously discovering internet-facing infrastructure, including previously unknown or unmonitored assets, shadow IT, and third-party dependencies. This gives defenders an opportunity to remove unnecessary exposure before a reachable vulnerability becomes an entry point.

Once the reachable assets are known, the next question is which weaknesses deserve immediate attention. Defenders need a way to prioritize exposure beyond CVSS alone. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management addresses this challenge through Exposure Score and prioritized security recommendations.

Prioritization incorporates threat and exploitability signals, breach likelihood, internet exposure, and asset criticality, helping teams focus remediation on vulnerabilities that create the greatest actual exposure.

An initial foothold is only part of the risk. Attack Path Analysis connects assets and threat actor techniques into end-to-end routes from an entry point to a critical asset. Microsoft Security Exposure Management Attack Path Analysis provides a cross-workload view spanning endpoints, cloud, and hybrid environments, using vulnerability context from MDVM, endpoint data from Defender for Endpoint, and cloud asset data from Defender for Cloud. Within cloud environments, Defender CSPM Attack Path Analysis adds detailed context about internet exposure, vulnerabilities, network connections, identities, and permissions across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud.

Together, these experiences show how an exposed workload could become a path through a privileged identity to sensitive data or another critical resource, helping defenders identify where to break the path before the initial compromise expands.

Patching remains essential, but it is not the only defensive action available. Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead, and identify opportunities to break attack paths before compromise spreads to critical assets.

Some 88% of the critical and high-severity weaknesses found in live attack tests on enterprise environments this year would not have been identified through vendor advisories or other outside sources, new data has suggested.

The figure comes from a report published on November 2 by Armadin, the offensive security startup launched by Mandiant founder Kevin Mandia, based on AI-driven attacks against its clients' live systems.

The clients span nearly a dozen industries, but Armadin did not disclose how many organizations or findings the data covers.

Read more on exposure management: AI Threats and Alert Fatigue Challenge Cybersecurity Teams

Most Severe Findings Sat Beyond Advisories and Logins

Defects in software the clients had written themselves made up 67% of the critical findings and 78% of the high findings that advisories could not cover. Vendor products deployed in ways no advisory describes, such as administrative consoles exposed to the internet, accounted for 24% and 22%.

The remaining 9% of critical findings, and under 1% of high ones, were zero-days Armadin found itself, including one in an identity governance platform whose vendor took almost four months to issue an advisory.

Nearly 70% of critical and high findings sat on the unauthenticated attack surface. Of the documented attack chains, 82% began without credentials, and 56% of those went on without a password or key ever being presented.

In more than 70% of client environments, Armadin said it reached a critical outcome in three steps or fewer without valid credentials.

Exposed Service Accounts Created Further Attack Paths

Just under half of the chains that started without authentication relied on an exposed credential, 71% of which belonged to applications or service accounts rather than people. Nearly 90% were reachable without extraction, often in repositories, configuration files, backups, logs or cloud settings.

In one engagement, Armadin started from an unprivileged domain account and used a flaw in backup software to read the credentials it held. That led to a hypervisor management server and, via a domain controller backup, to domain administrator hashes.

Fixing the severe findings meant shipping application code in 51% of cases, changing a setting, permission or policy in 43% and rotating an exposed credential in 32%, with many needing more than one step.

Armadin's recommendations included policies for provisioning, storing and rotating service account credentials, and checks of pipelines and code repositories for exposed secrets.

By its count, 93% of severe findings needed no third party to act, leaving the fix in each organization's own hands.

Title: Additional Ivanti Connect Secure zero-days exploited in the wild (CVE-2026-111357, CVE-2026-118527)
Context: Ivanti rates CVE-2026-111357, a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability (CWE-306), with a CVSSv3
Full Text:
Overview

On October 29, 2026, Ivanti updated its security advisory for Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) to include two additional vulnerabilities and released fixes for both. Ivanti rates CVE-2026-111357, a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability (CWE-306), with a CVSSv3.1 score of 8.8; it allows a local authenticated attacker to escalate privileges. CVE-2026-118527, classified as generation of predictable numbers or identifiers (CWE-340), has an Ivanti-assigned CVSSv3.0 score of 4.3 and, according to CISA's KEV entry, allows a remote authenticated attacker to upload attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk.

Per Ivanti, exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers when these flaws are chained with CVE-2026-104935, an authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290). Rapid7 covered the original disclosure on October 13, 2026, when a fix for CVE-2026-104935 was available but the privilege escalation component remained unpatched. Fixes are now available for all three vulnerabilities.

On October 30, 2026, CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 were added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation.

In its investigation, Volexity reports that UTA0576 used an exploit chain to gain unauthenticated root access to an appliance running 22.8R2.4, beginning on October 3, 2026. Its write-up identifies CVE-2026-104935 and CVE-2026-111357; Ivanti's updated advisory identifies CVE-2026-118527 as an additional component of the chain. Volexity observed credential theft and Active Directory queries for Windows LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

The combined impact warrants emergency remediation despite the individual CVSS ratings. Ivanti Connect Secure is an enterprise VPN solution deployed at the network edge and has a history of zero-day exploitation, including in 2024 and 2025.
