Title: Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause
Context: And guffaw-ingly, whereas in Italy they represent around 57% of all attacks, exploited vulnerabilities showed up in only 6
Full Text:
Italy is suffering from a disproportionately large number of cyberattacks, new data suggests. Not only that: The kinds of attacks hitting organizations in the country are vastly different from those hitting other places. Researchers have a triad of theories as to why.

It's true that certain regions and countries face greater cyber-risk thanks to economic, military, and political factors. Israel is a magnet for hacktivists and regional, state-aligned advanced persistent threats (APTs). Brazil's unique history makes it a hive of banking Trojans. The United States economy will always draw the most attention from scammers. It isn't so obvious, though, why Italy is such a popular mark for cybercriminals.

"One of the main reasons why we decided to look into the Italian threat landscape is because Italy kept appearing at the top of our stats in our monthly internal reports," says Gianluca Tiepolo, cybercrime analyst at Intel471. In a report shared exclusively with Dark Reading ahead of its release, Intel471 found that Italy is a total outlier in the global cyber threat landscape. Organizations there are being compromised at a rate beyond what one would reasonably expect, based on the country's size, economy, and politics. And exploits against vulnerabilities and Web infrastructure are far more common in Italy than elsewhere.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

"We wanted to understand what was driving those stats," Tiepolo says. In the end, though, the data paints a nearly inexplicable picture of what's going on in the land of pasta and Chianti.

Inexplicable Data From Italy's Threat Landscape

Italy is the 25th largest country in the world but, according to this new data, its organizations make up about 7% of all initial access data sold on cybercriminal forums. That's second only to the United States (30%) globally. Italy also ranks fourth among countries most targeted by ransomware.

Far stranger still are the types of cyber intrusions affecting organizations in Italy. According to the new data, initial access brokers (IABs) obtained their initial foothold through vulnerabilities in 57% of cases. Credentials only explained 23% of cases. Meanwhile, IABs have been selling access to victim-owned Web infrastructure in 49% of cases, with remote access and remote desktop tools making up 26% of cases.

So what? Maybe those figures don't pop off the page. Now, though, let's compare them with Intel471's own data from its 2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook report:

Globally in 2025, IABs targeted remote access and remote desktop tools 67% of the time — 41% more often, relatively, than in Italy. Meanwhile, Web infrastructure — by far the most at-risk asset in Italy — represented such a small fraction of Intel471's global data that it didn't even bother to cite it in their report.

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

In the same vein, according to the company's global data, credential-based attacks are eight times more common in general than any other type of attack today. It found that 49% of IAB listings advertised credentials as the attack type, compared to 23% in the Italian-specific data. And guffaw-ingly, whereas in Italy they represent around 57% of all attacks, exploited vulnerabilities showed up in only 6.5% of cases globally.

Theory #1: Poor Cybersecurity Hygiene

Though cybersecurity data reporting can be interpreted in different ways depending on the circumstance, Italy does seem like a kind of cyber-risk unicorn, Tiepolo says, adding that Italy has been falling behind on cyber readiness for a long time now.

"I'm Italian," he says. "I've been working with a lot of different Italian clients. What I can say is that Italy is probably slightly behind other European countries, simply based on security technology [adoption]. For example, endpoint detection and response (EDR) technologies became popular in Italy around 2020–2021. Before 2020, most Italian companies didn't use EDR technology. So maybe historically, Italy is a bit behind in actually investing in cybersecurity products and technologies."

Related:Nordic CISOs Handle Rising Cyber Threats Remarkably Well

Also, opportunistic cybercriminals are exploiting known, widespread, and often quite old vulnerabilities en masse to scoop up more victims in Italy than in other countries. "The data we saw last week from PHP2Shell, I think, validates this assessment. Italy is the country in Europe with the largest number of PHP 4, 5, and 7 versions, which are end-of-life," Tiepolo notes.

"A full 90% of initial access offers for Italy are what we call 'wholesale' offers," he posits. "They're not offers that are targeting Italy specifically, but simply exploiting vulnerabilities. Our assessment is that Italy is probably slower than other countries in patching their systems."

Theory #2: A Cyber Risk Network Effect

Another, related possibility is that Italy finds itself victim to a kind of cyber vulnerability network effect. The logic goes something like this: If certain technologies are especially common in a country like Italy, and organizations are slow to address vulnerabilities in those technologies, then that country becomes an attractive economy of scale.

As Intel471 wrote in its report, "Once an actor develops an effective exploitation method, the actor can apply that method to additional exposed systems without conducting a separate, extensive reconnaissance effort against each organization. This reduces the effort required to compromise businesses whose size or profile might otherwise offer limited incentive for a dedicated intrusion."

Researchers couldn't say exactly which technologies, vulnerabilities, or exploitations this theory might refer to, but noted that it does fold into the finding that 90% of initial access offerings to Italian organizations online are sold in bulk.

Without co-signing Intel471's data or conclusions specifically, representatives from the Milan-based cybersecurity firm Cleafy tell Dark Reading that they've observed broadly similar patterns.

"Our threat research does point to a related pattern: attackers reusing tools, infrastructure and techniques to scale campaigns across Italian banking targets," the company wrote via email. It pointed to cases such as the drIBAN Web injection kit, which attackers used to exploit the Certified Electronic Mail (PEC) system used widely across Italy. Cases like drIBAN "don't establish that Italy has a disproportionately large initial-access market, but they do illustrate how reusable attack techniques and infrastructure can help cybercriminals scale operations across multiple targets."

Theory #3: Small & Medium-Sized Businesses Shift the Data

There is one other, potentially significant contributing factor to why Italy looks so different from other countries in cyberattack datasets: its prevalence of small businesses.

Most businesses everywhere are small, but, at least in comparison to other advanced economies, it's especially the case in Italy. A May 2024 "data snapshot for Italy" by McKinsey found that "MSMEs" — micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises — contributed roughly 10% more to Italy's economy and employment compared to their relative share in other advanced economies. And last March, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) published a report that cited that 99.9% of Italian firms in 2023 were SMEs, and 94.8% were micro-enterprises.

"Italy has a lot of small and medium-sized companies," Tiepolo says. "One of the things that came out from the data — especially the extortion data — is that these groups are [disproportionately] targeting small- and medium-sized businesses. So this could be one of the reasons [Italy stands out] in comparison to other countries that have more large companies."

Title: Node2Shell: Reproducing CVE-2026-111497 in the Node.js Brotli decoder
Context: Datadog Cloud SIEM includes two detections that identify command execution associated with Node2Shell exploitation: Shell spawned by web server detects shells, download...
Full Text:
Key points and observations

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released fixes for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in its bundled Brotli decoder. The upstream flaw sits in the Google Brotli C library, so the blast radius reaches Python, Bun, .NET, Java brotli4j, Envoy, and Istio. Every affected runtime now has a fix available.

We reproduced the flaw on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image and verified that the patched build rejects the same bytes.

Capturing an application-level trace is difficult because the process continues running despite memory corruption.

Only patching fixes this vulnerability. The application process decodes the data, so neither the web server nor a web application firewall (WAF) ever sees the malicious content. An edge rule that rejects Brotli-compressed request bodies is a useful tripwire and nothing more.

What happened

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released security updates for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder. The CVE record gives the flaw a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 score of 9.2, or Critical, while Node.js rates its severity as High. Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 contain the fix, and end-of-life release lines carry the same vulnerable decoder but have no patch.

What looked like a Node.js problem on day one turned out to be far broader. Most runtimes embed the upstream Google Brotli C library, where the bug lives. Over the following week many consumers of that decoder shipped its own advisory:

Two details deserve special attention. Java's brotli4j bundles its own native Brotli build inside its jars, so patching the operating system's libbrotli does not fix it. Bun executables built with bun build \--compile embed the runtime and stay vulnerable until they are rebuilt.

Before the disclosure, Imperva demonstrated code execution on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux ARM64 image. Their exploit needed several attempts and was not released. A public proof of concept appeared on October 22, 2026. On standard builds it produces a crash and a limited memory read. As of October 29, 2026, there have been confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, and CISA's known exploited vulnerabilities catalog now lists the CVE.

How to know if you're affected

A service is exposed when it decompresses Brotli data that an attacker controls, which comes through two common paths. A few additional considerations apply to both.

Outbound requests (the quiet path)

Outbound requests are the harder path to see. Node.js's built-in fetch() decodes a Content-Encoding: br response automatically, whether or not the request asked for Brotli. The axios, got, and node-fetch clients advertise and decode Brotli by default. Any feature that fetches URLs supplied by users, such as webhooks, link previews, and feed readers, enables an attacker to force the encoding selection server side since the attacker controls the response headers, and fetch() decodes a body labeled br even when the application explicitly forces Accept-Encoding: identity.

In our testing, no exception surfaced at runtime: one crafted stream completed with an empty body and an HTTP 200, and the only visible signals were CPU usage and, under concurrency, a starved threadpool that still answered health checks.

The same holds outside Node.js: Python HTTP clients decode Brotli responses automatically whenever Brotli or brotlicffi is installed, even if application code never imports the package.

Inbound requests (the visible path)

Inbound attacks are easier to observe. A compressed request body is a recognizable attack surface, your reverse proxy or WAF can see the Content-Encoding: br header, and the framework parser is a known place to audit. Express 5 and body-parser 2.x accept Brotli-compressed request bodies by default in their JSON, raw, text, and URL-encoded parsers, and Koa and NestJS inherit the behavior. Express 4 rejects those bodies with an HTTP 415, and a bare Node.js HTTP server does not decompress anything. Parsers mounted before authentication expose the decoder to unauthenticated requests.

Other considerations

Both paths share a versioning trap: process.versions.brotli still reports 1.2.0 on the patched Node.js 24.22.1, because the cherry-picked fix does not bump the embedded version string. process.version is reliable only for official distributions from nodejs.org.

If you cannot patch immediately, set inflate: false on Express 5 and body-parser 2.x parsers, or reject Content-Encoding: br at the reverse proxy. These measures only mitigate the risk, as patching is the only complete solution. These mitigations could also break the functionality as they reject all compressed request bodies, do nothing for the outbound path, and break compressed bodies sent by legitimate clients.

How the vulnerability works

A Brotli stream is divided into blocks, and the decoder moves to a new block only when the current block's length budget runs out. A 23 MB stream of otherwise ordinary commands drains that budget while producing no output, and its closing commands request a block switch that the format forbids. These steps are where the attacker does the proper setup to exploit the bug.

In the next stage, we see the impact of the vulnerability. In Brotli 1.2.0, DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() returns a boolean, and it answers two different questions with the same "false" value: "this stream is malformed" and "I need more input". Callers cannot tell the two apart, and on the decoder's fast path the return value is dropped entirely.

The two arms then diverge. The first path is an overflow where the decoder parks the unconsumed bytes in a small internal buffer while it waits for more input. The copy has no bound check, so bytes past the end of the buffer land in adjacent decoder state. The write happens inside a single heap allocation, so the tooling built to catch memory corruption never sees it, and the process keeps running. The other path is that it keeps spinning. The decoder retries the forbidden switch in a loop, which pins a CPU core inside a single call that never returns: a one-request denial of service.

From memory corruption to code execution

In this case, memory corruption has impactful consequences. The corrupted decoder state controls where the decoder reads from and writes to next, so a crafted stream can redirect both operations. This gives an attacker two primitives:

A repeatable read of heap memory that leaves through the decompressed response.

A redirected write. In our lab, we aimed it at an unmapped page and produced a deterministic crash.

Both primitives are real. The read primitive is the most operationally interesting, because heap bytes returning over the wire are the first step of a staged attack.

Three obstacles stand between these primitives and a shell:

The addresses move. The heap layout that the corruption targets is randomized and changes between requests, so what one request leaks, the next request can’t reliably use.

The corruption bytes are also the decoder's input. The decoder consumes the bytes that steer the corruption again as it continues, so the values an attacker needs are constrained by the values the decoder will accept. This is the deepest structural obstacle we found.

A managed runtime stands in the way. Between the corrupted C state and control flow sits the machinery of a language runtime with its own allocator, its own compiled code, and its own defenses, none of which the original C library was designed around.

After measuring all three obstacles, we assess that the flaw is exploitable and that the gap between these primitives and reliable code execution is engineering effort. This matches Imperva's report of successful execution after several attempts on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image.

How the patch addresses the flaw

The patch is small and precise. The block-switch helper now returns a real error code, and both code paths treat a failed check as a hard stop instead of a request for more input. It rejects a crafted stream with a format error (-17) before anything is written to the decoder's state.

The release timeline is the troubling part. The fix was committed to the upstream Brotli repository on February 27, 2026, but the fixed library releases did not ship until October 21, 2026. For eight months, anyone who downloaded Brotli, or a runtime that embeds it, received the vulnerable version even though the corrected code sat in the public repository. The release also ships without a regression test or a changelog entry for this fix.

How to detect exploitation

This CVE involves no attacker-controlled infrastructure, so there are no conventional indicators. Detection rests on behavioral signals, and no single signal is conclusive. Correlate across three layers.

Decoder error signals

The vulnerable and patched builds respond differently to the same malicious bytes. Both responses appear in application logs and APM error spans and the error you see depends on whether the build is patched. On a vulnerable build, Node.js returns Z_BUF_ERROR with the message "unexpected end of file". On a patched build, Node.js returns ERR__ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH, and Python returns "brotli: decoder is unhealthy". The vulnerable signal also appears for benign truncated input so you have to still look a little closer and differentiate the benign truncated input vs real attacks.

Process signals

A worker that exits with signal 139 (SIGSEGV) right after a Brotli transfer is a crash attempt, and a process pinned at 100% CPU inside a decompression call is the spin arm. Correlate on workload identity (the container, pod, or service) and not the process ID, because the process that crashed is gone and a successful attempt may not crash at all. The strongest signal is behavioral: a shell or new outbound connections from the same workload.

The disclosure channel

Decompressed output that contains bytes the client never sent is the read primitive in action. Investigate any such output immediately. Because the leaked heap memory leaves through the decompressed response, start by listing the endpoints that return or reflect decompressed content back to the caller, such as echo, preview, conversion, or proxy features.

What does not work

Payload byte signatures, because the attacker-controlled parts of the stream change per target and the exploit is the decode process itself, not the decompressed content.

Content matching at the WAF, because the web server forwards compressed bytes and never decodes them.

Body-size limits, because the tested middleware counts decompressed bytes, so the 23 MB compressed trigger still reaches the decoder.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Cloud Security Management tracks CVE-2026-111497 and the related vendor advisories as vulnerability findings on hosts and container images, so your patching status lives in one place.

Datadog Code Security reports the vulnerable services that ship dependency inventories. Its library inventory identifies which services to prioritize: those running Express 5, body-parser 2.x, or Koa parsers, and those using HTTP clients that auto-decode Brotli.

Datadog Application Performance Monitoring (APM) helps you hunt for attempts. This query requires capturing Content-Encoding, which is not set by default in Node.js spans, so make sure to check how the language tracer you are using behaves. For example in Node.js it can be enabled by including content-encoding in DD_TRACE_HEADER_TAGS. Pivot on the services that accept Content-Encoding: br request bodies using this query, and review services that fetch user-supplied URLs. Decoder failures surface as APM error spans correlated with the request and the client address. The process telemetry that the Datadog Agent collects shows a crashed attempt as a worker restart with exit code 139.

Datadog Workload Protection includes coverage through the CVE-2026-111497 Node2Shell Exploit Content Pack. This pack includes a new security policy with three Agent rules that cover post-exploitation that surfaces a CVE-2026-111497 Node2Shell exploitation detected signal.

Datadog Cloud SIEM includes two detections that identify command execution associated with Node2Shell exploitation:

Shell spawned by web server detects shells, download utilities, and reconnaissance commands launched by web servers or web processes. It uses process activity events with parent process information.

Shell spawned by web process uses Linux auditd logs to detect shells or download utilities executed in a web server context.

Conclusion

CVE-2026-111497 shows how a single unchecked return value in a widely shared C library can ripple across nearly every major runtime. Because the decoder runs inside the application's own process, the flaw sidesteps the defenses most teams rely on. The eight months between the upstream fix and its release are a reminder that a fix in a public repository protects no one until it ships.

Exploitation has been confirmed, which further proves the primitives are real and the path to code execution is a matter of effort. Patch to Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1 or your vendor's fixed package, rebuild container images, restart every process, and inventory the other Brotli consumers in your environment.

Title: CVE-2026-101767: Critical Oracle EBS SQL Injection Actively Probed in the Wild
Context: CVE-2026-101767 disclosure and exploitation timeline The vulnerability was discovered by Horizon3
Full Text:
What is CVE-2026-101767?

A critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-101767, CVSS 9.8) was disclosed affecting Oracle E-Business Suite’s Application Object Library, allowing attackers to achieve full remote code execution and system takeover via an unauthenticated SQL injection in the Thin Client Framework servlet. Due to the potential for complete compromise of financial, payroll, and HR data managed by EBS, immediate patching is required.

How the Oracle EBS SQL injection leads to remote code execution

The issue originates from the Application Object Library’s TCF servlet at /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer, where missing authentication on a critical function combined with improper input sanitization leads to SQL injection as the privileged APPS database user. By sending specially crafted POST requests to the servlet instantiating oracle.apps.jtf.gantt.server.GanttDataServer, attackers can execute arbitrary SQL commands and chain to operating system command execution as the EBS application account, potentially achieving full takeover of the EBS instance and all data it manages. No authentication is required to exploit this issue.

CVE-2026-101767 disclosure and exploitation timeline

The vulnerability was discovered by Horizon3.ai and reported to Oracle on July 24, 2026. Oracle addressed it in the October 2026 Critical Patch Update, released October 20. Within a week of the patch release, threat intelligence firm Defused observed exploratory exploitation attempts hitting Oracle EBS honeypots on October 27. EBS has historically been a target for financially motivated threat actors, including the Cl0p group’s large-scale EBS campaign the previous year.

Which Oracle E-Business Suite versions are affected?

The following components are affected: Oracle E-Business Suite Application Object Library, versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15. Oracle notes that earlier unsupported versions are likely also affected. The vulnerable servlet passes through the default EBS URL firewall configuration, meaning any internet-facing EBS instance with default settings is exposed. Organizations running EBS for financial, payroll, HR, and procurement operations face elevated risk due to the sensitive data accessible through the APPS database user.

How to patch and mitigate CVE-2026-101767

Users should apply the October 2026 Critical Patch Update immediately (details in My Oracle Support Note KA923), and also patch the underlying EBS Database and Fusion Middleware components, which have separate CPU entries. As interim mitigations until patching is complete, administrators should remove /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer from the EBS URL firewall allowlist and restrict network access to the EBS web tier to trusted networks only.

Is CVE-2026-101767 being exploited in the wild?

At the time of writing, Horizon3.ai has published technical details of the attack chain, and active probing has been confirmed in the wild by Defused. The vulnerability is not yet listed on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Regardless, the severity and ease of exploitation make this vulnerability high risk, especially in internet-facing deployments.

What attackers can do with a compromised Oracle EBS instance

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to execute arbitrary SQL and OS commands as the APPS and EBS application accounts, exfiltrate or manipulate sensitive financial, payroll, and HR data, and potentially pivot to other systems within the network, leading to service disruption, data exposure, or full infrastructure compromise.

How Orca helps find and prioritize vulnerable Oracle EBS assets

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable versions of Oracle E-Business Suite, understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability, and asset criticality, and prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone. Orca’s platform highlights affected assets directly in the newItem view, helping security teams focus on the most critical remediation paths first

Title: Most Servers on the Planet Are Vulnerable to This Firmware Code-Execution Flaw
Context: With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits
Full Text:
Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.

The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.

The Cat Has Left the Bag

The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.

With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.

“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”

CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.

Title: CVE-2026-111497: Node2Shell / HTTP2Shell Vulnerability May Allow RCE
Context: ThreatLabz has observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting this vulnerability through Zscaler Deception, as detailed in the ThreatLabz Observations section below
Full Text: IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, the Node.js project disclosed CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Google’s Brotli decoder used by Node.js and other software. The vulnerability is also known as Node2Shell and more recently as HTTP2Shell. The CVE score, filed by Google as the numbering authority, is 9.2 (Critical) on CVSS 4.0. The flaw can be triggered when a vulnerable process decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. Successful exploitation may result in process crashes, disclosure of process memory, or remote code execution (RCE). Imperva reported demonstrating code execution in fresh containers running the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image, with multiple attempts required in its test environment. The vulnerable Brotli decoder may be present in a range of runtimes, libraries, and software packages, including Node.js, Bun, Python Brotli bindings, .NET, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Java brotli4j, libbrotli, curl/libcurl through Brotli dependencies, and Linux distribution packages. Applications may be exposed if they decompress attacker-controlled data using a vulnerable decoder. The vulnerability may be reachable through both inbound and outbound traffic paths. A malicious client could send a crafted request with Content-Encoding: br to a vulnerable server-side component that performs Brotli request decompression. Conversely, a malicious or compromised server could return a crafted Brotli-compressed response to a vulnerable client application that automatically decodes Brotli responses. ThreatLabz has observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting this vulnerability through Zscaler Deception, as detailed in the ThreatLabz Observations section below. RecommendationsZscaler recommends the following measures to address CVE-2026-111497 and monitor for potentially related activity:Patch vulnerable runtimes and libraries. Upgrade vulnerable runtimes, packages, and infrastructure components to the patched versions listed in the Vulnerable Versions table. Prioritize services that decompress untrusted Brotli data, including internet-facing applications that accept compressed request bodies and services that fetch content from external or user-controlled URLs. Validate each vulnerable component independently. Updating the system-wide libbrotli package may not remediate applications that statically bundle Brotli or ship their own decoder copy.Rebuild and redeploy containers. Use patched base images, runtimes, and libraries, and verify the versions in running workloads. Updating a host’s libraries does not update copies bundled within container images.Disable Brotli decoding where patching is delayed. If immediate patching is not possible, disable Brotli decompression on vulnerable paths where supported, following vendor guidance and testing for application compatibility.Monitor for exploitation and post-exploitation behavior. How It WorksBrotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It is used for HTTP compression to reduce the size of web content such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, and API responses. Brotli-encoded HTTP content is identified by the Content-Encoding: br header.Applications may use Brotli directly or through dependencies such as runtimes, frameworks, HTTP clients, and middleware. In some configurations, these components automatically decompress Brotli-encoded content without application code explicitly calling Brotli APIs.Vulnerability detailsThe flaw occurs in Brotli’s block-decoding logic. When a stream changes block type, the decoder determines the next block type and length. In vulnerable versions, there is a macro (in the fast-path logic) that does not properly check the return value of the DecodeBlockTypeAndLength function, which can cause the decoder to continue processing an invalid state (e.g., when provided a maliciously crafted Brotli stream). This can lead to an out-of-bounds write and be used as a primitive for RCE. Title: Millions of security cameras at risk: DoS vulnerability in Intelbras devices
Context: During our research, we discovered a denial-of-service vulnerability that affects Intelbras IP cameras systems
Full Text:
Background

Network-connected surveillance cameras are now widespread in both home and enterprise environments, so securing them is essential to safeguarding physical spaces and sensitive assets. As these devices continue to gain new features and network connectivity capabilities, vulnerabilities in their implementation can have significant security implications.

During our research, we discovered a denial-of-service vulnerability that affects Intelbras IP cameras systems. The flaw resides in a firmware update endpoint that is accessible without authentication and allows anyone with access to the local Wi-Fi network to knock cameras offline. A single request disrupts the camera for only about a minute, but sending periodic requests keeps the device offline indefinitely. We reported the issue to Intelbras, monitored the remediation process, validated the fix in the new firmware, and will now demonstrate the exploitation procedure step-by-step.

Following our notification, Intelbras patched the vulnerability and released updated firmware (R.260804) along with update instructions. A candidate ID of CAN-2026-2035970 has been assigned by MITRE following submission, pending the final CVE assignment. Additionally, the Intelbras team recently informed us that MITRE has classified the vulnerability as Medium, assigning it a score of 5.1 under the CVSS 4.0 framework. The issue discussed in this article is no longer present in the latest firmware version.

Firmware

Intelbras provides firmware files on its official website. While users can manually install these updates via an SD card, the cameras also natively support firmware upgrades over the local network via their web interface and mobile app. We obtained the firmware version v240927 for the iM3B-C (IM3 C) camera, which was the latest available version at the time of our research. According to Intelbras, the same firmware is also compatible with the iMX C, iM4 C, iM5 SC, iME 360 C, and iM7+ FC models. Below, we can view the firmware version and the camera model used as an example.

To provide context, we will explain how the camera’s authentication mechanism works and why it is relevant to accessing the camera’s endpoints. The main firmware component is an ARM binary named sonia, responsible for controlling the kernel drivers used by the camera hardware, authentication, and livestream recording, among other things.

How authentication works

The global.login RPC method handles authentication at the /RPC2_Login endpoint. First, the client, such as the mobile app or a custom script, sends the username and an empty password. The camera responds with an authentication challenge (a set of values to verify the password without transmitting it). This response returns a temporary session, the encryption type in the encryption field, a random value, and a realm (authentication scope). At this stage, a false response is normal and does not indicate a failed login, as the authentication process is not yet complete.

Next, the client calculates the response password from the authentication challenge. It first generates an MD5 (username:realm:original_password) hash as the base. It then calculates a second MD5 (username:random:first_md5) hash, where first_md5 is the result of the previous step. To complete the authentication, the client sends this final result back to /RPC2_Login in a second global.login call, passing the username, calculated password, and temporary session ID.

If the login is accepted, the camera returns true and a new, authenticated session. This session must be used for all subsequent RPC calls, including the camera’s other endpoints, for example, the one that reboots the device or those that expose sensitive information.

Affected endpoint

The affected endpoint is the firmware upgrade route http://<ip_address>/firmwareUpgrade_service/Demo, which lacks authentication checks; furthermore, it fails to verify whether the firmware is actually valid before initiating the upgrade process. This creates a serious issue because the upgrade requires the camera to reboot, and that is precisely when the problem occurs: the camera enters reboot mode and eventually shuts down, appearing offline to the user and anyone who has the camera registered on their device.

PoC: vulnerability exploitation

Now that we have outlined how the vulnerability works, we will use a Python script on an iM3B-C camera to exploit it for demonstration purposes. The exploit contacts the camera’s endpoint to upload firmware. Below, we can see sonia creating the endpoint responsible for the firmware upgrade.

Next, the exploit will hit the endpoint and cause the camera to reboot. Consequently, mobile phones running the Intelbras app will lose connection with the registered device. Below, we can see the camera operating normally: the green light is on and the app is showing it is available for viewing.

The camera is online

After the exploit executes, we can see the effects: the camera goes offline and loses connection to the registered devices.

The camera is offline

The exploit is quite simple: it sends an HTTP POST request with the firmware, which causes the camera to accept the request and initiate the reboot process. It does not matter whether the firmware is original; the reboot process will start regardless.

New firmware version

After we notified Intelbras about this flaw in the endpoint implementation, the company contacted the OEM vendor. As a result, a new firmware version was released that requires authentication to initiate an update through this endpoint.

Below, we can compare the new firmware, which validates cookies and session data, with the old firmware, which performed no authentication checks and proceeded directly to the update routine.

Real risk

An attacker can remotely trigger the camera firmware upgrade and reboot process without authenticating or supplying a valid firmware image. This may cause the device to go offline, which results in a denial-of-service condition preventing legitimate users from accessing live monitoring or managing the camera.

The potential impact is significant due to the number of affected users. The Intelbras Mibo Smart app, which the company provides to connect and manage the devices mentioned in this report, has over 4,000,000 downloads. Brazil represents the largest user base, followed by Paraguay, Ecuador, Colombia, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Bolivia, Uruguay, and Venezuela. As a result, exploitation of this issue affects a large number of users.

Takeaways

This is a medium-severity vulnerability that Intelbras is already aware of. The issue has been addressed in a newer firmware release (R.260804 along with update instructions), which mitigates this attack vector. Because the vulnerability directly affects the availability and normal operation of the affected cameras, it is highly recommended that users verify the firmware version currently installed on their devices and update to the latest available version as soon as possible. Keeping the firmware up to date is an essential security practice, especially for internet-connected surveillance devices, as outdated versions may remain exposed to known vulnerabilities.

Title: Detecting and mitigating ZDI-CAN-33367 and five other Linux flaws
Context: The vulnerability is a local privilege escalation (LPE), so an attacker needs code execution on the host first
Full Text:
This blog was originally published on October 24, 2026.

As of October 28, there are four important updates to note:

AlmaLinux has shipped a fixed kernel for AlmaLinux 9 (5.14.0-687.60.1.el9_8), which also covers CloudLinux 9. Patched kernels for 8 and 10 were in testing as of Oct 23.

KernelCare’s EL10 rebootless patch shipped on October 23, with EL9 shipped on October 26, and EL8 is ready for release. Debian and Ubuntu work is in progress with no date.

CloudLinux 7 hybrid and 8 fixes are in beta, and the upstream fix has been accepted but has not reached mainline.

The Hacker News lists ZDI-CAN-34076 with a CVSS score of 8.6, we previously did not have this rated.

A working root exploit for a Linux kernel bug is now public, before it has a CVE or a merged fix. On October 20, 2026, Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent one report, a bug in the ConnMan network manager, to the public ConnMan mailing list. On October 21, ZDI sent five reports to the Linux kernel security team and copied public mailing lists on every one. The reports included reproduction details, showing that several had no patch attached and no fix in any released kernel. Two of the Linux flaws have been rated as CVSS 9.0.

None of the six bugs has been assigned a CVE ID yet, and no in-the-wild exploitation has been reported as of the publication of this blog. However, security teams should work to get detections and mitigations in place now. TuxCare has reproduced the public proof of concept (PoC) for ZDI-CAN-33367 from the ZDI report. Exploitation leads to root access on current Ubuntu, Debian, and AlmaLinux distributions.

The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) reviewed the batch of Linux vulnerabilities and ranked the reports by how much each should affect what defenders do today. This report explores what was disclosed, who may be exposed, what runtime visibility can detect for each bug, and what defenders can do while patches are pending.

Timeline

Date

Event

Sept. 30, 2026

ksmbd maintainer Namjae Jeon writes a fix for an SMB1/SMB2 dispatch race, credited to a different reporter

Oct. 20–21, 2026

ZDI sends six reports to the kernel security team with public lists copied

Oct. 21, 2026

The ksmbd fix is committed to the maintainer's ksmbd-for-next branch

Oct. 21, 2026

SMB Direct maintainer Stefan Metzmacher asks the reporter to test his Linux 7.5 branch against ZDI-CAN-33549

Oct. 22, 2026

A v2 patch for skb_zerocopy() (ZDI-CAN-33367) is posted to netdev, reviewed by Eric Dumazet

Affected versions

Exposure risk varies greatly across the reports. One affects the mainstream distributions TuxCare tested, including Ubuntu, Debian, and AlmaLinux releases. Two affect only hosts running ksmbd, the in-kernel SMB server. Another affects only VMware guests.

Organizations should review their inventory before deciding how to prioritize these vulnerabilities.

Report

Component

Impact

Exposure

Fix status (as of Oct 22)

ZDI-CAN-33367

skb_zerocopy()

Local privilege escalation (LPE); public PoC. CVSS 7.8

Hosts that allow unprivileged user namespaces and load the specific networking modules the PoC needs

Patch posted to netdev, not merged

ZDI-CAN-33774

ksmbd protocol dispatch

Remote, pre-authentication; PoC leaks heap / crashes. CVSS 9.0

Hosts running ksmbd

Fixed in the ksmbd maintainer tree, not in mainline

ZDI-CAN-33549

ksmbd SMB Direct

Remote heap overflow; needs RDMA and a writable share. CVSS 9.0

Hosts running ksmbd with SMB Direct, an RDMA interface, and a writable share

Maintainer believes a 7.5-branch fix covers it, unconfirmed

ZDI-CAN-34068

vmwgfx (VMware guests)

LPE. CVSS 8.8

Linux guests on VMware

No patch

ZDI-CAN-34076

Information disclosure

Unknown

ZDI-CAN-32005

ConnMan DNS proxy

Userspace stack overflow, not a kernel bug

Not a kernel-level bug

Out of scope

ZDI-CAN-33367

Fix status

A small patch, “net: skbuff: propagate shared-frag marker in skb_zerocopy()”, is on netdev, reviewed by Eric Dumazet and tagged for stable. It has not been merged.

How the bug works: Dirty Frag again

Earlier this year, Dirty Frag (CVE-2026-43284) showed defenders how an unprivileged user could get the kernel's IPsec ESP code to decrypt in place over pages that belong to the page cache. Those pages back a file the user can only read, and decryption writes the attacker's bytes into the cached copy of that file. Targeting a setuid binary or /etc/passwd this way gives the attacker root without ever opening the file for writing.

The Dirty Frag fix marked those shared pages with a flag and taught ESP to copy before decrypting when it sees the flag. ZDI-CAN-33367 is a gap in that fix.

skb_zerocopy() moves the same pages into a new socket buffer but does not carry the flag across. ESP never sees the flag, decrypts in place, and the write lands in the page cache. According to TuxCare and Safeguard, the code path dates to kernel 3.14.

Not the first gap

The Dirty Frag fix only works if every piece of networking code that moves those pages around carries the flag along. Since May, the kernel's CVE team has published six follow-up CVEs where some other path lost it:

Frag-copy and shift helpers: CVE-2026-43503

Coalescing: CVE-2026-46300

IPTFS: CVE-2026-53363, CVE-2026-64566

An error-handling helper: CVE-2026-80977

Another error path inside skb_zerocopy() itself: CVE-2026-90049

CVE-2026-90049 is a different bug in the same function, so a kernel carrying its fix is not fixed for ZDI-CAN-33367.

Exploitation

The PoC needs unprivileged user namespaces and a handful of networking modules: nlmon, nft_queue, nfnetlink_queue, cls_u32, act_pedit, act_mirred, and esp4. It does not need a Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR) leak, or any capability the user doesn't already get inside their own namespace.

Each step of exploitation is a system call that can be made by an ordinary user process:

Unshare into new user and network namespaces, then write sysctls.

Bring up an nlmon interface.

Install XFRM state over netlink.

Add an nftables NFQUEUE rule.

Attach a tc pedit action with a redirect.

splice() into a socket on 127.0.0.1, which triggers the in-place decryption over the page cache.

Impact

TuxCare reproduced a root shell on AlmaLinux 8–10, CloudLinux 9–10, Debian 12 and 13, and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04. AlmaLinux was rooted with the Dirty Frag fix installed. CentOS 6 and 7 kernels are not vulnerable. The vulnerability is a local privilege escalation (LPE), so an attacker needs code execution on the host first.

ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549

Both CVSS 9.0 reports are in ksmbd, the in-kernel Server Message Block (SMB) server. Samba is not ksmbd.

If your file servers run smbd, neither report applies to you. To check whether ksmbd is running anywhere, look for the ksmbd kernel module, the ksmbd.mountd userspace daemon, and a kernel-owned listener on TCP 445.

ZDI-CAN-33774: The dispatch race

ksmbd decides per request whether it is handling SMB1 or SMB2. If an attacker packs a burst of short SMB1 packets and an SMB2 packet into the same TCP write, the worker threads can run an SMB2 handler over SMB1 data and read past the end of the shorter buffer. This works before authentication. The public PoC leaks 28 bytes of kernel heap per attempt and can crash the kernel. ZDI describes a write-past-buffer path that needs share access and labels the bug as remote code execution (RCE), but nothing public shows code execution as of this blog’s publication.

Maintainer Namjae Jeon says the bug is already fixed, and his tree bears that out. Commit 68f410faedaf ("ksmbd: wait for negotiation before receiving another PDU") was written on September 30, credited to a different reporter, and describes exactly this race. It is queued in ksmbd's ksmbd-for-next branch and has not reached a released kernel.

ZDI-CAN-33549: SMB Direct

An integer underflow in the Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) transport turns a crafted buffer descriptor into a heap overflow of up to eight KB. The bar is higher than for 33774. The host needs an RDMA-capable interface (hardware, or the rxe software driver), a client that negotiates SMB Direct, and a writable share. The public PoC crashes the kernel.

SMB Direct maintainer Stefan Metzmacher believes a fix already in his branch for Linux 7.5 covers it. As of this writing, that hasn't been confirmed. Ubuntu builds SMB Direct support; Debian does not.

ZDI-CAN-34068

ZDI-CAN-34068 is an out-of-bounds write in vmwgfx, the kernel driver for VMware's virtual GPU, rated as LPE (CVSS 8.8). Only the title is public. Kroah-Hartman's reply on dri-devel points to the dirty-tracking code. There is no patch.

The exposure is narrow. vmwgfx only binds to VMware's SVGA virtual display adapter, so the bug only matters on VMware guests: vSphere and Workstation VMs, and VMware-based virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI). In Sysdig TRT testing, it does not reproduce on Lima or EC2 instances, which don't present that device.

ZDI-CAN-34076 and ZDI-CAN-32005

ZDI-CAN-34076 (nvmet) is an uninitialized-memory information leak in the Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target's Get Log Page handling. Only the title is public, and the kernel team has said nothing can be done until details arrive.

ZDI-CAN-32005 (ConnMan) is a stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager's DNS proxy. It is a userspace bug, not a kernel bug, and is outside the scope of this post.

Detection

The four bugs that are the most impactful right now differ in what a syscall-level runtime sensor can observe:

ZDI-CAN-33367. The sequence of the exploitation is distinctive. The process unshares into new user and network namespaces, writes sysctls, brings up an nlmon interface, installs XFRM state over netlink, adds an nftables NFQUEUE rule, attaches a tc pedit action with a redirect, and then splice()s into a socket on 127.0.0.1. Nothing legitimate does all of that from a single unprivileged process. Of the four, this is the easiest one to detect.

ksmbd (33774 and 33549). A sensor can see that ksmbd is exposed: the module loads, ksmbd.mountd starts, and 445 is listening. It can see what an attacker does after code execution, once something spawns a process or touches files. It cannot see the race or the overflow itself. Runtime detection is the backstop.

ZDI-CAN-34068. The trigger is DRM ioctl() calls on the vmwgfx device node, made by a local process. That narrows where to look, but GPU ioctls are noisy on any desktop or VDI guest, so treat them as context for an investigation, not as a signal on their own.

Sysdig Secure customers are covered by a new runtime rule in the Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics policy, Page Cache Poisoning via Spliced File Pages to Loopback, which matches the syscall patterns as seen for ZDI-CAN-33367. Work on exploits for the other flaws in this disclosure continues, and the Sysdig TRT is writing detection rules for them as the techniques become clear.

Independently of the entry point, customers also keep post-exploitation coverage, which detects the effects of a successful exploit rather than the route in.

Recommendations

ZDI-CAN-33367

Patch as soon as your distribution ships the skb_zerocopy() fix. A kernel carrying only the CVE-2026-90049 fix is not covered.

Restrict unprivileged user namespaces. Setting user.max_user_namespaces=0 (or kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 on Debian) should block the public PoC, though TuxCare notes it has not yet validated this against the PoC. The cost is real: rootless containers, some browser sandboxes and some build tooling depend on user namespaces, so scope it to hosts that don't need them.

Avoid relying on Ubuntu's AppArmor user-namespace restriction. The PoC got past it through the AppArmor profile of a container launcher package.

Block the nlmon and act_pedit modules where you can. Denying them breaks this PoC, although TuxCare cautions it may not close every path to the bug.

Enforce seccomp RuntimeDefault on Kubernetes pods. The exploit starts by creating a user namespace, so containers that can call unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER) are in play. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks that call, but Kubernetes pods run Unconfined unless you set RuntimeDefault per pod or cluster-wide using the kubelet --seccomp-default option. This is a good week to make it the cluster default.

ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549

Inventory where ksmbd runs. Samba users are unaffected.

Unload ksmbd and block the module on hosts that don't need it.

Restrict TCP 445 to trusted networks where ksmbd must stay.

Disable SMB Direct unless your storage network depends on RDMA.

ZDI-CAN-34068

Inventory Linux guests running on VMware, and watch for the vmwgfx patch.

Disable 3D acceleration, or keep the vmwgfx module from loading, on guests that have no use for it.

Across all Linux flaws

Track the reports by ZDI ID and component name until CVEs are assigned.

‍

Conclusion

ZDI's decision to copy public lists put reproduction details for six bugs in front of attackers before several of them had fixes. As defenders know, a lack of an assigned CVE ID does not mean a lack of exposure. Only one of the six, ZDI-CAN-33367, combines a public root exploit, broad distribution exposure, and a fix that hasn't yet merged. It is the seventh path found to drop the Dirty Frag flag, reopening a bug class whose protection has already leaked six times since May 2026. The two ksmbd reports carry the highest scores, but they only matter where ksmbd — not Samba — is running.

For defenders, the practical takeaway is that this week's work is about exposure, not scanners. It’s also important to note that the bugs differ in what defenders should actually watch. The ZDI-CAN-33367 exploit runs as an ordinary user process through a distinctive sequence of systems calls, so teams can catch it in motion. The ksmbd bugs run inside the kernel worker threads with no attacker process on the host, so controlling exposure is key.

Affected organizations should immediately restrict unprivileged user namespaces and enforce RuntimeDefault seccomp where they can, find out whether ksmbd is running anywhere in their estate, and patch ZDI-CAN-33367 the day their distribution ships the fix.

Title: CVE-2026-35273: SSRF to RCE in Oracle PeopleSoft
Context: On September 25, 2026, Mandiant released a report regarding continued mass exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 by the ShinyHunters group
Full Text:
On September 25, 2026, Mandiant released a report regarding continued mass exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 by the ShinyHunters group. TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative first reported this CVE to Oracle on June 10, 2026, following an investigation I conducted with Minh Giang and Lucas Miller of TrendAI Research. Although Oracle issued a patch under a single CVE, we reported three distinct vulnerabilities across multiple PeopleSoft components. We are coordinating with Oracle to assign separate CVEs for each issue.

In this blog post, we will walk through each of these vulnerabilities, starting with a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability. We will also review the validateClient method that Oracle introduced to allow PeopleSoft system administrators to restrict access to certain functionality. Spoiler alert: the SSRF allows attackers to make requests that satisfy this validation and access endpoints vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE).

Overview

There are two main components involved here, both served as individual Oracle WebLogic applications.

The first, the PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB), is part of Oracle’s Environment Management Framework. This component implements the validateClient method, ensuring only trusted clients can reach PSEMHUB functionality. Because this is an internal management interface, it makes sense that Oracle would restrict access to its web endpoints. However, this also means it’s a prime target for attackers looking to pivot from their existing, low-privileged access.

The second, the PeopleSoft Integration Gateway (PSIGW), contains functionality for exchanging messages between the PeopleSoft server and remote systems. This is accomplished using a set of Listening and Target Connectors.

One such connector is the HttpListeningConnector, which translates data from inbound HTTP requests into the format supported by the specified Target Connector before routing the request to the desired URL. In this chain, attackers specify the HttpTargetConnector.

The diagram below shows how an attacker like ShinyHunters can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise PeopleSoft systems. Notice that the attacker cannot simply hit the PSEMHUB functionality directly:

Bug 1: PSIGW Server-Side Request Forgery (ZDI-CAN-31816)

Now let’s take a look at how the PSIGW SSRF provides attackers with a foothold in the PeopleSoft application. An example malicious request to PSIGW shows just how powerful this is for an attacker. We control the URL to hit AND the full payload to send!

At [1], the attacker sends a POST request to /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector

At [2], the HttpTargetConnector handler class is specified

At [3], the target is PeopleSoft on the loopback interface at http://127.0.0.1:8000, satisfying the validateClient logic

At [4], the full POST request payload is specified in the Data field, to be forwarded to the target URL at [3]

The HttpTargetConnector handler appears below. Note there is no validation to ensure this traffic is legitimate and bound for a valid target. I've done my best to pull out the important parts of this 800+-line function. If you want a fun side quest, go decompile this for yourself and check it out. I hope you like spaghetti!

At [1], retrieve the target URL from the attacker's request

At [2], create an httpObj using the URL from [1]

At [3], retrieve the HTTP method (POST) and apply it to the httpObj from [2]

At [4], send the content data seen in the Data tag of the network request. This content is sent as-is using the HTTP parameters configured in the httpObj

To fully understand why this SSRF is valuable, here is the validateClient method I mentioned earlier:

At [1] and [2], the validateClient method pulls the hostname and IP of the requesting client

At [3], a file path is built to the /envmetadata/config/allowedhosts.properties file, which contains the list of hosts allowed to access functionality protected by validateClient

At [4], the server checks if the allowedList set contains any entries. The first time this path is hit, the set is empty, so execution continues into the client list refresh block

At [5], that allowedhosts.properties file is read and iterated over

At [6] and [7], each allowed host is added to the allowedList set, including the default localhost entry alongside the server's resolved hostname and IP address

At [8] and [9], if the requesting host is found in the allowedList set, validateClient returns true

We can see the localhost entry in the default allowedhosts.properties that ships with PeopleSoft:

While this solution does restrict access, an attacker on any trusted host can still reach PSEMHUB. Because Oracle allows localhost by default, the PSIGW SSRF provides exactly that access.

Bug 2: PSEMHUB External Control of File Path (ZDI-CAN-31818)

Now that the attacker can make requests to the PSEMHUB endpoints using the PSIGW SSRF, let's see how they can turn that into RCE.

The first path to code execution uses an External Control of File Path vulnerability in the ExecuteProcessActivityCommand handler, which is designed to allow remote clients to write log entries to the PeopleSoft server’s filesystem.

However, callers of the command control both the file contents AND the absolute file path on disk to which that content is written. Here’s an example of the request made to PSEMHUB. Note that, in practice, each parameter value is a form-encoded serialized Java object. For clarity, I’ve decoded and formatted it here:

At [1], we see the request is being made to PSEMHUB’s central routing hub

At [2], note that the request is made to the loopback address 127.0.0.1. Since this request originates from localhost, the validateClient check is satisfied

At [3], the web shell contents are specified in the m_line parameter

At [4], the absolute path where the contents will be written is specified in the m_targetFile parameter

Looking at the handler for this request, we can see that no validation is performed to ensure that m_targetFile points to a legitimate log directory:

By writing this shell to the PSEMHUB WAR path, the attacker achieves immediate remote code execution in the context of the PeopleSoft service account.

Here's how those bugs look when chained together:

Bug 3: PSEMHUB Deserialization of Untrusted Data (ZDI-CAN-31817)

Using any file write primitive (like the ExecuteProcessActivityCommand seen above), an attacker can write a malicious XML file inside the [docroot]/envmetadata/data/environment/ directory. When the PSEMHUB HubServlet class initializes next (after a system or service restart, for example), it triggers a code flow that ultimately deserializes this XML file. Because this vector does not require writing a JSP web shell, it is less likely to be noticed by standard detection methods.

Specifically, on initialization, the PSEMHUB HubServlet class calls startServerPeer in the com.peoplesoft.pt.environmentmanagement.hub.Server class:

At [1], HubMBeanPersistance.getInstance() is called, which triggers the private constructor for that class

At [2], env_dir_path is set to <context_root>/envmetadata/data/environment/, which contains the malicious XML file placed by the attacker

At [3], all files from this folder are loaded into a list variable fl

At [4] and [5], the absolute path for each file in that directory is built

At [6], XMLDecoder is instantiated for each file

At [7], the content of the malicious XML placed by the attacker is deserialized

Java's XMLDecoder instantiates and configures the objects described in the XML during parsing, so the attacker's payload executes before the cast to Environment throws an exception.

Conclusion

The combination of the powerful PSIGW Server-Side Request Forgery primitive alongside the decision to allow access to PSEMHUB via the loopback address by default renders the validateClient protection ineffective. Attackers can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise affected instances of PeopleSoft.

The impact of SSRFs can sometimes be overlooked, especially if they have no standalone information disclosure impact. Under the right circumstances, however, the humble SSRF can open the door for complete compromise.

You can find me on Twitter at @bobbygould5, and follow the team on Twitter, Mastodon, LinkedIn, or Bluesky for the latest in exploit techniques and security patches.

Title: OpenAI Compaction Flaw Exposed AI Reasoning to Researchers
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Researchers have discovered a flaw in OpenAI's application programming interface (API) that allowed them to extract raw reasoning traces from its frontier models, exposing information OpenAI normally withholds from API users.

AI vulnerability discovery firm Xint disclosed the technique, dubbed 'compaction smuggling,' in research published October 26. According to Xint, OpenAI confirmed the issue, deployed a fix on October 23 and paid a $6000 bug bounty.

The flaw involved OpenAI's context compaction feature, which uses a model to compress a lengthy conversation into an encrypted item the user cannot read.

Xint found it could hide one model's reasoning inside a compaction and have another model hand it back.

Compaction Bypass Exposed Hidden Reasoning

OpenAI gives API users optional summaries rather than the raw chain of thought behind its reasoning models' answers. Xint said this is partly to prevent distillation, because raw reasoning, which shows abandoned approaches and corrections, makes much richer training data than final answers.

OpenAI added mitigations in August after the Stolen Thoughts paper showed that a frontier model's encrypted reasoning could be fed to a less capable model from the same company, an attack that affected Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.

Xint said those mitigations stopped reasoning being replayed into other models but did not cover compaction, which ran on the model that had produced the reasoning.

Xint generated reasoning with GPT-5.6 Sol, compacted it and asked the older GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o models to repeat their input word for word, from which it recovered the reasoning. It said the attack succeeded at every reasoning-effort setting it tested.

Read more: OpenCode Breach Could Affect OpenAI, Anthropic and Google

Compaction and Distillation Concerns Remain

The flaw was discovered by Xint in August and OpenAI's fix was not publicly described. The Xint post did not include a statement from OpenAI. Infosecurity has contacted OpenAI for comment.

Compaction has raised separate concerns for OpenAI and in a September report the company said that during training of an internal, unreleased model, the model had in rare cases written unauthorized instructions into its own compaction summaries, including one instructing the model to ignore developer messages.

Xint argued that the technique opened the door to distilling OpenAI's frontier models at scale, though it did not report training a model on the reasoning it extracted. It said the risk was real, citing an Anthropic report in September of seven distillation campaigns it attributed to China-based labs and OpenAI's September 30 disclosure that it had broken up an effort to pull hidden reasoning from its models.

Title: PHP2Shell: Exploitation Attempts and Remediation Trends
Context: When only one worker was available the exploit attempted heap-shaping by sending requests containing 1,001 fields of 3,000 bytes each
Full Text:
Last week, we published a report describing two major vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619). Since then, alongside much of the security industry, the Wiz Research team has been monitoring for related activity in the wild and reviewing publicly available exploit code. So far, we have observed a limited number of exploitation attempts in our telemetry and have not identified a publicly available proof of concept (PoC) demonstrating complete, general end-to-end exploitation against an arbitrary target. Some partners have, however, privately disclosed to us exploits that work against a variety of targets and we continue to experiment internally. Videos demonstrating our successful exploitations are available at php2shell.com.

This post summarizes what we have observed in terms of remediation efforts and exploitation attempts across real world environments and in our own honeypot data to date and shares findings from our ongoing investigation into these activities.

We will continue monitoring developments and update this post as new evidence emerges.

Observed exposure trends

Following PHP2Shell’s public disclosure on October 21, 2026, Wiz telemetry has recorded an approximate 67% decrease in the daily number of distinct Internet-exposed machines vulnerable to PHP2Shell over the past few days. Separately, among vulnerable Internet-exposed machines, the proportion running PHP version 7.3 or earlier fell from 8.3% to 5.7% over a period of five days. This measures the share of the observed population running older versions that did not receive official backports.

During this period, the number of significantly affected organizations - defined here as those with at least one exposed and vulnerable instance - fell by approximately 47.9% (see graph below). For reference, our data shows that PHP itself is in use by 65% of organizations in our dataset.

Together, these observations are consistent with organizations collectively reducing their exposure through a combination of patching, upgrading, retiring affected machines and restricting internet access (note that this data shows the overall trend, but does not establish the relative contribution of each remediation strategy; scan coverage and size of observed population can also affect the overall reported numbers over time).

Exploitation attempts observed by Wiz research

We have so far observed the following types of activities in this context:

Attempts using the PHP2Shell exploit mechanism, with techniques matching those of public PoCs.

PHP2Shell-branded tools unrelated to the vulnerabilities that instead relied on session poisoning and a separate local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerability in the application.

Attempts using the PHP2Shell exploit mechanism

We observed two variants of an open source exploit kit targeting PHP-based software. Neither completed the exploit chain in the attempts we captured. The older variant encountered request-size limits or failed to produce the expected memory-exhaustion condition. The newer variant did consistently exhaust PHP’s memory, but failed to obtain the memory addresses needed to continue.

Variant 1: the legacy chain

The first request to our PHP-CGI honeypot came from 3.37.227[.]134. It matched the kit’s older chain, found under archive/legacy-8m/exploit.py and its accompanying stage scripts. The first full exploit stage used a multipart body containing 1,005 parts, including a field named big filled with approximately 12 MB of padding:

POST / HTTP/1.1 Host: <honeypot> Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=SSSSSSSSSSSSSSSSS Content-Length: 12655437 [1,005 parts] 1001 x p0000 = "x" 1 x PHPSESSID = "\x00" 1 x PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS = "pwn" 1 x f (file) = "A" x 64 1 x big = "B" x ~12 MB

According to the kit’s notes, this stage attempts to exhaust memory during a session reset, leaving the session state available for a later request.

On our honeypot, it failed before reaching that code. The declared request size exceeded the configured 8 MB post_max_size limit, so PHP skipped processing the multipart body and logged:

POST Content-Length of 12655437 bytes exceeds the limit of 8388608 bytes

The author has since moved this chain into the kit’s archive directory.

A later attempt against Roundcube

In a later attempt, 103.151.172[.]95 sent a longer sequence from the legacy chain. It included stalled connections intended to occupy other Apache workers.

When only one worker was available the exploit attempted heap-shaping by sending requests containing 1,001 fields of 3,000 bytes each. These requests didn’t trigger the memory exhaustion flow required. So there is no evidence that this attempt reached the intended memory-exhaustion condition.

Variant 2: the current chain

Most IP addresses we captured used the newer chain, built from pure/mk_a1.py and pure/mk_leak_b.py. We observed this variant in multiple attempts.

This variant progressed further: its first stage consistently caused PHP to exhaust its memory. The following stage, which attempts to leak process memory, failed in every run we captured.

The server logged a fatal error indicating that PHP reached its limit, for example:

Allowed memory size of 134217728 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 81920 bytes) in Unknown on line 0.

Keeping requests on the same worker

The chain depends on consecutive exploit requests reaching the same Apache child process. To increase the chances of that happening, the kit attempts to occupy the other workers with incomplete requests. Each connection declares a large body, sends a single byte and stalls:

POST /index.php HTTP/1.1 Host: <honeypot> Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded Content-Length: 1048576 x

One address, 178.249.214[.]6, opened 399 of these connections alongside 400 GET requests before sending the exploit stages. The address is a VPN exit node, which limits what we can infer about the source.

Stage A1: triggering memory exhaustion

A1 is a chunked multipart request containing a null-byte session ID, 860 empty file parts with long, deeply nested array names and several groups of padding fields:

POST /?q0=v&q1=v&q2=v&q3=v&q4=v HTTP/1.1

Host: <honeypot> Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=CCCCCCCCCC Transfer-Encoding: chunked [1,060,211 bytes, 974 parts] 1 x PHPSESSID = "\x00" 860 x files[R00000KKKK...][a][a]... (file, empty) 14 x f0000xxxx... = "vvvvvvvv" 78 x b0000 = "B" x 8000 20 x u00 = "U" x 4000 1 x PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS = "k" x 4000

The request is designed to exhaust memory during session handling at a point that can leave the session ID pointing to freed memory.

Every A1 request we captured returned HTTP 500, accompanied by a PHP error matching:

Allowed memory size of 67108864 bytes exhausted ... in Unknown on line 0

This confirms that A1 reached the intended memory-exhaustion condition on our honeypot. It does not, by itself, confirm that the stale session state needed by the next stage was preserved.

Stage B1: attempting the memory leak

B1 followed roughly a second later. It sent another chunked multipart request containing PHPSESSID=a, PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS=k0and two large padding fields.

If this request reaches the same worker before PHP resets the stale session state, PHP can write reclaimed heap contents into a PHPSESSID response cookie. The kit then extracts heap and libphp addresses from that cookie to prepare the final exploit stage.

We observed no such leak. In all but one run, the connection closed without a response. The remaining run returned a normal 32-character session cookie. None of the sources sent the final exploit stage.

Why the leaks may have failed

The failed leaks highlight a broader challenge: building a generalized exploit that works reliably across PHP versions and deployment configurations is difficult. The kit’s B1 layout was calculated for the official php:8.4.26-apache image with a 128 MB memory limit. Other instances like our Roundcube honeypot ran the same PHP version from a different build, with additional extensions and a 64 MB memory limit. These differences can affect heap layout and memory reuse, potentially preventing the leak from working as expected.

Reliable worker pinning adds another challenge. Consecutive exploit requests must reach the same Apache child process while the required session state persists. Request timeouts, network latency and worker availability can disrupt this sequence. In our own testing, request timeouts combined with network latency were enough to prevent the chain from completing over an internet connection.

So far, we have not identified a publicly available, generalized solution for either worker pinning or information leaking across different deployments. Simply copying public PoCs and running them at scale does not address the work needed to turn a configuration-specific exploit into a reliable operational kit. We expect these barriers to diminish over time: some threat actors have the expertise needed to adapt the chain and build more robust tooling.

Other attempts

We also saw failed exploitation attempts from 15.204.59[.]70 and 162.35.99[.]94, but these scanners did successfully exploit Adel Karimi's honeypot, which was a likely contributing factor to CISA’s decision to include PHP2Shell in their KEV list.

PHP2Shell-branded tools unrelated to the vulnerabilities

We also observed tools labeled as PHP2Shell exploits that did not actually attempt to exploit either vulnerability. The earliest such traffic, from 85.11.187[.]35, matched a Go port of “Chain A” from WoYinDao/CVE-2026-109618-CVSS-9.2-Critical.

The tool used a longstanding session-poisoning technique, attempting to write PHP code into a session file through the upload-progress feature. The request below is abbreviated:

POST /index.php HTTP/1.1 Host: <honeypot> User-Agent: Go-http-client/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----php2shell-golang PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS = <?php echo "PHP2SHELL_XBu4Je"; system($_GET["c"]); ?> PHPSESSID = <attacker-chosen ID> f (file) = "Z"

It then attempted to execute that code by including the session file:

GET /lfi_sink.php?c=id&f=/tmp/sess_SUjKIKy3Rr6QsaJ1Ik7Rme8h3n HTTP/1.1

Crucially, lfi_sink.php is a vulnerable endpoint supplied by the PoC’s lab environment. The tool assumes that this endpoint exists on the target; without it or an equivalent local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerability, the chain cannot execute code.

A padded variant triggered our memory-exhaustion detection, but we observed no successful code execution. Despite the PHP2Shell branding, this activity relied on an unrelated technique and a vulnerable application endpoint.

Conclusion

We have not yet observed successful end-to-end PHP2Shell exploitation in our own telemetry. However, Adel Karimi’s public report and supporting data provide the most robust public evidence we have seen to date, correlating exploit traffic, memory disclosure and subsequent code execution on his honeypots. Notably, those targets used a favorable single-worker Apache mod_php configuration, so the findings do not establish reliability across other deployments.

Our observations show that triggering memory exhaustion alone is not enough to complete the exploit chain. Differences in PHP builds, memory limits and worker behavior can prevent subsequent stages from working. The challenge for opportunistic attackers is turning currently available public PoCs into similarly reliable operational tooling or developing it on their own. In our view, PHP2Shell remains a risk in both the short and long term and applying the PHP security updates or remediating through other means therefore remains essential.
