AhsayCBS.jsp

Loader for an encrypted payload hidden in a PNG, described below.

The folder locations where we found these webshells gave us further insight into how the attack might vary across operating systems. The impacted servers here ran Windows: however, the exploit also attempted Linux-style installation paths, suggesting the exploit was not tailored to one operating system.

In addition to webapps\cbs and webapps\rps in the real install, we found copies in directories matching Linux-style paths, including /opt/AhsayCBS, /usr/local/AhsayCBS, and /home/ahsay/AhsayCBS. On one of the affected Windows servers, these appeared as folders under C:\opt, C:\usr, and C:\home, with a staging folder, C:\ahsay_tf, holding another copy. That suggests the exploit was not designed for a specific operating system or install path, and simply tried every likely location.

The copies outside the live install were not served by the web application, so they probably cannot be used as shells on Windows, but they are a reliable tell. Several shells also sat in random six-character folders, each containing its own app, conf, and webapps\cbs subfolders. These imitate the structure of an AhsayCBS install, but none of the components are part of the real application. Some of those folders held empty pb_ marker files in the conf folder, and folders named ahsay_poc_*, ahsay_tf, ahsay_th and ahsay_t0 showed up in Program Files.

Figure 2: Shell locations on a Windows host: the live install, and the Linux-style paths the exploit also tries

A webshell that hides inside an image

One of the webshell families, AhsayCBS.jsp (in webapps\rps), was disguised as an image-preview service: it was designed to extract encrypted code from uploaded PNGs and run it in memory while making its traffic resemble ordinary image requests.

The webshell's disguise as an internal image preview service even extended down to a comment block describing a watermark endpoint. The webshell used only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, meaning it would compile on any servlet container and on Java Development Kit (JDK) 6 and later.

On the sample we saw, the webshell was designed to work as follows:

First, the operator POSTs a PNG.

Then the page reads the least-significant bit of each pixel's red, green and blue values, one pixel at a time.

It strings those bits together and packs them into bytes, with the first bit read becoming the most significant bit of each byte.

That rebuilds a four-byte big-endian length followed by that many bytes of payload, which it then decrypts with AES.

The key is hardcoded, and the cipher is Java's default AES transformation (translating to ECB mode with PKCS5 padding).

On the first request, the decrypted bytes are loaded as a Java class through a small custom ClassLoader and stored in the application context under the attribute name QuCh, and the page answers with its built-in cover image. On later requests, it creates an instance of that class, hands it the request, an output buffer and the decrypted data through calls to equals(), and calls toString() to run it. Whatever the class produces is encrypted again and written into a new PNG.

Passing arguments through equals() is a convention used by some open-source in-memory webshell frameworks, though we have not tied this one to a specific framework. The practical effect is that the functionality arrives per request and lives in memory. The access log showed what looked like image traffic, and there was no c or p parameter to search for. We analyzed the loader, not the class it receives, so we cannot confirm what the operator actually ran through it.

Figure 3: How AhsayCBS.jsp turns an uploaded image into running code

A webshell with a signed API

Not every shell was a one-liner. nsmind.jsp, also in webapps\rps, behaved like a small remote administration service.

In the sample we saw, every request must carry an X-Auth-Token header that matches a hardcoded API key, plus X-Timestamp, X-Nonce and an X-Signature header holding an HMAC-SHA256 of the request parameters. The timestamp has to be within five minutes of the server's clock, and each nonce is stored in the application context so a captured request cannot be replayed. A request that fails any check gets a short JSON error, so the page behaves like an ordinary API that rejects unauthenticated callers.

Behind the checks, the action parameter selects exec, cd, upload or download. exec runs the command through cmd.exe /c (after chcp 65001, so output comes back as UTF-8) and tracks the working directory between calls, so the operator gets a persistent shell. upload and download move files in chunks using an offset parameter, with a limit of 4 GB per file, which means a large file can be pulled off the server through many small requests.

On a server that holds backups, this download action is the part to worry about: it is a ready-made exfiltration channel that looks like normal API traffic. We did not see logs showing download in use, so we cannot say what, if anything, was taken.

The files also showed the operator iterating. In the same rps folder we found three timestamp-named folders, each holding a single copy of a shell. The oldest held the simple cmd, del and rm shell described above, and the two newer ones contained nsmind.jsp, which suggested the operator upgraded from a basic shell to this tool. We also found byte-identical copies of nsmind.jsp and AhsayCBS.jsp on two of the servers, which pointed to one operator or one script working across hosts.

A second miner, with its own persistence

The Edge-themed miner analyzed in our initial blog was not the only one: we also found another miner in our follow-up investigation.

The XMRig miner we observed (kvm-agent.exe) is configured like a standard XMRig build: donate level 0, MSR access enabled (the same capability the WinRing0 driver in the first post provides), and TLS connections on port 443 to SupportXMR pools. The wallet and password differed from the Kryptex pool and user listed in the first post, making us believe this was a separate miner and not a second copy of the first. We found the same file, with the same hash, on two servers, and the task on both was created the same night and edited within seconds of each other, which again points to one operator or one script working across hosts.

During our analysis, we found a scheduled task named kvm running as SYSTEM every minute. Its command used a tasklist to check whether kvm-agent.exe was running and, if it wasn't, it would start it from C:\Windows\SysWOW64\kvm-agent. This means that if the miner was killed, it would be back up and running within a minute. The task's start time was set well before the intrusion (making it look older than it was in task listings).

Figure 4: The kvm scheduled task (start time elided)

A Python implant that only runs where it was staged

The most interesting file we pulled was main.py, which sits in an embedded Python distribution under the SYSTEM profile and is started from a Run key through explorer.exe. The script is only a wrapper: Base64, then lzma, then a marshaled Python code object that it passes to exec. Decoding it without running it shows that the code was compiled from a file called heap_shellcode_runner_bound_weaponized.py.

The code computes the SHA-256 of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a file with that name next to main.py. Based on the bytecode, if the marker file is missing, the script exits. That would keep the implant from running in a sandbox or on an analyst's machine, because the marker only exists on the host it was provisioned for. We did not find a marker file in the folder we collected, so either it was not part of what we pulled or it was removed. If the marker is present, the script copies a 673 KB blob into an executable heap (HeapCreate, HeapAlloc, RtlMoveMemory) and starts it on a new thread with CreateThread.

Figure 5: The implant's execution flow, reconstructed from static analysis

Figure 6: The decoded logic, reconstructed from the code object

The blob starts with a short bootstrap that calls a reflective loader at the end of the blob, which in turn maps an x64 DLL carried inside it. The DLL is C++ with a JSON library and imports very little: bcrypt, KERNEL32, OLEAUT32 and SHLWAPI, with the networking functions resolved at run time. It has no export table, no PDB path and no version resource, so the usual attribution breadcrumbs have been stripped.

Its strings include the C2 URL hxxps://creepexplosiondarknight[.]com/d, a JSON content type, a mutex, and string fragments (dns.quad with 9.net, and dns.goog) consistent with DNS-over-HTTPS lookups through Quad9 and Google. It also reads MachineGuid and Windows version information, which fits host identification. We have not identified the malware family and have not watched the implant run, so what it does after it checks in is still an open question.

Figure 7: Selected strings from the embedded DLL (C2 defanged)

The rest of the toolkit

Around those pieces, the same environment held the tunneling tools gost and chisel, staged in .st<id> folders as wust<id>a.exe and wust<id>b.exe, the remote access tools AnyDesk, Atera and Splashtop, a local account named wdguest, and a Mimikatz package on disk. We also saw Microsoft Defender exclusions that covered C:\ProgramData, C:\Windows, temp folders, the dropper processes, and the AhsayCBS service process (cbssvcX64.exe). These exclusions would have reduced Defender's ability to scan files in those locations and files accessed by the excluded processes, creating broad blind spots for the operator's tooling.

Backup servers as a target

Everything above ran on servers whose purpose is to hold or manage backups. On a related Veeam server in the same environment, we also saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module: a PowerShell script, apparently launched remotely through WMI, that queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database for stored credentials and decrypted them with DPAPI. Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts. We cannot say how many of those credentials were retrieved, but the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query suggested the operator was interested in backup infrastructure on purpose, not by accident.

What to check for

Patching closes the entry point. It does not clean up what already happened, so on any server that was exposed before the hotfix, look for:

Unexpected .jsp files under webapps\cbs and webapps\rps, especially random names and the status_ and st_ patterns, and requests to UpdateReceivers.do in the AhsayCBS access logs

Folders named ahsay_*, home, opt, srv or usr at the root of the drive or in Program Files, and timestamp-named folders (year-month-day-hour-minute-second) next to the shells, which in some cases held a single copy of one

Scheduled tasks and services you did not create, including a SYSTEM task with a one-minute repeat that tests for a process with tasklist

Defender exclusions you did not add, especially for C:\ProgramData, C:\Windows and the AhsayCBS service process

An embedded Python install under the SYSTEM profile and a Run key that launches it

A few behaviors make useful detections even when the files are gone:

python.exe or pythonw.exe running from a path under the SYSTEM profile

Outbound requests to public DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers from a process that is not a browser

New .jsp files created under the AhsayCBS web directories

The parent-child pattern our earlier Sigma rule already looks for, where cbssvcX64.exe spawns a command shell.

If you find any of the above, we recommend a full re-image from a trusted backup and rotating credentials stored on or reachable from the server, including those saved in AhsayCBS and in any backup software on the same network.

Title: The Expanding Attack Surface Demands a New Operating Model
Context: Yet only a small percentage were patched during the critical first hours after disclosure
Full Text:
Why the Risk Operations Center Is Becoming the System of Record for Proactive Enterprise Risk Reduction

The cybersecurity industry has spent years improving how we discover vulnerabilities. The challenge now is no longer finding risk. It is reducing risk faster than adversaries can exploit it.

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities disclosed in October are a reminder of how quickly exposure can become exploitation. Within hours of disclosure, attack activity was already being observed. Across more than 10,000 customer environments, the Qualys Threat Research Unit identified more than 166 million PHP installations, approximately three-quarters of them internet-facing. Yet only a small percentage were patched during the critical first hours after disclosure.

This trend is only accelerating. Frontier AI is reducing the time and effort required for reconnaissance, vulnerability analysis, attack planning, and exploitation. The gap between disclosure and weaponization continues to compress, placing increasing pressure on defenders to prioritize and remediate risk at machine speed.

At the same time, the enterprise attack surface has fundamentally changed.

Risk is no longer concentrated in servers, laptops, and cloud workloads. It now extends into mobile devices, medical technology, healthcare environments, manufacturing operations, operational technology, connected devices, and other cyber-physical systems. Many of these assets support an organization’s most critical functions. They help deliver patient care, keep production lines running, support transportation networks, and operate critical infrastructure. Mobile devices have become equally important, providing access to corporate data, business applications, sensitive communications, and some of an organization’s most valuable information.

Yet these environments are often managed separately, with different teams, tools, workflows, and severity models. Attackers do not see those boundaries. They see a single attack surface.

That is why the Risk Operations Center matters.

The Risk Operations Center was never intended to be another dashboard, nor was it intended to replace the SOC. It is an operating model for continuously identifying, prioritizing, validating, and reducing risk across the enterprise before those vulnerabilities can ever be exploited. To fulfill that mission, the ROC must extend beyond traditional IT assets.

As attack surfaces expand and threats accelerate, organizations need more than visibility. They need a way to bring together technology, telemetry, and expertise into a single operating model capable of operationalizing cyber risk management at scale.

That is the vision behind the expanded Global mROC Alliance.

By bringing together the Qualys platform, specialized technology alliance partners, and a global ecosystem of highly trained Risk Operations Center experts, the Global mROC Alliance helps organizations move from identifying risk to systematically reducing it across the enterprise. The goal is not simply to see more risk. It is to help customers outpace increasingly sophisticated threats in the age of AI.

As part of that effort, Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management (ETM) now integrates telemetry from Lookout and NowSecure for mobile security, and from Claroty and Nozomi Networks for OT, IoT, healthcare, and cyber-physical environments.

This expands visibility into some of the least measured yet most consequential areas of enterprise risk.

More importantly, it creates a common operational model for reducing risk. Qualys ETM and TruRisk provide the visibility to understand exposure, the prioritization to focus on what matters most, and the remediation guidance needed to drive measurable risk reduction across the attack surface.

The objective is not simply broader visibility. The objective is better prioritization and faster risk reduction.

When a vulnerable mobile device, an exposed medical system, an industrial controller, and an internet-facing application are all evaluated through the same framework, security teams can focus on reducing the risks that have the greatest potential impact on the business rather than simply responding to the loudest alerts.

For mobile environments, that means bringing device posture, application risk, operating system vulnerabilities, and threat telemetry into the same risk conversation as cloud, endpoint, and infrastructure exposure. A compromised mobile device with privileged access may represent greater business risk than dozens of lower-priority infrastructure findings.

For healthcare, manufacturing, OT, and cyber-physical environments, it means incorporating risks that have traditionally existed outside mainstream security operations. Through Claroty and Nozomi Networks, organizations gain visibility into environments where operational continuity is paramount and active scanning may not be feasible. Just as importantly, those risks can now be prioritized and managed through the same remediation workflow as the rest of the enterprise. Where patching is not possible, compensating controls such as segmentation and access restrictions become part of the same risk reduction process.

This is the power of Qualys’ Global mROC Alliance.

Technology alliance partners contribute deep visibility into the environments they know best. Qualys ETM and TruRisk transform that telemetry into a common risk language through visibility, prioritization, and remediation. mROC Alliance partners help customers operationalize those insights through advisory services, implementation, managed risk reduction programs, and fully managed Risk Operations Center services.

Together, they provide organizations with a practical path to reducing risk across the entire attack surface, not just the portion that has historically been easiest to measure.

Find out more about the Global mROC Alliance.

Learn More

PHP2Shell is not the story.

PHP2Shell was just the opening act. The real story is that the time between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation continues to shrink while the attack surface continues to expand.

Organizations can no longer afford separate programs for IT, mobile, healthcare, OT, IoT, and cyber-physical risk. They need a common operating model, a common language for prioritization, and a single system for driving remediation.

The organizations that succeed will not be those that discover the most vulnerabilities. They will be those that reduce the most risk in the shortest amount of time.

That is the purpose of the Risk Operations Center.

And that is why the Risk Operations Center is emerging as the operating system for proactive cyber risk reduction in the age of AI.

Title: Email Addresses of 2.2 Million Sega Customers Leaked in Vendor Breach
Context: Sega has revealed that around 2
Full Text:
Sega has revealed that around 2.2 million customer email addresses have been exposed as result of a third-party incident.

The video gaming giant revealed on November 9 that an unauthorized third party leaked the email addresses after gaining access to Arara Inc., a Japanese email delivery provider used by Sega to distribute its email newsletter.

“We deeply apologize for the great inconvenience and concern caused to our customers and all parties involved,” Sega wrote.

“Currently, Arara is working to identify the causes of unauthorized access and prevent further damage, and we are working with Arara and related companies to confirm the details of the leaked information.”

The Japanese firm said the breach is limited to 2.196 million email addresses for various email newsletters, and 92,273 items related to distribution.

The leaked information does not include customer names, dates of birth, genders, addresses, phone numbers, credit card information or login passwords.

No misuse of the leaked data has been currently confirmed. However, Sega has warned customers to be vigilant for suspicious emails purporting to be from Sega or Sega Fave Corporation, or using product or service names operated by both companies.

Sega Fave is a subsidiary of the broader Sega group, which focuses on the production of toys and arcade machines.

“Please do not open or reply to URLs or attachments provided in emails you do not recognize. Accessing URLs or opening attached files may lead to entering personal information or affecting your device. Neither our company nor Sega Fave will ask you for your password or credit card information by email. If you receive such an email, do not access the reply or the provided link; delete it,” the company said.

Sega Breach Part of Large-Scale Third-Party Incident

Arara revealed it had been compromised in a statement issued on October 29, which said that unauthorized access was gained to certain server systems of its email distribution service a day earlier, on October 28 after a hacker exploited vulnerabilities in web servers.

The distribution service ‘Arara Message’ was suspended on October 31 and remains offline at the time of writing, according to a dedicated incident page set up by the firm to provide updates.

According to a report by The Japan Times, Arara’s parent company Paycloud Holdings confirmed on November 2 that hackers gained unauthorized access to servers operated by the subsidiary, which exposed information held by around 380 corporate clients using the service. This included 77 million email addresses.

Paycloud also noted that depending on the company, the breached data also included names, telephone numbers and addresses. However, it said that no credit card details have been exposed.

Title: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Targeted in Reported $133m Heist
Context: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa issued a statement on November 4 confirming that it had been a victim “of an attack that enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out
Full Text:
A leading French banking group has moved to reassure customers that their funds are safe after reports emerged of a $133m heist.

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa issued a statement on November 4 confirming that it had been a victim “of an attack that enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out.”

The hackers reached the bank’s network via the platform of a service provider, it added in an FAQ on the incident.

“The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account to make transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialized platforms,” it said.

“They did not, therefore, use customer accounts belonging to its federations or subsidiaries. We have communicated that this incident has no financial consequences for our customers. As soon as this attack was identified, our teams immediately activated the necessary security measures to contain the incident and prevent any further fraudulent activity against us.”

Read more on big-money heists: Brazilian Fintech Giant Sinqia Reveals $130m Heist Attempt

Suspicious Withdrawals Traced Across Multiple Exchanges

The incident first came to light on November 2 when blockchain investigator, “ZachXBT,” claimed in a Telegram post that an unnamed “EU entity” had lost $106m from “multiple centralized exchange accounts.”

ZachXBT ruled out the involvement of notorious North Korean hackers the Lazarus Group.

“Over the past 24 hours the illicit actor has been aggressively swapping USDC for ETH, transferring to instant exchanges (WellWallet, Kyrrex, etc), converting to XMR via Wagyu, and bridging across multiple chains,” they explained.

The investigator posted an updated the day after claiming to have spotted an additional $27m of fraudulent centralized exchange account (CEX) withdrawals.

“My working theory is a large financial institution in Western Europe was exploited and it’s currently being covered up,” they said. “No proper incident disclosure has resulted in $30m+ being laundered away which could have been frozen by EU law enforcement.”

However, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa noted in its FAQ that it was “still too early” to say for sure how much was taken.

“Our teams are continuing their work to precisely assess the financial consequences of this attack: some of the funds involved have been frozen, and other actions are underway to recover them,” it said.

“We can already confirm that the amounts involved are in no way likely to jeopardize the financial health and stability of Crédit Mutuel Arkéa.”

The bank urged customers to be on the lookout for potential phishing attempts in the aftermath of the incident and resulting publicity.

The news comes just days after North Korean hackers stole an estimated $6.3bn from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, in what has been described as the biggest theft of its kind ever seen.

Title: LNbits Urges All Operators to Shut Down Their Bitcoin Lightning Wallet Servers Amid Attacks
Context: The attack ran from 09:22 to 14:00 UTC yesterday, starting more than three hours before the project's first warning at 12:33 UTC
Full Text:
Everyone running LNbits, a free, open-source Bitcoin Lightning wallet system, should shut down their servers now because of a wave of attacks, the project said yesterday.

It has several security fixes to release and asked operators to be careful until they are out. One operator said new accounts used an exploit to withdraw 2,285,545 satoshis, about 0.023 bitcoin, from his server before he could stop it.

The shutdown notice came about 80 minutes after a first, narrower warning. That warning asked operators to disable Paywall, an add-on that makes people pay to view content, while the project looked into a possible bug.

As of 09:00 UTC today, the project had not released a fixed version. On X, it had not canceled the notice, offered another option, or told operators how to check whether their servers were hit before they were shut down.

Ben Arc, an LNbits developer, said in a patch estimate yesterday that patches "should be merged and available within 24-48hrs." Counted from his post, that means between about 14:00 UTC today and 14:00 UTC tomorrow.

The project also switched off all the LNbits instances it runs for users on its cloud service, my.lnbits.com, later yesterday. It said in a hosted-service notice that all services would be back within 24 hours, or by about 17:20 UTC today.

Kevin Ravensberg, the operator who reported the loss, said in a loss report on X that his server was exploited before the shutdown notice. The attack ran from 09:22 to 14:00 UTC yesterday, starting more than three hours before the project's first warning at 12:33 UTC.

He has promised to repay users of BitTipBot, a Telegram bot. They cannot reach their funds until the project fixes the flaws.

Later yesterday, Ravensberg said in a follow-up post that Arc and a team of security testers had confirmed "which exact extension exploit was used" on his server. Neither he nor the project had named that extension in posts on X as of 09:00 UTC today. The project also had not said whether it is Paywall, the add-on named in its first warning.

The shutdown notice covers LNbits servers and does not mention Lightning nodes or other wallet software. It did not say how many servers were attacked or how much was taken.

Title: Anti-Money Laundering Watchdog FATF Targets Scam Compounds
Context: Often staffed by trafficked victims, 120,000 of whom are forced to carry out online scams in Myanmar alone, these operations are also supported by crypto and instant payment...
Full Text:
A leading anti-money laundering (AML) organization has called for global action to disrupt the scam compounds responsible for a considerable volume of transnational fraud.

AML watchdog the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) warned in a new report that large physical scam compounds are a major driver of a global fraud economy estimated to be worth $500bn annually.

Often staffed by trafficked victims, 120,000 of whom are forced to carry out online scams in Myanmar alone, these operations are also supported by crypto and instant payment platforms, money mules, social media, messaging services and AI-enabled content, FATF said.

The trend is increasingly one of smaller and more mobile operations, with compounds created out of repurposed casinos, rented rooms, apartments, coffee shops and even moving vehicles, the report warned.

Read more on scam compounds: Scam Centers Expand Global Footprint with Trafficked Victims

The FATF report noted that countries are generally better at tackling scam compounds through downstream action such as asset tracing and targeting victim payments.

But it called on FATF member nations to combine these efforts with upstream disruption targeting things like fraudulent advertising, recruitment activity, malicious domains and suspicious phone numbers and telecom indicators,

“With criminals weaponizing AI and other technologies to intensify their scam operations, we need to urgently modernize and accelerate our response,” argued FATF president, Giles Thomson. “This means focusing on dismantling the criminal networks behind scam compounds, working proactively with technology, social media and communications sectors to prevent and disrupt more scams before they happen, and quicker intervention to freeze and seize the proceeds of scams once they’ve happened.”

Six Principles to Combat Illicit Money Flows

With this in mind, the FATF report promoted six pillars to its approach:

Shift the focus from physical compounds to criminal leaders, recruiters and traffickers, and other supporting players

Disrupt the infrastructure and services, including stopping, tracing, freezing and recovering victim payments

Share information between financial institutions, technology companies, telcos and authorities

Act at speed across borders, as the first 24-72 hours after a scam are critical for freezing funds and recovering assets

Ensure investigations put the protection of trafficked and scam victims front and center

Continuously update approaches as scam operations decentralize and adapt

Jonathan Frost, director of global advisory at BioCatch, welcomed the focus on compounds and the need for action by platform providers.

“Those platforms need to act on what they can already see. But when push comes to shove, banks are often the last and sometimes the only line of defense,” he added. “Funds can leave an account in minutes, and customers are often groomed into trusting the scammer over their bank. Banks must detect the manipulation itself, not just the transaction, and intervene before the money moves.”

A CybSafe report published last month found that over a fifth (22%) of Brits have received a scam call impersonating a familiar person’s voice or appearance. Over a third (36%) of these reports have led to their employer losing money or data.

Title: Taiwan-Based Hacker Used BOSSAI AI Agents to Steal Taipei Emergency Dispatch Records
Context: A single attacker using AI agents pulled emergency dispatch records covering seven Taipei districts, researchers at Acronis's Threat Research Unit said last week
Full Text:
A single attacker using AI agents pulled emergency dispatch records covering seven Taipei districts, researchers at Acronis's Threat Research Unit said last week.

The agents also found a Taipei fire department platform exposing patient data from 2018, including ECG readings and ambulance video footage, without a login.

The researchers are highly confident that the attacker is a single person based in Hualien City, Taiwan. He aimed the agents at hundreds of organizations in at least 11 countries, including emergency services, banks, universities and military systems. The agents collected data or accessed systems at about 10 of them in Taiwan, Mexico and Thailand.

The evidence comes from the attacker's own server, which initially appeared to be a misconfigured development system. It turned out to be his operational attack platform, containing more than 90,000 files, including the agents' conversations, his command history, hacking tools, credentials, and victims' data.

The agents did not communicate with each other, so the attacker manually pasted one agent's output into another. Commercial AI models mostly refused to help him attack. The attacking agents therefore ran almost entirely on "abliterated" models, meaning AI models run locally with their safety training removed.

What the Agents Reached

Taiwan was targeted far more heavily than any other country, according to the researchers' technical analysis. The most serious confirmed harm there involved emergency-services data.

The dispatch records came from a city's system for 119, Taiwan's emergency number for fire and ambulance services. The agents pulled them from the system's API, and they include incident times, response types, case status, and street-level locations. They are case records, not live ambulance tracking.

The researchers' summary says breaches at emergency services and universities led to the theft of medical and personal data. Their detailed account of the Taipei patient platform, however, says only that the records were exposed.

The agents also went after five other targets tied to Taiwan's emergency services:

Target

What the agents did

Result

Logged into its database admin panel with default root credentials. A web shell attempt through a known CVE failed.

Found a hardcoded AES-256 key in the site's front-end JavaScript that exposed session-cookie contents, including an administrator's identity

No confirmed compromise

The report does not say whether the affected organizations or Taiwan's authorities were told, or whether the exposed data can still be reached.

Outside emergency services, the agents pulled data from an account table at a Taiwanese lending firm through SQL injection. In Thailand, they collected data from three universities in the same way, after selecting 489 potential targets across 45 institutions.

In Mexico, they collected about 206,800 home phone records containing names and addresses, using government statistics, postal code lists, and telecom authority data.

About 15 more organizations were attacked without a confirmed break-in. In at least eight other countries, targets were only scanned or lined up for attacks that had not run by the time the researchers looked.

The researchers watched the operation for 12 days. One recorded exchange shows the attacker at work on July 25.

How the AI Was Used and Where It Failed

The setup, called BOSSAI, had 12 AI agents, with 9 in use. Some built and maintained the attacker's servers and tools, while others scanned targets and carried out attacks.

Commercial cloud models did most of the building, with Grok as the main builder. When the attacker directly asked them to attack, Grok and MiniMax M3 refused and requested written proof that the work was authorized. The researchers say it is unclear whether a fake authorization letter would have changed that.

Grok made one exception, repairing a broken proof-of-concept script that the attacker then handed to an attack agent. The attacker also redirected the coding agents Claude Code and Codex to an abliterated model, though they mostly did infrastructure work. Cursor, another coding agent, attacked a Taiwanese emergency-services site while running such a model.

The abliterated models were versions of DeepSeek, GLM, and Qwen.

The agents also got things wrong. One scanning tool invented CVEs, and more than half of its high and critical findings were false positives or wrongly classified. The main attack agent also reported results that had not happened.

Who Ran It

Acronis's attribution rests on mistakes the attacker made while hiding his identity, combined with publicly available information. He reused a single identity across his legitimate businesses and his attack servers, including a GitHub profile, a logo, an SSH key name, and an email address.

His home IP address appeared during an SSH session in one of his Grok conversations.

Why he did it is less clear. Some attacks on government, emergency, and military targets looked like the work of state-backed hacking groups, while others looked like ordinary cybercrime. The researchers think he probably wanted to make money, and it is unclear whether he works for anyone.

What Stopped the Agents

What the agents found was mostly data that was already poorly protected, according to the researchers: a medical data port left open since 2018, dispatch records on a public-facing API, a lender with 16 SQL injection points, and universities running unpatched Oracle databases.

The agents failed where logins were enforced, where paywalls required a valid session, and where endpoints were properly filtered. The AI made it cheap to find and reach many targets at once, but it did not get past defenses that held.

Nine IP addresses and nine domains from the attacker's setup appear in the indicator list at the end of the analysis. None is marked as active or inactive, and most come without a note on what they were used for.

Title: Fake GitHub Security Tools Infect Over 2,000 PCs With Malware
Context: Cybersecurity firm Doctor Web has found malware hidden in GitHub projects that look like security tools
Full Text:
Fake GitHub security tools are spreading malware that disables defenses, steals sensitive data and infects over 2,000 PCs.

Cybersecurity firm Doctor Web has found malware hidden in GitHub projects that look like security tools. The campaign targets blockchain game fans and, more recently, information security professionals. The researchers discovered that more than 2,000 PCs were infected.

“The attackers behind these compromised development projects target blockchain game enthusiasts and (most intriguingly) …information security professionals.” reads the report. “At the time of Doctor Web’s research into this matter, more than 2,000 PCs were infected.”

The campaign started two years ago with Visual Studio projects related to blockchain games, game bots and cheats. The attackers targeted people who used crypto wallets. They hid malicious code in project files, including commands that ran before a project was built and PowerShell commands stored in configuration files. They even provided instructions on how to install Visual Studio and download the projects from GitHub, making it easy for people with limited technical knowledge to use them.

Now the attackers are targeting cybersecurity professionals. Their new GitHub projects claim to offer tools for automated scanning, security testing and log analysis. Doctor Web found one that pretends to analyze and clean results from the Fscan security scanner.

The attackers also hide malicious code in Python and Go files, using large blocks of blank spaces to make it harder to spot. Some of these fake security tools even remove the antivirus software installed on the victim’s computer.

Once a victim opens the project, a PowerShell script runs and contacts the attackers’ servers and legitimate platforms, including YouTube, Telegram, Google Docs, GitCode and Pastebin. An encrypted string it retrieves holds a link to an archive, which unpacks into a folder disguised as a Windows Photos component. Its main program is Microsoft.exe, a modular app built with the Electron framework.

It does most of the damage. The loader collects system information and sends it to a Telegram bot, keeps itself running, raises its privileges, and turns off Windows Defender, UAC, System Restore and shadow copies. It also adds its own Defender exclusions, injects code into legitimate processes, and removes McAfee, ESET and Malwarebytes antivirus products.

Its default mode, called Mode3, stacks several evasion tricks. It fakes its parent process, disables Smart App Control, removes security software hooks from ntdll.dll, makes direct system calls, and patches event tracing and antivirus script scanning in memory. If that fails, Mode2 takes over, adding Defender exclusions and injecting through PowerShell.

Three payloads follow. AsyncRAT, a remote access backdoor, runs as two identical copies on different ports, which probably lets two operators control one device. A clipper swaps crypto wallet addresses in the clipboard while taking screenshots, and a stealer takes browser data, FileZilla, MobaXterm and Total Commander configs, VPN settings, messenger files, game accounts and Discord tokens. Everything is zipped and sent through Telegram, and the malware edits the hosts file to block antivirus vendors’ domains.

The attackers are still developing the malware. Doctor Web found an unfinished component that could install itself as a system service, download Microsoft.exe again if someone deletes it, manage startup and install updates.

“Attackers are constantly updating the Trojans to introduce new features. For example, Doctor Web’s researchers discovered certain unused routines that facilitate downloading and decompressing yet another archive—Lodge.7z.” concludes the report. “It contains an Electron project that hasn’t been completed yet. The executable file’s name is WUDFHost.exe. Its code offers us a glimpse of some of the trojan’s future features.”

Doctor Web advises users to keep their antivirus software up to date and scan every file they download. The researchers warn that attackers are constantly improving the Trojans and adding new features.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Fake GitHub Security Tools)

Title: On the hunt for ARTEX: understanding agentic attacks in AWS environments
Context: In early November 2026, Datadog tied ARTEX activity to IP addresses that resolved to a hosted console, and found hundreds of additional internet-exposed ARTEX consoles, often in...
Full Text:
Key points

In October 2026, Datadog observed in-the-wild activity from ARTEX, an AI-native penetration framework, against several AWS environments, with a focus on accessing financial data.

Using compromised long-term IAM access keys, ARTEX searched through CloudWatch using FilterLogEvents, hunting for financial information, file paths and secrets such as long-lived AKIA access keys and passwords.

We also observed unauthenticated abuse of public Amazon Cognito user pools, including anonymous sign-ups, token collection, and follow-up AWS account enumeration attempts.

In early November 2026, Datadog tied ARTEX activity to IP addresses that resolved to a hosted console, and found hundreds of additional internet-exposed ARTEX consoles, often in Mandarin and hosted with providers in locations including Singapore and Hong Kong.

Background on ARTEX

ARTEX is an AI-native penetration framework in which an operator supplies a target and an objective, and a team of LLM agents plans and runs the attack. A Chinese developer published it on GitHub in July 2026 and made it closed-source on October 8, after it had passed 12,000 forks.

Microsoft tied it to Storm-0940, a China-aligned actor behind a recent supply-chain compromise. In recent months, ARTEX has been documented attacking Okta, Entra ID and Cognito across IT and software vendors.

Those reports center on identity providers and web application logs. In this post, we provide more details on the cloud control-plane view, in particular how ARTEX behaves once it has compromised an initial set of AWS credentials, through leaked long-lived access keys or following a successful anonymous sign-up on a public Cognito pool.

First, we will dive into ARTEX as a platform. Then, we'll describe specific behaviors and indicators we identified in the wild.

Inside the ARTEX console

ARTEX started as a repository and has grown into a platform running on live infrastructure. Operators run it as a hosted web console, and many of those consoles face the internet. We found hundreds of hosts serving the same Chinese-language login page, titled ARTEX — 自主渗透测试控制台 (ARTEX — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console). We've also seen the same platform appearing under other names:

Page title

English translation

ARTEX — 自主渗透测试控制台

ARTEX — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console

ScopeWeaver — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console

(original in English)

LUCK — 自主资产控制台

LUCK — Autonomous Asset Console

观澜SEC渗透测试平台

Guanlan SEC Penetration Testing Platform

A similar console is rendered across many of these hosts.

The platform user supplies API keys to chosen AI inference providers and points ARTEX at almost any provider through three request formats:

openai: OpenAI Chat Completions and any compatible gateway, which covers OpenAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, MiniMax, OpenRouter-style resellers and self-hosted models.

openai-responses: OpenAI's newer Responses API.

anthropic: Anthropic's Messages API, plus vendors that expose an Anthropic-compatible endpoint, such as DeepSeek.

When one provider bans or cuts off a key, ARTEX moves to the next to continue activity. Therefore, a single campaign can be spread across several providers and keys.

An agent planner directs a small team of workers. The planner sends "intents" to workers, which run three at a time by default. A main agent handles chat with the operator, with a /btw command for side questions.

Everything is recorded on a "blackboard" graph of tasks, goals, intents, facts, findings, hints and compression digests. Each task carries operator-defined allow and deny constraints, a timeout with a wrap-up step, and a planner heartbeat of at least 10 minutes. A fixed task timeout would explain bursts that end at a consistent length, though we have not confirmed the value operators set.

Command interception rules, written as regex or plain strings, can allow, deny or ask a human for a judgment. In some versions, a global asset blocklist excludes .gov, .gov.cn, .edu and .edu.cn by default.

API paths expose core routes, such as:

/tasks /exploration/findings /exploration/graph /exploration/intents /traffic /companies /llm/profiles /llm/pool /intercept /mcp /skills /agents /notify

One version we observed shipped with a sample demo engagement. It walks through a full external-to-internal compromise, from a public web app to a DMZ foothold, internal lateral movement, and finally the Active Directory domain controller.

We often found the agent reading the front end of web apps hosted in S3, looking for build manifests and runtime configurations.

Wiz noted that before each fuzzing run, ARTEX requested a path that should not exist (/zzz-nonexistent-xyz123) to learn what "not found" looks like. We saw the same habit against S3, with keys such as zzz_nonexistent_abc.txt and Notexist-xyz. A request for an object named like a placeholder, right before a burst of guesses, is a useful signal to hunt on.

This behavior is one example from agentic pentesting tools, which continue to evolve whether they're used directly as a tool or hosted as an interactive platform.

ARTEX sightings in AWS environments in the wild

In this section, we share some activity we've identified in real-world AWS accounts, and that we have attributed to ARTEX usage.

The two initial access vectors we've witnessed ARTEX start from are:

Compromised long-term AWS access keys

Public Cognito user pools

Before either, every session we reviewed opened with unauthenticated S3 requests. In CloudTrail, these show a userIdentity.type of AWSAccount and an accountId of anonymous, calling GetObject, ListObjects and similar read APIs.

Activity cluster 1: Post-exploitation following compromised access keys

In one instance using a valid long-term access key, ARTEX's most frequent action was FilterLogEvents. The most common searches were various naming conventions of cryptocurrency companies, hedge funds, and related financial institutions. The terms combine a company name with words like Fund, Invoice, Billing and LLC.

Every FilterLogEvents call was set with a limit of 1000, below the API's 10,000-event maximum. That constant shows up across sessions.

On October 20, the same long-term key was used again from 103.54.154[.]40, an address associated with zeofast[.]cn. This session widened the search, looking for file and storage links, internal secrets, internal IP addresses, and database information.

Files and storage links

Databases, internal IPs and secrets

Errors

"s3://" || "presigned" || ".pdf" || ".xlsx" || ".csv" || "rawData_" || "transformedData_"

?mongo ?172. ?10. ?password ?AKIA

?Error ?❌ ?⚠

Activity cluster 2: Self-registration through public Cognito user pools

In an instance where no long-term access keys were obtained, ARTEX went after public Cognito user pools. Wiz reported account-recovery abuse through InitiateAuth, ForgotPassword and ResendConfirmationCode. We saw the agent go further, registering an account, collecting tokens, trading them for AWS credentials, then enumerating resources.

One example came as a spike on October 26 and 27 from 154.64.252[.]77. The observed SignUp calls sometimes named the tool in the user agent such as Mozilla/5.0 ARTeX, while other user agents included curl or typical browser user agents.

Getting through sign-up was noisy. The pool had a PreSignUp Lambda trigger that checked a tenant domain, and the agent iterated against it and continued probing. For example, below are errors generated as the agent continued attempting to sign up:

PreSignUp failed with error Invalid tenant domain: api[.]github[.]com. PreSignUp failed with error Invalid tenant domain: example[.]com PreSignUp failed with error tenantId does not match tenant domain. PreSignUp failed with error Invalid tenantDomain format: hxxps[://]artex-hqheizfk[.]invalid/x. Attributes did not conform to the schema: Type for attribute {custom:isAdmin} could not be determined

Once registered, it walked the standard user pool flow: SignUp, InitiateAuth, RespondToAuthChallenge, GetUser and GetTokensFromRefreshToken, followed by Get* requests and attempts to call ListUserPools.

In CloudTrail, that session appears under the CognitoIdentityCredentials role session name with short-term AWS credentials. The agent used it to try nearly every read-only discovery call it could, such as:

ListBuckets

GetBucket*

ListSecrets

DescribeParameters

ListTopics

DescribeLogGroups

GetRestApis

DescribeRepositories

ListFunctions20150331

In this case, all of them failed because the identity pool's authenticated role did not grant the required permissions.

Hunting for ARTEX activity

In this post, we've shared some in-the-wild sightings of ARTEX-attributed activity in cloud environments. It's important to remember that while ARTEX is an offensive AI-native orchestration framework, distributions we analyzed don't appear to have an opinionated methodology for targeting or performing post-exploitation in cloud environments: the playbook is therefore left to downstream AI inference, and can vary greatly depending on the model in use.

In this context, research such as "I Gave 14 LLMs AWS Keys. Here’s What They Wanted to Do Next" by Adan Alvarez is valuable for gaining a broader understanding of how LLMs tend to behave when faced with compromised credentials.

When hunting for ARTEX activity in your environment, we recommend following the methodology below.

Start with quick wins, namely ARTEX user agents (see IOCs), to identify noisy ARTEX probing or exploitation requests. Note that user agents can easily be changed, but they aren't always updated to a stealthier value.

Review your environment for activity originating from IP addresses known to be associated with ARTEX activity (see IOCs).

We've seen ARTEX behave noisily in a number of cases: identify large volumes of permission denied errors, enumeration of objects in S3 logs, unusual access patterns (for instance, credentials vended from an EC2 instance role being used by a non-AWS IP), and CloudTrail events that relate to known cloud attack techniques (Stratus Red Team, Datadog's Cloud Security Atlas and TrailDiscover are useful resources for these).

How Datadog can help

Cloud SIEM

Datadog Cloud SIEM contains several out-of-the-box (OOTB) rules that can detect ARTEX-related post-exploitation and initial access in your AWS environment:

Enumeration from multiple regions using a long-term access key failed

AWS Cloudtrail possible secret enumeration in multiple regions and secret retrieval

Cloud Security Misconfigurations

Datadog Cloud Security Misconfigurations ships with out-of-the-box (OOTB) rules to help you identify risky long-lived AWS credentials proactively:

Access keys should be rotated every 90 days or less

IAM access keys that are inactive and older than 1 year should be removed

Title: The Fridge-Hacking Spree Is an Internet-of-Things Wake-Up Call
Context: Amid an onslaught of AI vulnerability discovery and AI-assisted hacking, some of the most consequential critical infrastructure attacks this year may have little to do with the...
Full Text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Amid an onslaught of AI vulnerability discovery and AI-assisted hacking, some of the most consequential critical infrastructure attacks this year may have little to do with the technology at all—instead providing a stark reminder that cybersecurity fundamentals are still key to digital defense.

Three sites in France that handle blood and plasma bags were briefly impacted this week by widespread attacks on vulnerable internet-connected refrigerators. On Wednesday, the Établissement Français du Sang (EFS) confirmed that cold rooms storing blood were “raised to very high temperatures” on November 2. The blood samples, thankfully, weren’t altered or damaged, the EFS said, because the organization’s alarm facilities and staff quickly detected the changes and implemented fail-safe measures.

The incident, however, comes amid a wave of cyberattacks in recent days affecting supermarket chains in at least 11 European countries that also drastically increased the temperatures of their refrigerators. Pictures from across the continent show huge volumes of food being trashed following the spikes. Similar fridge attacks in October affected hundreds of French stores that were forced to throw away food. And in August, roughly six commissaries and grocery stores on United States military bases suffered similar incidents resulting in spoiled food. The Pentagon is investigating the incidents and is collaborating with French law enforcement, Reuters reported last week.

“It's been true for more than a decade now that our dependence on connected technology is growing faster than our collective will to protect it, which has exposed us to accidents, adversaries, and now potentially agents,” says longtime critical infrastructure researcher Josh Corman, who is currently the executive in residence for public safety and resilience at the nonprofit Institute for Security and Technology. “These fragile cold-chain systems are too critical to fail, but we keep experiencing hard lessons.”

It is still unclear who is behind the incidents and whether the attacks are all connected or being carried out by multiple actors. The first recent wave of attacks against French supermarkets last month appears to have been caused by attackers exploiting unpatched refrigeration controllers exposed to the internet—including software versions that allegedly used weak passwords formulated based on the date.

Many of the hacks stem from attackers exploiting vulnerabilities in temperature controllers made by the Danish firm Danfoss, and researchers say the attacks would not have been particularly difficult to pull off. Danfoss did not return WIRED’s request for comment.

Title: NHS breach helpline left staff carrying a 'significant emotional burden'
Context: NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review...
Full Text: NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review has found. The report [PDF] comes almost exactly a year after the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust disclosed a data breach affecting 8,003 people, including current and former trust staff and non-trust workers. A member of the public discovered the exposure in November 2025. An Excel workbook published in response to a Freedom of Information request in February 2023 retained underlying sickness absence records that users could reveal through its pivot tables. Staff assigned to the helpline described difficult calls involving shouting, anger, and distress. Particularly difficult calls involved people distressed by the sensitivity of the disclosures or potentially in danger from domestic abuse. Call handlers said they had to make safeguarding assessments without training or an established process. "Such occurrences of anger or distress were not infrequent, and this reflected the heightened emotions and distress experienced by callers to varying degrees due to the breach," the review noted. "This placed significant emotional burden on individuals working in the contact center, who were not prepared or provided support on how to deal with those." Members of the trust's clinical governance team were told just a day beforehand that they would staff the helpline. Despite their experience dealing with patient trauma, they received little preparation for the calls that followed. "The staff working in the call centers had a short training session and then the calls started coming in within minutes of the team being set up," the review noted. "Some staff had not finished reading the pre-prepared script which had arrived only 30 minutes before the center went live." Most call handlers only learned that their own data had been exposed while already working on the helpline, sometimes minutes before supporting others affected. Call handlers also said they had little choice about taking on the work and were expected to maintain their usual duties alongside it. The review stated that some staff members gave up weekends and worked long past their scheduled hours to meet the demands of both roles. "It's typical NHS, it runs on goodwill," one staffer told the team that compiled the report. The call center was only supposed to run for two weeks in December 2025, but due to the volume of calls, it was eventually stood down after 11 weeks, in February 2026. According to officials speaking at a trust board meeting on Thursday, the review and its findings have since been circulated among staff, and published online. How the spreadsheet slipped through Responding to a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request thought to be from a journalist researching a story about stress in the NHS, the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust uploaded a spreadsheet to its public FOI Disclosure log in February 2023. This contained personal data and inadvertently exposed sickness absence information and sensitive health data related to 7,715 staff, 288 non-trust workers, as well as a small number of unidentified records. Crucially, this spreadsheet was uploaded in a format that allowed users to access the pivot table from which some data was derived. The data in these pivot tables would normally have been too sensitive to be included in FOIA responses. The first failure was that the request was handled by the trust's e-Rostering team instead of the People Information Unit, which had the expertise in responding to FOIA requests with complex datasets. The e-Rostering team compiled the response using the team's own data, but incorrectly believed they had stripped the spreadsheet of the sensitive data that would later be exposed. Standard procedures instructed request handlers to follow several steps to ensure sensitive data was stripped before documents are published, some of which were skipped. For starters, one FOI officer assigned to the response either failed to run the spreadsheet through Excel's Document Inspector, which formed part of the usual procedures, or failed to act upon its recommendations. This feature can flag pivot tables and potentially hidden cached data, but cannot determine whether that data is sensitive or automatically remove the cache. Staff also failed to follow instructions to convert the spreadsheet to PDF. Investigators found that doing so prevented users clicking through to the underlying records, although they could not guarantee that no hidden data remained technically accessible. At the time, internal guidance did not require conversion to CSV, which would have removed the workbook's pivot-table functionality and embedded cache. The trust's sign-off process also focused on answering the request's questions and meeting their public relations duties, and falsely assumed that the data had been adequately sanitized before the final review. The spreadsheet was made available for 33 months, although the trust is not sure how many times it was viewed during that time. Its logs only covered the 12 months before a member of the public alerted it to the pivot table issue. These indicated that it had been accessed 340 times, although the review noted there was no way of knowing how many of these, if any, led to pivot tables being accessed, or even if it was viewed by a human, with web crawlers adding to the total view count. The trust has since implemented a number of changes to prevent a recurrence of the breach, including the mandatory password-protecting of any Excel workbook as part of FOIA responses. A senior information governance officer must now approve spreadsheet responses before executive sign-off. Revised guidance circulated in November 2025 also called for conversion to CSV, although investigators found that this requirement had not been incorporated into the formal operating procedure and recommended updating it. The review says the Information Commissioner's Office closed its case after the trust implemented its recommendations. A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall Hospitals said: "We are deeply sorry for the accidental sharing of sickness absence data which we reported in November 2025, and for the distress and concern it caused those colleagues whose data was involved. "An independent investigation has now been completed, and the report has been published in full on our website in the interests of transparency and accountability. "The investigation has helped us understand what happened and identify areas where improvements were needed. We have already implemented a number of measures to strengthen our processes, particularly around the management of Freedom of Information requests and responses. "The protection of personal information is of the utmost importance to us, and we remain committed to learning from this incident and preventing a similar event from happening again. "We continue to provide support to colleagues who have been affected." ®

Title: Free Chinese AI Models Are Getting Scary Good at Hacking
Context: The researchers found OpenAI’s most advanced cyber model, Daybreak, which is available only to trusted partners, to be the most capable, completing 81 percent of the tasks it...
Full Text:
Open-weight artificial intelligence models are now almost as capable of hacking into computer networks as the best closed ones, according to new research that heralds a much-anticipated turning point in the cybersecurity landscape.

Vals, a company that measures AI capabilities, set out to test how well different AI models could carry out complex, multi-step network instructions on mock corporate networks.

“The best frontier models, locked up inside the labs and available only through trusted access programs, are now starting to be matched by open models that anybody can download,” says Nikil Ravi, a researcher at Vals.

The company’s findings suggest that closed models no longer have a definitive edge in cyber skills, meaning recent efforts by frontier labs to limit access to their models, and thereby slow the proliferation of such capabilities, may potentially be moot.

The findings are also noteworthy given that the US frontier labs, particularly Anthropic, premised the limited release of new models—beginning with Claude Mythos Preview in April—on the idea that gated access would only buy time before advanced hacking capabilities were broadly available.

Anthropic's frontier red team lead, Logan Graham, told WIRED in April that the company’s Project Glasswing, which gives trusted access to the full capabilities of new models, was focused on getting those tools “in the hands of defenders to give a head start.”

“We need to prepare now for a world where these capabilities are broadly available in 6, 12, 24 months. Many things would be different about security,” he told WIRED at the time.

Seven months later, that transition seems to have arrived on schedule.

Vals tested AI models in two simulated scenarios, giving them various specific tasks to achieve. The first scenario involved a mock corporate network accessible through a public-facing website. The second involved two different company networks; a model needed to compromise the first in order to gain access to the second.

The researchers found OpenAI’s most advanced cyber model, Daybreak, which is available only to trusted partners, to be the most capable, completing 81 percent of the tasks it was given in an average of two tests. The Chinese open-weight model DeepSeek was not far behind, completing 73 percent of the objectives on average. The Vals researchers note that on some tasks, the two models scored equally.

The research also showed how much cheaper it is to use an open-weight model for this kind of task. Vals says it costs $17 to $46 in tokens for GPT-6-Sol to carry out an attack compared to $2 to $3 for DeepSeek. Open models are generally cheaper because they can be run on one’s own hardware. Rayan Krishnan, CEO of Vals, says this also provides a strong incentive for those playing defense to use open models rather than proprietary ones.
