Title: Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets
Context: Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks...
Full Text:
In this article

From exposed secrets to cloud compromise

Follow-on actions

Mitigating application credential abuse activity

Defending against agentic AI attacks

Microsoft detections

Advanced hunting queries

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to search public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, including credentials, application credentials, and AI inference-related API keys across multiple applications and cloud services. These threat actors can then use the secrets for further malicious activity against the compromised organization.

Searching open code repositories for exposed credentials, secrets, keys, and other authentication material is a well-documented technique that has historically been limited by the time required for human operators to find code repositories, review the data in the repositories, and leverage authentication material for further action. However, agentic tooling like ARTEX allows threat actors to not only scan for secrets across multiple repositories at a quicker pace but also use the agents to analyze the output and conduct follow-on attacks, cutting down on the need for the threat actor to have hands-on-keyboard interactions throughout the attack chain. In at least one case, Microsoft observed an AI agent advance from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes.

Microsoft has also investigated follow-on activity involving the misuse of valid application credentials. As early as October 28, 2026, Microsoft began observing successful service principal sign-ins from the IP address 199.19.77[.]84 involving multiple application IDs across some impacted customers, including cases where a multitenant application credential was compromised at the source (vendor-owned application) and used to access multiple downstream tenants. The threat actor used the compromised credentials for cloud resource discovery, and credential and data exfiltration, including from Azure Key Vaults and Storage Accounts, and abuse of Azure AI services consistent with the activity described above. Additionally, Microsoft observed malicious activity originating from two IP addresses potentially associated with this campaign. We identified malicious operations from 65.87.223[.]26, including indications of vulnerability exploitation by embedded shell commands in a user agent and attempts to obtain App Service authentication tokens. A similar campaign involving the same IPs addressed was also reported by Todyl. Separately, Microsoft observed reconnaissance operations from 157.22.126[.]128 targeting AI workloads deployed by victims on Azure AI services.

Microsoft encourages organizations to scan their code in GitHub and determine where any secrets are present. In addition to removing the secrets from the code base, affected organizations should immediately rotate any exposed keys or credentials. GitHub monitors public repositories by automatically scanning for secrets. In addition to scanning their own repositories, organizations can enable public monitoring through GitHub to detect secrets leaked in secondary public repositories across GitHub. This extends secret scanning beyond the repositories an enterprise owns to follow potential secret exposure across the platform. GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps scans for credentials and other sensitive content in source code. Push protection can also block supported secrets before they’re pushed. Organizations need either GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps or, for organizations using the standalone experience, GitHub Secret Protection for Azure DevOps enabled.

Secrets are exposed in public repositories when code containing the secret is committed to GitHub. Developers might store secrets in configuration files, scripts, or other code to quickly operationalize the OAuth application or avoid configuring more modern authentication flows. Organizations can reduce exposure by protecting workload identities and secrets, enforcing least privilege, safeguarding recovery resources, and enabling relevant Microsoft Defender for Cloud protections. Publicly exposed credentials remain usable until revoked or rotated; removing the original disclosure alone does not remediate the exposure. Microsoft recommends that developers migrate OAuth applications away from secret-based authentication. While storing long-lived application client secrets in code is a common practice, using managed identities for application authentication eliminates the possibility of secret exposure in code, manual processes associated with secret management, and barriers to securely scaling applications.

This activity illustrates an ongoing trend of threat actors accelerating all stages of the attack chain with agentic AI penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX. As these capabilities evolve, defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments.

From exposed secrets to cloud compromise

Starting in August 2026, Microsoft observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to submit large volumes of queries to GitHub for secrets. The queries submitted by the AI framework often included the name of a target organization, keywords for secrets, a keyword linked to cloud services, or a keyword linked to another AI service provider. Organizations that find their secrets exposed in public repositories must assume that the exposed secrets and associated applications are compromised.

Follow-on actions

Credential abuse via Entra ID

In one follow-on attack that began as early as October 28, 2026, an agentic framework used valid leaked or stolen application credentials to access Microsoft Entra ID tenants of certain organizations and connected Azure and Microsoft 365 resources. The sign-ins primarily came from two IP addresses: 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18. The latter IP address is a Tor exit node, which might be associated with unrelated malicious activity, including from unrelated sources. The agent successfully conducted service principal sign-ins on dozens of associated applications across multiple tenants.. Service principals are the identities that applications use to authenticate and give direct, programmatic access to whatever the application is authorized to reach.

The threat actor targeted operations that return credentials, including storage account keys, App Service settings, connection strings and publishing credentials, AI and machine learning (ML) connections and datastores, and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) user credentials. The compromised applications subsequently accessed SharePoint and OneDrive in the targeted organization tenants, including file downloads and mailbox-item access. In some tenants, the threat actor sent Microsoft Graph API requests, which were mostly searches to find content of interest. The threat actor enumerated subscriptions, resource groups, permissions, AI model deployments, and service configurations in Azure to map the environment.

Additionally, the threat actor attempted to validate stolen Azure resources, including compromised Azure AI services, as identified using Defender for Cloud’s AI threat protection. Observed activity suggests that the threat actor might have attempted to abuse some of these compromised AI resources to facilitate their broader attack activity.

Figure 1. Tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) observed across the credential abuse attack chain

Cloud API adjustments indicative of adaptive behavior

Additionally in this attack the agent’s operations on a victim’s Azure Resource Manager (ARM) instance originating from 199.19.77[.]84 demonstrated sequences consistent with adaptive troubleshooting, where failed cloud API requests were followed by changes to HTTP methods or API versions and subsequent HTTP 200 responses:

A batch of ARM requests attempting to enumerate secret metadata across multiple Azure Key Vault resources returned HTTP 400 (Bad Request). These requests specified a version associated with Key Vault’s data-plane APIs against ARM (control-plane) APIs. Approximately 28 seconds after the first failed response, a batch rerun began against the same vault resource paths using the ARM API version 2023-07-01 and returned HTTP 200.

A GET request to enumerate an Azure SQL server’s firewall rules specified an outdated API version and returned HTTP 400. Approximately 60 seconds after that request, a matching GET began using a supported version and subsequently returned HTTP 200. The URL changed only in its api-version parameter.

An ARM POST request to an Application Insights query endpoint returned HTTP 400 because an outdated API version was specified. Approximately 80 seconds after the failed request, another POST began against the same endpoint, specifying a supported API version, and subsequently returned HTTP 200.

OAuth application abuse

In multiple cases, Microsoft observed the same agentic AI tools subsequently obtain a token for a single-tenant OAuth application in the same target organization, then use the compromised OAuth application to enumerate other cloud resources within the organization. In some cases, the agents exfiltrated secrets from the organization’s Azure Key Vault. The agents once authenticated have also searched Azure DevOps for secrets. Until the secrets are revoked or rotated, they can allow a threat actor to maintain persistence in the organization, compromise additional identities, or hijack resources. In one observed case, an AI agent progressed from searching for the client secrets in GitHub to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

The agents also used the compromised OAuth application to use the Run Command, which runs scripts in Azure VMs. With access to this functionality on a VM, a threat actor can access unsecured credentials and other stored data, compromise associated workload identities, or run code that provides persistence or lateral movement.

During this activity, the AI agents repeatedly demonstrated a focus on credentials that provide access to AI services, such as API keys for major AI service providers and OAuth applications with access to Foundry Tools (previously known as Azure Cognitive Services). Multiple public reports have documented threat actors using agentic AI tools to compromise credentials for AI services, sometimes to run the same agentic AI workflow.

Mitigating application credential abuse activity

Microsoft recommends the following mitigation steps to contain, detect, and investigate this threat.

Containment

Block 199.19.77[.]84/32 as a named location in a Conditional Access policy targeting workload identities, assigned directly to service principals, and in a user-scoped block policy to cover replayed sessions. Note that workload identity policies require Workload ID Premium licensing and cover only single-tenant apps registered in your tenant. Block the exact IP rather than the whole ASN.

For affected users, revoke Entra sessions, Azure DevOps PATs and SSH keys.

For any affected application, remove all client secrets, certificates and federated credentials, including those added by the threat actor and disable the service principal if needed. Tokens already issued remain valid until expiry.

Rotate everything stored in any Key Vault the affected application could read, and any credentials found in accessed documents.

MSPs: Review Partner Center access, GDAP relationships, and customer tenants, and notify affected customers per your agreements.

Detection and hunting

Review Entra service principal and non-interactive sign-in logs for 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18 including failed attempts. Sign-in errors AADSTS7000215 (invalid secret) or AADSTS7000222 (expired secret) indicate someone holds a credential for your app; a failure followed by a success is urgent.

Review Azure Activity, Key Vault and Storage diagnostics, Entra audit, Azure DevOps audit and Microsoft 365 unified audit logs for the address, including secret reads, blob and file downloads, and changes to apps, permissions or pipelines.

In Azure DevOps auditing, review PAT creation and first use, federated service connections, pipeline runs and edits, and unfamiliar user agents. Enable auditing if it is off.

Look for behavior as well as the IP: one address authenticating to three or more service principals with mixed success, or one app requesting tokens across Azure Resource Manager, Key Vault, Storage and Graph in a short window. Search as far back as retention allows.

Defending against agentic AI attacks

Threat actors can and do change the source IP address, user agent strings, and other fingerprints left by the agentic AI penetration testing tools they use. This can make identifying and blocking malicious network traffic early difficult for defenders.

Several behavioral signals can help organizations determine that they are being targeted by threat actors using agentic AI. Agentic AI frameworks scanning a target send a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retry variations on the same technique or move on to next-stage actions at machine speed. Agentic AI frameworks use existing penetration testing tools. For example, ARTEX by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others. These tools may send network traffic with distinctive characteristics, such as default user agent strings. While blocking network traffic with these characteristics will not stop an attack by an AI agent, which will quickly change them, identifying them can alert defenders to the activity.

Defensive honeypots, decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as Microsoft Sentinel Deception give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal.

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.

Protect and continuously assess application credentials and secrets. Avoid storing service principal credentials, storage keys, connection strings, and other secrets in source code, configuration files, public repositories, issues, or other locations where they might be inadvertently exposed. To find credentials in source code, consider using tools like GitHub Advanced Security or other OWASP source code analysis tools.

Rotate compromised or exposed credentials immediately and establish credential lifecycle practices. Treat credentials that have been publicly exposed as compromised, even if the original location has subsequently been edited or deleted. Removing the content does not invalidate the credential or eliminate copies retained in edit history, caches, archives, logs, or other systems. Immediately revoke or rotate the affected credentials and investigate their historical use. Where supported, organizations should favor mechanisms that reduce reliance on long-lived credentials. Learn more about protecting secrets with Defender for Cloud.

Enable appropriate Microsoft Defender for Cloud plans for critical Azure workloads. Consider enabling workload protections relevant to the resources in your environment, including Defender for Resource Manager, Defender for Storage, Defender for Key Vault, Defender for App Service, and Defender for Databases. Learn more in the Microsoft Defender for Cloud overview.

Apply least privilege to service principals and other workload identities. Review the Azure role-based access control (RBAC) permissions assigned to service principals and restrict their privileges to the resources and operations required by their applications. Learn more about best practices for Azure RBAC.

Protect backup and recovery infrastructure as part of resilience. Restrict access to backup and recovery resources and closely monitor attempts to modify or remove their protection controls. Learn more about Azure Backup security best practices.

Hardening OAuth applications against compromise involves managing the permissions of the applications in your organization and securing application secrets. To triage applications in your environment, enforce security policies with new applications as they are created, and address existing applications over time beginning with the most recent ones.

Identify and catalog applications running in your cloud environment. The Cloud app catalog page in Defender for Cloud Apps is one service that can help accomplish this.

Use Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps Cloud Discovery tools to identify unmanaged apps, and prioritize the most frequently used apps to migrate and integrate.

Use Conditional Access policies for workload identities. Consider augmenting identity signals with workload identity risk protection.

Set permission restrictions to limit who can create an application in the tenant. This can be achieved by setting the ability for users to register apps to “No” and limiting the application developer role to privileged users. Review the list of least privileged roles by task to help scope role-based access control in your environment.

Integrate enterprise applications with Microsoft Entra ID.

Title: Feds warn grocers: Don't chill on cyber defenses as freezer hacking spree heats up
Context: Attackers exploit these flaws by bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and abusing weak configurations, according to the feds
Full Text: If you have any industrial smart freezers, look out. The US federal government is urging owners and operators to disconnect them from the internet, apply patches, change default passwords, and take other security measures to prevent the kind of attacks that have become prevalent in Europe. “We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk,” FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said in a statement. Since mid-October, unknown miscreants have hacked thousands of remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of grocery stores in France, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden. The attacks increase the temperature inside fridges to highs of 50ºC (122°F), spoiling food, and sparking fires. The Register asked the FBI if it has documented any successful or attempted attacks against refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in America. We had not received a response to our questions at the time of publication, nor are we aware of any documented digital attacks against these systems in American supermarkets. But there are signs that stateside operators are aware of the issue. Dutch grocery giant Ahold Delhaize, which operates US supermarket chains Food Lion, Giant Food, and Stop & Shop, last month said it proactively took IT systems offline following a cyberattack that affected most of its US and European brands. Delhaize supermarkets in Europe are among those hit by the destructive freezer attacks. The Pentagon is also reportedly treating a series of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the US in August as a suspected cyberattack, according to Reuters, which cited four officials familiar with the matter. In a Thursday advisory, the US FBI, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Health and Human Services, and departments of Agriculture and Transportation warned organizations about the ongoing cyber threats facing operators of industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems. “The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards,” the agencies said. Attackers exploit these flaws by bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and abusing weak configurations, according to the feds. Once criminals gain access to the systems, they can change the temperature to spoil food or temperature-controlled medications, start fires, and ultimately harm people who consume products that haven’t been stored at proper temperatures. How to stay frosty To prevent these scenarios, the government organizations urge owners and operators to “immediately” implement best practices and security protections. First and foremost on the list: do not expose industrial control systems and devices to the public internet. Iranian hackers used internet-accessible programmable logic controllers (PLCs) to break into more than 100 US water systems in July. This sort of exposed device, which often lacks password protection, is a boon to miscreants looking for an easy button to gain access to critical facilities. “Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities,” the feds advise. Other recommended tactics include: Create a dedicated VLAN for operational technology (OT) devices, to isolate industrial devices from business networks. Replace default passwords with strong passwords and policies, turning on phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA) whenever possible. Apply patches in a timely manner, and retire and replace legacy devices that no longer receive security updates from the manufacturer. Define and maintain a device and IP allow-list, and limit access to OT devices to only those on the list. Maintain and test backups. These should be kept offsite and offline. And finally: enable logging and regularly review logs for any unusual activity.®

Title: French banking group hit by supply chain cyberattack
Context: This attack comes amidst worries by European regulators about cyber threats to financial institutions as they become more reliant on interconnected systems and external service...
Full Text:
French regional banking group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa admitted Wednesday that attackers had accessed an internal account via an unnamed third-party service provider’s platform and transferred funds to other financial institutions. Those funds, it said, could have then been potentially converted to cryptocurrency by the thieves.

The day before, cryptocurrency news outlet CoinDesk reported that the attack had been detected on Monday by blockchain investigator ZachXBT, although at the time he did not identify the entity involved. On Wednesday, he identified the suspected victim as Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, which the banking group later confirmed. It did not, however, specify whether the stolen funds were originally in traditional currency or cryptocurrency.

This attack comes amidst worries by European regulators about cyber threats to financial institutions as they become more reliant on interconnected systems and external service providers.

The bank, which serves the West of France, temporarily suspended some transactions in the wake of the attack to prevent further fraudulent activity. It reported that, as of Wednesday morning, operations were returning to normal after the implementation of additional security controls. French law enforcement is investigating the breach.

In its initial announcement, the group reassured customers that their funds were safe. “This incident has no impact on [customer] assets, and has only resulted in a delayed execution of certain transfer operations. Their interests are fully protected, and safeguarding their assets is an absolute priority,” it said.

French regional newspaper Le Télégramme reported that the thieves had taken over €118 million (over $133 million); the bank would not confirm the amount but said that the order of magnitude was accurate.

The bank said it was still working to assess the precise financial consequences of this attack. “Some of the funds involved have been frozen, and other actions are underway to recover them. While it is therefore still too early to provide a final figure, we can already confirm that the amounts involved are in no way likely to jeopardize the financial health and stability of Crédit Mutuel Arkéa,” it said. The group has 5.8 million customers and manages more than €211 billion (about $237 billion) in assets.

Title: Phone return scams: where a real delivery and a fake return end up in a bill for you
Context: Available with Malwarebytes Premium Security for all your devices, and in the Malwarebytes app for iOS and Android
Full Text:
A caller offers you a free phone upgrade or an exclusive deal from your mobile provider. A new phone arrives at your home. So far, everything seems to check out.

Then comes another call: There’s been a shipping mistake. You received the wrong phone, and the company needs you to send it back. You send it back, but the phone never reaches your provider, leaving you with a large charge or long-term contract to pay.

Now police are warning about this scheme after residents lost devices and were left facing the associated payments.

How phone return scams works

The scam usually starts with a call from a spoofed number. In the US we’re seeing several examples in anonymized Malwarebytes Scam Guard records of the impersonated company being Canadian mobile provider Rogers.

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre warns:

“After collecting personal information required for credit checks, they’ll order a new phone in your name.”

Next, a genuine device arrives through a legitimate delivery service. That delivery makes the next part of the story easier to believe.

The caller gets back in touch and claims something went wrong. Perhaps the company sent the wrong device, or an extra phone arrived by mistake. To put things right, you need to send it back using the label or shipping QR code they provide.

The shipping label is the real trick. Rather than directing the package to the provider’s returns facility, it sends the device to an address chosen by the criminals.

The result: You no longer have the phone, but your provider has not received it back. Victims can be left facing a contract, financing agreement, or monthly payments for the missing device.

How to stay safe

The most important protection against most types of scams is having someone you can trust and deliberate whether something is a scam. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can be that partner if you’re on your own.

You don’t need to decide on the spot about whether a caller sounds convincing. Break the conversation and verify the offer separately. Pause and check if you encounter any of the following:

An unexpected call offering a free phone, loyalty reward, or unusually attractive upgrade.

A caller asking for personal, financial, or account information to arrange the offer.

A follow-up call claiming the wrong device was shipped or that another delivery mistake needs correcting.

Instructions to use a return label or QR code supplied by that caller.

A return destination that you have not confirmed directly with your provider.

If you’ve already sent a phone, contact your mobile provider immediately using verified contact details. Explain that you believe you were targeted by a phone return scam, identify the affected orders, and ask for a fraud investigation.

If you shared your account password or PIN, change it through the provider’s official channels. Rogers advises customers who disclosed their credentials to reset them and contact customer service to check for unauthorized transactions.

Keep the evidence: messages, emails, the shipping label, tracking details, order confirmations, bills, and a timeline of the calls. These records can help explain what happened to support a billing complaint and fraud report.

Something feel off? Check it before you click.

Title: NIKKE PC launcher compromise put players’ passwords and personal files at risk
Context: Game publisher Level Infinite has released fixes and added a malware-checking feature to the official PC client
Full Text:
Players of Goddess of Victory: NIKKE are being urged to check their PCs after attackers tampered with files used by the game’s Windows launcher. Opening the launcher could allow malicious software to run, potentially exposing much more than a player’s game account.

The incident occurred as part of a supply-chain attack, where services or software used by the company in question is compromised. In practice, this meant that instead of persuading players to download a fake game or install a suspicious add-on, the attackers compromised resources used by the legitimate launcher. Players could therefore encounter the threat simply by opening software they already trusted.

Game publisher Level Infinite has released fixes and added a malware-checking feature to the official PC client. However, fixing the delivery mechanism does not undo an infection, nor does it recover passwords and other information that may have been stolen.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

Independent researcher MotherSphere identified malicious code in four JavaScript files hosted on Level Infinite’s official content delivery network (CDN).

Players should be aware of a discrepancy in the published timelines. Level Infinite says malicious-program distribution began on October 30. while MotherSphere reports evidence of the remote-control agent running as early as October 23.

According to the researcher’s analysis, the distributed remote-control agent supported commands to:

Run programs and system commands.

Browse folders and download files.

Take screenshots.

Retrieve saved NIKKE login credentials.

Collect browser passwords and cookies.

Search for developer credentials, API tokens, and other secrets.

Collect cryptocurrency wallet-extension data.

The number of compromised PCs and the full extent of any data theft remain unclear.

How to stay safe

Mobile-only players are not affected, according to Level Infinite, so they do not need to take any additional security measures.

Level Infinite says it replaced three abnormal script files early on November 4, then refreshed the CDN’s cache for the remaining file later that day. MotherSphere subsequently reported that all four files were clean on the four CDN servers checked.

If you opened the Windows launcher during the period identified above, take the following steps.

Close the launcher and check your PC. MotherSphere’s report includes user-reported Malwarebytes detections for traces associated with the attack.

Follow the removal instructions published by NIKKE carefully.

Secure your accounts from a clean device. Do not change passwords on a computer that may still be compromised.

If a cryptocurrency wallet or its recovery phrase may have been exposed, use a clean device to move funds to a newly created wallet with a new recovery phrase.

Level Infinite asks players who believe they were affected, including those experiencing problems with external accounts or financial losses, to contact its customer support team, so keep relevant records without handing over personal information.

Please note that the NIKKE wiki’s unofficial cleanup guidance recommends scanning with Malwarebytes. Although the guide describes this as a one-time free option, Malwarebytes Free lets you continue running manual scans and removing detected malware after the Premium trial ends. The trial provides additional features, including real-time protection, so decide what is best for you.

Title: Binance heist is stark example of AI governance gaps and basic security failures
Context: The company described this as zero-day malware, but if endpoint protection tools were only capable of detecting known malware, then the whole industry has a problem
Full Text:
A chain of avoidable technical and human security failures enabled the largest crypto heist on record, the theft of approximately $6.34 billion from Binance. The improper monitoring and access scoping of an internal AI tool played a major role in helping the hackers, and should serve as a warning for enterprise CISOs to take AI governance seriously.

Binance’s initial findings report, published Nov. 3, describes a months-long, multi-stage campaign against its wallet-infrastructure engineers that resulted in malware being installed on developer machines in two separate incidents, only one of which was detected. The attackers were then able to pivot through an internal AI tool to additional developer systems, obtain an access token, and deploy a container on Binance’s infrastructure before executing the rogue withdrawals.

While Binance describes this attack as highly sophisticated, there were multiple security failures involved that could have been avoided, from weak or absent access controls to overly broad privileges, poor credential hygiene, and employee security awareness lapses or policy violations.

“Developer workstations have quietly become some of the most privileged assets in the enterprise, carrying deployment tokens, signing access, and now AI tools that can act across internal systems on an employee’s behalf,” warns Joe Brinkley, director of offensive security research and community at security firm Cobalt. “Once an attacker controls that machine, an AI tool with broad internal reach becomes one more trusted path they can use.”

He adds: “Security teams should treat engineers with production or signing access as a high-value attack surface, test the path from workstation to production the way an adversary would, and scope AI tool permissions as tightly as any service account.”

Two compromises, months apart

The FBI has attributed the Binance breach to North Korea, identifying the hacking unit as TraderTraitor, which other researchers consider part of the broader Lazarus operation that has stolen billions of dollars from cryptocurrency platforms over the past decade. Binance’s own report relays the FBI’s conclusion and notes that throughout 2026, the company’s security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea–linked cyber threat cases.

This suggests Binance has the Lazarus APT in its threat model, as it should, and is well aware of the group’s tools, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), which include software supply-chain compromises, the use of malware that masquerades as popular legitimate tools, tricking developers with fake job interviews, and long-horizon social engineering operations. Yet, two Binance engineers fell victim to exactly these tricks, raising questions about the company’s security awareness training as well as its technical controls.

In June, a wallet-infrastructure engineer searched the web for a popular AI coding tool and downloaded a tampered Homebrew installer rather than obtaining the software from a trusted source. Homebrew is a package manager and distribution channel for open-source applications on macOS. Binance’s security team detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and rotated all related credentials, but the attackers had already learned who the engineer was and who else worked on the wallet infrastructure team.

It’s good that Binance was able to quickly detect the breach, but the incident raises the question of why an engineer was installing software from a search result at all. Does Binance have a policy that employees install software only from approved sources, and is this enforced with technical controls such as application whitelisting?

Three months later, the attackers approached a second engineer through a job-hunting platform, posing as a project director recruiting for a company that did not exist. Two staged interviews followed: one with a purported HR representative who shared a social media account filled with personal photos and videos to build trust, and one with someone claiming to be the company’s CEO.

At the end of the second interview, the engineer was told to download a coding assignment onto their work computer from a repository. The assignment included malicious code, and this time Binance’s endpoint protection tools did not detect it. The company described this as zero-day malware, but if endpoint protection tools were only capable of detecting known malware, then the whole industry has a problem.

Either way, the developer’s actions raise a number of questions regarding security policies, procedures, and awareness at Binance, first among them: Why was the engineer doing job interviews and test assignments on their work computer? Why did they clone a repository directly on their system instead of using a virtual machine? If this is something they regularly do, then it points to lapses in security training or intentional policy violations. And companies cannot solely rely on employees always following policies. They need detection and enforcement mechanisms.

“The engineer did multiple things wrong,” says Tim Chase, AVP for cybersecurity at human-risk management company Fable Security. “A modern risk program should have ensured he understood the modern [attack] surface of social engineering that attackers are using today.”

Binance did not respond to CSO’s questions on whether it had policies in place that explicitly prohibited the developer’s actions on work computers and whether its employee training covered the fake recruitment social engineering tactic commonly used by North Korean hackers.

An overprivileged AI tool enables lateral movement

Once the attackers had malware running on the engineer’s computer, they were able to use an internal AI tool present on it to pivot to additional machines belonging to two other engineers from the wallet infrastructure team.

Binance did not clarify the purpose of this tool in its report or to CSO, but the fact that it could be used by one compromised user to access different computers suggests its privileges were too broad or that it lacked proper access controls. This is hinted at by the company in its list of remediation steps, which included: “Rebuilt the affected internal AI tool and access controls.”

On one of the additional engineering computers, the attackers found a token with permissions to deploy new containers on the company’s infrastructure. Nine days later they used this token on a different compromised engineering computer to deploy a container with a malicious script that interacted with the wallet signing service and initiated withdrawals.

This series of events raises additional questions about credential hygiene and access controls because Binance’s report doesn’t describe any additional checks. Why was the token long-lived and not ephemeral for a single operation? Did deployment of containers to production involve additional validation or approval steps? Is there any authentication between the deployed container and the signing service, or was being on the same trusted network enough? Binance did not respond to CSO’s questions about any of these points.

“An internal AI tool that can reach engineers’ systems holds the same kind of access as a privileged employee, and most organizations don’t govern it that way,” says Justin Beals, CEO of Strike Graph. “Expect more groups to copy this playbook against anyone holding signing keys, deployment tokens, or production access. Security leaders should treat engineers with production access, and the AI tools those engineers use, as privileged identities. That means restricting what gets installed on work machines, expiring deployment tokens quickly, and logging and reviewing what internal AI tools actually do.”

Shlomi Salem, co-founder of Neo, a startup focused on AI agent security, predicted the AI attack vector days before Binance released its findings. “I wouldn’t be surprised if investigators find a poisoned package, a misused agent, or both at the start of this chain,” he said on Oct. 30 after the breach was announced.

The takeaway for organizations is that internal AI tools are now part of the attack surface and need to be tested accordingly, Bri Frost, director of product management at Cloud Range, tells CSO.

“When an AI tool can reach other systems on an employee’s behalf, an attacker who controls that employee’s machine may inherit everything the tool can do,” she says. “That changes the question security teams need to answer. It’s not only whether the model gives good answers, but what it will do, and for whom, when a request comes from a compromised session.”

Title: Scammers use AI-generated images of missing pets to extort owners
Context: Messages like these exploit two powerful emotions in quick succession: relief that a beloved pet has been found, followed by fear that something terrible will happen unless the...
Full Text:
When your pet goes missing, it can be totally heartbreaking.

So hearing that they’ve been found is no doubt very welcome news. Even better to see a photo of them looking safe and well.

But while the photo may look exactly like your pet, that doesn’t mean the person who sent it has your pet or even ever saw it.

The BBC reports how criminals are sending owners AI-generated images of their missing pets, demanding money for their return, and sometimes threatening to harm the animals when owners refuse to pay.

The BBC interviewed two targets of this scam who were both contacted after posting a missing pet message on social media. The scammers sent them pictures of their beloved pets and demanded a ransom for their safe return.

Messages like these exploit two powerful emotions in quick succession: relief that a beloved pet has been found, followed by fear that something terrible will happen unless the owner acts immediately.

The scam typically follows this pattern:

A scammer finds a missing pet appeal, which is typically posted to social media or local sites with an accompanying photo and contact details.

The scammer contacts the owner and claims to have found the animal. An image fabricated with the help of AI makes the claim appear more convincing.

They ask for money which may be described as a reward or as payment for emergency treatment.

They add pressure. They might refuse to meet until payment arrives, or threaten to sell or harm the pet.

Our data backs this report up. Over the last month, people anonymously submitted three distinctive types of pet related scam attempts to Malwarebytes Scam Guard:

“We found your missing cat” message, with photos: Someone claimed to have found a user’s missing cat and had images of it.

Found pet callback lure: A voicemail claimed to have found a lost cat and supplied a callback number.

Humane Society impersonation and payment demand: A caller claimed a missing cat needed emergency surgery, and demanded successive Zelle payments.

How to stay safe

Sadly, while it can be very useful to use social media to retrieve lost pets, it also attracts scammers and other abuse.

You don’t have to stop asking for help online, but you can put some safeguards between an unexpected message and any payment.

Keep some identifying details private. Leave a distinctive feature out of the public description so you can ask a supposed finder about it later.

Do not pay in advance to secure a reunion. Be particularly wary of someone who insists that you send money before they will let you see the animal. Arrange any legitimate handover in a safe, public location, and verify that it is your pet before paying a reward.

Verify veterinary claims independently. If someone says your pet is at an animal hospital, find the hospital’s contact details yourself and call it directly. Do not rely on the number or payment link in the message.

A second pair of eyes can help you assess a demand without the same emotional pressure. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can help you identify whether a message might be a scam and how to proceed.

If someone is threatening your pet, remember that when they make threats to your pet, it is very likely they don’t have a clue where it is either, so don’t let them extort you.

Title: Bring a tent, I've got the coffee: Lessons from it-sa
Context: This commoditized threat allows even low-level actors to bypass security measures like Chrome's App-Bound Encryption and receive ranked target assessments, escalating the risk...
Full Text:
Welcome to this week's edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

I'm just back from an interesting and demanding week of booth duty at it-sa Expo&Congress in Nuremberg, where Talos had a Point of Demonstration at the Cisco booth.

I personally see it-sa as the German or European counterpart to the RSA Conference in San Francisco, with a slightly different center of gravity in at least two dimensions.

First, the expo is the main event, not the congress. The congress is organized by associations, industry groups, and exhibitors, and plays more of a supporting role. Second, the focus is more local and European. Major topics were (of course) AI for defense tooling, securing AI systems themselves, and post-quantum cryptography. And here comes the local touch (in my opinion): digital sovereignty and regulatory compliance, with NIS2, CRA, and DORA.

But local doesn't translate to small, or to the city of Nuremberg. With more than 1,000 exhibitors and 33,000 visitors from 70 countries over three days of exhibition, preceded by a congress day, it was huge. Even as a trade show veteran, I was overwhelmed.

My conversations at the booth had a different focus, though. It was a lot of chatter about vulnerabilities like php2shell or broccoli2shell and state-sponsored actors, but again with a local touch: education.

I was very surprised how many teenagers stopped by to ask for advice. Here in Germany, you mainly have two paths for your career. One is the university route, and the other is vocational (apprenticeship). Across all industries the split is roughly 50/50, while in IT it is more like 80% university, 20% apprenticeship. The common minimum age to start university is 18, while it is 16 for apprenticeships. Reality is way more complex, but the details don’t matter for the point I want to make.

For university opportunities in cyber, I count close to 30 bachelor programs. For apprenticeships, I count ZERO. There is the "IT Specialist" (Fachinformatiker), but it only has specializations like application development, system integration, digital networking, or data and process analysis. That is why an initiative exists to get an "IT Security" specialization going.

Even the degree route is thin. There are no official statistics, but my guess is 800 to 900 graduates a year, compared to a demand of more than 100,000. We need a second route into the field for the 16-year-old who finished various CTFs or Hack the Box challenges and wants to join the good side now. Honestly speaking, I would rather have them on our side of the fence at 16 than wonder at 26 where they ended up.

How does it look in your country?

On a personal note: If you consider visiting it-sa in 2027, book your accommodation early. The hotels are gone fast. That is the one downside, because Nuremberg isn't exactly a city with the infrastructure for more than 30,000 visitors. (Don't ask me how I learned that there are also camping spots close to the exhibition area.)

The one big thing

Cisco Talos recently discovered VOLTA, a mature, self-deleting Windows infostealer that uses AI to act as a personal intelligence analyst for cybercriminals. After harvesting a massive haul of credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to a large language model to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value. The malware even uses stolen session access to enrich this data, searching the victim's emails for purchase receipts to corroborate home addresses. If an AI model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA seamlessly fails over to a multi-model chain to ensure the attackers get their prioritized dossier.

Why do I care?

VOLTA replaces the manual work of data sorting with automated, AI-driven victim profiling. By letting an LLM determine a target's worth, attackers drastically reduce the human effort required to monetize stolen data. This commoditized threat allows even low-level actors to bypass security measures like Chrome's App-Bound Encryption and receive ranked target assessments, escalating the risk of severe follow-on attacks.

So now what?

Organizations should implement application control policies to restrict or alert on processes launching Chrome with the --headless flag. Defenders must also enforce best practices for storing credentials in hardware-backed stores.

Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device. Title: Inside ARTEX: How Autonomous AI Agents Are Being Used in Real-World Cyberattacks
Context: Attacks can run almost entirely autonomously: Once operators set an initial goal, agents handled vulnerability discovery and exploitation with little to no further human direction
Full Text:
AI agents are already changing how cyberattacks are carried out. Check Point Research (CPR) analyzed ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing platform increasingly adopted by cybercriminals and gained rare visibility into how attackers are using autonomous agents from inside their own operator consoles.

The findings show that attackers can set an initial objective and leave AI agents to independently find vulnerabilities, exploit systems and pursue that goal at scale, often with very little human involvement.

Key Findings

ARTEX is already operating at scale: CPR identified 2,557 systems that hosted ARTEX, including 1,608 live, publicly accessible instances at the time of the research.

Attacks can run almost entirely autonomously: Once operators set an initial goal, agents handled vulnerability discovery and exploitation with little to no further human direction.

One campaign generated 400,791 agent messages across 292 objectives without further operator prompting, showing the scale at which autonomous attacks can operate.

AI agents achieved serious compromises: They exploited vulnerabilities including remote code execution, exposed databases and cloud credentials, and in one case independently identified and executed a supply chain compromise.

Autonomy still has limits: Despite finding serious vulnerabilities, the crypto campaign generated $0 for the attacker, with agents sometimes mistaking successful API responses for successful cryptocurrency theft.

What Is ARTEX?

ARTEX is an open-source, AI-powered penetration testing platform originally designed to help security teams test systems they own or are authorized to assess. It connects large language models (LLMs) with multiple AI agents that can plan tests, run security tools, investigate vulnerabilities and document their findings.

After ARTEX was observed in attacks against South Korean banks, its developer made the original project closed-source. However, maintained forks and backups have kept the platform available.

CPR identified 2,557 systems that currently or previously hosted ARTEX panels, including 1,608 live and publicly accessible instances at the time of the research. Many additional ARTEX deployments are likely to be inaccessible from the public internet because they operate behind firewalls or within local networks.

Most importantly, researchers discovered 10 misconfigured ARTEX instances exposing their full databases. This provided visibility into the operator side of the attacks, including the models being used, instructions given by operators and the steps taken independently by the AI agents.

Figure 1 – ARTEX Panel

How Autonomous Are ARTEX Cyberattacks?

The research shows that in many observed cases, ARTEX required remarkably little interaction from its operators once an objective had been established.

Rather than continuously directing attacks step by step, operators frequently issued a goal and left the agent fleet to work toward it. Human interactions were largely limited to checking progress, asking whether a target had been compromised or occasionally adjusting priorities.

In one cryptocurrency campaign, 292 campaign objectives produced 230 findings and 400,791 agent messages without any additional operator prompting after the initial goals were set.

This provides a direct look at how agentic hacking changes the role of a cybercriminal. The human can establish the desired outcome, while AI agents perform much of the reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery and exploitation required to pursue it.

Which AI Models Are Cybercriminals Using With ARTEX?

Across the 10 exposed ARTEX instances analyzed by CPR, Chinese AI models dominated, with models from the DeepSeek Flash family appearing most frequently.

American models were configured on three instances. Researchers observed guardrails being triggered only while Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 was being used, after which the operator switched to more permissive Chinese models.

The findings suggest that attackers are not simply experimenting with AI models. They are selecting models according to practical operational considerations, including capability, cost and restrictions.

Which Industries Are Being Targeted, and Where Is ARTEX Infrastructure Hosted?

The observed campaigns were predominantly opportunistic and financially motivated, rather than attacks focused on a single predefined organization.

CPR observed agents targeting organizations and infrastructure connected to:

Cryptocurrency and digital asset services

Online gambling, slots and card-game platforms

Payment infrastructure and crypto payment services

Over-the-counter crypto trading and custody services

Gray-market iOS application signing services

Attack objectives ranged from stealing cryptocurrency and code-signing certificates to compromising gaming accounts and conducting denial-of-service attacks against gambling websites. Agents exploited vulnerabilities including weak or hardcoded passwords, missing authentication, insecure direct object references and remote code execution.

The infrastructure behind ARTEX also has a significant global footprint. Among the live ARTEX servers identified by CPR, 882 (54%) were hosted in the United States, 295 (18%) in Hong Kong and 103 (6%) in China. These figures describe the hosting locations of ARTEX servers, not the geographic distribution of attack victims.

Figure 2 – Location of observed ARTEX C&C servers

How Did ARTEX Agents Steal Apple Code-Signing Certificates?

One operator tasked ARTEX with attacking gray-market iOS signing services to obtain Apple code-signing certificates that could potentially be resold.

Two ARTEX consoles operated in parallel for roughly two weeks, targeting 10 signing shops. Instead of directing agents through every stage of the attack, the operator primarily asked questions such as “What’s the progress?” and “Which one is closest to the goal?”

The agents independently searched compromised systems for certificate databases and then validated stolen certificates by checking passwords, private keys, Apple revocation status, expiration dates and associated provisioning profiles.

They ultimately obtained more than 300 certificates and their passwords, with three certificates passing the full validation process, meaning they could be used to sign arbitrary iOS applications.

The scale came at a relatively low cost. The operation processed approximately 36 billion tokens, with CPR estimating the AI model costs at $700 to $1,500 based on official DeepSeek API pricing at the time of writing.

Figure 3 – Example gray-market signing certificate service with more than 90,000 subscribers

Can Autonomous Hacking Agents Carry Out Supply Chain Attacks?

A second campaign shows how far an AI agent can progress independently once given a broader financial objective. An operator tasked agents with stealing cryptocurrency from hundreds of targets. During a later attempt to identify and compromise the infrastructure associated with a specific cryptocurrency wallet, an agent discovered an unauthenticated API exposing AWS S3 credentials.

Those credentials provided write access to a bucket containing iOS applications and landing pages for a cryptocurrency service. The agent independently reasoned through the possibility of compromising this distribution infrastructure, executed the write and verified the attack chain.

The original file was later restored, and there was no evidence that the operator ultimately profited from the compromise. However, the activity demonstrates that an agent pursuing one objective can identify and act on a supply chain compromise opportunity without being explicitly instructed to do so.

Where Do Autonomous Hacking Agents Still Fail?

Autonomy does not necessarily translate into successful outcomes. In the cryptocurrency campaign, the agents processed 167.5 million tokens and identified multiple vulnerabilities, including remote code execution and exposed databases. Yet across 292 objectives, 230 findings and 400,791 agent messages, the attacker made no money.

Some agents even incorrectly reported successful cryptocurrency cash-outs because APIs returned a “success” response. The attacker’s wallet showed a $0 balance and no transactions, exposing a significant weakness: agents can successfully execute technical tasks while still misunderstanding whether the intended real-world objective has actually been achieved.

What Does Agentic Hacking Mean for Cybersecurity Teams?

ARTEX shows that agentic hacking is already part of the cyber threat landscape. CPR observed more than 1,600 live publicly accessible ARTEX instances, while the exposed databases provide direct evidence of agents operating with very limited human supervision.

For defenders, the important change is scale and speed. A cybercriminal can task agents with investigating large numbers of targets simultaneously, allowing vulnerabilities across internet-facing systems to be discovered and exploited with considerably less manual effort.

At the same time, the research demonstrates the current limitations of these systems. Agents hallucinate, misunderstand results and may fail to achieve their underlying objective even after successfully compromising systems.

Organizations should therefore expect greater automated pressure against exposed infrastructure. Internet-facing systems should be continuously tested and hardened, with particular attention paid to weak authentication, exposed APIs, credential leakage, remote code execution vulnerabilities and cloud storage permissions.

The ARTEX campaigns provide a glimpse of a threat model that is already taking shape: attackers define the objective, while increasingly autonomous AI agents do much of the work required to pursue it.

For the full technical analysis, read the research from Check Point Research here.

Full Text:
Key Points Agentic hacking platforms like ARTEX, where AI models autonomously drive vulnerability discovery and exploitation, have been observed to be used by various cyber criminals. Check Point Research’s analysis of the current landscape observed more than 1,800 publicly exposed instances for ARTEX alone, showing a massive scale of deployments. While previous threat reports on ARTEX focused on the observed telemetry on the victim side, we present artifacts from the operator consoles. This data shows which models were used as well as how the operators prompted their agents. Most attacks were fully autonomous besides the initial goal setup. Threat actors barely interacted with their agent fleets. In the observed activity, Chinese models are most prevalent, with Deepseek Flash taking the lead. Operators mostly only interacted with their agents to check the progress of the current operations – attacks were almost fully autonomous. The goals set by the attackers were exclusively to carry out opportunistic, financially motivated cybercrime, mostly on a broad scale. Agents abused various web vulnerabilities, such as Remote Code Execution (RCE), to achieve their goals. In some cases, agents were using the access gained to actively carry out supply chain attacks. Introduction ARTEX is a Chinese open-source, AI-powered penetration testing platform designed to help security teams assess systems they own or are authorized to test. It uses large language models (LLMs) to coordinate multiple AI agents that plan tests, run security tools, and record evidence of potential vulnerabilities. Its web dashboard brings together assets, testing progress, captured traffic, and findings, allowing users to monitor activity and guide the agents. By linking each investigation to specific assets and supporting vulnerability retesting, ARTEX aims to reduce repetitive work while keeping human oversight central to the testing process. After the tool was observed in attacks against South Korean banks, its developer decided to make the project closed-source on October 8th. However, various maintained forks and backups of the original repository keep the tool publicly available to threat actors. Figure 1 – ARTEX Panel. As described further below, artifacts obtained by Check Point Research show that these systems can work fully autonomously after the initial goal has been set by the operator. Using agentic hacking frameworks like ARTEX, threat actors can carry out attacks at a previously impossible speed, on a broad scale and without any technical knowledge, opening the field to a large set of people. Besides ARTEX, other frameworks such as CyberStrike, Cairn or PentAGI offer similar capabilities. Check Point Research also observed various other custom agentic hacking frameworks in the wild. While some of these are based on open-source tools such as those mentioned above, others are written from the ground up. Figure 2 – Custom agentic hacking framework “PZZ”. While many ARTEX instances are hidden behind firewalls or are set up in local networks, threat actors often expose administrative interfaces to the internet, to make them accessible remotely. Check Point Research found 2,557 systems hosting or having hosted ARTEX panels, with 1,608 live and publicly available instances at the time of the research. A metadata analysis of these servers gives valuable insights into the distribution and usage. Additionally, 10 instances were misconfigured to expose the full ARTEX database – giving a rare insight into how actors prompted their agents, which models were used and the exact steps and attacks the agents carried out. Model Usage In the analyzed 10 instances, Chinese models dominate the share of configured LLMs, with models of the Deepseek Flash family being the most prevalent. With American models configured on 3 different instances, we observed guardrails being hit only when using Anthropic’s Opus 5.5. Here, the actor subsequently switched to more permissive Chinese models. Figure 3 – Model usage. Observed Campaigns The campaigns observed, targeted various industries, with goals ranging from acquiring cryptocurrency, and stealing code-signing certificates or gaming accounts from grey-market infrastructure to carrying out Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks against gambling sites. Almost all of these campaigns can be classified as opportunistic cybercrime – operations with a broad scope instead of a single target. Three example campaigns are described below. The observed ARTEX instances were running in default configurations using default tools. To get around WAF restrictions, IP blocks and obscure traffic, many operators configured their agents to use residential proxies. One operator created a dedicated skill for proxy-usage. Campaign 1 – Apple Certificate Heist Apple’s iOS code-signing ecosystem has given rise to an underground market for .p12 code signing certificates and their associated provisioning profiles. Possession of such a certificate enables signing iOS apps and sideloading them, bypassing the official App Store. A 2026 study found that these certificates are distributed in a network of gray-market certificate marketplaces and signing services, with a large share of them located in China. Use-cases range from modifying existing applications to bypass restrictions or add features to injecting libraries that exfiltrate sensitive data or introduce other malware. Figure 4 – Example gray-market signing certificate service with more than 90,000 subscribers. One ARTEX operator was observed tasking their agent fleet with compromising those gray-market signing shops themselves in order to steal their certificates and resell them. The operator ran two ARTEX consoles in parallel for roughly two weeks (from 2026-10-14 to 2026-10-29) using the Deepseek v4.1 Flash and Kimi K3.1 Pro models. In total, the operator worked through 36 billion tokens, consisting of 2.13 billion input tokens (cache miss), 33.79 billion input tokens (cache hit), and 473.9 million output tokens. According to the official DeepSeek API prices at the time of writing, this amounts to a cost somewhere between $700 and $1500. The operator targeted a total of 10 different signing shops, with the goal of the task set to “get a p12 certificate + password”. Once an agent managed to break into a signing shop, the agents searched for the 证书库 (cert library), a database full of .p12 files and their respective plaintext passwords. Once that database was obtained, agents ran a validation pipeline on each compromised key: Validate the password by trying to decrypt the key Check if the private key matches the certificate Check Apple’s OCSP for revocation Checking the expiration date Checking if there is a matching In-House profile (a .mobileprovision file which is needed to complete signing of an application) To gain initial access to the signing shop’s infrastructure the agents used the following vulnerabilities: Hardcoded administrator passwords in SPA JavaScript bundles Missing authentication on Web APIs Remote Code Execution (RCE) through command injection Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR) Weak administrative credentials RCE through Server Side Template Injection (SSTI) One case additionally involved privilege escalation on a Linux host from a low privileged user to root through overly permissive folder access. In total, the agents managed to get more than 300 certificates and their passwords. After the agents validated them, three certificates passed the checklist. These could thus be used to sign arbitrary iOS applications and be sold by the operator. Operator prompting The interaction of the threat actor with its agents was minimal: most messages are simply asking about the progress of the operations and whether specific certificates have already been obtained. As such, the agents were working almost entirely autonomously. With Deepseek v4 Pro being used, which is more expensive than its Flash counterpart, the costs for this operation can be estimated somewhere between $145 and $300. However, the original manifest file was restored later by the bucket owners and the operator’s wallet still shows a balance of 0 and zero transactions, which means that the write was successful, but the compromise was not properly exercised. In this campaign, the goal was money instead of access. Across 292 campaign objectives, 230 findings and 400,791 agent messages, not one cent moved to the attackers pockets. While agents found loads of RCEs and were able to dump databases, there are no signs that the actor is interested in turning these into money through traditional means, such as brokering data or access on cybercrime forums. Testing found that roughly 3,3% were still valid – which sums up to around 6,000 compromised accounts. 已实证有效：分层抽样验证出 29 组账号实时可用，含 Lv417 超凡I(3451分)、Lv232 铂金III、Lv226 超凡II 等高价值账号，可读到游戏列表/时长/段位/封禁/禁言/点券/金币/Q币。REDACTED 主库 19 万条抽样命中率 3.3%（推算约 6000 条仍有效）。 “Proven effective: Stratified sampling has verified that 29 sets of accounts are currently active, including high-value accounts such as Lv417 Superb I (3,451 points), Lv232 Platinum III, and Lv226 Superb II. These accounts allow access to game lists, playtime, rank, bans, mutes, points, gold, and Q Coins. REDACTED Main Database: 190,000 records with a hit rate of 3.3% (estimated to have approximately 6,000 records still valid).” Besides this unauthenticated attack surface, the agents discovered various hardcoded administrative credentials in frontend JavaScript bundles and HTML source code. This campaign demonstrates exactly what makes agentic hacking dangerous: it is not necessarily the complexity of attacks, but the breadth and perseverance at which LLMs can audit a scope and test every endpoint, front end bundle and site, non-stop until an objective is achieved. Operator Prompting None. Beyond the initial task goals, the agents ran fully autonomously. Analysis of C&C Infrastructure The individual campaigns provide insight into ARTEX’s operational use cases and the actors using it. However, examining the full set of identified Command-and-Control domains and IPs offers a more comprehensive view of its infrastructure. Timeline of ARTEX C&C Servers Following the deletion of the original ARTEX project on September 8, numerous forks emerged. The number of newly created ARTEX C&C servers spiked in mid-October, coinciding with prominent public reporting about the project. Figure 6 – ARTEX C&Cs created. Geographic Distribution Inspecting the geolocations of live ARTEX servers shows that the largest amounts are hosted in the US (882, 54%), Hong Kong (295, 18%) and China (103, 6%). Figure 7 – Location of observed ARTEX C&C servers. Version Statistics ARTEX exposes a version tag, which is either set to the default of dev or derived from the latest Git commit, if ARTEX is built in a Git tree. This tag can thus serve as a campaign- or actor-identifier. Figure 8 – ARTEX versions/tags. The default dev tag, which was most commonly observed, does not indicate a relationship. Other more unique tags, when combined with signals such as a shared ASN and other services running on the same hosts, show the following three clusters, which we believe with high confidence are managed by the same operators: Tag IPs Total Hosts ASN Country sco-fix2 38.11.173.1-125, 38.11.221.1-125, 198.200.59.85-89 255 AS54600 PEG TECH INC USA Changing tag, e.g. dev-db-resilience-20261031 . Observed update of all hosts at the same time. 103.122.245.194, .198, .199, .204, .214, .215, .216, .217, .218, .219 10 AS152918 Liberally Network LLC Thailand Rolling slug (0.3.15-pro.* ). Observed synchronous version bump, where * is a rolling version 192.236.172.197, 198.44.123.66, 204.44.66.81, 104.168.112.237 5 AS36352 HostPapa USA It is important to note that a shared tag by itself simply means that the ARTEX versions were built from the same or a similar commit (or being run from the same docker base image); the tag is thus more of a clustering hint than an unique identifier. Conclusion Agentic hacking tools like ARTEX are already a part of the threat landscape: more than a thousand publicly available servers have been observed for ARTEX alone, and many more are hidden in local networks or behind firewalls. These tools allow cybercriminals to execute operations at an unprecedented speed and with capabilities beyond the actors actual technical proficiency. Analysis of agent conversations revealed that these systems work almost fully autonomously, once the initial goal is set: most actors barely interacted with their agent fleets and mostly asked for progress or directed the agents to a new target. The vast majority of the analyzed actors used Chinese AI models, with models of the Deepseek Flash family being the most prevalent. These models did not show any signs of guardrails when executed under the “Pentest” framing of ARTEX and provide a good balance of capabilities and cost. Agents have been observed to exploit various vulnerabilities, from weak or hardcoded passwords, to remote code execution (RCE) and business logic vulnerabilities – with the impact of system compromise, data leakage or even supply chain compromise. Companies can expect to be exposed to a high volume of attacks, if being target of an agentic hacking campaign. Systems in the exposed perimeter should be tested and hardened accordingly. Context: In September, purchase order and payroll lures used disguised archives to deliver Agent Tesla, malware commonly used to collect credentials and other information
