Title: Dreeze raises $33 million to automate recovery of entire cloud applications
Context: “With cyber threats increasing and AI introducing new risks, enterprises need to assume that critical applications will go down
Full Text:
Dreeze emerged from stealth with $33 million in seed funding and announced the general availability of its Application Revival platform for Amazon Web Services (AWS). Norwest and Bessemer Venture Partners led the round, with participation from Claltech. The platform helps enterprises recover complete cloud applications by restoring data, infrastructure, and dependencies in the order they need to come back online.

A successful backup can still leave a business offline. Cloud applications rely on infrastructure, configurations, identities, secrets, keys, and connections that must be restored alongside the data. When those pieces are missing, IT teams have to track down credentials, consult old runbooks, and rebuild dependencies by hand. Dreeze calls this the “recovery scramble.” It can leave an application offline for days or even weeks after its data has been restored.

“Our customers have moved production workloads into the public cloud, and most of them can back up that data without much trouble. Recovery is what worries them: getting a whole application running again, with every dependency in the right order,” said Jeremy Miller, CEO of Coravant. “Dreeze was built around that problem, which is why we wanted to work with them from the start.”

Application Revival gives teams a way to test recovery before an outage. The platform maps each application’s dependencies as its environment changes, backs up the resources it needs, and automatically generates a recovery plan. Teams can run that plan end to end to verify that it brings the application back online.

“Companies have spent years getting better at backing up data, but getting the data back doesn’t mean the business is back,” said Ziv Kedem, CEO of Dreeze. “With cyber threats increasing and AI introducing new risks, enterprises need to assume that critical applications will go down. We started Dreeze because recovery needs to go further. Our goal is to make Application Revival the new standard, so companies know they have a proven path to bring their applications back when something goes wrong.”

Introducing Application Revival

Know – Autonomous Dependency Mapping: Maps cloud resources and dependencies to the applications they support and generates a recovery plan based on the live environment as it changes.

Protect – Vaulted Backup: Backs up the data, configurations, keys, and other resources an application needs to run. Backups are stored in an immutable, air-gapped vault, with optional replication across regions.

Orchestrate – Revival Automation: Runs the recovery plan, restoring data, infrastructure, configurations, identities, and connections in dependency order.

Validate – Revival Confidence: Runs an automated, end-to-end recovery test that brings up a working application without affecting production or requiring manual cleanup.

“At Kashya, Zerto and now at Dreeze, Ziv, Oded and Avi have spent decades together building recovery technology that enterprises rely on. They know first-hand how the market needs to evolve,” said Dror Nahumi, general partner at Norwest. “As cloud environments grow more complex and the cost of downtime rises, enterprises need a better way to prepare for failure. Few teams understand the recovery problem as deeply as this one.”

Dreeze for Microsoft Azure is in early access, with general availability planned for early 2027.

Context: The window between a vulnerability going public and being exploited has shrunk from years to weeks
Full Text:
In October, two critical PHP vulnerabilities went public before a patch was ready. PHP runs beneath a large share of the web, often inside software that bundles it without saying so, so updating the applications on top of it changed nothing. Hundreds of thousands of internet-facing systems were exposed, and many had never been watched as risks.

This is the new normal. The window between a vulnerability going public and being exploited has shrunk from years to weeks. Title: JFrog Names Nine Global Winners for Inaugural Software Supply Chain Excellence Awards

Full Text:
JFrog announced completion of the first-ever Software Supply Chain Excellence Awards, recognizing the teams who have turned their software supply chain into a competitive advantage – unifying development, security and operations around a governed, automated ecosystem that delivers trusted software at scale.

The nine honorees span the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific, across three categories: Unified Platform, Trusted AI Adoption, and Software Supply Chain Security.

“Agents now write, review and deploy code faster than ever, while malicious AI models, agent skills and extensions are turning up in the registries developers use daily. Increasing regulations require proof at every step – from code to runtime,” said Roie Shorer, Chief Growth Officer at JFrog. “The companies that pull ahead in the AI era will be those going beyond simply automating for speed and scale. They will be the ones who can see exactly what’s shipping and why, as they bring trust, control and adaptability to their development operations. This year’s winners didn’t just add tools; they established a single source of truth where developers, security, and compliance teams can operate using the same data and the same rules. We’re very proud of all of them and thrilled to be part of their journey.”

Software supply chains are being put under new strain as developer teams grapple with AI-era software challenges. In its 2026 Software Supply Chain Security report, JFrog identified over 900 malicious AI agent skills carrying high-impact payloads alongside 495 malicious AI models on Hugging Face and 56 malicious extensions on OpenVSX. Attackers are no longer just targeting code; they are targeting the autonomous tools that write, review, and deploy it.

This year’s JFrog Software Supply Chain Excellence Award winners are working to reduce their exposure to these emerging threats by building a system of record that governs and secures artifacts from end-to-end – mastering the AI surge with speed and trust.

THE CONVERGENCE AWARD

The Convergence Award recognizes teams that unify a fragmented software delivery workflow – bringing previously disconnected repositories, scanners and tools into a single governed system of record.

Here are the winners:

Ford (Americas): Ford Motor Company has more than 15,000 developers spread across 80-plus global plants, which previously ran on separate repository tools and scanners with no shared visibility between them. By consolidating operations into a unified ecosystem with the JFrog Platform, Ford reduced tool sprawl and turned multiple blind spots into a single pane of glass view for IT and security teams. As a result, the team now manages more than 43 million artifacts on the JFrog Platform with 99.99% uptime. The team credits the consolidation with recapturing an estimated $8 million a year in developer productivity.

SCHOTTEL Industries (EMEA): Schottel replaced fragmented artifact storage and open-source consumption with the JFrog Platform. Over six months it delivered more than 32,000 artifacts, curated over 2,300 open-source packages and automatically blocked more than 900 risky ones. Manual dependency approval processes that previously delayed developers by months were replaced by automated governance and security controls, enabling faster adoption of new technologies while helping maintain its compliance and security standards.

Rakuten Symphony (APAC): Rakuten Symphony runs 28 self-hosted JFrog Enterprise+ instances across India, Japan and Singapore, that are all connected by JFrog Federated Repositories into one collaborative environment. With JFrog Curation and JFrog Advanced Security moving controls to the point of ingestion, the company cut manual triage efforts by roughly 60% in a single month across more than 600 releases, reclaiming more than 500 engineer-hours and pre-triaging over half of its vulnerability workload automatically.

THE TRUSTED INTELLIGENCE AWARD

The Trusted Intelligence Award recognizes teams that bring enterprise-grade governance to AI and model lifecycles, helping trust extend far beyond just supporting application code.

Here are the winners:

NVIDIA (Americas): Models repositories are under enterprise identity control, with a shared curation and scanning policy,which means a downloaded model faces the same checks as a package before it reaches production.

NVIDIA brought its AI model distribution surface under a governed perimeter by applying curation, scanning, and policy enforcement directly to its model mirrors. Thousands of AI model seats are now managed inside a controlled, auditable boundary, transforming what was once an unmanaged distribution surface into a demonstration of DevGovOps operating at true enterprise scale. To get there, NVIDIA leveraged JFrog Curation and JFrog’s scanning and policy tools, piloting them on the infrastructure through which its AI models flow.

Husqvarna Group (EMEA): Husqvarna’s autonomous divisions, across forest, garden and construction equipment, had accumulated overlapping scanners with limited shared visibility into software supply chain risk. After consolidating around the JFrog Platform and introducing software package scanning and policy-based controls earlier in the software development lifecycle, builds were progressively onboarded, providing teams with greater visibility into open-source dependencies and a more consistent approach to software component governance. Husqvarna Group validated JFrog Curation and JFrog Advanced Security in a hands-on pilot ahead of full deployment, and says the centralized visibility helps streamline security and governance workflows while supporting software traceability and reporting needs associated with evolving regulatory requirements, including the EU Cyber Resilience Act and NIS2.

Singapore Airlines (APAC): Singapore Airlines moved from “trust by verification” to “trust by default.” JFrog Curation and JFrog Xray now help intercept malicious, risky or non-compliant assets before they reach a build, including AI models, MCP servers, agent skills and IDE extensions. More than 95% of AI and open-source dependencies are onboarded through curated channels prior to integration. As a result, late-stage release blocks from non-compliant dependencies are down 60-75% and the airline has full visibility of its compliance posture.

THE GUARDIAN AWARD

The Guardian Award recognizes software supply chain security operating at real enterprise scale – blocking threats before they reach production across large, highly distributed environments.

Here are the winners:

S&P Global (Americas): S&P Global’s five divisions ran on independent JFrog Artifactory clusters with no shared policy enforcement which could potentially increase risk. By putting JFrog Curation at each point of ingestion – backed by continuous rescanning – S&P addressed that gap without slowing down development teams. Critical vulnerabilities across 30 images fell by 90%, from 141 to 14. S&P reports that about 99% of malicious npm and PyPI packages are now blocked at the point of ingestion, with JFrog Curation deployed as a synchronous gate for every division and JFrog Xray continuously rescanning artifacts already in use to catch newly disclosed threats.

TSB Bank (EMEA): TSB built a continuous governance platform based on JFrog’s APIs, using GitHub Actions and Open Policy Agent, as well as a versioned Python library published to JFrog Artifactory. Automated weekly audits check configuration drift, access control, artifact integrity and artifact authenticity. In the first seven months of using the platform there were 75 governance issues, 74 of which were resolved, with 11 production repositories verified for integrity every week.

Iress (APAC): Iress put the SaaS implementation of JFrog Artifactory at the center of their 600 developer operations, and added JFrog Curation and JFrog Xray to help keep zero-day threats from entering the development environment. In just eight months, the curation initiative mitigated six critical security incidents, while eliminating 90% of reactive vulnerability triage – saving the team an estimated 13,705 engineering hours for the year.

THE SELECTION PROCESS

Award winners were selected by a cross-functional panel of JFrog leaders and industry voices who scored each submission on the breadth of its story and the strength of its metrics. The complete list of winners and full category criteria are available at jfrog.com/software-supply-chain-awards.

You don’t have to be an award winner to experience the advantages of the JFrog Platform. Schedule a demo today and perhaps your team will be joining us on the podium next year.

Delinea has been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Privileged Access Management (PAM) for the eighth consecutive time.

This is our eighth time running in the Leaders Quadrant, and it comes at a moment when the identity landscape looks nothing like it did even two years ago. They're managing a fast-growing population of AI agents that need access to systems, data and each other, often with no human in the loop at all. We believe this year's recognition reflects how seriously we've taken that shift.

What changed this year

Over the past twelve months, we added just-in-time runtime authorization for AI agents. In plain terms, the same granular, time-bound access controls we've long applied to human and machine identities now extend to autonomous agents operating inside enterprise environments. An agent gets exactly the access it needs, exactly when it needs it and that access goes away the moment the task is done. Decisions are made in real-time and governed by policy.

The centralized control, session monitoring and credential management features are particularly valuable, as they help enforce strong security policies while maintaining smooth operational workflows. Lead Engineer - IT Services

We think this is what will be required for authorization going forward. Access shouldn't be a standing grant that sits around waiting to be misused. It should be a decision made in the moment, based on context and revoked automatically once that moment passes. The Gartner evaluation noted our placement on the Ability to Execute axis, and we believe our shift toward dynamic, real-time authorization is a major reason why.

Why this matters to you

If you're evaluating PAM vendors right now, here's the practical takeaway: The market is being reshaped by AI agents faster than most security programs are ready for. Every agent your teams deploy is a new identity that needs governing, and static, standing access to critical infrastructure. This is exactly the kind of attack surface that gets exploited. We feel a Leader placement is just that. We see it as an independent signal from Gartner that a vendor's approach to this problem holds up in the market on both vision and execution.

Delinea Secret Server has consistently demonstrated its value as a comprehensive and scalable PAM solution. Director, IT Security and Risk Management - IT Services

For prospects comparing options, it's a data point worth weighing alongside your own evaluation, not a substitute for it.

Where we believe Gartner evaluates us

Just-in-time (JIT) PAM has emerged as a core capability to counter potential rogue agentic AI. Delinea has delivered enhanced cloud-native JIT capabilities along with protocol-level ephemeral credential injection for servers, databases and Kubernetes. In practice, this means credentials are issued at the protocol level for the exact moment they're needed and never persist as standing access.

That eliminates a huge chunk of the attack surface that traditional privileged credentials create, because there's no credential sitting around to be stolen, harvested or forgotten about.

This is the same philosophy extended across three populations at once: humans (workforce), machines (workload) and now AI agents. One authorization model, applied consistently, rather than three separate systems bolted together.

Reliability isn’t an afterthought

None of this matters if the platform isn't there when you need it. We guarantee a 99.995% monthly availability SLA across our global regions, including the US, EU, Canada, Southeast Asia, the UK, Australia, and the UAE. When you're enforcing access controls at scale, and especially when those controls are making real-time decisions for AI agents, the platform making those decisions has to be dependable. We treat that as table stakes, not a bonus feature.

Customer experience as a differentiator

We've heard directly from customers that what sets Delinea apart isn't just the technology; it's how straightforward the platform is to deploy, how much support is available when questions come up, how clearly we help teams understand where they sit on the maturity curve and what to tackle next. Mapping against 70 real-world use cases isn't a marketing exercise; it's a practical tool that helps security teams figure out what "good" looks like in their specific environment, rather than guessing.

Delinea is a trusted partner of ours. We have received first-class product support and service through the years. Our organization values this vendor relationship. IT Security & Risk Management Associate - Banking

Looking ahead

Eight consecutive times as a Leader is a recognition we don't take lightly, and it's also not the finish line. The identity landscape keeps moving. AI agents are only going to multiply, attackers are already using AI to move faster and the organizations that get ahead of this will be the ones treating authorization as something dynamic and continuous rather than something you configure once and forget.

We plan to keep building in that direction by extending runtime authorization further, tightening the connection between identity context and access decisions and making sure that whatever population of identities shows up next in your environment, AI agent, human or machine, gets governed with the same rigor.

Title: Proofpoint CEO Sumit Dhawan On ‘Market-Changing’ $6.3B Varonis Deal, IPO Goal
Context: 3 billion deal for publicly traded Varonis was announced—Dhawan said that the planned acquisition seeks to bring together complementary technologies for securing data and AI...
Full Text:
The planned acquisition of publicly traded data security vendor Varonis will enable Proofpoint partners to deliver a ‘comprehensive data security solution to their customers,’ which is primed for combating AI and agentic risk, Dhawan tells CRN.

Amid the surging adoption of AI agents, Proofpoint’s “market-changing” deal to acquire Varonis is aimed squarely at helping partners and customers to protect the data those agents can access, Proofpoint CEO Sumit Dhawan told CRN.

In an interview Friday—a day after Proofpoint’s $6.3 billion deal for publicly traded Varonis was announced—Dhawan said that the planned acquisition seeks to bring together complementary technologies for securing data and AI agents, while giving partners an even more strategic role with their customers.

[Related: 5 Things To Know On Proofpoint’s $6.3B Acquisition Of Varonis]

The deal ultimately is positioned to enable Proofpoint partners to deliver customers a broader data security platform that is primed for combating AI and agentic risk, he said.

With the combined Proofpoint-Varonis platform that is envisioned, partners will be enabled to “take a comprehensive data security solution to their customers—becoming more strategic, providing more value-added services,” Dhawan said. “And No. 2, they now can work with a single [data security] provider with a larger business.”

The combination of Varonis with Proofpoint, which was itself publicly traded until its acquisition by private equity firm Thoma Bravo in 2021, is also poised to strengthen Proofpoint’s positioning for an initial public offering, Dhawan told CRN.

“We think it’s going to be even more attractive to public investors, and our goal would be to assess that after close,” he said.

The combined company would have more than 8,000 employees with annual recurring revenue (ARR) of more than $3 billion, according to figures disclosed by the companies.

Upon completion of the combination of the two vendors, “it’s a top-five cybersecurity company with healthy growth—and more importantly, [providing] the next frontier of protection, which is data,” Dhawan said.

What follows is more of CRN’s interview with Dhawan.

What does this deal mean for the industry and the channel?

It’s a game-changing moment—just bringing together Varonis and Proofpoint makes us the [premier] data security solution in the market, especially in the world of AI. So we’re very excited.

It sounds like the ultimate plan is for this to be a combined solution from the two companies, as opposed to being Varonis operating independently of Proofpoint?

[Varonis CEO] Yaki [Faitelson] and I started the conversations a while ago. And we always compare notes on the market and whatnot. [We are] largely complementary. And earlier this year, as this whole agentic era starts shaping up, we said, look, there is clearly a next frontier on cybersecurity emerging, which is data. AI is attacking data from outside, and AI is attacking data [from] inside. And data protection needs to be done holistically. That was the vision that brought us together—to say, not just that we can have one house that will be able to serve all the portfolio. But if you’re really providing data protection, it needs to be done with machine speed. And machine-speed level of protection, in the world of AI, means integrations of our signals and control points. And that’s what our vision is. We believe we can accomplish that very, very quickly, based on just how complementary our technology stack is.

What are you hearing from your customers and your partners about how urgent of a need there is for something like this?

The whole conviction of ours is rooted on the principle that this is a board- and CEO-level priority. [When] you think about it, AI and cybersecurity, those are the two priorities for the board and CEOs. And they go hand-in-hand. Without data security, you can’t enable and adopt AI. So to me, that sort of is the grounding fact for the conviction that we have, on why data becomes the next frontier for cybersecurity—and why Proofpoint and Varonis becomes the only player that no other [vendor] can do, [providing] a full and comprehensive solution for protecting data in today’s AI-accelerated risks.

Can you say whether the combined company will operate entirely under the Proofpoint brand, or whether Varonis will still exist as a brand in some form?

We’re going to talk through it—we’re going to think that through. Those things get sorted out as we go. [Both companies have a] strong product, strong following in the customer base. So we don’t have any desired intent to make one change or the other. But it’s something we’ll figure out between now and close [of the deal].

As far as what Varonis brings in product capabilities, what specifically are you most excited about? And what do you think partners are going to be really excited about from Varonis?

What Proofpoint has built is sensing how people and AI behave when they’re interacting with data and each other—that’s our focus area. Intent-based protection, as we’ve always talked about, when people, AI and data come together. What Varonis has built is making sure that [businesses understand] where the data is and how it is getting protected based on privileges and usage. So these are a complementary set of signals. We are getting the signals on the intent and behavior, and they’re getting the signals at the data layer. Combining the two together gives you the right protection of data in today’s AI and machine-speed era. That’s the complementary nature of the solution. I’ve gotten so many positive feedback in less than 24 hours, and it’s all been about this—[they’ve been] waiting for [a vendor] who brings data security together. And Proofpoint and Varonis, because of the complementary nature of the solution, [can] become that company.

It sounds like some of the capabilities that Varonis has in certain areas are bringing something a bit different to your platform?

We already have data security solutions. We’re the market leader for DLP [data loss prevention]. We’re the market leader for insider risk solution. Those are complementary to the data security and access governance solution that Varonis brings. You combine them together, and now you can protect data at rest, and you can protect data in motion, as used by humans and AI. So think of it as data security at two different layers, working together, through a combination of signals and protection.

Are you saying how many employees the combined company will have?

Varonis has more than 2,500 employees [and] publicly we have said we have closer to 5,500 employees. As a combined company, it’s an at-scale company. We have publicly said that our ARR exiting midyear was closer to $2.5 billion. They have publicly said a little shy of $800 million exiting June. So you’re talking about a company of scale. It’s a top-five cybersecurity company with healthy growth—and more importantly, [providing] the next frontier of protection, which is data.

Envisioning the bringing together and combining of these two companies, you would say this is going to be very differentiated?

If you look at other top-five cybersecurity companies, none of those platforms were designed and built to do data protection. They’re [from] different eras of cybersecurity—endpoint, network. We become, together, the company that protects data from external threats as well as insiders. Both are being accelerated because of AI.

On the partner front, what should partners of both companies know about what this means?

Partners are excited. It happened to be that yesterday we had a European partner council, and our head of Europe was running that partner council when the news broke. And many of them said, “Hey, look, Varonis is one of our top partners. Proofpoint is one of our top partners. Together, you become maybe the No. 1 or No. 2 partner of ours going forward.” From a partner’s perspective, No. 1, most importantly, they can take a comprehensive data security solution to their customers—becoming more strategic, providing more value-added services. And No. 2, they now can work with a single provider with a larger business—which is what partners want, anyway.

Previously you talked about potentially going public at some point—probably it’s not something you would be looking at doing prior to closing this, but is there any update there?

Like you said, our focus is going to be on [closing the acquisition]. And we hope to go through the regulatory process and close the transaction as early as possible. And then we think that the combined company is quite attractive to the public investors. It’s an at-scale company, driving protection of one of the key pillars, just like any other major cybersecurity platforms are doing. We think it’s going to be even more attractive to public investors. And our goal would be to assess that after close.

Agents are something that so many businesses are grappling with, and it sounds like this combination is very much going to be tuned toward helping companies with that?

Exactly. There isn’t a day that goes by whereby we don’t read the news about risks that AI agents pose. Risks that AI agents pose doesn’t mean you have to slow down the adoption. It just means that you need to adopt AI with the right degree of security. What are these risks going after? You read all these stories. Eventually, the issue is that these AI agents go to data [systems], and the data is captured in so many different places. So enterprises need comprehensive solution that can both work on protecting the behavior of AI and protecting the data, regardless of where it exists. And that’s what Proofpoint and Varonis offers. It provides a solution that enables enterprises to go pick any agents of their choice. They’re not locked in. Go pick and enable access to any data of their choice. And in that environment, their data is protected, and they can adopt AI with speed.

There are so many different vendors coming out and saying they’re going to have some solution to this. But it sounds like part of the idea here is if you’re already protecting the data—as you and Varonis are—then you’re really in the best position to help with the agent problem, if the agent is ultimately trying to access data?

That’s 100-percent right. There is no use solving a sliver of the problem. These are interconnected problems—because eventually, agents have to access data. By protecting data, you extend that protection to protecting AI agents. So that’s why our solution in protecting agentic security—through an extension of protecting data—becomes even more powerful and real for customers.

Overall, what is the message for your partners out of this, and what is the major opportunity for them?

Firstly, I want to thank the partners that have really built the business for us. We couldn’t do it without them. And this is game-changing. It’s a market-changing, game-changing [deal], really helping customers together with partners. We can be their strategic advisors, a platform for protecting the next frontier of cybersecurity, which is data, and all driven because of AI.

Combination creates a new cybersecurity powerhouse to deliver a complete security platform that protects against AI-accelerated threats and data risks

MIAMI, FL and SUNNYVALE, CA – October 15, 2026 – Varonis Systems, Inc. (Nasdaq: VRNS) (“Varonis”), the data and AI security leader, and Proofpoint, Inc. (“Proofpoint”), a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, today announced entrance into a definitive agreement under which Varonis will be acquired by Proofpoint, a portfolio company of Thoma Bravo, in an all-cash transaction valued at approximately $6.3 billion.

Under the terms of the agreement, Varonis shareholders will receive $49.75 per share in cash. This purchase price represents a premium of 52% to Varonis’ closing stock price of $32.71 on June 22, 2026, the last full trading day prior to initial rumors about a potential sale of the Company, and a premium of 17% over Varonis’ closing stock price of $42.35 on September 1, 2026, the last trading day prior to additional media reports speculating about a potential sale of Varonis. The transaction values Varonis at approximately 53x LTM Free Cash Flow and 8.4x LTM Revenue.1

The combined company will serve more than 16,000 enterprises and millions of organizations globally, creating one of the world’s leading pure-play cybersecurity companies and establishing the industry's largest data and AI cybersecurity organization. Together, the combined company intends to deliver a unified platform that helps organizations adopt AI with confidence: finding and protecting sensitive data, controlling what people and AI can access, and stopping data loss. Following closing, Proofpoint intends to move quickly to integrate the companies’ capabilities, align go-to-market efforts, and accelerate delivery of the combined platform to customers.

“Today begins an exciting new chapter for Varonis and our customers. It’s a testament to the incredible work of the Varonis team over two decades,” said Yaki Faitelson, Varonis CEO, Co-Founder and Chairman of the Board of Directors. “Our mission is to secure AI and the data that powers it. By joining forces with Proofpoint, we can achieve this mission faster than ever.”

Faitelson continued, “This announcement follows a comprehensive evaluation led by a committee of independent members of our Board of Directors, which included extensive outreach to a range of potential strategic and financial buyers. This transaction is an excellent outcome for the company and our shareholders, representing a realization of immediate, significant, and certain value well in excess of the risk-adjusted value of delivering against our standalone plan.”

“As AI becomes embedded across the enterprise, the data it can access determines both its value and its risk. AI agents are increasingly accessing sensitive information and taking action across systems, making it critical for organizations to understand not only what data needs protecting and who can access it, but how it is actually being used,” said Sumit Dhawan, CEO of Proofpoint. “By connecting communications, identities, permissions, data, and AI, we are creating an intelligence advantage that helps customers see risk more clearly, respond faster, and defend against the next generation of AI risks. This is a defining step in Proofpoint’s evolution into a cybersecurity platform built for the future of AI.”

Transaction Details

The transaction, which has been unanimously approved by the Varonis Board of Directors, is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to customary closing conditions, including approval by Varonis shareholders and receipt of regulatory approvals. Thoma Bravo is providing committed equity financing, and has secured debt financing commitments, to fund the purchase. Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan has also agreed to make an investment into Proofpoint in connection with the transaction. Until the transaction closes, Proofpoint and Varonis will continue to operate as separate and independent companies. Upon completion of the transaction, Varonis' common stock will cease trading on the Nasdaq, and Varonis will become a private company.

Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results

Varonis will announce its financial results for the third quarter 2026 following the close of the U.S. financial markets on November 3. The news release will be available on the Investor Relations section of the company’s website. In light of the announced transaction, Varonis will not conduct an earnings conference call.

Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC is acting as exclusive financial advisor and Paul Hastings LLP is serving as legal counsel to Varonis.

BofA Securities, Inc., Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, UBS Securities LLC, and Mizuho Securities USA LLC are serving as financial advisors, and Kirkland & Ellis LLP is serving as legal counsel to Proofpoint.

About Varonis

Varonis (Nasdaq: VRNS) secures AI and the data that powers it. The Varonis platform gives organizations automated visibility and control over their critical data wherever it lives and helps ensure safe and trustworthy AI from code to runtime. Backed by 24x7x365 managed detection and response, Varonis gives thousands of organizations worldwide the confidence to adopt AI, reduce data exposure, and stop AI-powered threats.

About Proofpoint, Inc.

Proofpoint, Inc. is a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, securing how people, data and AI agents connect across email, cloud and collaboration tools. Proofpoint is a trusted partner to over 80 of the Fortune 100, over 14,000 large enterprises, and millions of smaller organizations in stopping threats, preventing data loss, and building resilience across people and AI workflows. Proofpoint’s collaboration, data, and AI security platform helps organizations of all sizes protect their people, defend their data, and adopt AI securely and confidently. Title: Railway breach leads to $740,000 in fraudulent AI charges
Context: The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway's build infrastructure to escape filesystem isolation and obtain an internal...
Full Text:
Cloud hosting provider Railway says hackers exploited vulnerabilities in its infrastructure to steal customer authentication secrets and generate approximately $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage, potentially exposing credentials for up to 100,000 workspaces.

The company disclosed the incident on October 22, warning customers to rotate their secrets after detecting unauthorized access to systems storing environment variables.

In a new incident report published today, Railway confirms that attackers gained access to its internal source code and the decrypted customer environment variables for at most 1.85% of its workspaces, or approximately 100,000.

The company says this figure represents the maximum number of potentially impacted workspaces, rather than the confirmed number whose secrets were stolen.

The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway's build infrastructure to escape filesystem isolation and obtain an internal credential.

The attackers used the credential to access stored build histories and retrieve a copy of Railway's internal source code, which they then analyzed to identify additional ways to compromise the platform.

The attackers then exploited a second vulnerability involving an improperly configured trust relationship to gain further access to Railway's infrastructure and obtain credentials used to decrypt customer environment variables.

Railway says the attack became a roughly 26-hour battle between its engineers and threat actors using AI-powered agents to identify and exploit vulnerabilities across its infrastructure. At the same time, defenders worked to secure the systems.

"This was not a single breach followed by a single fix. The attacker probed many potential routes, in parallel, with Railway similarly hardening the routes in parallel," Railway said.

"The escalating situation became a contest of agent speed, with Railway defending against abliterated models and a harness similar to ARTEX, according to Wiz."

Railway says its investigation found that the attackers specifically searched for AI provider credentials, although some queries also targeted cloud, database, and payment service credentials.

The stolen credentials were subsequently used to generate approximately $740,000 in unauthorized AI usage, with Railway working with affected providers to reimburse customers. The company says it will cover charges that providers decline to refund.

The breach also exposed linked-account tokens belonging to 1,852 users, including GitHub OAuth tokens and AI agent keys. Railway says it reset those tokens and notified affected users.

Railway believes the attackers were focused on stealing AI credentials for resale or use in AI model distillation, linking the incident to a recent wave of attacks against AI developer platforms that security firm Wiz has dubbed "Black October."

This campaign has targeted numerous AI development platforms during the past month, including Northflank, OpenCode, Warp, and Lightning AI.

The company says the attackers were fully removed from its systems on October 21 and that all exploited vulnerabilities have since been remediated.

Railway also found no evidence that the hackers downloaded customer Git repositories or accessed customer databases.

Title: The next name on CISA's door.
Context: The streamlined questionnaire collects more granular incident data—categorizing intrusions across malware, social engineering, and insider threats—while integrating the MITRE ATT&CK framework to align observations with known adversary techniques. While only civilian federal agencies face mandatory reporting...
Full Text:
Palantir’s CISO gets the nod for CISA. Tehran takes the rap for sabotaging European grocery freezers. Russia’s Turla turns victim Exchange servers into passive spy hubs. Barracuda battles actively chained gateway zero-days. Vanderbilt grapples with a BYOD ransomware outbreak. CISA rushes patches for critical IBM and SignalWire flaws, while revamping its national incident portal. ENISA tracks the EU’s cyber maturity gap. Cryptographers debate whether AI will crack modern encryption. Our guest is Duncan Greatwood, CEO at Xage Security, discussing the cybersecurity problem you can’t patch away. Chinese AI labs set up shop in Silicon Valley's backyard.

Today is Tuesday November 10th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Trump nominates Palantir’s CISO to lead CISA.

The White House has tapped private-sector defense experience to take the helm at CISA.

President Trump nominated Michael LoSapio, chief information security officer at Palantir Technologies, to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The nomination was sent to the Senate on November ninth and awaits confirmation. If approved, LoSapio will succeed acting director Nick Andersen as the agency’s Senate-confirmed leader.

LoSapio brings over twenty years of systems engineering, cloud infrastructure, and cybersecurity experience to the role. At Palantir, he directed defenses against sophisticated nation-state adversaries, following earlier infrastructure roles at SingleStore and high-performance computing engineering at New York University.

The nomination was announced in an official statement from the White House.

CISA upgrades incident reporting portal with MITRE ATT&CK taxonomy.

CISA is revamping how organizations report cyber incidents, leaning on standardized frameworks to turn disparate breach alerts into actionable national intelligence.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency rolled out an updated reporting form on its Incident Reporting Portal. The streamlined questionnaire collects more granular incident data—categorizing intrusions across malware, social engineering, and insider threats—while integrating the MITRE ATT&CK framework to align observations with known adversary techniques. While only civilian federal agencies face mandatory reporting requirements under FISMA, CISA urges all critical infrastructure operators to voluntarily submit disclosures.

Standardizing intake across public and private sectors enables analysts to spot broader adversary campaigns faster, proving that one enterprise's early detection can secure an entire ecosystem.

Details were announced in an official agency release citing CISA’s Chris Butera.

ENISA charts EU cyber maturity amid AI and infrastructure threats.

The European Union is taking stock of its collective cyber defenses, and while overall maturity is climbing, the regional threat ecosystem refuses to stand still.

According to ENISA’s biennial State of Cybersecurity in the Union report, the bloc averaged 71.5 points out of 100 on its 2026 Cybersecurity Index. Executive Director Juhan Lepassaar credited robust supply chain governance and research initiatives, but cautioned that recent disruptions—including cyber incidents hitting industrial refrigeration systems—spotlight persistent operational gaps. The assessment also identified uneven incident response capabilities among national CSIRTs alongside an expanding global cyber skills shortage.

While legislative frameworks like the NIS2 Directive push baseline compliance, operational realities diverge as frontier artificial intelligence accelerates automated vulnerability discovery and ideologically driven hacktivism dominates incident volume.

ENISA published the report in cooperation with the European Commission and the NIS Cooperation Group under Article 18 of the NIS2 Directive.

Western officials link Iranian cyber unit to European supermarket sabotage.

State-sponsored cyber sabotage has crossed into everyday retail operations across Europe, spoiling tens of millions of dollars in food.

French officials, backed by American investigators, have tied a wave of cyber incidents affecting supermarket freezers and refrigerators across at least six European nations to Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. In France alone, actors remotely altered temperatures at over seven hundred supermarkets, forcing units into defrost cycles and triggering fires and equipment failures. The Paris prosecutor is now pursuing international arrest warrants for the group's leadership.

Targeting internet-accessible industrial control systems reveals a deliberate pivot toward low-complexity, high-impact civilian disruption, testing Western infrastructure resilience well beyond conventional military targets.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot announced the attribution during a G-7 gathering in Paris, while U.S. and European agencies continue ongoing investigations.

Cryptographers debate whether AI advances could unravel modern encryption.

While cybersecurity planners have spent years preparing for quantum decryption, a nearer-term challenge may be arriving from artificial intelligence.

Advances in machine learning are accelerating mathematical discoveries, prompting some researchers to question whether algorithmic shortcuts might unravel the foundational math securing modern encryption. Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green points to recent breakthroughs in theoretical computer science, while Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin has called for the industry to proactively develop “post-AI cryptography.”

However, other leading voices urge restraint. Coinbase head of cryptography Yehuda Lindell contends that current post-quantum algorithms are resilient, arguing that speculative panic is premature and that artificial intelligence is just as likely to help defend and harden existing cryptographic primitives.

At stake is the core premise of modern digital trust: if computational shortcuts render previously intractable mathematical problems solvable, upgrading legacy protocols before adversaries exploit them becomes a race against time.

Attackers chain Barracuda ESG flaws for root access in targeted attacks.

Barracuda Networks is urging administrators to patch immediately as threat actors actively target two critical vulnerabilities in its Email Security Gateway appliances.

Tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, the flaws allow attackers with access to an appliance's administrative interface to bypass authorization controls and execute arbitrary commands with root privileges. While patched last week, Barracuda confirmed on Monday that attackers are already exploiting the chained flaws against a limited number of customer environments. Several other Barracuda products, including its Load Balancer and Web Application Firewall, share the command injection vulnerability.

Securing perimeter email gateways remains a priority for enterprise defense, especially given past nation-state campaigns that weaponized edge appliances for persistent espionage.

Turla deploys stealthy "Cereal" malware targeting Exchange servers.

Russian state-sponsored operators are turning victim email servers into their own operational infrastructure.

ESET Research has detailed "Cereal," a sophisticated, modular .NET malware toolkit attributed to the Russian threat group Turla. Deployed against national government bodies in Kazakhstan and Romania, the malware eliminates dedicated external command-and-control servers. Instead, a passive backdoor listens for incoming malicious web requests disguised as legitimate Outlook Web Access and ActiveSync traffic. Another module, CerealBox, injects directly into Exchange's transport service, in-memory hijacking existing mail handlers to filter and stage messages involving NATO and European Union addresses.

By operating entirely within legitimate enterprise processes and unmanaged .NET image caches, the campaign evades traditional network defenses while weaponizing mission-critical servers as long-term intelligence collection hubs.

Vanderbilt University investigates a cyberattack claimed by BYOD ransomware.

Vanderbilt University is actively responding to a significant cybersecurity incident affecting campus devices, enterprise systems, and cloud infrastructure.

University officials instructed students, faculty, and staff on Monday to power down institutional hardware, disconnect from campus Wi-Fi, and alert IT to suspicious behavior. While the university has not officially confirmed the specific nature of the intrusion, the relatively new BYOD ransomware gang claimed responsibility on its data leak site. The group claims to have encrypted databases and exfiltrated research files alongside personal records for over one million individuals.

Targeting major academic research hubs underscores how rapidly evolving ransomware operations threaten both critical intellectual property and sensitive community data.

CISA adds actively exploited IBM and SignalWire bugs to KEV catalog.

CISA has added critical vulnerabilities affecting IBM Aspera Faspex and SignalWire FreeSwitch to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Both flaws carry CVSS scores of 9.8. The Faspex bug permits authorization bypass for full administrative takeover, while the FreeSwitch defect enables arbitrary command execution via crafted SIP messages. Mandated under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, federal civilian agencies must apply vendor patches within three days.

Rapid cataloging of these flaws underscores federal urgency to seal network-accessible enterprise tools before widespread automated exploitation takes hold.

Title: CISA Expands Incident Reporting Form While CIRCIA Mandate Waits
Context: More Granular Questions Add ATT&CK Terms The revised form asks whether an incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat
Full Text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has rolled out a revamped cyber incident reporting form that asks more granular questions about incident types and frames observed activity in MITRE ATT&CK terms.

CISA outlined the changes in an announcement published November 9 and the updated web-based questionnaire is available through its Incident Reporting Portal.

The agency said better data quality will help it connect related threat activity into broader trends that would otherwise look like separate incidents. The update draws on community feedback CISA has received over the years.

More Granular Questions Add ATT&CK Terms

The revised form asks whether an incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat. Questions about observed activity now use MITRE ATT&CK, a framework for describing adversary behavior that CISA said is familiar to the cyber community.

The changes are meant to support rapid but thorough threat analysis, according to CISA.

"In the team sport of cybersecurity, one organization's detection is another's protection," said Chris Butera, CISA's acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity. "As the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity and resilience, CISA is able to leverage such incident reporting to identify emerging cyber campaigns, warn potential targets, and strengthen the Nation's collective defense."

For now, only federal civilian agencies are required to report incidents to CISA. The agency encouraged other organizations that experience an incident to report voluntarily, and information they submit can be protected from disclosure under the Protected Critical Infrastructure Information (PCII) Program.

CIRCIA Rule Remains at White House

The update comes as the final rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) awaits approval. The rule went to the White House for review on October 1 and remains listed as pending.

Read more on CIRCIA: US Critical Infrastructure Braces for Sweeping New Cyber Reporting Rules

Once the rule takes effect, covered critical infrastructure organizations would have to report qualifying cyber incidents within 72 hours of reasonably believing they occurred and ransom payments within 24 hours of making them, according to CISA.

CISA published its proposed CIRCIA rule in April 2024 but missed an October 2025 statutory deadline to finalize it. Many comments on the proposal asked for a narrower scope, less burden and closer alignment with other federal reporting rules, according to CISA's regulatory agenda.

CISA's announcement did not mention CIRCIA or whether the enhanced reporting form would be used under the pending rule.

Title: Blind Eagle Uses Fake Court Notices to Deliver Remote Access Trojan Across Latin America
Context: Attack chains begin with phishing emails targeting individuals who handle cases, contracts, judicial, or institutional service requests to trick them into opening a malware-...
Full Text:
The threat actor known as Blind Eagle has resurfaced with a new campaign targeting organizations in Latin America through judicial and administrative-themed phishing lures to deliver a remote access trojan (RAT) that shares its lineage with AsyncRAT and DCRat.

"The campaign uses Portuguese and Spanish lures that resemble court notifications, fiscalía notices, tutela proceedings, and administrative documents," Zenox said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

Assessed to be a Spanish-speaking group and active since 2018, Blind Eagle (aka APT-C-36) has a track record of using spear-phishing lures to distribute commodity RATs like AsyncRAT, BitRAT, Lime RAT, NjRAT, Quasar RAT, and Remcos RAT.

Attack chains begin with phishing emails targeting individuals who handle cases, contracts, judicial, or institutional service requests to trick them into opening a malware-laced attachment.

One email containing a Colombian judicial-themed XHTML file has been identified as a weaponized Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) image that renders a bogus web page impersonating Colombia's Fiscalía General de la Nación, also referred to as the Office of the Attorney General.

The web page, for its part, employs a technique known as HTML smuggling to assemble the next-stage ZIP archive payload locally in the web browser using ZipCrypto, thereby circumventing email security controls.

Present within the ZIP archive is a JavaScript dropper that masquerades as Network Configuration Auditor version 2.7.298. The JavaScript code conducts environment reconnaissance, and collects details such as system version, network profile, installation date, memory size, computer name, environment variables, and directories localized in Portuguese and Spanish.

Upon execution, it launches a Visual Basic Script that performs Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) bypass, while displaying a fake criminal-citation page as a distraction mechanism.

In parallel, the malware also takes steps to delete the original XHTML artifact, clears Mark of the Web (MotW) metadata, and sets up persistence on the host under the Windows Startup folder so that it's automatically executed on system startup.

The attack culminates with the use of PowerShell to decode and launch the final RAT payload in memory. The trojan is an AsyncRAT fork with DCRat lineage based on code structure, configuration, build characteristics, and observed behavior.

"The targeting of judicial, fiscal, administrative and educational organizations gives the operation access to highly sensitive legal, financial and institutional information," Zenox said.

"Combined with the Portuguese and Spanish lures, Brazilian infrastructure, operational timezone and regional victimology, these elements establish the campaign as an APT-C-36 operation conducted through a Brazilian operational cluster."

Zenox told The Hacker News that it could not confirm whether any of these attacks had succeeded against real-world targets. However, during the campaign period between late October and early November 2026, it observed a large-scale wave of targeted phishing involving nearly 3,300 malicious emails.

While not all of these messages targeted organizations in Colombia, the country continues to remain a priority target for Blind Eagle for a combination of reasons.

"The repeated targeting of Colombia likely reflects multiple factors, with one of the main enabling factors being the structural vulnerabilities and uneven security maturity across parts of the country's critical, public, financial, and private-sector infrastructure," Zenox security researcher Gabriel Alves said.

"These conditions may increase the likelihood of successful compromises and offer greater opportunities to monetize access, steal sensitive data or funds, or reuse compromised credentials against critical systems. This is further supported by regional actors' familiarity with the Colombian context and is consistent with patterns observed among Latin American threat actors."

(The story was updated after publication to include additional insights from Zenox.)

Title: France Blames Iran for Supermarket Fridge Hack, Requests International Arrest Warrants
Context: Laure Beccuau, the Paris Public Prosecutor, said on social media the investigation found links between the October 11 to 12 cyber-attack and the Shahid Kaveh and Shahid...
Full Text:
The recent wave of cyber-attacks targeting refrigeration control systems across 700 supermarkets sites in France was coordinated by Iranian hacking groups, according to French authorities.

Laure Beccuau, the Paris Public Prosecutor, said on social media the investigation found links between the October 11 to 12 cyber-attack and the Shahid Kaveh and Shahid Shoostari groups, two elite offensive cyber units tied to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

In a technical attribution notice published on November 9, the French Computer Emergency and Response Team (CERT-FR) said Shahid Kaveh is linked to a range of purported hacktivist groups, including CyberAveng3rs, Soldiers of Solomon, Mr. Soul and Cyber Isnaad Front.

Investigators from the Anti-Criminality Office (OFAC) and the French domestic intelligence service (DGSI) found IP addresses linked to Iran-based endpoints and observed Farsi words in the traces left by the hackers.

Additionally, the techniques, tactics and procedures (TTPs) employed by the attackers were consistent with previous Shahid Kaveh campaigns.

CERT-FR named three leaders of the IRGC and Shahid Kaveh linked to the cyber-attacks.

The Paris prosecutor's office has now opened a judicial investigation into the cyber-attacks and the damage caused.

France Vows to Take Punitive Measures

According to another statement issued by the French government on November 9, Paris intends to take a series of diplomatic and punitive measures in response to the cyber-attacks.

The government announced that it would summon Iran’s Ambassador to France to formally convey its strongest condemnation of the attacks.

It also stated that it would urge its European partners to introduce additional sanctions targeting Iranian individuals and entities allegedly involved in the cyber-attacks against France, as well as other malicious cyber activities.

The French government stressed that it reserves the right to take further measures, both public and undisclosed, should they be deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to the cyber threats.

Frist Nation-State, Sabotage-Focused Cyber-Attack on French Soil

Historically, France has rarely attributed cyber-attacks to a single country, making this move particularly significant.

“This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, marking the first cyber-offensive campaign carried out purely for sabotage purposes on French national territory,” the French government explained in its statement.

Commenting on the attribution, Gary Barlet, public sector CTO at Illumio, said he is also “impressed” that France is planning to pursue sanctions at a European level.

“It's not yet clear what form those sanctions will take, so that will be interesting to see. But this needs to happen more often. Too often an attack gets publicly called out, there's outrage, and then nothing happens. It sends a message to attackers that the cost of doing this is close to zero,” Barlet added.

In the CERT-FR technical notice, the French Cyber Crises Coordination Center (C4) said this attack added to a series of other incidents that have been attributed to IRGC-linked groups since at least 2020. These include destabilisation campaigns targeting satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and a French digital display company in 2024, in the context of the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

This attribution does not include the cyber-attack on the French Blood Service (EFS) that occurred in early November.

Title: U.S. urges critical infrastructure orgs to secure refrigeration systems ASAP after EU supermarket and blood bank attacks
Context: Visualize attack paths and prevent lateral movement: Threat actors frequently exploit web-exposed IT infrastructure to pivot laterally into critical OT environments
Full Text:
Following recent cyber attacks on French blood banks and European supermarkets, U.S. federal agencies are urging critical infrastructure organizations to immediately secure industrial refrigeration systems against remote tampering and temperature manipulation.

Key takeaways

Cybercriminals are actively targeting unpatched flaws, misconfigurations, and weak or hard-coded passwords in commercial cold-chain and refrigeration controllers globally.

Attackers are gaining remote access to manipulate temperature controls and spoil essential products, such as blood and food.

CISA, the FBI, and other U.S. agencies are advising organizations to isolate OT systems, secure or remove remote access, patch critical vulnerabilities, and replace end-of-life devices.

Critical infrastructure organizations in the healthcare, chemicals, transportation, and food and agriculture sectors must urgently harden their industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems to protect food, medicines, and other essential products against ongoing cyber attacks.

That’s the call from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and other U.S. government agencies, following a series of alarming breaches against refrigeration systems in French blood banks and European supermarkets.

“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” CISA Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera said in a statement.

Attackers are remotely targeting electronic-temperature and commercial-refrigeration controllers used in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. They’re looking for unpatched vulnerabilities and other security flaws, such as misconfigurations, according to the agencies.

Once attackers gain remote access to these systems, they try to tamper with these machines’ temperature controls to damage their refrigerated products. The temperature changes could also trigger fire hazards.

In a joint fact sheet, the agencies recommend organizations immediately take the following steps:

Use strong authentication mechanisms and change systems’ default passwords.

Keep systems updated and promptly patch critical vulnerabilities.

Replace legacy devices that have reached end-of-life status.

Identify systems accessible from the internet.

Isolate operational technology (OT) systems from business networks.

Remove unnecessary remote access.

Secure necessary remote access.

Maintain offsite backups.

“This fact sheet provides clear, practical steps that network defenders can take to reduce that risk and protect operations,” said Brett Leatherman, cyber branch operations director at the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), one of the authoring agencies.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the U.S. Department of Transportation (DoT) also contributed to the joint fact sheet.

Attackers hit hundreds of grocery stores in France several weeks ago that caused food to spoil and triggered fires. The National Cybersecurity Agency of France (ANSSI) recently told Cybersecurity Dive it has been investigating the attacks since they started in mid-October and is aware of compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series controllers, as well as Copeland and Dixell XWEB controllers.

Title: CISA and the FBI Warn Of Attacks against Industrial Refrigeration Controllers
Context: Attackers may exploit flaws in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to change settings remotely and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles
Full Text:
US agencies warn attackers are going after industrial refrigeration controllers. The fixes are basic, and most start with getting them off the internet.

CISA, the FBI, HHS, USDA and the Department of Transportation published a joint advisory on attacks against industrial refrigeration controllers and cold chain monitoring systems. The activity is global. Healthcare, chemical, food and transport companies use these systems to watch temperatures, keep logs, run defrost cycles and save energy, including in refrigerated trucks.

“The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities.” reads the advisory published by CISA. “The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.”

The targets are electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers used in grocery stores and cold-storage sites. Attackers may exploit flaws in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to change settings remotely and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles. In plain terms, someone could cook your freezer from the other side of the world.

The agencies identify three ways in: bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and exploiting weak configurations. Once inside, an attacker can change temperatures, which can shorten equipment life, create a fire hazard and destroy stock. Spoiled products that reach consumers can also create a safety risk.

“The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.” continues the adviosry.

An attacker can also hide the damage. Operators lose sight of current temperatures, and that’s a bad moment to learn a cold room has been warm for hours.

CISA’s Chris Butera adds that every organization that depends on these systems should assume it’s a target. The advice follows the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals from CISA and NIST, a minimum set of practices for any organization.

Start with exposure. Keep controller panels off the internet, and if you need remote access, put an up-to-date firewall or similar gateway in front of it. Then separate industrial equipment from the office network with its own virtual network.

Next, fix the basics. Change default passwords, use strong ones, and add phishing-resistant multifactor authentication where you can. Update firmware, and retire or replace devices the maker no longer supports.

Allow only trusted devices and IP addresses to change system settings. Keep tested backups in a separate location, disconnected from the network. Enable logging and regularly check the logs. If devices do not record activity, monitor the network traffic between them.

U.S. organizations should report suspicious activity to CISA’s 24/7 operations center or the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center. Healthcare organizations can also contact HHS.

Reports should include the date, time and location of the incident, a description of the activity, the number of people affected, the equipment involved, and a contact person within the organization.

One control gets forgotten more than the rest. A controller shouldn’t be able to push a freezer past what’s safe, whoever is giving the orders.

“The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems.” concludes the report. “To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations:

United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT“

Title: The code and the court: Why your email security thinks like Napoleon
Context: A codified system is only as current as its code
Full Text:
In 1804, Napoleon gave France a code that much of the world still runs on. The Code civil replaced a tangle of local customs with a single written statute: orderly and knowable. In that tradition, the judge’s job, in Montesquieu’s phrase, is to be the mouth of the law, nothing more. Certainty was the point.

Certainty has a cost. A codified system is only as current as its code. When the world produces something the code did not anticipate — a new technology, a new fraud — there is no statute to apply, and everyone waits for someone to write one.

Your email security works exactly this way. That is the problem.

Security by statute

A signature is a statute. Someone observes an attack, writes a rule that describes it, and from that moment you are protected against that attack and its close relatives. It is fast, certain, and blind to anything the code has not been written to see.

Signatures alone were never enough, so the industry made the code bigger. Anomaly detection and behavioral models are a thicker statute book, trained on what already happened and scoring how far a message deviates from it. More sophisticated than a signature, but not a different philosophy. A zero-day is a crime with no statute.

The strongest evidence against codified defense is not the attack that fails a check. It is the attack that passes every one. When a supplier’s mailbox is compromised, the message arrives from a real domain, with valid credentials and earned reputation. Every check comes back clean because the infrastructure is genuine. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that breaches involving a third party now account for 48% of the total, up 60% in a single year. Authentication did exactly what it measures: it confirmed the letter came from who it said, and had no rule for whether it should be believed. The code was consulted. The code said valid. The message was a theft in progress.

Attackers understand this. A codified defense is cheap to walk around. You do not break the code; you do something it was never written to cover. The FBI’s 2025 Internet Crime Report put business email compromise losses above $3 billion in a single year, much of it carried by messages that broke no rule because no rule described them.

The other tradition

The English-speaking world chose a different system. Common law does not always wait for the legislature. A judge facing a situation no statute anticipated can reason from principle and precedent to a verdict. It adapts case by case. It is not simply a code that has to be rewritten. It is a court that knows how to weigh a new set of facts.

That is the difference between detecting and reasoning. The fair objection is that a reasoning system also learns from the past. True. But there is a difference between matching a case to a stored pattern and applying a principle to a case you have never seen. A judge who has never encountered your particular dispute still knows how to weigh evidence.

None of this means throwing out the code. Most mail is open and shut and should be settled that way in milliseconds. You keep the fast rule for the easy calls and save a full hearing for the contested ones.

A court can also answer a question a code struggles with: why. A codified system can say “this matched” or “this deviated.” A verdict can cite its evidence: what the sender actually is, whether the relationship supports the request, what the message is asking for. You do not have to trust the reasoning. You check the evidence, because a ruling stands or falls on whether its facts hold up, not on the private thoughts of the judge. It is the opposite of a black box: a decision you can read, challenge, and overturn.

None of this retreats from zero trust. Zero trust governs access, who gets in and what they can touch, and assumes nothing. This is about the verdict, whether a message is what it claims to be, and there the posture is not to presume guilt or innocence but to let the evidence decide.

The court of last resort

For the highest stakes matters, a mature legal system does not let the machinery decide alone. In security, some decisions belong with the person whose money is about to move.

When a message asks for a wire, a change to vendor banking details or a payroll redirect, the right design does not render a silent verdict and hope. It escalates and asks the owner to approve the action itself. Reasoning handles the general docket. The human is the court of last resort, reserved for the decisions that deserve one. Match the process to the stakes.

No analogy is perfect. Real judges in both traditions do more than this, and civil-law systems evolve through their own doctrine.

The question worth ending on

For most of this industry’s history, there was no choice, because machines could apply a code but could not weigh evidence and reason for a judgment. That is no longer true.

There is a simple way to find out which system you are running. Ask your team how many attacks that reached a user came from infrastructure you already trust: a compromised vendor, a real account, a genuine DocuSign or Microsoft notification bent to a purpose it was never meant for. If that number is high, your defenses are not failing to enforce the code. They are enforcing it perfectly; against threats the code was never written to describe.

So, the question is not whether your defenses are up to date. A code is always, by definition, up to date with yesterday. The question is whether your security is a code or a court, and whether it can rule on the case it has never seen, because that is the only case that was ever going to hurt you.
