Title: Addressing protocol security gaps in multi-tenant Kubernetes
Context: In the Cuttlefish deployment (Cuttlefish is Google’s configurable virtual Android device that runs in containers), the first approach routed this traffic through a bastion host...
Full Text:
Protocols like Android Debug Bridge (ADB) and Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC), by default, use unencrypted channels for network communications and don’t support enterprise authentication mechanisms like JSON Web Tokens (JWTs). In a multi-tenant Kubernetes cluster—including Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS)—pods can reach other tenants’ open ports by default unless you configure network policies to restrict cross-namespace traffic. Also, modifying each protocol individually doesn’t scale. This post describes an architecture built on three reusable components: namespace-scoped mutual TLS (mTLS) gateways, managed TURN relay through Amazon Kinesis Video Streams, and JWT identity chains tied to an enterprise identity provider (IdP). The post focuses on architecture decisions and learnings rather than step-by-step deployment.

This post assumes an EKS cluster with namespace isolation configured, an enterprise IdP that issues JWTs, and AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA)—a managed service for issuing private certificates—set up in your account. cert-manager—an open-source Kubernetes add-on that automates certificate issuance and renewal—and the AWS Private CA issuer plugin should already be running in the cluster. The architecture also assumes permissions to deploy Envoy Gateway, a Kubernetes API gateway built on the Envoy proxy. The key authentication mechanism used is mTLS, where both client and server present certificates to verify each other.

The challenge: Unauthenticated protocols in multi-tenant Kubernetes

ADB, a command-line tool for communicating with Android devices, requires a proxy or custom API to handle authentication; its unencrypted channel exposes data in transit. Virtual Network Computing (VNC), a protocol for remote desktop access, and similar TCP services share this problem: their credentials are local to the protocol, with no path to a central identity store.

In the Cuttlefish deployment (Cuttlefish is Google’s configurable virtual Android device that runs in containers), the first approach routed this traffic through a bastion host to the Amazon EKS control plane, as Figure 1 shows.

Figure 1: Previous architecture (superseded), shown for comparison only. Communication flow between developer workstation, bastion host, and Amazon EKS control plane

Figure 1 shows a common pattern across the industry to access a private Amazon EKS cluster. We share it to help others identify and migrate away from similar designs for low latency environments. Do not implement this design. The current architecture is described and shown later in this post.

In the now deprecated architecture, a custom API handles authentication by checking each user’s identity against the enterprise IdP and enforcing pod-level authorization. The custom API powers a command-line interface (CLI) that lets you list pods in your assigned namespace and connect to your devices.

The JWT identity chain maps each user to an AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) RoleSessionName, so every AWS API call in the audit log traces back to a specific person, even in a multi-tenant environment.

Those credentials set up a two-hop port forward that goes from your machine to the bastion, then from the bastion to the target pod. Because all traffic was routed through the Kubernetes API server, concurrent sessions created a throughput bottleneck even though the cluster itself stayed private.

Why self-managed relay infrastructure falls short

A TURN server—a media relay—is needed when communicating parties are behind a NAT Gateway and can’t set up direct peer-to-peer connections.

The initial deployment used STUNner, an open source Kubernetes Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) and Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) gateway designed for WebRTC media ingestion. STUNner introduced three operational and security challenges.

Because STUNner had no native integration with AWS services or the enterprise IdP, we built a custom token-exchange service to convert IdP tokens into time-limited, namespace-scoped TURN credentials. As usage grew, patching, monitoring, and scaling the TURN servers became a recurring burden. Pod migrations between Availability Zones required manually updating routing rules, and STUNner dropped WebRTC connections during peak usage.

WebRTC’s signaling server introduced a separate security risk. WebRTC encrypts media using Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) and Secure Real-Time Transport Protocol (SRTP) but doesn’t define authentication or encryption for the signaling server; you must build that yourself, which leaves control-plane signaling exposed.

The architecture doesn’t use the Kinesis Video Streams signaling channel because integrating it required substantial changes to the Cuttlefish source patch. The Cuttlefish source code was patched to support non-Google TURN servers, and further changes to support non-Google signaling servers deviated the deployment further from upstream Cuttlefish, risking compatibility issues. Instead, the architecture kept the default Cuttlefish signaling server, with JWT-based session validation and TLS termination at the signaling endpoint designed around it at the application layer.

Namespace-scoped mTLS gateways and managed media relay

The architecture retains namespace isolation, JWT-based authentication, the custom authorization API, and the Cuttlefish patch; the last three of which are custom to this deployment. All components except Cuttlefish patch are reusable.

The reusable components include namespace-scoped Envoy Gateway for mTLS-authenticated TCP proxying, cert-manager-driven certificate rotation through AWS Private CA, and Kinesis Video Streams as a managed TURN provider.

The mTLS gateway assumes several other controls are already in place:

Default-deny NetworkPolicy in each tenant namespace. Without this, traffic can bypass the gateway.

JWT-based authentication through the custom API. The API validates each user’s identity against the enterprise IdP before returning connection details.

Namespace-scoped mTLS certificates issued by AWS Private CA through cert-manager.

Kubernetes namespace isolation with scoped role-based access control (RBAC).

ADB connectivity through mTLS

For ADB connectivity, the architecture uses mTLS authentication with Envoy Gateway. Each namespace runs its own Envoy Gateway instance, which routes traffic only to pods within that namespace. cert-manager, running in the cluster with the AWS Private CA issuer plugin, requests short-lived mTLS certificates from AWS Private CA for each namespace at creation time. In production, apply NetworkPolicies before deploying the gateway and issuing certificates.

The certificate commonName uses the convention <user-namespace>.eks.internal so that Envoy can validate the certificate against the expected namespace during the mTLS handshake. The .eks.internal suffix is a naming convention for internal cluster certificates; choose a domain that doesn’t conflict with your organization’s DNS. The usages field specifies both client authentication and server authentication because the same certificate authenticates the client to the gateway and the gateway to the client during the mutual TLS exchange. A cluster-scoped AWSPCAClusterIssuer is used instead of a namespace-scoped AWSPCAIssuer so that a single CA configuration can issue certificates across all tenant namespaces without duplicating issuer resources in each one.

Before deploying Envoy Gateway, each tenant namespace needs a NetworkPolicy that enforces a default-deny ingress posture.

Each certificate is issued with a 12-hour lifetime. A shorter lifetime means a compromised certificate expires quickly without requiring Certificate Revocation List (CRL) or Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) infrastructure, while the 4-hour renewal window gives cert-manager multiple retry attempts before expiry. cert-manager tracks expiry and re-requests a new certificate from AWS Private CA before the current one lapses (by default, renewal starts at the two-thirds mark of the certificate’s lifetime). Envoy Gateway picks up the renewed certificate through Kubernetes Secrets using its Secret Discovery Service (SDS), with no pod restart required.

You first authenticate with the enterprise IdP through the custom CLI, which calls the custom API. The API validates your JWT, confirms your namespace assignment, and returns connection details for the appropriate namespace-scoped Envoy Gateway, including the client certificate for that namespace. The API delivers the certificate over HTTPS. Because certificates are namespace-scoped and expire in 12 hours, a compromised response yields access only to the holder’s own namespace for a limited window. The CLI then presents this certificate to establish a direct mTLS connection, through Envoy, to the target pod. The JWT proves who you are, and the mTLS certificate proves which namespace the connection belongs to.

Envoy proxies the TCP stream directly to the pod and pools connections to reduce latency. The hop between Envoy and the pod isn’t encrypted by mTLS. NetworkPolicy restricts ingress so that only the namespace-scoped Envoy Gateway can reach the ADB port on the target pod. For environments with compliance requirements, extend mTLS to the pod using a sidecar proxy or pod-level certificates. Evaluate this gap against your organization’s data classification and regulatory requirements.

For the REST API path, the custom API sits behind AWS WAF. The ADB data path has no WAF protection; it relies on mTLS, NetworkPolicies, and namespace isolation.

Figure 2: ADB communication flow using Envoy Gateway and custom REST API

Figure 2 shows this ADB communication flow using Envoy Gateway and the custom REST API. It logs your authenticated identity, namespace, and timestamp. The mTLS certificate doesn’t carry a user identifier in its subject field. This applies when namespaces are strictly 1:1 with users. For shared namespaces or regulated environments requiring granular attribution, issue per-user certificates from AWS Private CA.

WebRTC relay through Kinesis Video Streams

Kinesis Video Streams provides built-in STUN and TURN infrastructure and signaling channels. It replaced the self-managed STUNner because it integrates with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), so the custom token-exchange service is no longer needed. This is an important factor in reducing operational costs. For implementation details, see the Amazon Kinesis Video Streams WebRTC developer guide, which covers signaling channel setup, IAM policies, and TURN credential retrieval.

Kinesis Video Streams WebRTC charges per active signaling channel, per signaling message, and per TURN streaming minute. Idle namespaces incur no TURN cost. See Amazon Kinesis Video Streams pricing for latest pricing and Amazon Kinesis Video Streams with WebRTC service quotas for service quotas.

Figure 3: Final architecture with ADB and WebRTC communication channels

Figure 3 shows both ADB and WebRTC communication channels in the completed architecture. Each path has different controls: ADB traffic flows through the namespace-scoped Envoy Gateway, where mTLS and NetworkPolicies enforce access. WebRTC media relay runs through Kinesis Video Streams, with IAM scoping credentials per session. The custom REST API is the only HTTP-based path; it runs over HTTPS with AWS WAF at the edge.

The JWT identity chain connects all three paths: the custom API validates each user’s identity before any connection opens, so the audit log records who connected to which namespace and when.

Applying this pattern to other unauthenticated protocols

The mTLS gateway and certificate rotation pieces transfer directly to most TCP protocols. The TURN relay is specific to WebRTC and similar media-streaming protocols that need NAT traversal. The JWT identity chain requires custom work and isn’t directly transferable. You need to build the API that validates tokens and maps users to namespaces, and a client that retrieves and presents the certificate. The Cuttlefish source patch is specific to this case study and not reusable.

Two common protocol families show how the reusable parts apply:

VNC and RDP both store credentials locally, with no path to an enterprise identity provider. Wrapping VNC in mTLS through Envoy replaces the shared password model with certificate-based identity. RDP benefits similarly: certificate authentication works without domain-joining the containers, so you don’t need Active Directory inside each one.

MQTT, SIP, and similar TCP protocols often encrypt the payload but skip session-level authentication entirely; meaning you can verify what was sent but not who sent it. Wrapping these protocols in mTLS through Envoy closes that gap without modifying the protocol itself.

JWT identity chain secures session establishment at the application layer. For Internet of Things (IoT) device management, industrial control, or game streaming, Envoy Gateway adds mTLS to TCP protocols that lack built-in encryption in transit. Managed TURN through Kinesis Video Streams handles NAT traversal for WebRTC-based streaming components.

Performance results

Application installs through the dual port-forwarding chain (local machine to bastion, bastion to pod) took 3–4 minutes, and individual ADB commands took 1–2 seconds per round trip.

After migrating to the mTLS Envoy Gateway, ADB commands added under 50 ms of gateway latency compared to local setup. The latency was measured as the difference in round-trip time between a command sent through Envoy and one sent to a local Android device. Through Envoy, individual ADB commands completed in under 100 ms and application installs finished in under 30 seconds, because Envoy proxies the TCP stream directly to the pod instead of routing through the Kubernetes API server. This was an improvement from 1–2 seconds for ADB commands and 3–4 minutes for application installs using bastion host setup.

Key implementation lessons

The main concern addressed by replacing bastion-host forwarding with mTLS proxying was latency compared to local setup. Gateway overhead stayed under 50 ms and met developer expectations.

After migrating to Kinesis Video Streams, WebRTC connections stayed stable during peak usage, and pod migrations between Availability Zones no longer required manual updates to routing rules. Because Kinesis Video Streams integrates with IAM, new protocols added to the cluster are automatically covered by the same audit trail with no additional logging configuration needed.

Security considerations

mTLS authenticates both ends of a connection and encrypts traffic in transit, but it only works when other controls are in place. The NetworkPolicy and pod security controls described in the preceding ADB connectivity section must be in place before mTLS adds value. Without default-deny ingress rules, traffic bypasses the gateway entirely. At the application layer, the custom API validates each user’s JWT before issuing connection details and logs the identity, namespace, and timestamp for every session. Certificates expire after 12 hours and cert-manager rotates them automatically. Short-lived certificates reduce exposure, but if your threat model requires immediate revocation, you need CRL or OCSP infrastructure on top of AWS Private CA. Envoy Gateway is a trust boundary. Review its configuration, resource limits, and access controls against the Envoy security best practices.

The custom API is the primary trust boundary in this architecture. Apply the same rigor to its security review, logging, and access controls as you would to any authentication service.

Conclusion

With namespace-scoped mTLS gateways and managed TURN relay, you can secure unauthenticated protocols on shared EKS clusters without modifying the protocols themselves. ADB command latency drops from 1–2 seconds to under 50 ms, and WebRTC connections remain stable during pod migrations. See the Envoy Gateway documentation, cert-manager documentation, and Amazon Kinesis Video Streams WebRTC developer guide to build and deploy this architecture.

Title: Brute Force Sentry for Managed SIEM | Huntress
Context: Brute Force Sentry normalizes both into one authentication surface, so a single detection can follow the attack from the first failure to the login
Full Text:
Today, Huntress Managed SIEM's Brute Force Sentry is available to all Managed SIEM customers. It turns the brute force attacks our SOC sees in the field into detections that fire earlier, with the evidence and hardening guidance you need to close the gap. Brute Force Sentry watches your internet-facing login surfaces, including RDP, RD Gateway, and the RDWeb portal on Windows and SSH on Linux. When a run of failed logons ends in a successful one, the Huntress SOC investigates.

Every exposed login gets knocked on, and most of that knocking is bots cycling through "administrator" on a gateway someone set up years ago. The trouble is that one burst out of thousands ends in a working login, and a generic threshold rule treats it the same as the rest.

Brute Force Sentry is built to find that one.

RDP is still a front door attackers use

Huntress research ties RDP to 10–20% of how advanced attackers break into networks. Plenty of organizations don't realize their RDWeb portal or RD Gateway is reachable from the internet until someone starts working through usernames on it.

RDWeb and RD Gateway behave a lot like an SSL VPN portal. Authentication happens at the web portal, before the user ever reaches an endpoint, so that portal is where attackers line up.

Most SIEMs handle brute force with a single threshold rule, something like "X failed logons in Y minutes." Set it low and your team drowns in alerts from bots that never get in. Set it high and a slow spray across dozens of accounts slips right under it. In both cases, the rule can't answer the question you care about: did one of those attempts work?

How Brute Force Sentry works

Brute Force Sentry reads the authentication telemetry your Managed SIEM already collects across all three platforms: Windows Security events (4624, 4625, 4740, 4776) and RD Gateway's own connection log, Linux sshd, and macOS, and splits "brute force" into the distinct tradecraft it really is:

Traditional brute force: one source guessing against a few accounts until something works

Distributed brute force: many sources working the same account, each staying quiet enough on its own to look unremarkable

Spraying: a short list of common credentials tried across many accounts

Credential stuffing: username and password pairs from earlier breaches, tested to see which still work

Username enumeration: repeated attempts against accounts that don't exist, probing for valid names before the guessing starts

It reads each platform in its own language. Windows spreads a single authentication across several event IDs, with the failure reason buried in a status code and the credential check sometimes landing on a domain controller instead of the machine being attacked. Linux writes one sshd line that already separates a wrong password from an attempt against an account that was never real. Rather than flatten both into a lowest common denominator, we normalize them into one authentication record that keeps what each platform knows, so the detection logic is identical everywhere and nothing is lost in translation.

It's tuned per surface, not set once.. Each one gets its own narrow correlation detection in place of a single noisy rule. Our researchers tuned every detection per login surface against historical partner data, then validated it against simulated real-world attacks in the lab before the SOC got it.

It correlates across providers. The failed sign-ins and the success that follows are often recorded by two different systems on the same host. Brute Force Sentry normalizes both into one authentication surface, so a single detection can follow the attack from the first failure to the login.

It turns itself on, and tells you when it can't. Brute Force Sentry activates per organization once the telemetry it needs is flowing. If that telemetry is missing, it shows as unavailable along with the reason, so a quiet dashboard means Huntress checked and found nothing.

The accounts they go after aren't the ones you're watching

Across the compromises Huntress has worked, the accounts that fell weren't always domain admins. They were the ones nobody owns; shared logins created for a device, a front desk, or a one off integration, with a password nobody has rotated since and an MFA exemption nobody remembers granting. They don't surface on a privileged-account review, and they don't belong to anyone who'd notice them being used. That's exactly why attackers reach for them first, and the pattern holds whichever door they come through: a Windows desktop or gateway, a Linux server, or a Mac sharing its screen.

Brute Force Sentry surfaces the usernames being attempted, not just how many times. That includes the ones that don't exist. A run of failures against accounts that were never real is username enumeration, someone working a list, learning your naming convention before they start guessing passwords in earnest. Catching that tells you an attack is being set up rather than already underway. And seeing which real accounts an attacker keeps returning to tell you which credentials to rotate tonight, not next quarter.

About 1,700 attempts in 72 seconds

In June 2026, the Huntress SOC handled a compromise at an organization running Remote Desktop Gateway. The attacker hit eight accounts with 212 to 215 failed logons each, roughly 1,700 attempts in 72 seconds, and then got in.

Every one of those failures was sitting in the gateway host's event logs. The successful login that came right after was recorded by RD Gateway, a different provider on the same host. Connecting the two took a detection that didn't exist yet, and Brute Force Sentry was built to make that connection.

To see how often this pattern shows up, we reviewed 30 confirmed RDWeb/RDG compromises during the first four weeks of testing. In 20 of them, Brute Force Sentry's signal would have reached the SOC up to an hour earlier. That's an hour between the attacker's first guess and their first move inside the network, and it's an hour our analysts can spend containing the account.

An attacker who gets in through your gateway keeps moving, so the sooner you see the login, the less of the network they've touched.

What you'll see in the portal

Most brute force activity never succeeds, and until now partners haven't seen any of it. Brute Force Sentry shows it as it happens, so you can act on your own terms before something breaks through:

Exposed surfaces: which internet-facing login surfaces are under attack, including ones you may not have known were reachable

Targeted accounts: the accounts attackers keep coming back to

Sources: where the attempts come from, and which sources keep returning

Compromises: successful logins that followed a run of failures, each linked to its Incident Report

You're notified on compromise, and you can opt in to notifications for every attempt, successful or not.

Figure 1: Brute Force Sentry dashboard

Less noise for you, more proof for your customers

If you're an MSP, you've probably told a client their RD Gateway needs MFA or belongs behind a VPN. Brute Force Sentry gives you their own data to make that case, starting with whether the portal should be exposed at all: which accounts were targeted last week, how many attempts were made, and where they came from. Pair that with the hardening guidance in each finding, and the conversation moves from "we should" to "here's what happened."

Internal IT teams get the same benefit. You don't have to become a Windows event log specialist to tell whether a burst of 4625s was background noise or the start of an intrusion, because the Huntress SOC is already looking at the ones that matter.

Built from the attacks our SOC works

Brute Force Sentry started with a real incident and a gap our analysts could name. That's how we want Managed SIEM to keep growing: take the attacks our SOC sees in partner environments and turn them into detections that fire earlier, with the evidence attached.

Every exposed login gets knocked on. Now you'll know which knock got answered.

Title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly in Cybersecurity - Week 45 (2026)
Context: Once connected, attackers instructed victims to launch Quick Assist, a built-in Windows remote-help tool, and read back connection codes to grant full remote desktop control
Full Text:
The Good | Global Authorities Dismantle Investment Scams & VasyGrek Infrastructure, Indict University System Hackers

Law enforcement in Europe, supported by Europol and Eurojust, arrested seven suspects and seized over 100 servers targeting a crime-as-a-service (CaaS) investment fraud infrastructure. Operating from Cyprus and Israel, an unnamed vendor supplied fraudulent trading websites to criminal call centers across Albania, Kosovo, North Macedonia, and more.

Following a four-year investigation initiated after victims reported missing funds, investigators linked the infrastructure to fake foreign currency, stock, and cryptocurrency schemes affecting victims in at least 50 countries. Scammers used fake online account profits to coerce larger transfers before cutting contact, leaving victims unable to recover their funds.

In the U.S., a federal grand jury indicted two Canadian nationals, Ryan James Roach and Mathiew James Stubbings, for conspiring to breach multiple American universities to mine for cryptocurrency. Between June 2016 and December 2019, the co-conspirators deployed virtual private servers to infect academic networks across Massachusetts, New York, North Carolina, and Tennessee with malware.

Once inside, the defendants stole user log-ins and data, deployed cryptocurrency mining software, and hijacked high-performance campus supercomputers to conduct unauthorized network vulnerability research. Both men face up to ten years in prison and $250,000 fines following formal extradition proceedings from Canada.

Russian law enforcement authorities arrested three suspected members of the VasyGrek threat group (aka Fluffy Wolf) and dismantled its operational infrastructure. Active since 2016, the financially-motivated group was known for targeting organizations across metallurgy, energy, healthcare, and finance sectors in Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan.

Attackers would send phishing emails with malicious accounting attachments to drop remote access trojans and steal corporate funds. Police seized computer equipment and server assets after uncovering a broad network of fake financial domains, dark web remote administration tools, and Golang backdoors used to execute unauthorized commands.

The Bad | Impersonators Abuse Microsoft Teams and Active Directory Certificate Services

According to a new report, threat actors have been posing as IT help desk staff on Microsoft Teams to message and call corporate employees and leverage external support-themed tenants to trick users into handing over workstation access.

Once connected, attackers instructed victims to launch Quick Assist, a built-in Windows remote-help tool, and read back connection codes to grant full remote desktop control. The intruders then dropped malicious software archives into Downloads folders, unpacking and executing payloads via portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes disguised as legitimate Windows system updates.

After establishing initial persistence, the attackers abused weak configuration templates within Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) to request digital authentication certificates for privileged domain accounts. In one documented intrusion, threat actors exploited an ESC1 misconfiguration to obtain certificates for three highly privileged identities—access that persisted even after password resets or workstation wipes. The attacker used one of those certificates to compromise a domain controller, execute DCSync credential dumping, and exfiltrate internal corporate files to an external server via Rclone.

In a second intrusion, attackers targeted an ESC8 configuration by deploying the ‘PetitPotam’ technique to force a domain controller to authenticate against an attacker-controlled endpoint. The relayed NTLM authentication allowed the actors to request a certificate directly for the domain controller without credentials, securing a persistent Kerberos ticket-granting ticket. The customer isolated the affected workstation, and no further attack progression was observed.

Because these intrusions exploit misconfigured certificate enrollment policies rather than underlying software vulnerabilities, Microsoft advises organizations to confirm unexpected support requests via internal channels, enforce Extended Protection for Authentication on web enrollment endpoints, and audit certificate issuance rules.

The Ugly | Threat Actors Disrupt European Refrigeration Systems Across Retail and Healthcare Sectors

Threat actors have targeted internet-exposed refrigeration control systems across Europe this week, altering temperature settings and activating defrost cycles across facilities just three weeks after similar attacks on hundreds of refrigeration systems in French supermarkets.

So far, this second wave has impacted retail chains across Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Sweden. In several stores, attackers set cooling units to generate heat or raised temperature setpoints to 50°C.

The activity extended into critical healthcare infrastructure when a cyberattack on refrigeration supplier Coolworld Rentals raised temperature thresholds at French Blood Establishment (EFS) cold-storage facilities managing vital blood supplies. However, automated monitoring alarms enabled staff to relocate stored blood products before any inventory was lost.

SentinelLABS’s breakdown notes that similar attacks targeted Israeli and Russian facilities in 2022, a Los Angeles meat processor in 2024, and U.S. military commissaries in August 2026. The intrusions primarily targeted commercial supervisory platforms, such as Danfoss AK-SM, AK-SC, and Copeland Dixell XWEB controllers, that centralize site cooling operations.

At the time, ANSSI indicated that adversaries gained control by exploiting publicly accessible administration interfaces and weak default credentials rather than executing novel software zero-days.

While Russian-aligned hacktivist collectives including CARR, NoName057(16), and Z-Pentest claimed responsibility for specific disruptions, law enforcement authorities have not formally confirmed attribution. Opportunistic scanning against unhardened building management systems allows multiple threat groups to execute similar disruptions.

To mitigate ongoing operational risks, government advisories from CERT-FR instruct operators to immediately disconnect exposed control panels from the public internet, restrict remote maintenance access to secure virtual private networks, enforce strong authentication controls, and replace legacy end-of-life hardware.

Title: Pinpointing Location of Videos from Background Airplane Sounds
Context: Much of this information is publicly available
Full Text:
Pinpointing Location of Videos from Background Airplane Sounds

This is fascinating:

The video describes a technique that can reveal where an otherwise unidentifiable recording was made by analyzing its audio for the faint sounds of passing aircraft. The technique is both fascinating and frightening.

It works by looking at Doppler curves, which plot the way a plane’s sound changes as it passes overhead because of the Doppler effect. This is the same familiar Doppler effect that causes the frequency of a siren to rise as it approaches and then fall as it passes by and moves away. More generally, it’s the phenomenon whereby the frequency of a wave perceived by an observer changes when the observer and the source of the wave are moving in relation to one another.

[…]

It’s sound that’s relevant here, though, and specifically the sound of aeroplanes. Early in his video, Colsto brings up a map of the flights that were in the air at the time the video he’s tracing was recorded. Much of this information is publicly available. Aircraft equipped with Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) transmit data about their position, velocity, and altitude, which flight-tracking services collect and make available to the public. While not every plane is tracked, the system provides an enormous amount of information about aircraft movements.

Title: AI Agent Security: 5 steps to take before the rules are written
Context: Lock your most critical systems to known users and usage patterns only
Full Text:
In April 2026, an AI coding agent deleted a company’s entire production database in under ten seconds. When asked why, it admitted to guessing rather than verifying.

The story sounds concerning, but actually, there’s a lot we can learn from it—namely because the agent didn’t malfunction. It was asked to clean up a staging environment, found a forgotten API token an unrelated file, and used it. That token worked like a master key, so one wrong guess reached production, and the rest is history. Or it will be, anyway.

And this isn’t an isolated incident. I recently had the opportunity to speak with Susanne Senoff on our podcast, Identity Decoded, and she shared a similar story where an agent went rogue, looking like a threat actor to complete its task.

So, the agent didn’t act maliciously or make a bad judgement call. It could just access too much, and that makes it an identity problem. But, because I’m a bit allergic to FUD, I’m happy to share that this is a problem organisations can start solving now.

I recently sat down with CNBC Explains to chat about the increasing risks of AI Agents (and what to do about them). You can watch the full segment here, or continue reading to see how I would get ahead of stories like the one we’ve just discussed:

Agents have identities, so onboard them like digital workers

A new hire gets an identity, a manager, and access scoped to their job. AI agents need the same. They authenticate, hold credentials, and act inside (and sometimes outside) your systems, often without human supervision, ownership, or guidance. When an agent gets it wrong, early legal thinking points the same way: the business that deployed it owns the outcome.

All AI agents’ access permissions must be treated with the same rigour as humans’. When thinking about agents, we need to get into the habit of asking: “what can this identity reach if it gets something wrong?”

Best practices are coming, but here’s what you can do in the meantime

In the grand scheme of things, agents are really new, and that means no one is completely certain how we should protect them (and our businesses). I’ve noticed this affecting many identity and security teams, who are hesitant about picking an approach to securing agents without the guidance of established, time-tested best practices.

This leads to a kind of analysis paralysis: should agents have their own identities and credentials, or not? Should you wait for proven approaches or act now as the risk grows—as more and more business are adopting agents?

I’m a strong believer in mastering your risk and in progress over perfection. Here are five steps that can be taken today to help you understand your agents, reduce risk, and build maturity without waiting for best practices—or an incident.

#1: Find your agents. Yes, all of them.

Inventory the agents running in your environments, including ones other teams set up themselves, and the credentials and access each one uses. Expect surprises (that’s the point of looking) and expect to find a lot more than you anticipated, especially as you’re likely experimenting with multiple agentic platforms.

You don’t have to find every single one before you start protecting (see tip #5 for more on this), but you should aim to catch ‘em all!

#2: Give each agent its own identity and a human owner.

No shared tokens or borrowed developer access. Every agent should trace back to a distinct identity and an accountable human, so you know who to ask, what to switch off, and how to manage it.

#3: Limit what each agent can reach.

Apply Least Privilege properly. Scope credentials tightly by starting with what you absolutely DON’T want an agent to touch, and verifying existing permissions; for example, to payment systems, regulatory systems, customer databases, etc. Hunt down forgotten tokens, let agents work on a copy rather than production, and keep backups out of reach. An instruction in a prompt is a request. An access policy is a control—and it’s one that’ll stop these kind of incidents.

Listen

What happens when a well-intentioned AI agent goes rogue?

Hear it from a CISO: When a sanctioned AI agent started acting like a threat actor on one of Conga’s most important databases, Susanne Senoff’s team had to act fast. Hear what happened, and why she treats agents like teenagers, on Identity Decoded.

Listen now

#4: Control agents at runtime and prepare your environment for the fast and curious.

There are two sides to protection, and you need both.

The first is controlling what agents do, as they do it. A valid credential isn’t proof that an action is right, so you need to be able to check each request at the moment of access. Is it unusual, risky, or out of character for the agent? Answering that inline, before access is granted, turns policy into protection, and lets you stop an agent from overstepping.

The second is making your environment ready for things that are both fast and curious. Lock your most critical systems to known users and usage patterns only. Build it into platform engineering and governance, so every new account is born with restrictions and an accepted use case. Even an agent you haven’t yet vetted is then far less able to wander into something they shouldn’t.

#5: Don’t wait for the work to be done before you switch on enforcement.

I’ll say it again: progress beats perfection. Waiting until you have a complete inventory, perfect ownership map, and finished clean-up before you can reduce your exposure to rogue or over-permissioned agents isn’t going to do you any favours. It’ll just leave you with a headache and a to-do list that feels like it’ll never end.

So, I suggest putting runtime guardrails around every identity—human, non-human, and AI—regardless of your current set-up or tech debt. Start by stopping the worst-case scenarios first, and go from there. This keeps access in check while you catch up, reducing risk now, not when the to-do list is finished.

learn more

Secure in spite of legacy: The IAM leaders' guide to controlling identity risk

Take a look at my blog on how to get secure in spite of your tech debt—and how to master your identity risk.

Read the blog

The bottom line

Stopping AI agents from going wrong starts with access, not intent. Find your agents, give each one an identity and an owner, limit what they can reach, and make progress towards reducing your risk today, and for what matters most to your business.

Title: Integrate Aquasec and Jenkins to Stop Unsafe Images Before They Run
Context: How does the Aquasec and Jenkins integration work
Full Text:
How does the Aquasec and Jenkins integration work?

The Aqua Security Scanner plugin is installed from the central Jenkins plugin repository, or deployed manually from its .hpi file. It is configured under Manage Jenkins, System, in the Aqua Security section. There an administrator sets the Aquasec scanner image, the Aquasec server URL and a scanner token. Both values come from the deployment command of a CI/CD scanner group. Aquasec SaaS accepts token authentication only, so username and password authentication is not an option for SaaS environments.

The plugin works in Pipeline and Freestyle jobs. In a pipeline, the aqua step goes into the pipeline script, and the Jenkins Snippet Generator can build the syntax. With the Docker engine, the plugin scans local images, images hosted in a registry and docker-archive tar files. With Podman, supported from plugin version 3.1.2, it scans local images as a root or non root user.

Each job chooses what happens to a noncompliant image: never fail the build, or perform the actions defined in the Image Assurance Policy. Local images and archives are evaluated against the Default Image Assurance Policy. Registry images are evaluated against every policy whose scope includes them. Optional settings register the image with Aquasec after a successful scan, hide base image vulnerabilities and run a shell command when an image fails.

Results appear in Jenkins as an Aquasec scan report organized like the image view in the Aquasec UI. A View in Aqua Platform button opens the image under Workload Protection, Images & Functions, Images, CI/CD Scans. A separate Aqua Security Serverless Scanner plugin scans function code for vulnerabilities, sensitive data and excessive permissions.

Title: The post-quantum future of web privacy

Full Text:
The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS.

Privacy Pass is a protocol used by site operators like Cloudflare to help protect applications from abuse. One way we do this is by rate limiting individual clients so that no one client consumes too many of the site's resources. Normally this involves some combination of friction or loss of privacy for users: CAPTCHAs or other challenges to moderate traffic, along with accounts and fingerprinting to identify traffic.Privacy Pass was designed to avoid this tradeoff between friction and privacy. The basic idea is that a client gets issued a number of tokens, which they can redeem in exchange for access to the site. Crucially, each token is unlinkable to the client it was issued to, ensuring the client can use the site as they always had without sacrificing privacy.

With 10 years of deployment experience under our belts — using Privacy Pass for applications such as privacy proxies (like iCloud Private Relay) and relays (like Privacy Gateway) — we, along with others, are collaborating to bring the next generation of this technology to the web. One of our goals is to develop more sophisticated tools for managing agentic traffic that would otherwise consume too many resources and degrade performance for human visitors. Another goal is to foster a more open ecosystem by making it easier for more types of clients to participate. Achieving these goals requires developing new capabilities beyond what Privacy Pass offers today.

Given the trajectory, in this post we look at the prospects for post-quantum. In fact, we're in better shape than one might think. Privacy Pass still relies on classical cryptography, like RSA and elliptic curves. This means that a quantum attacker will be able to forge tokens at will and use them to bypass whatever security mechanism the site operator wants to implement (such as rate limiting). On the other hand, Privacy Pass is unconditionally private, meaning no attacker, quantum or not, can link the redemption of a token to its issuance. What's more, the new capabilities we're developing for this new generation of private authentication technology can and will be instantiated in a way that upholds the same guarantee: your interaction remains private even after Q-day.

This gives us a little breathing room, but we will need an alternative soon. This is an active area of research that has made significant strides in recent years. Still, just as is the case with other aspects of the transition, the primary challenge is the sheer size of post-quantum alternatives: ML-DSA-44 signatures are a whopping 2,420 bytes, while ECDSA-P256 signatures are just 64 bytes. And there's not much hope for drop-in replacements any time soon. Just as for TLS, we'll have to settle for primitives with higher cost and re-engineer our systems to bear this cost.

But what will those primitives be? In this post, we'll explore one potential future for post-quantum privacy on the web, made possible by a recent breakthrough in the design of blind signatures.

What we need to build: a brief look at MOLE

Let's start with an overview of this new technology, which is presently called MOLE ("Moderation Of unLinkable Endorsements"). We'll have much more to say about MOLE later on, but for now we'll highlight the details that are most relevant to cryptography.

One of the core components of Privacy Pass is a blind signature scheme, which allows a client to obtain a signature under an issuer's secret key without revealing to the issuer the message that it signed. The client can then reveal the message and blind signature later on without linking the signature to its issuance.

One type of Privacy Pass token consists of the message and blindly issued signature. To verify the token, the verifier needs the issuer's public key, and so necessarily learns the identity of the issuer. Thus while these tokens protect the identity of the client, they don't protect the identity of the issuer.

Of course, this is exactly what we want for some use cases. The identity of the issuer tells us something about what type of client is connecting to our edge, a signal we use to make decisions in some of our products and for some of our customers. For instance, a client might use a token issued by one of our customers to prove it is authorized to use the customer's VPN product.

However, for many use cases, this is more information than we actually need to make a decision to grant a client access to a resource. Normally we only care that the token was issued by some entity we trust. In fact, MOLE takes this a step further: the token should hide the identity of the issuer altogether so that we can't treat tokens differently based on who issued them. This guarantees equal treatment regardless of the type of client, making it easier for more clients to participate.

This issuer-hiding property is achieved through a new object called an endorsement. An endorsement is issued by an anchor and redeemed by a moderator. Before redemption, the client and moderator agree on an anchor set, the public keys of the anchors trusted by the moderator. During redemption, the client proves it was issued an endorsement by one of the anchors in the anchor set without revealing which one. Upon acceptance, the moderator issues the client the MOLE credential it will use to moderate the client's interaction with the site.

An endorsement can take many forms, but its key property is that it can be redeemed while hiding the identity of the anchor that issued it. There will also be many types of credentials, but because they're intended to be used by a particular moderator, they needn't be anchor-hiding or even publicly verifiable. This means that everything from blind signatures to anonymous credit tokens or anonymous rate-limited credentials can be used to instantiate MOLE credentials.

Now that we have a sense of what we're building, let's look at our options for post quantum.

A feast of cryptography

When designing cryptographic protocols, adaptability and efficiency are often in tension. Sometimes we know exactly what we want to build and can tailor a construction for that purpose; but the more we tailor the protocol for that use case, the harder it becomes to adapt that construction to a different use case.

Adaptability is essential for a system like MOLE. We're not just building one kind of credential system, but many. And the types of credentials we need are likely to change over time, especially on the web where we must constantly adapt to new traffic patterns and attacker behavior. To keep up, we need a set of building blocks that can be composed together into different protocols to meet different requirements.

Most of the post-quantum cryptographic schemes in wide use today come from larger families of constructions, but have been tuned for their particular application. ML-DSA is a good example here: the cryptographic framework from which this scheme was derived can be used to build a variety of things, but to make ML-DSA as compact as possible, its parameters have been carefully tailored to build an efficient and secure digital signature scheme. However, the same parameters would not necessarily be secure for other use cases.

We have come to view this as the central challenge for post-quantum anonymous credentials: to decouple parameter selection from protocol design. Classical credential systems take this for granted: for the most part, protocol designers don't need to think about the parameters of the elliptic curve they're using, allowing even non-experts in the design of elliptic curve cryptography to build useful things with it. Unfortunately, designing efficient post-quantum credentials still requires an enormous amount of expertise.

This situation seems to have changed, however. Earlier this year, we saw a breakthrough that represents a potential sea change for anonymous credentials.

VOLE-in-the-Head

The roots of this breakthrough go back several years. We'll pick up the story three years ago, with the VOLE-in-the-Head (VOLEitH) zero-knowledge proof system (Baum et al., Crypto 2023). A zero-knowledge proof system allows one to prove knowledge of a hidden witness, satisfying some public statement while keeping the witness private. For example, a zero-knowledge proof can be used to prove knowledge of an AES key K for which Y=AES(K,X), where X,Y are public. This proof can be transformed into a digital signature whose security reduces to the security of AES, with X,Y as the public key and K as the secret key. This is exactly the FAEST digital signature, a candidate in NIST's ongoing signature competition.

Compared to many contemporary proof systems, VOLEitH is relatively simple to understand and implement securely. VOLE stands for "Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation" and is an interactive technique that gives two parties correlated random values. These correlations act like authentication tags, allowing the verifier to check that a computation on the hidden witness was performed correctly. In VOLEitH, the prover prepares locally what the two parties would normally generate together — hence “in the head” — then commits to those values and uses the Fiat-Shamir transformation (a widely used tool in cryptography) to select the parts the verifier checks. This step turns the interactive VOLE process into a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof.

Apart from its simplicity, VOLEitH is a fairly unremarkable proof system. It's not succinct in the way many other proof systems are: its proofs are asymptotically linear in the size of the witness and the arithmetic complexity of the statement being proved. However, VOLEitH is concretely very efficient for a particular type of statement, namely one that can be expressed as a set of equations over small binary fields.

One example is the relation Y=AES(K,X) we just discussed. We don't normally think of AES as a set of equations, but many of its computations are designed around arithmetic in GF(28), a field whose elements are single bytes. FAEST proofs for this statement are only about 4KB (NIST Round 3, 128s).

Another example is the KuMQuat signature scheme, in which the signer proves an instance of the Multivariate Quadratic (MQ) problem. Here we're given a system of random, quadratic equations of multiple variables over a small field, like GF(28). Mathematically, this MQ map P looks something like P(s) = (sTA1s + b1s,…,sTAms + bms) where s and each bi are length n vectors and each Ai is an n-by-n matrix. Given P,P(s) for random s, the MQ problem is to find s. We call it quadratic because we multiply the elements of s by itself.

The MQ problem is believed to be hard to solve even for a quantum computer. But because P is made up of quadratic equations, proving knowledge of a solution with VOLEitH is fairly cheap, yielding KuMQuat signatures as small as 2.6KB.

When compared to other post-quantum signatures like ML-DSA or FN-DSA, these numbers don't look especially impressive. But how VOLEitH compares to other schemes in a particular category of constructions is beside the point. For MOLE, we'll need to strike a balance between performance and the ability to build many types of credential systems. To that end, we need one more ingredient.

Multivariate signatures

Another way to build signatures from MQ maps involves embedding some additional mathematical structure into the map. In the Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) signature scheme, the public key is an MQ map P, and a signature is a vector s satisfying P(s) = t, where t is obtained by hashing and salting the message to be signed.

The secret key for this signature scheme is a trapdoor for P with which the signer can derive solutions to the MQ equations. The trapdoor reveals to the signer a hidden partitioning of the variables of each quadratic equation into “oil” and “vinegar” variables. Oil variables are never multiplied by one another, so fixing the vinegar values turns the equations into a linear system that the signer can solve for the oil values. In the public key, oil and vinegar variables are mixed together in a way that hides this structure in the map.

UOV is also a candidate in NIST's ongoing signature standardization effort. It has one of the smallest signatures among the candidates, at just 135 bytes. The trade-off is that it has the largest public keys, at 46.6KB. MAYO is another multivariate candidate with much smaller public keys, at the cost of slightly larger signatures.

The key thing to take away here is that the arithmetic complexity of evaluating a UOV (or MAYO) signature is comparable to evaluating an MQ instance. Both are public quadratic maps over small binary fields, making them a good fit for VOLEitH. This brings us to the breakthrough.

Blind signatures from VOLE-in-the-Head and UOV

Earlier this year, a blind signature called PoMFRIT was published (Baum et al., USENIX Security 2026) that achieved what at the time was a record for candidate post-quantum constructions: 6.7KB for the blind signature itself and just a few hundred bytes for issuance. PoMFRIT is based on VOLE-in-the-Head and the MAYO multivariate signature. We can easily drive the size of the signature down to 4.3KB by swapping MAYO out for UOV. (This figure uses NIST round 3 parameters for UOV (uov-Ip) and FAEST-EM-128s.) The trade-off is larger public keys, but this pays off in applications where a public key can be cached and used sufficiently often.

This is competitive with state-of-the-art lattice-based constructions. But the really good news is that building blocks of PoMFRIT can easily be reconfigured into all of the credential systems we've considered for MOLE, including endorsements. More on this in a bit: for now, let's look at how PoMFRIT works in more detail.

A well-known paradigm for designing blind signatures is the following. First, the client places the message in the cryptographic equivalent of a sealed envelope, called a commitment. For our purposes, a commitment is simply the hash of the message together with some randomness generated by the client. To complete issuance, the signer simply signs the commitment directly.

To construct the blind signature, the client produces a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of the signature and the randomness it used to compute the commitment, called the opening. A verifier would use the signer's public key to verify this proof.

Let's define a bit of notation to make this clearer:

The client generates an opening r and sends a commitment c=H(m,r) to its message m to the issuer.

The issuer produces a signature s=Sign(sk,c) and sends it to the client. It doesn’t learn the message as it’s hidden behind the hash.

Finally, the client produces a proof π of knowledge of s,r for which Verify(pk,H(m,r))=1,

The proof π is the blind signature. It can be verified by any party in possession of the issuer's public key pk and the message m.

Unlinkability comes from the client presenting entirely different objects during the two phases: a commitment is shown to the issuer during issuance, and a zero-knowledge proof is shown to a verifier during presentation. Even if the issuer and verifier collude or are the same entity, they cannot link the sessions.

The size of the proof π is dominated by evaluation of the hash, so we need to choose a hash function that is friendly for our proof system. For most proof systems, such proof-friendly hashes are not well studied, but for VOLEitH it turns out that the Keccak permutation used in SHAKE and TurboSHAKE is a good choice. Keccak’s bitwise operations translate natively into VOLEitH constraints: XOR becomes addition, AND becomes multiplication, and rotations simply rearrange values. (Many popular SNARKs, by contrast, are designed for large prime fields, making byte- and bit-oriented operations less natural to express.)

Nevertheless, Keccak evaluations end up being the largest component of the VOLEitH proof, so we need to make sure we're using only the minimum necessary number of permutations. PoMFRIT requires two: one for the commitment and another for the signature. Concretely, the statement we prove is roughly P(s)=H(H(m,r),rs) where s is the signature, rs is a salt chosen by the issuer, P is the issuer's UOV public key, and H denotes the Keccak permutation with the output truncated to the appropriate length, which also prevents anyone from inverting.

From blind signatures to endorsements and beyond

Recall that for MOLE endorsements, we need something like a blind signature, but one that doesn't reveal the anchor that issued it. That is, we now have a sequence of anchor keys P1,…,PN, and the statement we now want to prove is Pi(s)=H(H(m,r),rs) for some anchor key Pi whose index i is now part of the hidden witness.

With some care, we can write this as a set of constraints with roughly the same cost: two hashes and one MQ evaluation. We need to prove a bit more about the witness. What exactly? We won't spoil it for you: ZK circuit design is part of the craft of cryptographic engineering that makes it so fun. We'll just say the kind of thinking needed here is transferable to just about any modern proof system you might encounter.

Even more advanced credential systems can be constructed in this framework, including the aforementioned anonymous credit tokens and anonymous rate-limited credentials. In both of these cases, the primary cost is an additional hash or two. Each of these also requires proving that part of the witness (e.g., the credit count) is in some expected range, but this is low cost in VOLEitH.

Indeed, for every construction we have considered so far for MOLE, the primary cost is the size of the Keccak evaluation and how many times we need to evaluate it. This means that finding ways to reduce the amount of hashing yields improvements across the board.

Optimizations

Before we go any further, we need to acknowledge that cryptanalysis of multivariate cryptography is still relatively immature. We have seen advances against several parameter regimes in just the last couple of years, Both UOV and MAYO have weathered these attacks well, and an outright break of UOV and even MAYO seems more unlikely with every passing year. But we should at least expect the parameters to change in a way that adds a bit of cost to our constructions.

On the other hand, it's not uncommon for credential systems used in practice to adopt a less-than-conservative security posture for the sake of performance in so far as it affects forgery resistance. This typically means relying on stronger-than-usual computational assumptions. That is, it's possible that a (pre-quantum) attack might come along that breaks anonymous credit tokens, but not ECDSA, despite the fact that they both use the same elliptic curve.

Using fewer hashes

PoMFRIT achieved its size record by doing precisely the same thing. Recall that the blind signature requires proving two hash evaluations, one by the client and the other by the issuer. PoMFRIT observes that VOLEitH proof generation can be split into two stages. In the first stage, the client commits to a random mask. It then hashes the message normally (outside of the ZK circuit), combines the result with the mask, and sends the masked target to the issuer. The issuer uses the UOV trapdoor to find a preimage of this target. In the second stage, the client completes the proof that the preimage and previously committed mask are consistent. The hash remains part of the protocol, but the issuer — acting as the VOLEitH verifier — can compute it directly rather than requiring the zero-knowledge proof to reproduce it.

This strategy substantially reduces proof size, but it also changes our security posture. The plain UOV assumption is that no (quantum) attacker can find a pre-image for a random target without knowledge of the trapdoor. The corresponding one-more-UOV assumption (analogous to the one-more-MAYO assumption in the PoMFRIT paper) neatly captures the additional information available to the attacker as a result of this kind of optimization. The assumption, then, is that this additional information doesn't lead to an attack.

This assumption may turn out to be overly optimistic. Recently, researchers at the University of California, San Diego, and INRIA managed to forge a 1024-bit RSA signature using a Privacy Pass issuer as a signing oracle. Fortunately, Privacy Pass uses 2048-bit RSA, which, in concert with other defense mechanisms, provides a pretty good security margin. Likewise, for UOV we might consider using NIST Level 3 parameters instead of Level 1.

In any case, a bit more study will be required before we rely too heavily on these kinds of optimizations. It's worth emphasizing that a break here would only impact an attacker's ability to forge tokens, not the attacker's ability to violate a client's privacy.

Making each hash cheaper

Standard SHAKE uses a 1600-bit Keccak state with 24 applications of an underlying round function. However, since the SHA-3 standard was published, many have come to believe that 24 rounds is just too much crypto. TurboSHAKE works the same way, except the permutation uses 12 rounds instead of 24. This substantially reduces the size of VOLEitH proofs. In fact, we're quite comfortable with this security margin, and not just for this application.

Another change to Keccak that reduces the proof size is to reduce the size of the state. 256 bits of the state are reserved for the capacity to get 128 bits security. That leaves 1344 bits that can be hashed in one go, which is more than we need. Reducing the state by half to 800 bits leaves us with a rate of 544 bits, which is plenty. On top of that, it even increases the security at the same number of rounds, as an attacker has less to play with. The smaller state means we’re using half the multiplications in our circuit, which reduces the size of the proof.

Leaning into multivariate

In an ideal world, we could avoid proving conventional hashes altogether by replacing each hash with something that composes more natively with the algebraic structure of our primitives. Indeed, those familiar with Pedersen commitments and their use in elliptic curve cryptography may wonder if commitments can be constructed from multivariate cryptography.

This might look something like this: Fix public, random MQ maps F and G and commit to a message m using c=(m+F(r),G(r)). The advantage of this approach is that the degree of the constraints is the same as the degree of the constraints for the UOV signature. Not only does this make the proof smaller, it makes it far simpler, since we avoid evaluating symmetric crypto in ZK altogether.

We experimented with this approach for our application, and it yielded some impressive results. However, it's not at all clear yet if the parameter regime in which multivariate commitments yield an improvement is also secure. Notably, the risk here is not just to unforgeability, but also to client privacy. A lot more study is needed.

Another direction is to build an MQ-friendly pseudorandom generator (PRG).

For typical VOLEitH parameters, adding an extra witness bit adds ten bits to the proof. There is a neat trick to make this a lot cheaper: only one bit of proof per bit of witness! Instead of using VOLEitH directly, we commit to a (relatively) short key. That key we stretch into a larger bitstream using a PRG with low-degree so that it can be computed cheaply in the circuit. Now, to add a witness bit w, we get one extra bit k from the PRG, and store the bit w XOR k in the proof.

There is a performance trade-off: we need to compute the PRG and the witnesses start at degree 2 instead of 1. That especially increases prover time. Also the benefits on proof size only start to pay off when you need a decent number of witness bits.

And of course you need a PRG! You can create a PRG using a random MQ instance, but that’s very slow and seems overly conservative. At the other end is the Goldreich PRG, which can be seen as an as-sparse-as-possible MQ PRG. We’d want something in between, but such PRGs haven’t received much study.

Is MOLE ready for post-quantum?

We already have post-quantum privacy today, so we have some time before we need to have a solution in place, but now is the time to develop alternatives.

Multivariate cryptography looks to be a promising basis for easily building a variety of anonymous tokens and credentials. We're currently developing two schemes in this framework: VOLE-IHAT, a candidate for MOLE endorsements, and VOLE-ACT, a candidate for MOLE credentials. Our current cost estimates for these are shown in the table below. The numbers here are subject to change as we analyze and develop these constructions. We use UOV (uov-Ip) in each case, which means the public keys are all 46.6KB. VOLEitH uses the same parameters as FAEST-EM-128s:

issuance

presentation

PoMFRIT (with UOV)

<1KB

4.3KB (redemption)

VOLE-IHAT

5.6KB

6.5KB (redemption)

VOLE-ACT

5.4KB

12.0KB (spend)

These numbers are significantly larger than their classical counterparts. This comes as no great surprise, as "PQ is big" is really the main hallmark of the transition across the board. However, replacing RSA blind signatures with PoMFRIT has comparable overhead to replacing ECDSA with ML-DSA. The runtimes of these protocols are also excellent: each operation takes just a few milliseconds with our implementation. (Runtime can be improved by quite a bit, though at the cost of higher communication.)

If these numbers hold, then we've already reached an important milestone: the transition to PQ anonymous credentials for the web can now shift from cryptography design to protocol engineering. In other words, we think we can make these numbers work. For example, whereas classical blind signatures might be cheap enough to redeem on every request, we'll have to figure out how to amortize a single redemption over multiple requests.

We have some work to do before we get there. First, we need to make sure our protocols are sound, in particular by producing security proofs for them that show they are secure as long as UOV is secure. Second, we need to wait a bit for cryptanalysis of UOV to catch up. We encourage cryptographers to spend time with multivariate cryptography. Once the parameters stabilize, we believe these schemes will find a place in a ton of useful applications. We've only just scratched the surface so far.

Title: Beyond Unified Detection: What Email Security Teams Need to Control
Context: Evaluate the Workflow, Not Just the Integration Microsoft announced the ICES Vendor Ecosystem in June 2025, and Proofpoint’s participation adds its API-based detections to...
Full Text:
For email security teams, evaluating an integration means understanding both the detections it brings together and the quarantine management and administrative workflows it supports. Proofpoint’s integration with Microsoft’s Integrated Cloud Email Security (ICES) ecosystem brings its post-delivery detections into Microsoft Defender and consolidates investigation and remediation workflows. For customers, the next step is to understand how that integration supports their requirements for administrator-configured enforcement.

Within ICES, Microsoft applies enforcement based on submitted verdicts, verdict severity, and configured policies. Proofpoint contributes its assessments within that model; a third-party engine does not independently override a Microsoft malicious verdict through ICES. Customers can evaluate how this division of responsibilities fits their operational requirements.

Check Point Email Security brings Microsoft’s detection information and native quarantine into its platform alongside Check Point detections and quarantines, combining quarantine management with administrator-configured actions. Where Check Point’s classification differs from Microsoft’s, customers can configure workflows to restore eligible messages that Check Point classifies as safe, including eligible messages classified as high-confidence phishing, and manage supported Junk-folder placements. These actions use a separate workflow from the ICES verdict-precedence mechanism.

For customers, the practical distinction is how each approach combines visibility, quarantine management, and enforcement actions within the workflows their teams use.

Where Will Your Team Manage Quarantined Email?

For customers using both a Secure Email Gateway (SEG) and an API-based integration, the scope of each workflow matters. Proofpoint’s ICES integration applies to its Core Email Protection API and post-delivery detections; its SEG can block or quarantine messages before they reach Microsoft 365. In a deployment using both, the operational responsibilities span two environments:

Proofpoint: Gateway policies, pre-delivery enforcement, and messages quarantined before reaching Microsoft 365.

Microsoft Defender: Microsoft-native detections and Proofpoint’s API-based post-delivery detections shared through ICES.

The announcement describes consolidation of API-based detections in Defender. For a gateway-plus-API deployment, customers also need to confirm how messages stopped by Proofpoint’s SEG are represented and managed, including whether they appear in Defender’s unified quarantine and how enforcement workflows span the two environments.

Check Point’s Unified Quarantine was built to bring Microsoft-native and Check Point-enforced messages into the same administrative and end-user experience.

Managing Conflicting Email Security Verdicts

Combining security engines brings together independent assessments. The operational value also depends on how those assessments inform investigation, quarantine management, and remediation.

Layered security enables independent engines to contribute additional threat assessments. When Check Point identifies a malicious message in a mailbox, it remediates the message; with Proofpoint’s ICES integration, Microsoft performs remediation based on the shared detection. Both approaches support layered protection, with a different division of remediation responsibilities.

When Microsoft and Check Point assess a quarantined message differently, administrator-configured policies determine whether Check Point Email Security automatically restores an eligible message that it classifies as safe. Supported scenarios include eligible messages Microsoft classified as high-confidence phishing.

Example: A finance team is waiting on a quarterly invoice from a long-standing supplier. Microsoft’s filtering, appropriately cautious given the payment-related content, quarantines it as high-confidence phishing. Title: A Kubernetes CVE just dropped. Here’s how to find and fix what matters.
Context: ” Step 4: Map the attack path from node to cloud A node escape is only as dangerous as what the node can access
Full Text:
Critical Kubernetes CVEs arrive constantly. Some hit an operator or controller, some the Linux kernel underneath your nodes, others the container images your teams ship every day. Each one comes with a CVSS score and an urgent recommendation to patch.

What it doesn’t come with is context. A CVSS score tells you how bad a flaw could be in theory. It can’t tell you whether the vulnerable component runs in your clusters, whether anyone could actually exploit it, or what it can reach. Without those answers, teams either scramble to patch everything at once or let the CVE sit in a backlog until it’s forgotten.

Kubernetes makes this harder than most environments. Workloads are ephemeral, permissions are spread across roles, bindings and service accounts, and a single foothold can travel from a pod to a node, from a node to the cloud account, or through a privileged operator to everything it manages.

This post walks through a repeatable approach for triaging any Kubernetes CVE in Orca, then puts it to work on a real example: Copy Fail, a Linux kernel flaw affecting nodes across nearly every major cloud and operating system.

How to triage a Kubernetes CVE: Four questions to ask

Whatever the CVE, effective triage comes down to the same four questions. Orca answers each one from a single platform for cloud security, across every cluster and the cloud accounts they run in.

Where does it run?

Is it internet exposed?

Is it exploitable?

What can it reach?

Each answer narrows the list for the next, so a CVE that touches dozens of clusters ends with a short, ranked set of actions. Here’s how that looks on a real example.

The example: Copy Fail (CVE-2026-31431)

Copy Fail is a bug in the Linux kernel that lets an ordinary user quietly give themselves full admin (root) access. In Kubernetes, that means an attacker who gets into any container can take over the node it runs on, and from there, potentially everything that node can reach. Here’s how Orca takes you from the headline to a fix.

Step 1: Find which nodes and images are affected

Orca’s emerging threats feed, From the News, flags Copy Fail with a plain-language summary and recommended fix. From there, search CVE-2026-31431 in the Vulnerabilities view, part of Orca’s agentless vulnerability management, to see every affected node, node pool and image across clusters and clouds, with the fixed kernel version for each.

Prefer plain English? Ask Orca AI, an AI reasoning engine for security teams, “Which Kubernetes nodes are affected by CVE-2026-31431?” and get the same answer in seconds.

Step 2: Check whether affected nodes or pods are internet exposed

Copy Fail needs a foothold inside a pod first, so checking the node alone isn’t enough. A node can sit on a private network and still run a pod that’s reachable from the internet through a LoadBalancer or an Ingress. If that pod is compromised, the attacker lands on the node’s kernel just the same. Click into an affected node to see its asset details, including whether the node or any workload running on it is publicly accessible, and how many high-severity risks it carries. Nodes with any internet-facing path go to the top of the list. Nodes with no exposure still get patched, just on a normal cycle.

Step 3: Confirm whether the CVE is exploitable

Open the Copy Fail risk on that node to see the vulnerable kernel package it affects, along with Orca’s exploitability and risk scoring details. Copy Fail has public exploit code, so the answer is yes, and on a node with an internet-exposed workload, that moves it from “patch soon” to “patch now.”

Step 4: Map the attack path from node to cloud

A node escape is only as dangerous as what the node can access. Use attack path analysis to see how an attacker could move to the cloud roles, secrets or crown jewel data within reach, all in one ranked path. That’s the alert you patch first.

Go further with Orca: Remediate, prevent, and prove progress

That’s the triage done. But finding the risk is only part of the job, and Orca helps with the rest too.

Prove progress to leadership. When leadership asks where things stand, you shouldn’t need to scramble and pull a spreadsheet together to answer. The K8s & Container Security dashboard shows how many clusters and nodes are still affected, and that number drops as patches roll out, so one view shows both your current risk and your progress.

Patch without letting new risk in. Teams keep deploying while patches roll out, and every new pod is a possible foothold. Orca’s Admission Controller checks each workload before it’s admitted, stopping new privileged or host-namespace pods, which make it easier to take over a node from a compromised container, from landing in affected clusters. Policies can warn or block depending on what you need, and every decision is logged in Orca alongside the CVE you’re tracking.

Stay audit-ready. An unpatched critical vulnerability is an audit finding waiting to happen. Orca automatically maps it to the regulatory compliance frameworks you report on, such as PCI DSS 4.0 and SOC 2, so you know which controls are affected now and have the evidence ready once remediation is done, instead of scrambling for it later.

Cut the time to fix. Orca opens tickets in tools you already use with the affected nodes and fixed kernel version already filled in, so engineers start fixing instead of investigating, and you can track every ticket through to closure. Where patching has to wait, disabling the affected kernel module is a quick interim mitigation.

Catch an attack before the patch lands. Rolling new images across a fleet takes time, and that window is when attackers move. Orca’s cloud detection and response monitors affected workloads for suspicious activity, so if someone tries to use the foothold, you know right away and can respond.

Together, that’s the difference between knowing about a CVE and being done with it.

A repeatable workflow for the next Kubernetes CVE

Kubernetes CVEs aren’t slowing down, and patching everything the moment it’s disclosed isn’t realistic. The teams that stay ahead are the ones that know where those CVEs are throughout their environment, and which ones need to get remediated first.

Orca helps you do exactly that. From the first alert to the closed ticket, the Orca Cloud Security Platform shows you where a CVE runs, whether it’s exposed, whether it’s exploitable, what it can reach, and how it affects your compliance posture. Copy Fail is one example. The same workflow works for whatever CVE lands next.

See it in your own environment. Request a demo and we’ll walk through how Orca triages the Kubernetes CVEs that matter most to your clusters. To go deeper on Orca’s Kubernetes and Container Security capabilities, download the data sheet.
