That's defense in depth: none of them is enough alone, none of them is redundant, and together they cover each other:

OpenShell is prevention. Hard limits, enforced below the agent. It decides what's possible at all.

Prempti is judgment. It understands the agent's actions, can stop the obvious stuff early, and ask a human when something looks off.

Falco is ground truth. It sees what ran, no matter how it got there, from a place the agent can't reach.

So, who watches the watchmen? Something the agent can't touch. OpenShell and Prempti stand right next to the agent, and that's exactly why they're useful: they can stop things before they happen. Falco stands outside, and that's why it's useful: it sees everything that happens, including what happens to the watchmen.

Try the three watchmen workflow

Everything is in the demo repo. You need Docker 28+, a Just command runner, and the OpenShell CLI and gateway. nix develop gives you all three, and just gateway starts a local gateway.

just gateway # once: local OpenShell gateway just falco # terminal 1: Falco with the OpenShell rules just openshell # terminal 2: Claude Code in a sandbox, with Prempti just prempti-logs # terminal 3: Prempti's verdicts

No Anthropic API key? Run the simulated evil agent instead and watch Falco light up:

openshell sandbox create --name evil --no-keep --from openshell-claude-prempti \ -- bash -c "$(cat test/evil-agent.sh)"

test/kill-prempti.sh and test/hijack-prempti.sh replay Scene 5 the same way.

We tested this on macOS (Apple Silicon) with colima, OpenShell 0.1.2, Falco 0.45, and Prempti 0.2.1.

One thing we learned running real sessions: Claude Code does a lot in the background (telemetry, claude.ai connectors, a plugin-marketplace clone). OpenShell's policy blocks all of it, as it should, and Falco reported every blocked connection and credential probe: about 160 alerts in a session where nothing bad happened. Three Claude Code environment variables in the entrypoint and a few narrow rule exceptions brought that to 0. Tune detection against real agent sessions, not just the attacks you script.

No single layer was enough: each caught something the others missed. The demo is repo available, so you can run the scenarios yourself and see what each layer catches and misses

Title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
Context: We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation
Full Text:
On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected.

Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens.

After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation.

Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs.

What happened

GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day.

This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.

The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions.

Immediate remediation

After disabling the model, we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it:

To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context. We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid request. This alone prevents the bug from being exercised.

To fix the engine, we also made the rejection path safe. Relying on pool size alone is fragile: any change to quantization, tensor parallelism, CUDA graph sizes, or a future model version changes the pool size in a way that's easy to miss. Furthermore, there may be other situations in which the prefill scheduler can reject a request and trigger the same bug. To prevent this, we also patched the engine so that a request carrying a pending rejection is retired at the disaggregation admission queue, with its original error, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer happens. We proposed this upstream as #38704, which also had the decode node verify that the number of tokens transferred matches the number it reserved. The fix was already on SGLang main in #36988, merged September 6 for a related failure path but not yet released. The maintainers also merged #38935, which rejects these requests earlier, following our approach.

We validated both changes against the researcher's reproduction script and our own canary-marker tests before restoring the model.

Background: how we serve GLM 5.3

Workers AI runs GLM 5.3 with SGLang in a disaggregated configuration: a pool of prefill GPUs processes the prompt and produces the model's KV cache for it, then hands that cache over remote direct memory access (RDMA), via Mooncake, to a pool of decode GPUs that generate the response. We have written about this architecture before in our posts on high-performance LLMs and smaller, faster, safer models.

The KV cache in GPU memory is a shared pool of fixed-size pages. Each request is assigned pages when it is admitted and releases them when it finishes. Pages are not currently zeroed between requests; the next request that gets a page simply overwrites it. This approach is common among inference engines and is necessary to achieve the best performance, but it means that the inference engine is responsible for tracking ownership of these memory pages. KV cache page ownership and lifetime tracking has to deal with not just shared ownership within a node (KV cache offload and token generation both access the memory with different lifetimes), but also ownership that is technically shared with the remote prefill node (which holds a simultaneous mutable reference to the page).

Furthermore, the size of this pool is not a configuration value. SGLang sizes it at startup from whatever GPU memory remains after loading the model weights. The model's advertised context length is a separate configuration value. Nothing forces the two to agree, and it is our job to check that they do.

Issue one: misconfiguration

On our GLM 5.3 prefill nodes with our configuration, the pool came to 681,280 tokens while the model's context length is 1,048,576 tokens. The selected KV pool size is printed by SGLang in logs during startup and exposed as a metric. We were aware of this size mismatch; however, during pre-launch testing we observed successful HTTP status codes and a streaming body with no error frames during benchmarking. We assumed that the engine was capable of gracefully handling the difference between the KV cache pool and requested context window via streaming or some other mechanism.

This was one critical gap in our testing: we only validated HTTP response codes and engine performance at long contexts, without validating model output and coherence. We now check KV pool size against context length directly, from the running engine, before any disaggregated deployment change ships, rather than inferring it from response codes.

Issue two: SGLang bug

In v0.5.21, the SGLang team has now addressed this bug in how it was handling prompts longer than the KV pool size. Here’s what was happening before.

When a prompt arrived that was longer than the KV pool could hold, SGLang's scheduler rejected it. The rejection path (Req.set_finish_with_abort) recorded the error to be returned to the client and swapped the prompt for a one-token placeholder so that the request could drain through the normal batch machinery without allocating real memory. On a single-node deployment this worked: the placeholder ran, the batch finished, and the client received an error.

In disaggregated mode such as we operate, the admission queues on both prefill and decode checked whether a request was finished, not whether it was rejected. A rejected request reported itself as live. So:

Bootstrap. The router told the decode node the prompt length (8 pages in the diagram). Decode reserved 8 KV pages for the request.

Prefill admission. The prefill admission queue admitted any request where req.finished() was False. A rejected request stored its rejection in to_finish, not finished_reason, so finished() still returned False. The rejected request was admitted.

Prefill forward pass. Rejection had already replaced the prompt with a one-token placeholder. Prefill ran a trivial forward pass on that one token.

KV transfer. Prefill sent one page of KV to decode and signaled that the transfer was complete.

Decode admission. Decode's admission queue had the same finished() check, so it accepted the handoff.

Decode attention. Decode started generating and attention read all 8 reserved pages. Only page P0 had been written by this request. Pages P1 to P7 still held what earlier requests left in them: other users' prompts and partial generations.

Response. The client got HTTP 200 instead of HTTP 400. prompt_tokens matched the long prompt and the reply was coherent. It arrived faster than an 8-page prefill should take, and it contained content from other users' KV pages.

Every request over the threshold behaved this way. This bug had been reported to SGLang by another user as issue #30233 on July 6, 2026, which Cloudflare noticed while investigating this incident. We had been flagging these types of issues with SGLang since v0.5.10 and this security incident sped up work that Cloudflare had already started in collaboration with the SGLang team. The patch for this issue was released in SGLang v0.5.20, with follow-ups in v0.5.21 and v0.5.22, and is available for all other operators dependent on SGLang to use. We highly recommend all operators update SGLang dependencies to v0.5.22 or later. For more details on specific PRs, read on below.

GLM 5.3 was the only model affected by this bug. Every other disaggregated deployment on Workers AI has KV pools larger than its context length on both prefill and decode, so no request could reach the rejection path. We have applied the engine fix and the hardening described below to every model we serve with SGLang, and our deployment checks require them for every new deployment.

Ongoing hardening effort

This bug belongs to a class of KV cache memory-safety bugs that Cloudflare has been working to address for several months. In each case, a page is freed, reused, or read while something else still has a claim on it. We see two common causes.

The first is page lifetime within a single node. Several tasks on a decode node can hold the same page at once: token generation, offload to host memory, the KV transfer receiver, and the abort and error paths. If one of them frees the page while another is still using it, a new request can be given that page while it is still being read or written. Our earlier fixes for decode offload (#24226, #30899) and double release on grammar errors (#30937) were of this kind.

The second is a race across nodes. When a request is aborted while prefill is still writing its KV cache to decode over RDMA, the writes already sent cannot be recalled. If decode frees those pages right away, those pages can be given to another request, and the late writes land in that request's KV cache. Cloudflare has contributed to the effort to fix this race through proposed fixes (#31357, #38961) and a reproduction script (#32564). In both cases the result is corrupted output, or one user's data in another user's response, with no error raised. The bug in this incident was different: a rejected request went through the handoff every time, rather than by a timing accident. But it had the same result: decode reading pages this request never wrote. None of these covered the failure in this incident in which prefill rejected the request, and decode never learned of it.

Since the incident, we have:

Extended deferred release to hold prefill's source pages as well, and to cover every failure type, not just aborts. We proposed it upstream as #38961, which was superseded by #40645, #41402, and #41404.

Deployed bounded Mooncake transfer batches (#32758, from the SGLang community), so no single transfer call can outlast the release timeout.

Changed our load balancer so a client disconnect no longer aborts a request mid-transfer. It holds the prefill connection until prefill finishes and the decode connection until the first token, then closes both.

Added a check to every disaggregated deployment change: KV pool size measured against context length, deferred release on both roles, transfer batch bounds inside the release timeout, and all required patches applied.

All of these changes were released to our disaggregated production deployments.

Working with the SGLang team

We met with the SGLang maintainers at RadixArk on September 10, the day after the incident. We agreed that RadixArk would investigate the race conditions we had reported, upstream the integrity-checking idea, and build reproduction tests for this class of bug.

The following have landed on SGLang main to address this incident and related KV cache race conditions, and all but one are included in v0.5.22. Operators running disaggregated SGLang should update to v0.5.22 or backport these patches as needed.

What we recommend to other operators

If you run SGLang in disaggregated prefill/decode mode, we recommend the following:

Measure your KV pool and compare it to your context length, on every prefill and decode node, from the engine's startup log, after every change to weights, quantization, parallelism, or memory fraction. If the pool is smaller, lower the context length to fit. Do not rely on a proxy to enforce the limit, and do not assume the engine will reject what does not fit. This is the check we did not enforce.

Upgrade to a build that includes #36988 and #38935 (v0.5.22 or later), so an over-length request is rejected before handoff regardless of pool size. This is the engine-side fix, and it is the backstop for the day your check in step one is wrong.

Run with deferred KV release on both roles (default after #41023), and bound your Mooncake transfer batches so a single timed-out call cannot leave an unbounded tail of writes.

Turn on corruption detection where your model supports it. --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum and --kv-canary do not yet cover every model architecture. Check your logs to confirm requests are being verified. We are working with the SGLang team to extend both checks to more architectures, including GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, and DeepSeek V4.

Ensure your proxy is not generating unnecessary aborts. Configure your load balancer to allow requests to proceed up to the first token, so that you do not trigger an abort that requires cross-node coordination.

Longer term

Integrity by construction

Configuration checks and lifecycle fixes reduce the number of ways a page can be misused. They do not make misuse impossible, and this incident is a reminder that the next bug will have a shape we have not seen. The durable answer is for the engine to detect, at read time, that a request is about to attend over a page it does not own, and fail that one request rather than return someone else's data.

We built a prototype of this over the summer and described it in August. Every physical KV page carries a tag that changes when the page is reallocated, each request records the tags it expects, and the mapping is checked before decode reads the cache. In our tests it cost under 1% in throughput and tail latency. We tested it on GLM 5.2 in mid-August, but disabled it shortly afterwards due to reliability issues.

The prototype was also tied to specific attention backends and model architectures, so it could not be a general fix. We are working with the SGLang team to build a production version into the engine that works across every model, rather than maintaining Cloudflare-specific patches. The per-transfer checksum in #39500 is a first step: it validates the handoff from prefill to decode. Page-level tags go further, because they check every read, including reads long after the transfer.

Integrity by mathematical impossibility

RDMA copies data directly from one node’s memory to another’s. It’s vital for the two machines to agree on where the data goes, how large it is, and when it’s finished; any mismatch can cause the receiver to read the wrong data. This bug is an example of a consistency failure in a distributed system, in which the two machines had inconsistent views of the state of that system.

Elsewhere in Cloudflare, we have put effort into proving the safety of distributed systems using formal verification methods. Topaz enables conflict-free IP selection for our authoritative DNS servers. Models of Meerkat’s QuePaxa implementation have demonstrated consistency bugs that were subsequently fixed.

We are now directing our experience in formal methods to KV cache transfer engines. This will start with modeling and proving the safety of an RDMA-based KV cache transfer protocol. The goal is to model our production SGLang’s distributed KV cache system using Mooncake, then track and fix any divergence from the safety properties we want to guarantee. The aim is to prove — as far as possible — that a bug like this cannot occur again. Realistically, we expect gaps in what the provers can tell us, but proving the rest of the system allows us to more closely review and monitor those gaps.

Coordinated disclosure

We are publishing this report as part of a coordinated disclosure. We want to thank the researcher, Gadi Evron, who reported this through our HackerOne program with a clear, reproducible script and gave us time to fix it and to coordinate with the SGLang maintainers before publishing. We also want to thank the SGLang team at RadixArk, who treated this as their problem as well as ours and landed the upstream fixes with urgency.

Read more at the post from the SGLang team.

If you find a security issue in Workers AI, please report it at hackerone.com/cloudflare.

Full Text:
Learn how to use Tenable solutions to find vulnerable PHP versions, prioritize remediation, and patch the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) faster.

Key takeaways

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) put security teams in a race against attackers. PHP runs on more than 70% of websites, so organizations need to quickly find where they’re affected and update PHP to fixed versions.

Tenable helps you find PHP2Shell across your attack surface. Tenable One Attack Surface Management discovers externally facing PHP assets. Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center provide detections, including local checks for Linux distribution packages. Tenable One Web App Scanning assesses web applications, and Tenable One Cloud Exposure covers cloud workloads.

Tenable accelerates remediation. Tenable Patch Management matches exposures to the right patches, launches patch workflows, and validates fixes with post-scan checks. Tenable One with Tenable Hexa AI lets you find vulnerable assets, create exposure initiatives, and generate remediation tickets with simple prompts.

Respond faster with Tenable solutions

The recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) have put security teams in a race against attackers to remediate or mitigate exposure before their systems are targeted. PHP runs on more than 70% of websites, and many of those sites run unsupported, legacy branches that no longer receive upstream support. Organizations need to quickly find where they’re affected and update PHP to fixed versions.

To help cybersecurity teams accelerate emergency response, this blog outlines tips for using the Tenable solutions to identify vulnerable versions of PHP, prioritize remediation decisions, and implement patches as quickly as possible.

External Attack Surface Management

Tenable One Attack Surface Management (ASM) helps you discover externally facing assets running PHP. ASM continuously scans public data sources, such as DNS records, IP addresses, Autonomous System Numbers (ASN), WHOIS registrations, and neighboring IP ranges, to discover forgotten, rogue, or shadow IT assets that might be vulnerable to PHP2Shell. This is one of the first steps to take. It shows your digital footprint from the attacker’s perspective and identifies potential entry points into your organization.

Important ASM tips include:

Use ASM to find additional top-level domains related to your organization. Suggested Domains helps you identify additional domains you may own based on ASN, brand, domain name, IP range, subdomain, or nameserver. You can also adjust the suggestion rules to prioritize domain names based on the likelihood of ownership.

Search the inventory for PHP deployments. Create a query in ASM to identify PHP as a programming language filter. This gives you a quick starting point to assess locations, asset details, and software versions for further analysis.

Continuously monitor for changes in your attack surface. Use Subscriptions in ASM to receive event-driven notifications and understand important changes in your attack surface that may create new exposure. Choose from hundreds of pre-built event categories or create a customized subscription. Two subscriptions apply to PHP: PHP in applications and PHP end-of-life installs.

Explore the solution walk-through to learn more about Tenable One Attack Surface Management.

In Explore > Asset Inventory, review the inventory of assets facing the outside world. To add another inventory source, click '+' and choose an option from the drop-down menu, such as 'Add Hostnames or Domains.' In the pop-up menu, enter a new hostname, for example 'tenable.com.' To narrow the results to assets running PHP, use the query bar to set 'Programming Language' equal to 'PHP.' The results show 265 assets with PHP listed as their Programming Language. Create a 'PHP2Shell' tag and apply it to the selected assets so they can be grouped and prioritized. The Tags column then displays the 'PHP2Shell' tag. Subscriptions can be used to view and assess PHP. Subscriptions provide a growing list of events, including predefined lists and categories. Search for 'PHP' and add the 'PHP - v1' subscription. After subscribing, create an alert for the subscription. The subscription is set to 'Programming Language' contains php, so it filters assets and sends an alert when a new asset meeting this criteria is identified.

Vulnerability Management

Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center both help you find PHP2Shell vulnerabilities with detections for PHP, including local checks for PHP packages from Linux distributions. Tenable will release additional detections as vendors publish fixes in their security advisories.

Both solutions help you create out-of-band, tactical scans based on your preferred scan policy. Additional tips include:

Update plugin feeds before running a scan. Tenable One Vulnerability Management automatically manages and updates plugin feeds through cloud synchronization by default. In offline or air-gapped environments, Tenable Security Center may require manual plugin feed updates.

Use thorough testing to discover more vulnerabilities. Enabling thorough testing and paranoia mode in your scan policy conducts deeper assessments of your attack surface using multiple methods to discover risk. This is very important when you need to scan software across all system drives or investigate deep component-level software vulnerabilities where default settings may result in false negatives.

Assign tags to indicate exposure. Use dynamic tagging to identify PHP2Shell on existing and newly discovered assets.

Title: PHP2Shell Is a Wake-Up Call for Every Business Leader
Context: AI is changing how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited for defenders and attackers alike, and the practical effect is that the time organizations have between a flaw...
Full Text:
AI is changing how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited for defenders and attackers alike, and the practical effect is that the time organizations have between a flaw being found and a flaw being exploited keeps shrinking. Today, we have more known vulnerabilities than at any point in history, and they’re being exploited faster than ever. Nearly 87% of exploited vulnerabilities in 2026 have been exploited before or on the day they were disclosed, up from 48% in 2024 and just 19% in 2018, according to zerodayclock.com, a neutral, independent observatory for cybersecurity telemetry.

More code, more bugs, and AI-aided discovery have all influenced this volume. The systems exposed are often the same systems that run revenue, operations, and customer relationships. Leaders now need to focus on something bigger than prevention alone. They need to build cyber resilience, the ability to withstand an attack, continue operating, and recover quickly. Every organization is racing against the clock to build that resilience.

We saw this play out recently during a week that saw multiple high-profile vulnerabilities and security incidents emerge in rapid succession. PHP2Shell, the name given to two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in PHP, became one of the most visible examples of how quickly newly disclosed flaws can become immediate operational risks. Researchers using frontier AI models identified the flaws and worked with the PHP Foundation to prepare fixes, but details leaked before the planned release. Patches were pushed early, but between the time the vulnerability was disclosed and the patch was available, exploitation attempts began appearing almost immediately. Our Arctic Wolf Labs researchers used aggregated, anonymized telemetry from across our customer community to spot spikes in scanning activity and to analyze exploitation attempts and uncover attacker payloads tied to PHP2Shell. Labs also replicated attacker techniques in controlled environments.

Those findings fed new detections, threat hunt queries, and immediately valuable customer remediation guidance, but detection and response work like this is most effective when an organization already knows what it needs to protect. While PHP2Shell captured much of the industry’s attention, it was only one example in a week that underscored how quickly new exposures can emerge across technologies and attack surfaces. The broader lesson is that organizations need resilience before the next disclosure arrives, and that the time to build cyber resilience into an organization’s ecosystem is now. Jason Clinton, Deputy CISO at Anthropic, warned on X following the PHP2Shell disclosure that security leaders need to prepare their boards as soon as possible for the new threat landscape.

“As bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse before they get better. security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now. not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)” — Jason Clinton, Deputy CISO at Anthropic

Organizations best positioned during that window already knew where PHP ran in their environment, which of those systems faced the internet, and how quickly they could patch, restart, and verify each one. A flaw in a system you cannot see cannot be fixed in the hours that matter. Those are the basics boards need to fund. Because the gap between discovery and exploitation will keep shrinking, the organizations that win the race against the clock are the ones that build that foundation of continuous visibility into their attack surface and disciplined exposure management before the next disclosure arrives.

Machine Speed Is the New Normal

AI accelerated both sides of the PHP2Shell situation timeline. The underlying flaws in the code had reportedly been in PHP for years, and turning them into a usable exploit required a level of complexity that would have been extremely difficult and time-consuming for most researchers to achieve on their own. Attackers gain the same AI efficiencies defenders do. They’re using AI to write malware, build exploits, find vulnerabilities, and automate actions. This means the gap between a flaw being disclosed and being exploited will keep narrowing. Patching alone cannot keep pace when that gap is just a few hours long.

In many circumstances, a vulnerability is disclosed before a patch is available. PHP2Shell showed us that. In those moments, security leaders need a way to detect exploit attempts and respond effectively. Machine speed meets that moment, especially when an exposure is widespread, and security leaders should recognize that machine-speed attack and defense are the new normal.

That shift has implications far beyond the security team. Cyber risk now deserves the same level of ownership, accountability, and investment as financial and operational risk. Boards and executive teams need to treat security as a business issue, not just a technical one. That starts with the fundamentals, including maintaining an accurate inventory of assets, applying patches on a defined timeline, enforcing strong identity controls, and maintaining continuous visibility across the environment. These aren’t new security practices, but they become far more important as AI compresses response timelines. You can’t remediate a vulnerability in hours if you don’t know the system exists.

The Four Fundamental Principles of Threat Protection for the AI Era

Vulnerabilities aren’t the only path to a breach. Initial access comes from social engineering (which is scaling with AI), internet-facing misconfigurations, and internet-facing vulnerabilities. Once an attacker is inside, more internal exposure means faster movement. We want to close the opportunity through configuration health and security hygiene.

Security fundamentals only work when teams can operationalize them consistently.

Exposure management strategies turn security hygiene upkeep into a repeatable process. Start with full visibility of your attack surface, including shadow IT and configuration gaps. Then connect asset management with vulnerability and patch management so each cycle improves on the last. Find known and hidden assets, assess them in the context of one another, identify where vulnerabilities are present and controls are missing, and mitigate the highest impact exposures first.

True resilience requires a continuous cycle of risk mitigation over time. Fewer exposures mean fewer opportunities for attackers, and organizations of every size can better defend against AI-driven threats with AI-driven defense and expert oversight. That means operating at machine speed with experts overseeing the work, and it requires knowing your environment, maintaining strong security fundamentals, and responding quickly when new threats emerge. In an era of machine-speed attacks, resilience belongs to organizations that can move just as fast.

Security operations must evolve as well. Human-only processes can’t keep pace with the speed and volume of modern threats. At the same time, fully autonomous security without oversight introduces its own risks. AI should handle most of the volume of investigation that slows down teams, while experienced analysts focus on validation, judgment, and the genuinely complex threats that require context. We’ve built Arctic Wolf around that principle. Our patent-pending Swarm of Experts™ combines specialized AI agents with expert human oversight, allowing us to operate at machine speed. Large teams of AI agents perform investigations, analysis, and response activities at scale, while experienced security experts remain involved where judgment matters most.

Leaders also need to prepare for the reality that one day, their organization may fall victim to AI-driven adversaries, with tested response plans and the ability to restore operations quickly. As the threat landscape rapidly evolves, this scenario appears increasingly likely, especially for businesses that lack the resources to staff their own security team.

We built Arctic Wolf for moments like this one. Internal staffing around the clock is difficult and costly, even for large organizations. Attackers don’t care about holidays, and AI cares even less. That’s why a partner matters. By combining AI-driven automation with expert human oversight, we help customers respond with speed and confidence when new risks emerge. Through our global partner ecosystem, we’re bringing that capability to organizations around the world and helping security leaders turn cyber risk into cyber resilience.

PHP2Shell won’t be the last vulnerability to remind us how quickly the threat landscape can change. This isn’t a risk to sleep on or push to next year’s budget. The time to act is now. The organizations that come through these moments will be the ones that understand their environments, maintain strong security fundamentals, and can respond decisively when new threats emerge. There has never been a better time to get proactive about cyber resilience.

This blog reflects the author’s views as of the publication date and contains forward-looking statements and opinions about technology trends. Actual outcomes may differ based on attacker behavior, customer environments, and broader market and regulatory developments.

Title: The apps are only the beginning.
Context: Attackers target critical PHP flaws, and former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI’s role in the vulnerability surge. So far, HPE says it has found no publicly available exploit code or evidence that attackers are exploiting these vulnerabilities in the wild.
Full Text:
Attackers target critical PHP flaws, and former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI’s role in the vulnerability surge. Railway confirms a cyberattack. HPE patches critical ArubaOS flaws. Quest Diagnostics investigates a disruptive intrusion. Capcom reports a data breach. China-linked hackers put AI-powered attacks on autopilot. And researchers uncover a Microsoft 365 campaign that hijacks authentication tokens to bypass MFA. Our guest is Anudeep Parhar, COO at Entrust, sharing his thoughts on AI kill switches. eMudra throws in the certificate towel.

Today is Friday, October 23rd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Attackers ramp up attempts to exploit critical PHP vulnerabilities.

Attackers are ramping up attempts to exploit two critical PHP vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell, but researchers have yet to confirm a successful compromise in the wild.

The flaws allow unauthenticated remote code execution and prompted emergency patches on October 21. Sophos identified attempts to deploy Potassium, a Mirai botnet variant, although the attack it examined was unsuccessful.

Researchers say exploitation is proving more difficult than initially feared, largely because successful attacks require specific server configurations or ways around memory protections.

VulnCheck has developed an exploit that bypasses one such protection, while an exposed attacker server revealed custom exploitation tools and unsuccessful attempts against dozens of targets.

Meanwhile, patching remains a challenge. Qualys estimates roughly 110 million PHP instances run unsupported versions that won’t receive fixes.

Security researchers have identified 426 mobile apps connecting to servers running PHP versions potentially affected by the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities.

NowSecure analyzed more than 15,000 Android and iOS apps, finding that 170 connected to servers running outdated PHP versions that no longer receive official security updates.

The vulnerabilities affect backend servers, not the mobile apps themselves, and could allow attackers to execute malicious code remotely without authentication.

Importantly, researchers caution that identifying a potentially vulnerable PHP version doesn’t establish whether a server remains unpatched or exploitable.

The findings also highlight the risks of third-party dependencies. One advertising provider’s server was contacted by 151 different apps.

NowSecure recommends developers work with their infrastructure providers to verify patching, upgrade unsupported PHP installations, and investigate potential exploitation.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI and PHP.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs says artificial intelligence is fueling an unprecedented surge in software vulnerability discoveries, creating what some are calling “Black October” for cybersecurity.

Appearing on CNBC, Krebs said AI-powered tools are uncovering security flaws at a pace that threatens to overwhelm organizations’ ability to patch them.

He pointed to the recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities as an example. While attackers have attempted exploitation, Krebs said no successful compromises have been confirmed.

His biggest concern isn’t necessarily large enterprises, which generally have the resources to respond quickly. It’s smaller businesses, rural hospitals, utilities, and managed service providers that lack dedicated security teams.

Krebs warned that vulnerabilities in third-party services could expose entire networks, while legacy systems can complicate patching.

He expects the situation to get worse before it improves, as AI continues uncovering vulnerabilities faster than organizations can address them.

Cloud development platform Railway has confirmed a cyberattack.

Cloud development platform Railway has confirmed a cyberattack that may have exposed customer passwords, API keys, and other secrets stored in encrypted environment variables. The company believes the breach affected a subset of customers but is urging all users to revoke and rotate their credentials as a precaution. Railway temporarily suspended new builds and deployments while investigating. The number of affected customers, the attack’s root cause, and the systems compromised remain unknown.

Railway suspects the incident is part of a broader campaign targeting AI inference providers. Earlier this week, AI coding tool OpenCode reported a similar attack that exposed credentials belonging to more than one percent of its customers. Railway says it plans to publish a detailed post-mortem.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise patches critical vulnerabilities in ArubaOS.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise has released security updates addressing 72 vulnerabilities in ArubaOS, including eight maximum-severity flaws that could allow attackers to bypass authentication or remotely execute malicious code.

The vulnerabilities affect multiple versions of ArubaOS 8 and 10, which power enterprise wireless networking equipment, including access points, controllers, and gateways. All eight maximum-severity flaws can be exploited remotely without authentication, using relatively simple attacks that require no user interaction.

HPE is strongly urging customers to install the patches, citing the number and potential impact of the vulnerabilities. The company also recommends restricting access to management interfaces through network segmentation and firewall controls.

So far, HPE says it has found no publicly available exploit code or evidence that attackers are exploiting these vulnerabilities in the wild.

Quest Diagnostics is investigating a disruptive cyberattack.

Quest Diagnostics is investigating a cyberattack that may have exposed patient information and disrupted access to medical test results.

The company discovered unauthorized access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager platform, which healthcare providers use to order tests and retrieve results. Quest took the system offline Thursday and temporarily paused several other systems as a precaution.

The company believes some patient data was accessed but hasn’t determined what information was compromised. Quest says its other operations weren’t affected and is working with law enforcement.

Healthcare providers can use paper requisitions while the system is unavailable. Quest expects to restore service Friday.

The company says the attack is unrelated to recently disclosed PHP vulnerabilities. No threat actor has claimed responsibility.

Capcom discloses a data breach.

Japanese gaming giant Capcom has disclosed a data breach affecting nearly 11.8 million records associated with its CAPCOM ID service.

The compromised information includes email addresses, account identifiers, and login activity. Attackers also changed passwords on 196 accounts, which Capcom has since reset.

The company says it has no evidence that customers’ original passwords were compromised, and credit card information remains unaffected.

Capcom has contained the unauthorized access and notified Japanese authorities. Customers are being warned to watch for phishing attempts impersonating the company.

Megaman, please call your office.

A China-linked threat actor is using Artex to automate cyberattacks.

Microsoft says a China-linked threat actor is using an open-source AI penetration testing framework called Artex to automate cyberattacks against hundreds of organizations.

The group, tracked as Storm-0940, used the tool in an October campaign targeting ConnectWise customers, accelerating reconnaissance, password spraying, and abuse of OAuth applications.

Microsoft observed more than 151,000 failed login attempts, along with successful authentication using compromised ConnectWise application identities.

The attackers attempted to access more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, sometimes progressing beyond authentication to modify credentials, manipulate directory settings, and establish persistent access.

In one burst of activity, the group targeted more than 300 accounts across eight organizations at over 2,900 attempts per minute.

Microsoft says the campaign illustrates how AI-assisted automation can dramatically accelerate established attack techniques, giving defenders less time to respond.

Researchers uncover a campaign that compromises Microsoft 365 accounts by stealing and replaying authentication tokens.

Security researchers at Huntress have uncovered a ten-week campaign that compromised Microsoft 365 accounts at 79 organizations by stealing and replaying authentication tokens.

Attackers used adversary-in-the-middle phishing and other techniques to capture legitimate login sessions, allowing them to bypass multifactor authentication without needing victims’ passwords.

Huntress observed at least 497 successful sign-ins alongside more than 200,000 failed attempts. Once inside, attackers registered 48 rogue devices, replaced victims’ authentication methods, and created hidden inbox rules to conceal suspicious communications.

In one case, a compromised account was used to send a payroll-related email to an outside contact.

The attacks relied partly on infrastructure belonging to a German hosting provider.

Huntress recommends properly configured Conditional Access policies and warns that password resets alone won’t eliminate persistent access. Organizations must also revoke sessions and remove unauthorized devices and authentication methods.

eMudra throws in the certificate towel.

From our “you can’t fire me, I quit!” desk, Indian digital trust company eMudhra is getting out of the global SSL/TLS certificate business following a security incident that attracted considerable scrutiny.

The company says it revoked the affected certificate authorities within 14 hours, with no infrastructure compromise, data breach, or affected customer certificates issued.

But eMudhra’s chairman says the resulting social media attention was disproportionate, particularly for a business representing just one percent of company revenue.

Add rising compliance costs and competition from free certificates, and the board decided it was time to pursue other opportunities.

eMudhra promises a smooth transition, including free replacement certificates for affected customers.

Its other digital trust services remain unaffected.

And so, after careful consideration, eMudhra has decided that SSL certificates just aren’t its thing anymore.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: PHP2Shell: What to Expect and What to Do Next
Context: Attackers were exploiting PHP2Shell before the patch existed Amazon's threat intelligence team saw the first exploitation attempt on October 17, 2026
Full Text:
What you will learn

Why PHP2Shell runs before your app code does, why a clean investigation proves nothing, which secrets to rotate first and how vaulting and just-in-time access limit what a stolen credential can reach.

Roughly seven in ten websites run on PHP. An unpatched PHP server can be broken into with one web request and no password. That hole has been there for 14 years, and attackers reached it before the patch did.

The flaw is PHP2Shell: two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime itself, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The fix shipped on October 21, 2026, four days after the first exploitation attempts were seen. PHP sits behind 69% of websites whose server-side language is known.

Upgrading PHP is the easy part. The hard part is what attackers already took: database credentials, API keys, session tokens and personal data, each still valid until someone rotates it. Treat every secret the server could read as stolen, including any it fetched from a vault.

A vault with automated rotation makes the cleanup fast. Without one, it is slow, manual work. Either way, rotation fixes the stolen credentials and does nothing about the other two problems. The leaked personal data will fuel targeted phishing and identity attacks for months, and breaches will spread from organizations that patched late to those that depend on them.

This is the first week of a long event.

Four reasons PHP2Shell is more dangerous than a typical critical flaw

Critical web vulnerabilities surface most weeks, and most of them don't deserve the label "dangerous". PHP2Shell does, for four reasons.

1. PHP2Shell runs before your application code does

With Apache mod_php, PHP is embedded in the web server itself. On those servers the exploit fires while PHP is still parsing the request, before any application code runs. PHP-FPM and other setups are affected too, under extra conditions.

The danger: the attack is over before your login page, your multi-factor check or your application's logging is reached. It can succeed and leave no trace where you would normally look.

2. PHP2Shell can leak server memory without leaving a web shell

PHP's advisory for CVE-2026-109619 lists memory disclosure as a confirmed impact. The process that handles requests keeps credentials, tokens and session data from earlier requests in memory, and an attacker can read it without dropping a file or running a command.

The danger: There may be no web shell to find. An investigation that finds nothing has not shown that nothing was taken. Rotate the server's credentials anyway.

3. Attackers were exploiting PHP2Shell before the patch existed

Amazon's threat intelligence team saw the first exploitation attempt on October 17, 2026. The CVE identifiers leaked on October 20, 2026, so PHP released the fix a day early. Proof-of-concept exploits were circulating hours before the planned release, and Amazon now describes PHP2Shell as broadly exploited in the wild.

The danger: A server patched the day the fix shipped may already have been compromised, and the gap between disclosure and mass exploitation was hours, not days.

4. PHP2Shell has been in PHP since 2012

Calif Research, the firm that found the bugs, traces the earliest affected code path to PHP 5.4.0, released in 2012. A related flaw surfaced in a 2024 audit, but nobody proved it exploitable, so nobody fixed it.

The danger: 14 years of PHP releases are exposed, and more than a third of PHP-powered sites run PHP 7 or older, branches that will never get an official fix. Those servers stay exploitable for months.

A web server is a credential store

Next to the PHP code on a typical server: a config.php with the database password. A .env file with API keys, cloud access keys, mail credentials and OAuth client secrets. Process memory holding the tokens and personal details of whoever was signed in. The PHP process reads all of it, so an attacker whose code runs inside that process can too.

With those secrets, the attacker no longer needs the vulnerability. Every login looks like legitimate traffic, and none of it trips a detection written for the PHP flaw. The vulnerability was the entry. The identities are the payload. A PHP vulnerability becomes an identity problem.

PHP2Shell's aftershocks will come in three waves

This is a forecast, based on how credential theft has played out before.

Wave 1 is now and runs for weeks. Automated exploitation of anything unpatched. Web shells and cryptominers installed. Config files and environment variables harvested at scale. Active sessions hijacked.

Wave 2 starts within a week and continues for months. The harvested credentials are used: database logins from new places, cloud keys to pull data and OAuth secrets to mint tokens for SaaS applications. None of it requires an exploit, and all of it appears to be authorized access.

Wave 3 runs for months or more. Leaked personal data and session details fuel targeted phishing and account takeover against your customers and employees. Some organizations will be breached through a vendor, partner or SaaS provider that ran PHP, patched late and rotated nothing. Their incident becomes yours.

What to do about PHP2Shell, in order

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged immediate patching but, at the time of writing, hasn't listed either CVE as known to be exploited. That is not a reason to wait; the first attempts came before any detection signature existed.

In the next hours. Find every place PHP runs, including appliances that bundle it. Upgrade to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or to your vendor's backported package; there is no complete workaround. Isolate anything you can't patch. Investigate from October 17, not the disclosure date.

In the next days. Assume any secret the server could read is in someone else's hands. Inventory them, rotate them starting with the ones that reach the most systems, and invalidate active sessions. Then audit the systems those credentials open for use you didn't authorize.

In the next months. Change what a web server is allowed to hold. Static secrets in files on an internet-facing host are standing privilege. Move them into a vault that rotates them automatically. Give applications and services just-in-time access scoped to the task, so a stolen credential stops working quickly and reaches only what the task needs. Put phishing-resistant authentication in front of the people who will be targeted. Ask your vendors which of these they've done.

Where identity security does its work

If a credential is stolen, the damage should stop at that credential. The Delinea Platform is built for that outcome; it limits how far an attacker can move and what they can reach if they get in.

Credentials are vaulted and rotated automatically, and in brokered sessions they are injected at the proxy at the moment of use, so database passwords and API keys no longer live in config.php or .env. Access is granted just-in-time, scoped to the task and revoked when it's done. Each privileged action is authorized as it happens and tied to a named identity, so when the board, auditors or regulators ask what happened and why it was allowed, you have an answer.

Patch today, then treat the patch as the beginning. Exploitation started before disclosure, so patching does not mean the attacker is gone, nor does it restore a single credential that was stolen. This is week one. Plan for the year.

See how the Delinea Platform vaults and rotates the credentials PHP2Shell exposes.

Title: Okta and Auth0 are removing trust in the eMudhra emSign ECC Root CA – G3
Context: On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys of eight intermediate eMudhra certificate authorities were generated with insufficient entropy and could be...
Full Text:
What happened?

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys of eight intermediate eMudhra certificate authorities were generated with insufficient entropy and could be derived from their public certificates. The derived private keys can be used to issue certificates for any domain, and software that trusts the eMudhra root will accept them.

Mozilla, Google, Apple, and Cloudflare have blocked the affected intermediates. Mozilla has removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 from its trust store, and Chrome will remove it on October 27, 2026. eMudhra has revoked the intermediates.

Okta’s response

Okta and Auth0 are removing trust in emSign ECC Root CA – G3 and the eight affected intermediates across our services.

Security Patching Services: The change has been deployed across Okta’s production environment. The change is continuing to roll out across Auth0 production.

No Evidence of Exploitation: To date, Okta and Auth0 have observed no evidence of exploitation.

Do I need to do anything?

Only if Okta or Auth0 connects to a server you control and that server's certificate chain includes the eMudhra emSign ECC Root CA – G3. Inbound access to Okta and Auth0, including sign-in, is not affected.

The case to check is a non-browser connection or webhook that calls your own API, such as an Okta Inline Hook or Event Hook, or Auth0 Action, Custom Database connection, or Auth0 Federated Connection.

These connections may not have shown you any error before now. Run

openssl s_client -showcerts -connect <your-host>:443

and look for "emSign" in the chain. If you find it, replace the certificate with one from another trusted CA. Connections to that endpoint will fail once our change is applied to your tenant.

References

eMudhra Statement on distrust of select Global TLS Intermediate and one Root CA

Google - Protecting Chrome and Android Users from Compromised eMudhra Intermediate CA Certificates

Mozilla - Protecting Firefox users following the compromise of eMudhra intermediate certificates

Title: How to contain shadow AI, as it takes on multiple forms and spreads throughout your environment
Context: That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data
Full Text:
Shadow AI used to be confined to a few simple scenarios, such as AI chatbots and AI browser extensions. Today, it spans a broad spectrum of complex vectors, making it harder to detect and control. In the latest installment of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, learn how employee security training, AI usage governance, and exposure management can help you tackle shadow AI successfully.

Key takeaways

Integrating shadow AI into security awareness training helps employees recognize its risks and learn how to safely adopt AI tools. Security teams should foster open communication with employees and try to understand why they use unsanctioned AI products.

Shadow AI now spans local models, AI coding assistants, autonomous agents, and many other asset types across your environment, making it a pervasive and complex problem.

You can reduce shadow AI incidence by enacting an AI acceptable use policy that provides clear guidelines and a list of approved AI tools, and by addressing shadow AI as part of your unified exposure management program.

It’s an ordinary workday at a typical mid-to-large enterprise, and the following is happening without the knowledge of the IT and security departments:

A marketing manager installs an unvetted, open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) server to secretly bridge his desktop AI assistant with the company’s internal customer database.

A sales executive downloads a free AI browser extension to summarize a web page, unknowingly granting a third party read-access to her confidential CRM dashboards.

An accounting supervisor creates custom AI chatbot skills to automate his reporting, feeding unredacted financial projections into a public generative AI tool.

An engineer bypasses software restrictions to download and run an unvetted, locally hosted AI model, creating a massive blind spot for endpoint security.

A business analyst hands over her broad administrative credentials to a consumer-grade AI agent so it can autonomously crawl the company’s private data warehouse.

A developer pastes proprietary, unreleased source code into a free, web-based AI assistant for quick debugging, inadvertently surrendering corporate IP to a public model’s training set.

Yes, we’ve come a long way from the days when instances of shadow AI consisted mostly of employees oversharing work information with their personal AI chatbot. With AI now permeating enterprises’ operations, shadow AI has spread and morphed accordingly across the attack surface. It has become riskier and harder to detect, especially as autonomous AI agents proliferate.

For example, security incidents involving organizations’ shadow AI assets have more than doubled to 43%, compared with 20% last year, according to IBM’s “2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report.” Meanwhile, the average data breach cost of shadow AI-related incidents hit $5.39 million, about $400,000 above the global average.

IBM's report found a direct impact on data privacy, operations, and compliance:

Almost half of shadow AI security incidents resulted in data loss or data compromise

42% caused operational disruption

21% triggered regulatory fines

During a 30-day period earlier this year, the Tenable One Exposure Management Platform found 457 million security issues across 7,000 customer environments using 274 detection plugins built specifically for AI. That averaged out to about 62,000 AI-related exposures per customer.

“The enterprise AI landscape of 2026 bears little resemblance to the AI landscape of even three years ago,” the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) wrote in its April report, “The Invisible Enterprise: Shadow AI and the Ungoverned Frontier.”

Because AI adoption has “dramatically outpaced” organizations’ AI governance, many enterprises now have a dangerous “invisible layer of AI infrastructure” that hasn’t been inventoried, and thus isn’t subjected to policy enforcement, access controls, or audits, according to the CSA report.

In this third installment of Tenable’s weekly Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, we’ll unpack best practices organizations can adopt to tackle shadow AI in its multiple forms — AI code assistants, models, applications, APIs, embedded features, agents, MCP servers, training data, browser extensions, and more — and mitigate its risks, such as compliance failures, system breaches, and data leaks.

3 steps to help you mitigate the risk from shadow AI

1. Boost employee and leadership awareness and education

A logical place to start your campaign against shadow AI is by teaching employees and leaders how to recognize and prevent the issue.

Employees

Just last month, the U.K. government stressed how important it is for organizations to address the human factor in shadow AI, specifically the disconnect between employees’ fast adoption and organizations’ lag in approving AI tools and setting AI usage policies.

For example, 34% of employees polled in Thomson Reuters’ “Future of Professionals 2026” report admitted to knowingly and deliberately using AI wares their organization hasn’t approved.

Why? “They are frustrated by the quality of sanctioned tools or the lack of a clear AI strategy,” reads a Thomson Reuters article about the report, published in June.

The U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) recommends focusing on three key elements:

Understand why staffers use unapproved AI tools.

Establish a “positive cybersecurity culture” marked by open communication between employees and the security team.

Securely integrate AI systems into the workplace.

“By raising awareness of the risks of shadow AI use within your organization and understanding the needs of employees, you can help them get the benefits of new technologies while using them securely,” an NCSC cloud researcher wrote in the blog “The hidden risks of shadow AI.”

In other words, focus on employee education, not punishment, and include shadow AI in your security awareness program training.

Business unit leaders

Proactively reach out to business unit leaders to learn about the AI tools they’re using, their reasons for using them, and the benefits they yield. Engaging in this needs-assessment exercise can help you decide which AI tools to allow and which ones to prohibit.

2. Establish a clear AI governance policy

Avoid being seen as an enemy of AI adoption. Extremely restrictive approaches, such as “block by default” policies, tend to backfire because they drive employees and teams to push their AI usage further underground, especially if these tools boost their productivity.

Instead, you should adopt an AI acceptable use policy that outlines clear rules for who can use AI, which tools they can use, and what data they can input, in a way that doesn’t compromise security and compliance.

Your AI policy should also clarify levels of accountability by outlining the responsibilities of employees, managers, and the AI governance team. For example, it should stress that employees must verify the accuracy of AI-generated content, because each individual is ultimately responsible for the quality of their work.

The comprehensive policy should clearly outline AI usage guardrails, such as rules for data handling, detail the formal process and criteria that the security and IT teams will use for approving and adopting AI tools, and provide a curated list of authorized tools.

It should further help you assess whether you should outright block a discovered shadow AI tool, or whether you can allow it with the appropriate controls.

Some questions to ask:

Does the AI vendor claim ownership of what your users input into its tool?

Does the tool encrypt data in transit and at rest?

What are the vendor’s vulnerability and incident disclosure processes?

Does the product comply with regulations relevant to your organization, like HIPAA?

Does the vendor use your data to train public AI models?

In which geographic region does the vendor house your data?

Which types of industry compliance does the AI vendor adhere to?

Finally, the AI usage policy should be a living document your organization continually revises, as AI technology advances and the organization’s usage evolves.

“Leaders should focus on creating a governance framework that balances innovation with risk management, ensuring employees feel empowered to use GenAI responsibly,” reads Deloitte’s “GenAI Workforce Survey,” which was published in September. The report found that 31% of U.K. employees use AI tools without their organizations’ permission.

3. Address shadow AI as part of your broader exposure management program

With AI now pervasive across most enterprises, shadow AI is present throughout your IT environment in a wide variety of manifestations. This is precisely the type of complex and multidimensional security issue that a unified exposure management platform helps untangle.

At Tenable, we believe that trying to detect and control shadow AI as a standalone problem with isolated point tools is the wrong approach.

To successfully mitigate AI security risks, including shadow AI, you need to gather contextually rich AI security data, so you can correlate and analyze it alongside your other exposure data. That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data.

These are some key ways in which an exposure management platform can help you address shadow AI risk.

Obtain comprehensive visibility of your AI environment via a continuously updated inventory of your AI assets – what they are, who and what can access them, and which data they can access – wherever they are in your environment including in your:

Data centers

Endpoints

Web apps

Cloud workloads

Network traffic

Application development pipelines

Enterprise AI platforms

Operational technology (OT) systems

IoT infrastructure

Detect shadow AI assets’ security flaws, including vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, excessive permissions, insecure output handling, and exposed training data.

Contextually map and prioritize the security issues that require immediate attention across your entire attack surface based on factors like AI asset criticality and business impact.

Take action and automate remediation, including by leveraging agentic AI capabilities, to carry out the fixes needed to close your shadow AI exposures.

Reduce the risk of data getting shared improperly via AI prompts and uploads by:

Discovering and classifying sensitive data

Auditing AI assets’ permissions and enforcing least-privilege policies

Monitoring data flows in real time

Detecting and blocking sensitive intellectual property, proprietary source code, and customers’ personally identifiable information (PII) before exposure or compromise

Title: Cloud Security Maturity Lags Despite Widespread Adoption, SANS Warns
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Nearly all organizations now run production workloads in the cloud, yet only 40% consider their cloud security strategy advanced or optimized, highlighting a significant maturity gap, according to SANS.

This is according to the 2026 SANS Cloud Security Survey Insights report which surveyed 400 IT and security professionals.

SANS found that 51% of respondents were running enterprise-scale (2501 to 10,000 workloads, containers, or instances) or hyperscale (more than 10,000) environments and 73% already having a dedicated cloud security team or role.

The report also noted that 93% of organizations already run production workloads in the cloud and 65% run more than one provider.

SANS noted that because so many respondents have a dedicated team for cloud security, it indicates that a maturity gap persists despite organizations being well-resourced.

Overall, 45% of respondents described their cloud security strategy as “intermediated” with partial implementation of a defined strategy.

This partial implementation is an issue, according to the report, and leads to security incidents.

Misconfiguration Make Up Nearly Half of Critical Cloud Incidents

The report found that misconfiguration is the leading cause of critical cloud incidents (45%), close to double that of the next highest factor, credential theft, which made up 22% of incidents.

What’s more, misconfigurations often remain in place for significant periods, with around half of organizations (49%) found to need more than 24 hours to close a known critical gap.

"Misconfiguration is not an exotic attack class. It is a known gap sitting in an account somebody already owns," said Serge Borso, SANS Principal Instructor. "What makes it persist is not the attacker. It is the distance between finding the gap and fixing it, across too many consoles with nobody clearly owning the result. That is why consolidation and enforcement matter more right now than implementing yet another detection tool. The industry has finished deciding to move to the cloud and is now paying for how fast it did.”

Despite the security maturity gap, cloud security budgets were found to be increasing for most, with 28% of respondents reporting significant investment to modernize or adopt new technology such as AI or Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP), and another 42% reporting incremental growth.

Overall, 70% of organizations are spending more on cloud security than a year ago. Only 7% reported budget cuts.

Just 21% of respondents said their organization runs a single consolidated CNAPP platform. Meanwhile, 31% still maintain separate point solutions across Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM), Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP), and Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM). Of those surveyed, 23% are actively evaluating a move to consolidate.

The SANS data points towards three priorities for security teams in the year ahead:

Strengthen cloud security by enforcing automated policy checks in infrastructure-as-code pipelines, preventing misconfigurations before deployment

Reduce security tool sprawl by consolidating posture management, workload protection and identity security tools into unified platforms

Extend zero trust beyond authentication by adopting continuous, context-based controls that limit what users and workloads can access after login
